PassBitmask.semantics: Each of the two bitmask rows has a checkbox beside its label. Clear one and elements on that side of the verdict keep the flags they arrived with, which is how a block marks only passes or only failures. The operation carried on each row (`=`, `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, `XOR`) is what combines that row's mask with the flags already on the element.
PassBitmask.trap: A row left at its defaults is a mask of zero combined with `OR`, which moves no bit. The attribute is still created, so the symptom is a result attribute full of zeroes.

FailBitmask.tooltip: Operations executed on the flag if when filters fail

fields.name: Mode
fields.tooltip: How the bitmask value is constructed. Direct uses raw value, Mutations applies per-bit operations.

fields.name: Bitmask
fields.tooltip: Base 64-bit mask value. In Direct mode, used as-is. In Mutations mode, modified by operations.

fields.name: Op
fields.tooltip: How the final mask is combined with existing flags when applied.

fields.name: Mutations
fields.tooltip: Per-bit operations applied to the base bitmask. Only used in Mutations mode.

fields.name: Compositions
fields.tooltip: Additional bitmask references combined with the result.

FPCGExFloodFillEdgeDirectionDetails.name: Flood Fill Edge Direction Details
FPCGExFloodFillEdgeDirectionDetails.purpose: A spread across a cluster gives every connection it crossed a natural direction, the way it travelled, and this block records that as a vector on the edges. **Cluster : BFS Depth** and **Cluster : Flood Fill** both carry it, as `Edge Direction Output` under their outputs, and it is off on both until asked for. Edges the spread did not order, because it reached both ends at once or reached neither, still get a vector: they fall back to the ordinary edge direction rule the rest of the plugin uses.
FPCGExFloodFillEdgeDirectionDetails.situation: The cluster needs to carry which way a fill ran, so a later node can orient meshes, drive tangents, or tell upstream connections from downstream ones.

mechanism.text: One vector per edge, written onto the Edges dataset. An edge whose two endpoints were reached at different depths is oriented from the shallower endpoint towards the deeper one, so it points away from where the spread came from. Every other edge, one whose endpoints came out at equal depth or one with an endpoint the spread never reached, is handed to the `Direction Settings` block instead and oriented by that rule. `Invert Direction` then negates whatever came out, on every edge, both kinds alike. Every edge in the cluster ends up with a value, including the ones well outside the filled region.

bOutputDirection.tooltip: Write the traversal direction onto edges (depth order where it exists, Edge Direction Settings elsewhere).
bOutputDirection.semantics: This is also what decides whether the host copies its Edges input at all: left off, the Edges data passes straight through, and turning it on makes the node produce its own copy to write into. If the fallback below is set to `Endpoints Sort`, turning this on is also what grows the required **Direction Sorting** pin on the host.
bOutputDirection.trap: A `Direction` name that is not a legal attribute name does not stop the node. It raises a warning at start-up and switches this back off, so the run completes with no direction attribute anywhere.

DirectionAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'FVector' attribute to write the direction to.
DirectionAttributeName.semantics: Every edge is written, so an existing attribute of this name is replaced rather than added to. Both hosts start at the same name, which means running one after the other over the same cluster leaves only the second node's answer unless one of them is renamed.

bInvertDirection.tooltip: Invert the written direction (multiplied by -1) for every edge.
bInvertDirection.semantics: The negation is applied last and to every edge, so it flips the depth-ordered edges and the fallback edges together. It cannot be used to bring the two halves into agreement with each other; it only reverses the whole set.

DirectionSettings.tooltip: Fallback orientation for edges with no depth difference (equal-depth, frontier or unvisited edges).
DirectionSettings.semantics: This governs the edges the spread left no order on: both endpoints at the same depth, one endpoint unreached, or the edge entirely outside the filled region. On a fill that reached everything it is unused; on a fill stopped early it decides most of the cluster.
DirectionSettings.trap: The two halves order edges by opposite conventions. The depth half points the vector at the endpoint reached **later**, away from the seed; the fallback points it at the endpoint that sorted **first**. Setting the fallback so the shallower endpoint sorts first therefore produces the reverse of the depth-ordered edges beside it, not a continuation of them.

hints.text: On **Cluster : Flood Fill** each diffusion counts its own depth from its own seed, so an edge whose two endpoints were claimed by different diffusions is oriented by comparing two counters that started in different places, and can end up pointing towards a seed rather than away from one. **Cluster : BFS Depth** counts hops to the nearest seed in one shared pass, so its depths are comparable everywhere.

FPCGExGeo2DProjectionDetails.name: Projection Details
FPCGExGeo2DProjectionDetails.purpose: The plane a node works on when it works in two dimensions. A great many operations only make sense flat, and this is where every one of them says which flat. It appears on more nodes than any other shared block, and what it decides is not a detail of the result but the frame the whole result is expressed in.
FPCGExGeo2DProjectionDetails.situation: Any node that has to reduce three dimensions to two, and needs telling which two.

mechanism.text: A normal defines the plane, points are projected onto it, and the work happens there. Where a node's output is spatial the results are carried back afterwards, so the projection is a working frame rather than a destination. The normal can be fixed for the whole run, or taken per point where the node supports a local tangent, which is what lets a projection follow curving data instead of cutting across it.

Method.tooltip: How to map the graph to a workable 2D/surface space. See each method's own tooltip.
Method.semantics: Where the plane's normal comes from. A fixed normal treats every input the same way, which is what makes results comparable across datasets. Deriving it from the data instead fits the plane to whatever arrived, so the same graph run on differently oriented inputs projects each one onto its own plane.

ProjectionVector.tooltip: Normal vector defining the projection plane. Points project perpendicular to this direction.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

ProjectionVector.semantics: The normal itself, when it is authored rather than derived. It names the direction being flattened away, not the direction being kept, which is the usual point of confusion: projecting along the world up is what gives a plan view.

hints.text: Anything the projection collapses is gone for the duration of the operation. Data spread mostly along the projection normal projects onto a line or a point, and what follows is degenerate rather than merely inaccurate: triangulations produce nothing usable and inclusion tests answer arbitrarily.

On nodes that offer a per-point tangent, the plane can follow the data rather than staying flat across all of it. Nodes without such a tangent ignore that entirely, so the same block behaves differently depending on where it is embedded.

FPCGExGeoMeshImportDetails.name: Geo Mesh Import Details
FPCGExGeoMeshImportDetails.purpose: A mesh turned into a cluster arrives as bare positions and connections, and this block is what else comes with it. Three things are on offer: vertex colours, per-vertex normals, and any of the mesh's UV channels under names you choose. **Mesh to Clusters** and **Dynamic Mesh to Clusters** are the nodes that carry it, and everything it writes lands on the Vtx half.
FPCGExGeoMeshImportDetails.situation: The cluster from a mesh needs to keep something the mesh knew, a paint layer or a UV set, so a later node can read it back off the vertices.

mechanism.text: Nothing here changes which points or connections exist. The Vtx are the mesh's vertices after the host has merged the split copies that hard edges and UV seams produce, and this block only decides what values ride along on them. That merge is why the two hosts differ on the same setting: **Mesh to Clusters** gives a merged point the values of one of the raw vertices behind it, whichever one created the point, while **Dynamic Mesh to Clusters** averages the values at that vertex. Where a Vtx stands for a triangle rather than a vertex, which is what the dual and hollow modes produce, the three corners are averaged. Colours land on the point's own colour, normals on its rotation, and UVs as named attributes.

bImportVertexColor.tooltip: Import vertex colors from mesh as point attribute.
bImportVertexColor.semantics: The destination is the point's own colour, so it reads back as `$Color` and no named attribute is created. A mesh with no colour data leaves the points at their default colour and raises nothing.

bImportVertexNormals.tooltip: Import per-vertex normals from the mesh, if available, by orienting each point so its Up axis (+Z) faces the vertex normal.
bImportVertexNormals.semantics: This one creates no attribute either: it spends the point's rotation, which a generated Vtx would otherwise leave at identity. Anything downstream that reads Vtx transforms, spline meshes and staging among them, inherits the surface orientation for free, and anything that wanted to write its own rotation onto those points is writing over this. A mesh with no normals leaves the rotations alone.

bImportUVs.tooltip: Import UV coordinates from mesh as point attributes.
bImportUVs.semantics: Turning this on grows a **UV Imports** input pin on the host node. Attribute sets wired there are read as name and channel pairs and added to the mapping below, so the mapping can come from data instead of being typed into the node.

UVChannels.tooltip: A list of mapping channel in the format [Output Attribute Name]::[Channel Index]. You can output the same UV channel to different attributes.
UVChannels.semantics: Each surviving row becomes a two-component attribute under the name on the left. A channel index outside 0 to 7 is refused outright, as is a name that is not a legal attribute name, and a name used twice keeps its first row; each of those raises a warning and the rest of the mapping still runs.
UVChannels.trap: A refused row gets no placeholder, whatever `Create placeholders` says, because it never reaches the point where a placeholder could be written. An index of 8 and an index of 3 on a two-channel mesh fail in visibly different ways.

bCreatePlaceholders.tooltip: If enabled, will create placeholder attributes if a listed UV channel is missing. This is useful if the rest of your graph expects those attribute to exist, even if invalid.
bCreatePlaceholders.semantics: This covers one case: a legal channel index that the mesh does not have that many of. The attribute is created and every point carries `Placeholder Value`, so a graph built around a four-channel mesh keeps working when a two-channel one comes through.

hints.text: A UV seam is several mesh vertices sharing one position with different coordinates, and the merge collapses them into one point. On **Mesh to Clusters** that point keeps one side's coordinates, so imported UVs are only faithful away from seams. Widening the host's vertex merge tolerance merges more, not less.

FPCGExGraphBuilderDetails.name: Graph Builder Details
FPCGExGraphBuilderDetails.purpose: The step between a node finishing its connections and a cluster arriving on the pins, labelled **Cluster Output Settings** wherever it appears. It decides which components survive, what the edge points look like, and whether the finished cluster is handed downstream prepared or as raw attributes. Twenty-five nodes carry it, and making a cluster from nothing is only half of them: **Cluster : Connect Points**, **Cluster : Delaunay 2D** and **3D**, **Cluster : Voronoi 2D** and **3D**, **Cluster : Convex Hull 2D** and **3D**, **Cluster : Cell Diagram**, **Cluster : Edge Dual Graph**, **Cluster : Build Custom Graph**, **Path : To Clusters**, **Mesh to Clusters**, **Dynamic Mesh to Clusters**, **Clipper2 : Decompose**, **Cluster : Refine**, **Cluster : Filter Vtx**, **Cluster : Fuse**, **Cluster : Simplify**, **Cluster : Cut** and **Cluster : Repair** all pass their result through it, and five more do in the companion plugins: **Valency : Lattice**, **Valency : Grow Points**, **Valency : Find Bridges**, **Get Sketch Data** and **Staging : Load Sketch**.
FPCGExGraphBuilderDetails.situation: A generator produced more islands than wanted, or its edge points came out as bare dots when they were expected to look like the connections they stand for.

mechanism.text: Connections become cluster data here. A pair of Vtx can be joined once, whichever way round the connection is made, and a Vtx is never joined to itself, so no cluster leaving this step carries a duplicate edge or a self-loop. Vertices that ended up with no connection are dropped, what remains is split into connected components, and every component that clears the size limits becomes one Edges dataset paired with the single surviving Vtx dataset. A component that fails the limits takes its vertices out of the Vtx dataset with it, so pruning changes both halves, and the limits are read from counts alone, before any edge point exists. Each surviving edge then gets its point: placed between its two endpoints at `Edge Position`, optionally rotated and stretched to span them, optionally carrying its own length as an attribute.

off_label.claim: Set `Build And Cache Clusters` to `Disabled` on the node that makes the cluster and nothing downstream can pick a prepared cluster up from that data, so the count-only staleness check has nothing left to be fooled by and every consumer rebuilds from the attributes. It costs that rebuild at each node, and it does not repair topology a vanilla node genuinely broke.
off_label.grounded_in: FGraphBuilder's constructor sets Graph->bBuildClusters from WantsClusters(); FSubGraph::CompilationComplete only attaches a cluster to the edge data when that flag is set, and Helpers::TryGetCachedCluster returns nothing when no cluster is attached.

EdgePosition.tooltip: Edge position interpolation between start and end point positions.
EdgePosition.semantics: The whole `Solidification` group below is gated by the same checkbox, so an axis picked there does nothing while edge positions are not being written. With the checkbox clear, each edge point keeps the transform it arrived with: the origin where the node built the cluster from nothing, and the source edge point's own transform where it rebuilt an existing one.

BasicEdgeSolidification.tooltip: If enabled, does some basic solidification of the edges over the X axis as a default. If you need full control, use the Edge Properties node.
BasicEdgeSolidification.semantics: With an axis picked, the edge point is rotated so that axis lies along the edge and its bounds are stretched to reach both endpoints on that axis, with the other two axes sized by the radius. `Edge Position` splits the box: at 0.5 the point sits at the midpoint with half the length either side, at 0.2 it sits a fifth along and the box is still exactly as long as the edge. Radius comes from the endpoints' own scaled extents rather than from anything on this block, so it tracks the Vtx points' bounds and scale, and `Lerp` samples between the two endpoint radii at `Edge Position`. For anything beyond a single axis and one radius rule, **Cluster : Edge Properties** is the node that owns edge point transforms.
BasicEdgeSolidification.trap: The panel shows `Solidification Axis` defaulting to `None`, but seven hosts construct the block with it already set to X: **Cluster : Connect Points**, **Cluster : Delaunay 2D** and **3D**, **Cluster : Voronoi 2D** and **3D**, **Path : To Clusters** and **Clipper2 : Decompose**. On those nodes the edge points arrive already oriented and stretched, and `None` is a change rather than the starting state.

MinVtxCount.semantics: A component is dropped when either count falls short, not both: three vertices joined in a line clears a `Min Vtx Count` of 3 and still fails a `Min Edge Count` of 3, because it has two edges. Both numbers are counted per component, and a component that fails loses its vertices from the Vtx dataset as well as its Edges dataset.

MaxVtxCount.semantics: The same either-or rule as the minimums, applied from the other side: a component over `Max Vtx Count` or over `Max Edge Count` is dropped.
MaxVtxCount.trap: Both maximums start at 500, which most real generator output clears. Turning the checkbox on without raising them discards nearly everything.

bRefreshEdgeSeed.semantics: An edge point's seed is derived from where that point ended up, so it moves with `Edge Position` and is stable across runs that produce the same geometry. Left off, the derivation runs only for edges whose seed is still zero, which on a node rebuilding a cluster means the surviving edges keep the seeds they came in with. Turned on, it runs for every edge.

BuildAndCacheClusters.tooltip: If the use of cached clusters is enabled, output clusters along with the graph data.
BuildAndCacheClusters.semantics: `Default` reads `Default Build And Cache Clusters` from the plugin's project settings, which ships on. Whatever this says, the plugin-wide `Cache Clusters` switch above it has the final word: with that off, no cluster is ever attached and every downstream node rebuilds from the attributes.

FaceEnumeratorProjection.tooltip: Projection settings for the pre-built face enumerator. Downstream nodes with matching projection will reuse the cache.
FaceEnumeratorProjection.semantics: The prepared face data rides along with the cluster, so it is built only while a cluster is being attached at all. With `Build And Cache Clusters` resolving to `Disabled`, or the plugin-wide `Cache Clusters` off, the checkbox is inert. Downstream reuse also needs the projection here to match the one the consuming node is set to, otherwise that node projects again for itself.

bPreBuildChains.tooltip: Pre-build node chains for path extraction and cluster simplification operations.
bPreBuildChains.semantics: Chains are the runs of binary vertices between leaves and complex vertices, and the nodes that walk them are the path extraction and simplification ones. Like the face data, this rides on the attached cluster and does nothing when cluster caching is off.

EdgeLengthName.tooltip: Name of the 'double' attribute edge length is written to.
EdgeLengthName.semantics: The value is the straight distance between the two Vtx positions. `Edge Position` and solidification move and resize the edge point without changing it.
EdgeLengthName.trap: A name that is not a legal attribute name raises an error and writes nothing while the rest of the node carries on, so the cluster arrives looking correct with the attribute missing.

FPCGExInfluenceDetails.name: Influence Details
FPCGExInfluenceDetails.purpose: How much of an effect actually lands. The iterative nodes compute a full result and then apply a fraction of it, which is what turns an all-or-nothing operation into something that can be dialled back, masked per point, or reversed.
FPCGExInfluenceDetails.situation: An operation whose full effect is too strong, or which should apply to some points and not others.

mechanism.text: The computed change is scaled by the influence value before it is applied. The range runs from minus one to one, so a negative figure applies the effect backwards rather than not at all, and zero leaves the point exactly as it was. Read per point, it becomes a mask: an attribute can hold a value per point and the same node then affects each one differently.

InfluenceValue.tooltip: How much effect is applied. Range is -1 to 1.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

InfluenceValue.semantics: Read per point, and signed. Zero is no change, one is the full effect, and negative values apply it in reverse, which is not the same as not applying it. That is what lets one node both relax and disturb depending on what an attribute says.

bProgressiveInfluence.tooltip: If enabled, applies influence after each iteration; otherwise applies once at the end of the relaxing.
bProgressiveInfluence.semantics: Decides when the scaling happens on a node that iterates. Applied after each pass, a reduced influence changes what the next pass sees, so passes compound differently; applied once at the end, every pass runs at full strength and only the final result is scaled. The two produce visibly different results at the same value, and only the second is a straight blend toward the untouched input.

hints.text: It ships progressive, so a half influence over several iterations is not half of the full result. Turn it off when the intent is to blend between the untouched input and the fully applied effect.

FPCGExJustificationDetails.name: Justification Details
FPCGExJustificationDetails.purpose: Where a fitted thing sits inside the space it was fitted to. Scaling something to fit leaves it smaller than its container on at least one axis, and this decides what happens to the slack: centred, pushed to a face, or aligned by a pair of reference points you name.
FPCGExJustificationDetails.situation: Assets fitted into bounds that do not match their proportions, where the leftover room should go somewhere specific.

mechanism.text: Each axis is justified on its own, by naming a point on the thing being placed and a point on the space it is going into, and bringing the two together. That pairing is what makes the block general: aligning a mesh's base to a bound's base is the same operation as centring it, with different reference points. An axis left unjustified keeps whatever the fitting produced.

fields.name: From
fields.tooltip: Reference point on the object being positioned. Min/Center/Max/Pivot or Custom for attribute-driven.

fields.name: CustomFrom
fields.tooltip: Attribute for custom 'From' position. 0 = bounds min, 0.5 = center, 1 = bounds max.

fields.name: To
fields.tooltip: Target point in the container bounds to align to. Same = match 'From', or Min/Center/Max/Pivot/Custom.

fields.name: CustomTo
fields.tooltip: Attribute for custom 'To' position. 0 = bounds min, 0.5 = center, 1 = bounds max.

JustifyX.semantics: Justification is per axis and each axis is off by default, so a block with nothing enabled leaves the fitting's own placement alone. The axes are independent, which is what lets a mesh sit on the ground while staying centred horizontally.

fields.name: From
fields.tooltip: Reference point on the object being positioned. Min/Center/Max/Pivot or Custom for attribute-driven.

fields.name: CustomFrom
fields.tooltip: Attribute for custom 'From' position. 0 = bounds min, 0.5 = center, 1 = bounds max.

fields.name: To
fields.tooltip: Target point in the container bounds to align to. Same = match 'From', or Min/Center/Max/Pivot/Custom.

fields.name: CustomTo
fields.tooltip: Attribute for custom 'To' position. 0 = bounds min, 0.5 = center, 1 = bounds max.

fields.name: From
fields.tooltip: Reference point on the object being positioned. Min/Center/Max/Pivot or Custom for attribute-driven.

fields.name: CustomFrom
fields.tooltip: Attribute for custom 'From' position. 0 = bounds min, 0.5 = center, 1 = bounds max.

fields.name: To
fields.tooltip: Target point in the container bounds to align to. Same = match 'From', or Min/Center/Max/Pivot/Custom.

fields.name: CustomTo
fields.tooltip: Attribute for custom 'To' position. 0 = bounds min, 0.5 = center, 1 = bounds max.

CustomFrom.tooltip: Vector attribute where X/Y/Z components provide 'From' positions for corresponding axes. Overrides per-axis attribute settings.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

CustomFrom.semantics: The reference point on the thing being placed, used where an axis is set to a custom justification rather than a named one. Read alongside the matching to value, which names the point on the destination it should meet.

CustomTo.tooltip: Vector attribute where X/Y/Z components provide 'To' positions for corresponding axes. Overrides per-axis attribute settings.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

hints.text: The reference values can be shared across the three axes or read per axis. Sharing is the common case and keeps the data smaller; per-axis is for the rarer arrangements where each axis justifies against something different.

FPCGExManhattanDetails.name: Manhattan Details
FPCGExManhattanDetails.purpose: Turns a straight line between two points into a staircase of axis-aligned steps. Rather than travelling directly, the route moves along one axis at a time, which is what produces the boxy right-angled runs that read as built rather than grown.
FPCGExManhattanDetails.situation: Connections that should look like corridors, pipework or circuitry rather than direct lines.

mechanism.text: The span between two points is decomposed into moves along each axis in turn, and `Order` decides which axis is travelled first, which is what makes an L-shaped route bend one way rather than the other. `Grid Size` sets the step, either as a distance or as a count depending on the method. `Space Align` decides what the axes are relative to, so the staircase can follow the world, the span itself, or an authored orientation.

Order.tooltip: Order in which axes are processed for subdivision.
Order.semantics: Which axis is consumed first, and therefore where the corner falls. On a two-axis span the two orderings give the two mirror-image L shapes, which is a visible difference rather than a technicality.

GridSizeValue.tooltip: Grid Size -- If using count, values will be rounded down to the nearest int.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute name to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

GridSizeValue.semantics: Read per element, and its meaning follows the method: as a size it is a distance in the aligned space, and as a count it is a number of steps, rounded down. That rounding is one-directional, so a count derived from a computed value tends to come out one step short rather than nearest.

SpaceAlign.semantics: What the axes mean. Aligned to the world, every route steps along the same global directions and a field of them reads as a grid; aligned to the span or to an authored orientation, each route has its own axes and the result follows the data instead.

OrientValue.tooltip: Orientation of the subdivision space. Represented as a rotator; attribute source is read as a rotator.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

OrientValue.semantics: The orientation the steps follow when the alignment asks for an authored one. Read per element as a rotator, so a field of connections can each step along its own frame.

FPCGExMatchingDetails.name: Matching Details
FPCGExMatchingDetails.purpose: The block a node embeds to accept match rules. It adds the Match Rules pin, decides how the verdicts of the rules on that pin combine, caps how many matches a target may take, and says where data that matched nothing goes. The same block appears on the samplers, on Copy to Points and Cluster : Copy to Points, on Copy to Path, Path : Insert, Path : Stitch and Path × Bounds Intersection, on Copy Tags, Merge Points, Best Match Axis, Pathfinding : Plot Edges and the Clipper2 nodes, and it hides different parts of itself depending on which kind of node it landed on.
FPCGExMatchingDetails.situation: A node showing a Mode dropdown and a Match Rules pin, and the question of what the settings under it do once rules are attached.

mechanism.text: Mode is the switch. Left Disabled, the block does nothing: the Match Rules pin drops to advanced and every input is paired with every target. Set to All or Any it becomes required, and each candidate is tested against each target through the rules on that pin, All needing every rule to pass and Any needing one Optional rule to pass before the Required ones are checked. What matched goes on to the work the node exists for. What matched nothing is routed by Split Unmatched, either onto an Unmatched pin or back into the ordinary output.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: The rule stack. Required while Mode is anything but Disabled, and demoted to an advanced pin when it is.
inputs.condition: required when Mode is All or Any

inputs.label: Match Rules (Edges)
inputs.note: A second, independent stack applied to the Edges half of a cluster.
inputs.condition: only on a cluster node with Cluster Match Mode set to Separate

outputs.label: Unmatched
outputs.note: Data that matched no target. Cluster nodes replace it with Unmatched Vtx and Unmatched Edges. Normal while Split Unmatched is on, advanced otherwise.
outputs.condition: only on nodes that declare the outputs of the block, which Path : Stitch does not

Mode.tooltip: Whether matching is enabled or not.
Mode.semantics: It is also the pin switch: Disabled leaves Match Rules as an advanced pin and lets every combination through, so a node that appears to be ignoring its rules is usually a node left on Disabled. All and Any differ in more than strictness, because Any starts from a negative and needs an Optional rule to pass before any Required rule is consulted at all.
Mode.trap: On Merge Points, Path : Stitch and the Clipper2 nodes there is no Targets pin, and Mode groups the inputs against each other instead of pairing them with targets. The rules there answer about two inputs, not about an input and a target.

ClusterMatchMode.tooltip: Which cluster component must match the tags
ClusterMatchMode.semantics: It decides which half of a cluster the rules are asked about, and the word tags in the tooltip is narrower than the behaviour: every rule kind applies, not only the tag rules. Vtx and Edges tests both halves and needs both to pass. Any tests either and needs one. Separate is the only value that changes the pin set, adding Match Rules (Edges) so the two halves can be given different rules.
ClusterMatchMode.trap: Under Any the test is short-circuited on the Vtx side, so a target matched there never registers against the edge side. With Limit Matches on, the cap therefore counts edge-side matches only.

bSplitUnmatched.tooltip: Whether to output unmatched data in a separate pin
bSplitUnmatched.semantics: On, unmatched data is redirected to the Unmatched pin. Off, it reveals the two settings below it, which decide whether that data reaches the ordinary output and whether anything is said about it.
bSplitUnmatched.trap: It also gates the match cap. With Split Unmatched off, Limit Matches and its Limit stay visible and stop having any effect.

bOutputUnmatched.tooltip: If enabled, outputs data that got no valid matches. Not all nodes support this options.
bOutputUnmatched.semantics: It is read whether or not it is visible. Turning it off while Split Unmatched is off, then turning Split Unmatched back on, leaves the setting hidden at its off value and the Unmatched pin permanently empty.

bQuietUnmatchedTargetWarning.tooltip: If enabled, will throw a warning when there is no valid target matches.
bQuietUnmatchedTargetWarning.semantics: The name is the behaviour and the tooltip has it backwards: on, the warning is suppressed. It defaults to on, so with Split Unmatched off nothing at all is reported about data that matched nothing.
bQuietUnmatchedTargetWarning.trap: Between that default and unmatched data being dropped, a rule that can never match looks exactly like a rule that works and found nothing.

bLimitMatches.tooltip: Whether to limit the number of matches or not
bLimitMatches.edit_condition: Mode != EPCGExMapMatchMode::Disabled && Usage != EPCGExMatchingDetailsUsage::Sampling && Usage != EPCGExMatchingDetailsUsage::Filter
bLimitMatches.semantics: The cap is per target rather than per graph, and only Copy to Points and Cluster : Copy to Points honour it. Copy Tags, Merge Points, Path : Stitch, Pathfinding : Plot Edges and the Clipper2 nodes run their matching uncapped, so the setting is visible and inert on all of them.

LimitValue.edit_condition: bLimitMatches && Mode != EPCGExMapMatchMode::Disabled && Usage != EPCGExMatchingDetailsUsage::Sampling && Usage != EPCGExMatchingDetailsUsage::Filter

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

LimitValue.semantics: In Attribute mode the value is read from the target being matched rather than from the input, so different targets can accept different numbers of matches. The default selector is @Last.

hints.text: The samplers hide Limit Matches and its Limit, and a filter using this machinery hides the whole block behind a Mode setting of its own. What a given node shows is decided by the kind of node it is, so two panels carrying the same block can offer different halves of it.

Merge Points reads Split Unmatched as a question about group size: a group of one counts as unmatched. It never consults Output Unmatched or Quiet Unmatched Warning, and it falls back to merging everything into one dataset when the rules fail to load. Path : Stitch goes further and declares no Unmatched pin at all, so all four of the unmatched settings are inert there.

FPCGExNodeSelectionDetails.name: Node Selection Details
FPCGExNodeSelectionDetails.purpose: Seeds and goals are ordinary points that know nothing about the cluster they aim at, so something has to turn each of them into a Vtx to start from or end at. This block is that step, and it appears on every node that takes such points: **Pathfinding : Edges** and **Pathfinding : Plot Edges** carry two of it, one for seeds and one for goals, while **Pathfinding : Grow Paths**, **Pathfinding : Find Cells**, **Pathfinding : Find Cells (Bounded)**, **Cluster : BFS Depth**, **Cluster : Flood Fill**, **Cluster : Diffuse** and **Cluster : Edge Order** carry one for seeds. It decides whether a point is near the cluster at all, what counts as nearest, and how far away is too far.
FPCGExNodeSelectionDetails.situation: A pathfinding node came back with fewer paths than there were seeds, or a fill started from a vertex on the wrong side of the cluster.

mechanism.text: One point in, one Vtx out, through gates that run in a fixed order. `Within Cluster Bounds` comes first and judges the point alone: a point outside the cluster's bounds, expanded by `Bounds Inclusion Offset`, is rejected before any search runs. `Picking Method` then decides what the search measures against, and the answer is a Vtx either way: `Closest edge` finds the nearest edge and then takes whichever of its two endpoints is nearer to the point, so the edge is a way of choosing a vertex rather than a thing that gets picked. `Max Distance` is checked last, against the Vtx that came back. A point failing any gate is dropped from the run rather than snapped to something further away, and every point is resolved on its own, so one rejection costs one seed or one goal and the node carries on with the rest.

off_label.claim: Because the test is per point rather than per node, `Max Distance` doubles as a spatial gate on the seed set: hand the node every candidate and let the distance decide which of them are near enough to a cluster to act, instead of narrowing the seeds upstream.
off_label.grounded_in: PCGExPathfinding::FNodePick::ResolveNode returns false on a failed WithinDistance, and the per-seed loops in PCGExBFSDepth.cpp and PCGExPathfindingGrowPaths.cpp skip that seed and continue.

PickingMethod.tooltip: Drives how the seed & goal points are selected within each cluster.
PickingMethod.semantics: `Closest vtx` measures to vertex positions, which is the literal answer and the one that misbehaves on sparse clusters: a point sitting beside the middle of a long connection can be nearest to a vertex that is nowhere near that part of the structure. `Closest edge`, the default, measures to the connections themselves and then hands back the nearer endpoint of the winning one, which keeps the answer local to where the point actually sits.
PickingMethod.trap: **Pathfinding : Find Cells** and **Pathfinding : Find Cells (Bounded)** never read this. They always work from the edges, so the picker is on their panel and changes nothing.

bWithinClusterBounds.tooltip: Requires the point to lie within the cluster bounds (expanded by Bounds Inclusion Offset) to be selected. Resolved before any distance check.
bWithinClusterBounds.semantics: The gate that judges the point before anything is searched for. Off, every point reaches the search and only `Max Distance` can turn it away. On, a point outside the cluster's own bounds is rejected outright, which is what stops a far-off seed being pulled onto the nearest edge of a cluster it was never near. The test is against the whole cluster's bounds rather than against any one Vtx, so it costs nothing per Vtx and it answers before the picking method is consulted.

BoundsInclusionOffset.tooltip: Per-axis padding applied to the cluster bounds for the inclusion test. Negative values shrink the bounds.
BoundsInclusionOffset.semantics: Padding added to the cluster bounds before the inclusion test, per axis. The shipped 100 on each axis admits points sitting a little outside the cluster, which is usually what a hand-placed seed needs. Negative values shrink the box instead, so a point has to sit well inside the cluster to survive the gate.

MaxDistance.tooltip: Max distance at which a node can be selected. Use <= 0 to ignore distance check.
MaxDistance.semantics: The measurement is to the Vtx the search returned, so under `Closest edge` a point can be right against a connection and still be rejected, because what gets measured is the run to that connection's nearer endpoint. On a cluster with long edges that distance is a large fraction of the edge length. The exception is again the cell nodes, which compare against the distance to the edge itself.
MaxDistance.trap: The default shown here is -1, meaning no limit, and five hosts override it to 200 in their own defaults: **Cluster : Edge Order**, **Cluster : BFS Depth**, **Cluster : Flood Fill**, **Cluster : Diffuse** and **Pathfinding : Grow Paths**. On those nodes seeds further than 200 units from a vertex are dropped before anything runs.

hints.text: Nothing reports a point that was rejected. The symptom is arithmetic: fewer paths than seed and goal pairs, a fill that started from only some of its seeds, or an empty result when every point missed.

FPCGExPathEdgeIntersectionDetails.name: Path/Edge Intersections
FPCGExPathEdgeIntersectionDetails.purpose: Where a path crosses an edge, and whether that crossing should become a point on it. It asks the same question the edge-to-edge block does, from the path side: which crossings are genuine junctions and which are two runs of geometry that happen to touch.
FPCGExPathEdgeIntersectionDetails.situation: Paths crossing a cluster's edges, where the crossings should become points rather than being passed through.

mechanism.text: Each path segment is tested against the edges, and crossings within `Tolerance` are candidates. The angle limits then reject the shallow and the square ones, so what survives is the set of crossings that read as junctions. Self-intersection is separately switchable, and separately supported: a node that does not support it at all leaves that setting inert.

bEnableSelfIntersection.tooltip: If disabled, edges will only be checked against other datasets.
bEnableSelfIntersection.semantics: Whether a path is tested against itself as well as against the edges. The embedding node declares whether it can do this at all, so on a node that cannot, the setting is absent from the panel rather than present and inert.

Tolerance.tooltip: Distance at which two edges are considered intersecting.
Tolerance.semantics: How near a path and an edge must come to count as crossing, in world units. Generated geometry rarely intersects exactly, so this is what makes the test usable rather than a refinement of it.

MinAngle.tooltip: Minimum angle between edges to be considered an intersection.
MinAngle.semantics: Rejects crossings shallower than this. A path running alongside an edge produces many near-parallel near-crossings, and admitting them turns a clean run into a row of redundant points.

MaxAngle.tooltip: Maximum angle between edges to be considered an intersection.

CrossingAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute to flag point as crossing (result of an Edge/Edge intersection)
CrossingAttributeName.semantics: Marks the points created at crossings so a later node can tell them from the path's original points, which is otherwise unrecoverable.

FPCGExPathOutputDetails.name: Paths Output Settings
FPCGExPathOutputDetails.purpose: A size gate on paths a node invents rather than receives, shown in the panel as **Paths Output Settings**. Three nodes carry it, and all three produce paths whose length nobody chose in advance: **Pathfinding : Edges**, **Pathfinding : Plot Edges** and **Tensors : Extrude**. Both bounds ship switched off, and a path that fails one is discarded whole rather than trimmed, tagged, or sent anywhere else.
FPCGExPathOutputDetails.situation: A pathfinding run came back with as many single-hop paths as real routes, and only the longer ones are wanted.

mechanism.text: One path in, kept or discarded, with its point count the only thing consulted. Two points is a floor that applies whether or not either switch is on, so nothing shorter reaches the output however the thresholds are set. Both bounds keep the value shown: a path sitting exactly on `Min Point Count`, or exactly on `Max Point Count`, passes. The test runs before the output data is built, so a path that fails is never written rather than written and then removed, and nothing is logged either way.

off_label.claim: The cap discards instead of truncating, and **Tensors : Extrude** has its own truncating limit, so setting `Max Point Count` just under the node's `Max Points Count` keeps only the extrusions that stopped for some other reason: a stop filter, an intersection, a length limit, or a closed loop.
off_label.grounded_in: FExtrusion::Advance stops the run once ExtrudedPoints reaches the node's per-seed MaxPointCount, and FExtrusion::Complete hands the final ExtrudedPoints count to FPCGExPathOutputDetails::Validate.

MinPointCount.semantics: Clamped at 2, so it can only tighten a floor the block already enforces. At its default of 3 the switch removes exactly the paths that are a single hop long, which on **Pathfinding : Edges** means a seed and a goal that turned out to be neighbours.
MinPointCount.trap: The number tested is the finished path, so **Add Seed To Path** and **Add Goal To Path** count toward it. With both on, a single-hop route arrives as four points and clears a threshold of 3.

MaxPointCount.semantics: A whole-path decision like the minimum: a path over the cap is discarded, never cut down to it. The switch is one click and the value behind it defaults to 500, so enabling it caps output length at a number that was not chosen for the graph.
MaxPointCount.trap: **Tensors : Extrude** carries a second limit one letter apart. `Max Points Count`, under Limits on the node itself, stops an extrusion once it has that many points and keeps what it built. `Max Point Count` here throws the finished path away.

hints.text: Nothing reports a path the gate dropped. The symptom is arithmetic: fewer paths than seed and goal pairs, fewer than plots, or fewer than the seeds that started an extrusion.

FPCGExPathStatistics.name: Path Statistics
FPCGExPathStatistics.purpose: The block behind `Visited` output mode. **Pathfinding : Edges** and **Pathfinding : Plot Edges** both offer a second way of answering a batch of queries: instead of handing back the routes, forward the cluster and write onto each Vtx and each edge how many of those routes crossed it. This block names the two attributes those counts land in, and decides whether a run starts the tally from zero. On both nodes it is labelled **Visited** on the panel and appears only once `Output Mode` is set to `Visited`.
FPCGExPathStatistics.situation: A batch of queries is being run to find out which parts of a network carry traffic, and the routes themselves are of no interest.

mechanism.text: One count per output path, not per traversal step. Every Vtx a resolved route passes through and every edge it crosses is incremented by one, so the number on an element is how many of the run's paths touched it, and an element nothing reached stays at zero. Queries that fail to resolve contribute nothing. On **Pathfinding : Plot Edges** the whole plot counts as one path even though it is solved leg by leg, so a junction two consecutive legs share is still worth a single increment.

off_label.claim: Turn the reset off and chain several pathfinding nodes over the same cluster, and the counts add up across all of them into one combined traffic map rather than each run overwriting the last.
off_label.grounded_in: bResetValues selects EBufferInit::Inherit rather than EBufferInit::New when the writable is acquired, in both PathfindingEdges and PathfindingPlotEdges

PointUseCountAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write the per-vtx visited count to.
PointUseCountAttributeName.semantics: The count lands on the Vtx dataset, and one Vtx dataset can be shared by several Edges datasets, so what accumulates here is the traffic from every cluster built on those Vtx rather than from one cluster alone. Leaving the toggle off forwards the Vtx untouched instead of copying them.

EdgeUseCountAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write the per-edge visited count to.
EdgeUseCountAttributeName.semantics: Counted per Edges dataset, so each cluster tallies its own. The default name matches the Vtx one, which is harmless because the two live on different datasets, and a cluster no query reached still gets the attribute written as all zeroes so the output stays uniform across clusters.

bResetValues.tooltip: If disabled, increment existing attributes otherwise reset to 0.
bResetValues.semantics: Decides whether the run starts from zero or from whatever attribute of that name already exists on the data. Left on, an incoming attribute is replaced. Turned off, the run adds to it, which is what makes several passes over one cluster accumulate into a single tally.

hints.text: **Pathfinding : Grow Paths** carries this block too, under `Settings|Advanced`, and its element never reads it. Nothing is written and no warning is raised, so counts configured there are silently absent from the output.

`Visited` mode changes the shape of the node, not only its attributes: the **Paths** output pin is replaced by the forwarded **Vtx** and **Edges** pins. A graph switched from `Paths` to `Visited` loses its downstream wire.

FPCGExPropertyOutputSettings.name: Property Output Settings
FPCGExPropertyOutputSettings.purpose: The shared answer to which declared properties get written out, and under what attribute names. Two inputs sit side by side: an explicit list that renames and disables row by row, and Property Schema assets whose whole resolved set is written under its own names. Three nodes carry it, and one of them carries it twice: **Get Collection Data** (as **Properties** and again as **Source Schema Properties**), **Staging : Load Properties**, and **Get Properties Data**.
FPCGExPropertyOutputSettings.situation: A schema declares more than this graph wants on its points, or one of its properties needs a different attribute name here than everywhere else.

mechanism.text: The two inputs merge into one list before anything is written: every row of **Properties Mapping** in author order, disabled rows included, then each schema's resolved entries appended under their own names, skipping any name already taken. Collisions are first-wins in that order, so an explicit row beats a schema and an earlier schema beats a later one. A row writes when it is enabled, names a property the source declares, and resolves to a usable attribute name; anything else drops out. **Included Schemas** resolve through their own imports recursively and are cycle-safe, so one asset can stand for a whole tree of declarations.

off_label.claim: A row with **Enabled** off is a suppression. It still reserves its property name against the schema half, which removes one output from a shared Property Schema without editing the asset or dropping the rest of it.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExPropertyOutputSettings::GetEffectiveConfigs adds every Config with a set PropertyName to SeenNames regardless of bEnabled, and the schema walk skips names already in that set.

Configs.tooltip: Explicit configs win over IncludedSchemas-derived entries on name conflict, regardless of bEnabled -- a disabled explicit entry suppresses the schema's same-named output.
Configs.semantics: Rows are emitted in author order, so a consumer that respects attribute order sees the list as it was written. Leaving **Output Attribute Name** blank falls back to the property name with anything PCG cannot take in an attribute name cleaned out of it, which is how a property named with a dot still writes.
Configs.trap: A name typed into **Output Attribute Name** is taken strictly instead: if it is not a valid attribute name the row is dropped with nothing logged. Blank never fails, so an output that disappeared right after a rename is the first thing to check.

IncludedSchemas.tooltip: Each asset's Collection is resolved recursively (locals + ImportedSchemas, cycle-safe); every resolved entry contributes an enabled config keyed by its Name.
IncludedSchemas.semantics: Each resolved entry contributes a row whose attribute name is the property name, so nothing on this side can be renamed. An explicit row naming the same property is how one of them gets a different name, and it takes the slot rather than adding a second output.

hints.text: **Get Collection Data** carries this block twice, and the two resolve differently. **Properties** reads each entry's own overrides and falls back to the collection's declared value. **Source Schema Properties** reads the collection's declared value only, and never looks at an entry override, so the same property configured identically in both blocks can come out with different values.
**Get Properties Data** reads this block only in Explicit output mode. In All Found the block is hidden, and every property the resolved component carries is written under its own name.

**Staging : Load Properties** keeps a second, separate list for time-sampled properties, **Sampled Properties Mapping**. It is the same three fields plus a per-point time, it is not merged with this one, and a property can appear in both.

FPCGExSelectorFactoryBaseConfig.name: Selector Base Config
FPCGExSelectorFactoryBaseConfig.purpose: The concerns every selector carries beside its own picking strategy. How the per-point seed is built, whether picks are restricted to a category, and how the second pick inside a chosen entry is made. Every selector node embeds it, the modifiers included, so the block reads the same wherever it appears. Only the selector wired to the consumer's **Selector** pin has its copy read, so a selector nested inside a modifier contributes its strategy and nothing from here.
FPCGExSelectorFactoryBaseConfig.situation: Two selectors reading the same points keep producing the same picks, or picks need restricting to a slice of the collection by name.

mechanism.text: A consumer reads this block from the selector on its **Selector** pin. With **Use Categories** off, every point draws from the whole collection; with it on, each point's category name chooses a pool, a blank name selects the uncategorized entries, and a name the collection cannot serve falls through to **Missing Category Behavior**. **Seed Components** and **Local Seed** decide what the per-point roll folds in on top of the point's own seed attribute. **Sub Distribution** decides the second pick made inside the chosen entry, which today means a mesh entry's material variants.

off_label.claim: A **Selector Modifier : Cascade** with a single child overrides that child's seed, category and sub-pick settings without editing the child, because the outer factory's copy of this block is the only one read and child 0 receives the unsalted seed.
off_label.grounded_in: FSelectorHelper::Init reads ActiveFactory->BaseConfig alone; FPCGExEntryCascadePickerOp salts child seeds by child index, leaving index 0 unsalted.

SubDistribution.tooltip: Entry-level (micro) distribution -- picks material variants etc. within a picked entry.

fields.name: Distribution
fields.tooltip: Distribution type

fields.name: IndexSettings
fields.tooltip: Index settings

SubDistribution.semantics: Applies to the secondary pool inside the chosen entry, which today means a mesh entry's material variants. An entry without one is unaffected whatever this is set to. The sub-pick is packed into the same pick hash as the entry, which is what lets **Staging : Randomize Materials** re-roll it later without changing which entry was picked.

Category.tooltip: Category name source (constant or per-point attribute).

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute name to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

Category.semantics: A constant, or a name read per point from an attribute. A blank name is a real value rather than a wildcard: it selects the uncategorized entries, and only counts as a miss when the collection has none of those.

MissingCategoryBehavior.tooltip: What to do when a point asks for a category the collection cannot serve. A blank key selects the uncategorized entries, and only counts as missing when there are none.
MissingCategoryBehavior.semantics: **Use Main** falls back to the whole pool, so a point that asked for a category it could not get can still be given a categorized entry. **Use Uncategorized** skips the point when the collection has no uncategorized entries, which makes it behave as Skip on a collection where every entry is categorized.
MissingCategoryBehavior.trap: A category that exists but whose pool failed to prepare is a miss too, so this setting also decides what happens to an empty or invalid category rather than only to a misspelled name.

SeedComponents.tooltip: Which components contribute to per-point seed generation.
SeedComponents.semantics: **Settings** and **Component** are not separable: setting either one folds both the node seed and the component seed into the roll. With no flags set, the roll uses the point's own seed alone, so the same points and collection reproduce across graphs and components.

LocalSeed.tooltip: Per-factory seed offset applied on top of SeedComponents.
LocalSeed.semantics: The knob for decorrelating two selectors that otherwise read the same points with the same strategy.
LocalSeed.trap: It reaches the roll only when **Local** is set in Seed Components. Both ship at zero, so a Local Seed typed into a fresh selector changes nothing until that flag is on.

hints.text: Only the outermost selector's copy of this block is read. A **Selector Modifier : Cascade**, **Anti-Repeat** or **Quota** answers for everything wired below it, and its children's seed, category and sub-pick settings are ignored. Cascade states this on the node itself; the other two do not.

FPCGExSocketOutputDetails.name: Socket Output Details
FPCGExSocketOutputDetails.purpose: One shared block for turning sockets into points, carried by the nodes that emit a Sockets pin. It decides which of an asset's sockets survive, what each socket point records about the socket it came from, and how much of the host point's scale and metadata travels with it. **Staging : Load Sockets** and **Sample : Sockets** always show it; **Staging : Distribute** shows it behind its **Output Sockets** toggle, and drops both the block and the pin in Micro Cache redistribution.
FPCGExSocketOutputDetails.situation: An asset carries more sockets than the graph wants, or the socket points need to say which socket and which asset they came from.

mechanism.text: Each host point contributes one new point per surviving socket, on a Sockets pin of its own; the host points are untouched by this block. Sockets are filtered once per distinct asset rather than once per point, and a socket has to clear the name filter and the tag filter both. A socket point takes its transform from the socket's transform composed with the host point's, its seed from the resulting world position, and its metadata by inheritance from the host point, which is what Carry Over Settings then prunes. The four write toggles add what the socket knew about itself: its name, its tag, its entry's category, and its asset path.

off_label.claim: With Socket Name Filters set to Include on a single name, the Sockets pin becomes a filtered copy of the host points: one point per host that owns that socket, sitting at it. Hosts without it contribute nothing, so the pin doubles as a test for which staged assets carry a given attachment.
off_label.grounded_in: FSocketHelper::Compile sizes the output at Count times the surviving socket count per asset and skips hosts whose mapping is empty, after FilterSocketInfos has reduced each asset's socket list.

SocketTagFilters.tooltip: Include or exclude sockets based on their tag

fields.name: FilterMode
fields.tooltip: How the names are processed.

fields.name: Matches
fields.tooltip: List of matches that will be checked. Any success is a pass.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNames
fields.tooltip: A list of names separated by a comma, for easy overrides. The limitation is that they all use the same shared filter mode.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNameFilter
fields.tooltip: Unique filter mode applied to comma separated names

fields.name: bPreservePCGExData
fields.tooltip: If enabled, PCGEx attributes & tags won't be affected.  Cluster-related nodes rely on these to work!

SocketTagFilters.semantics: ANDed with the name filter: a socket has to clear both to survive. Both run once per distinct asset, before any socket point exists, so a long match list costs nothing per point.
SocketTagFilters.trap: A socket with no tag carries an empty string, which matches no Include entry. Switching this filter to Include therefore removes every untagged socket, whatever the name filter was set to keep.

SocketNameFilters.tooltip: Include or exclude sockets based on their name

fields.name: FilterMode
fields.tooltip: How the names are processed.

fields.name: Matches
fields.tooltip: List of matches that will be checked. Any success is a pass.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNames
fields.tooltip: A list of names separated by a comma, for easy overrides. The limitation is that they all use the same shared filter mode.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNameFilter
fields.tooltip: Unique filter mode applied to comma separated names

fields.name: bPreservePCGExData
fields.tooltip: If enabled, PCGEx attributes & tags won't be affected.  Cluster-related nodes rely on these to work!

SocketNameAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name to write socket name to.

SocketTagAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name to write socket tag to.

CategoryAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name to write category to.
CategoryAttributeName.semantics: The category written is the collection entry's, not the socket's, so it is the same value for every socket point coming off one entry.
CategoryAttributeName.trap: **Sample : Sockets** reads sockets off a mesh with no collection entry behind it and leaves the category unset, so this writes None on every socket point there. It carries real values only on **Staging : Load Sockets** and **Staging : Distribute**.

AssetPathAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name to write asset path to.
AssetPathAttributeName.semantics: The entry's staged asset path on the staging nodes, and the sampled mesh's path on **Sample : Sockets**.

TransformScale.tooltip: Which scale components from the sampled transform should be applied to the point.
TransformScale.semantics: Selects which of the X, Y and Z scale axes the socket point takes from the composed transform, meaning the socket's own scale multiplied by the host point's. An axis left off keeps the socket's authored scale rather than falling back to one, so clearing all three gives socket points exactly the scale baked into the socket. Location and rotation always come from the composed transform; this touches scale alone. The default of 7 is all three axes on.

CarryOverDetails.tooltip: Meta filter settings for socket points, as they naturally inherit from the original points.

fields.name: bPreserveAttributesDefaultValue
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will preserve the initial attribute default value.

fields.name: Attributes
fields.tooltip: Attributes to carry over.

fields.name: bDataDomainToElements
fields.tooltip: If enabled, data domain attributes are promoted to the elements domain (the single @Data value is broadcast to every point). Off by default; Merge Points is the node that enables it. Not used by all nodes.

fields.name: Scope
fields.tooltip: Scope

fields.name: Tags
fields.tooltip: Tags to carry over.

fields.name: bTestTagsWithValues
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

CarryOverDetails.semantics: Socket points inherit the host point's attributes through metadata parenting, and this narrows that inheritance rather than adding to it. Leaving the Attributes filter on All carries everything across, the staging pick included.
CarryOverDetails.trap: Only the Attributes half is read on the socket path. The Tags filter beneath it, along with Flatten tag value, Preserve attributes default value and Data domain to Elements, are consumed by other nodes and do nothing to socket output.

hints.text: The four attribute names are validated whether or not their toggle is on. Clearing one to blank fails the node with an invalid attribute name error, even though nothing would have been written to it.

FPCGExTensorHandlerDetails.name: Tensor Sampling Settings
FPCGExTensorHandlerDetails.purpose: Everything the node reading a field does to the answer once the tensors have finished with it. It runs one time per read, after each tensor's own **Sampling Mutations**, and it settles four things: whether the field's own magnitude survives or is replaced by a length of your choosing, whether the answer is turned round, a scale applied on top of both, and which sampler takes the reading. The block appears on **Tensors : Extrude**, **Tensors Transform**, **Probe : Tensor**, **Heuristics : Tensor** and **Filter : Tensor Dot**, and on two nodes in the Valency plugin.
FPCGExTensorHandlerDetails.situation: An extrusion is stepping too far or barely moving, or a field is wanted for its direction alone and its magnitude keeps getting into the result.

mechanism.text: One read hands back a direction carrying a length, a rotation, and a count of the sources that reached. **Normalize**, which ships on, discards that length and puts **Size** in its place, read per point from the node's own input, so what the effectors made of the magnitude stops mattering and **Size** alone decides it. **Invert** then turns the direction round, and **Uniform Scale** multiplies what is left. Two of the consumers use the length: **Tensors : Extrude** and **Tensors Transform** step by it. The other three normalise the direction again for themselves, so on **Probe : Tensor**, **Heuristics : Tensor** and **Filter : Tensor Dot** the length work here changes nothing and only its sign survives.

off_label.claim: Setting **Uniform Scale** negative is a second mirror, and it is the one that reaches every consumer: on the three that normalise the direction for themselves the sign is the only part of this block's length arithmetic that survives, so a negative scale flips them while leaving the reported rotation alone, which **Invert** does not.
off_label.grounded_in: FTensorsHandler::Sample applies UniformScale to DirectionAndSize after the bInvert branch, and the probe, heuristic and filter each call GetSafeNormal on the result.

bInvert.tooltip: If enabled, sampling direction will be inverted.
bInvert.semantics: The mirror for the whole composited field, applied after **Size** has set the length so the two do not fight. Each tensor carries an **Invert** of its own inside **Sampling Mutations**, acting on that tensor alone before the field is built, and the two stack.
bInvert.trap: It rewrites the reported rotation as well as the direction, and the expression building that rotation uses the Y component twice and never reads Z, so what comes out describes no orientation the field gave. It reaches a reader through **Tensors Transform** and **Tensors : Extrude** in their `Absolute` and `Relative` modes, both of which ship on `Align`, which reads the direction.

bNormalize.tooltip: If enabled, normalize sampling. This effectively negates the influence of effectors potency.
bNormalize.semantics: Switched off, the length of every answer is what the tensors made it, which is the effectors' **Potency** averaged by weight. Switched on, that length is thrown away and **Size** stands in for it. Either way **Tensor Weight** keeps deciding how the tensors share the direction, so this changes how far, never which way.
bNormalize.trap: Switched off, an extrusion's step length becomes the effectors' **Potency**, which ships reading `$Density` from the effector points. A default effector dataset therefore gives steps around one world unit long, which reads as an extrusion that has stopped rather than one crawling.

Size.tooltip: Size applied after normalization. This will be scaled

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

Size.semantics: Read per point from the node's own input, so an attribute on the incoming points sets the step length point by point. It reaches the two consumers that use the sample's length; on **Probe : Tensor**, **Heuristics : Tensor** and **Filter : Tensor Dot** the direction is normalised again downstream and this value never surfaces.

UniformScale.tooltip: Uniform scale factor applied to sampling after all other mutations are accounted for.
UniformScale.semantics: Applied last, on top of **Size** and after **Invert**, so it multiplies whatever the block has finished making. A negative value turns the direction round the way **Invert** does and leaves the rotation alone, which **Invert** does not.

SamplerSettings.tooltip: Uniform scale factor applied to sampling after all other mutations are accounted for.
SamplerSettings.semantics: What sits in here is the sampler class and the five values it might read: **Radius**, **Min Step Fraction**, **Max Step Fraction**, **Error Tolerance** and **Max Sub Steps**. A sampler is picked as a class from the dropdown, which ships on **Default**, and never wired in as a sub-node; this block is the only place its parameters can be authored, because they are copied onto the pick when the run starts. Which of the five do anything follows from the pick: **Default** reads none of them, **Six Points** and **RK4** read **Radius** alone, and **Adaptive RK** reads all five.

hints.text: Two blocks with similar names sit on either side of the field. **Sampling Mutations** lives on each tensor and runs on that tensor's answer before anything is composited. This one lives on the node reading the field and runs once, on the result.

FPCGExTensorSamplingMutationsDetails.name: Tensor Sampling Mutations Details
FPCGExTensorSamplingMutationsDetails.purpose: The last thing one tensor does to its own answer before that answer joins the field. The panel calls the block **Sampling Mutations** and it lives on the tensor, so a stack can carry one tensor mirrored and another flattened while the rest are left alone. Three changes live here: a mirror, a per-axis scale, and a test that turns the answer round when it disagrees with the facing of whatever is being asked. Every **Tensor :** node carries the block apart from **Tensor : Null**, where the panel hides it, and **Tensor : Inertia (Constant)**, whose panel does not offer it at all.
FPCGExTensorSamplingMutationsDetails.situation: A field that is right in plan and wrong in elevation, or one tensor in a stack that has to push the other way from the rest of them.

mechanism.text: Three changes, run in a fixed order that is not the order the panel lists them in: **Invert** first, then **Scale**, then **Bidirectional**. The first two act on the direction alone and act the same way at every position. **Bidirectional** compares the direction it is handed against one axis of the transform being asked about and turns the answer round when the two disagree, which makes it the only one of the three whose decision varies point by point and the only one that also rewrites the rotation. What comes out is what this tensor contributes, weighted by its **Tensor Weight**, alongside everything else on the pin.

bInvert.tooltip: If enabled, sample will be mirrored. Computed before bidirectional.
bInvert.semantics: It mirrors the direction and leaves the reported rotation as it was, so a tensor mirrored here still reports its old facing to anything reading the rotation instead of the direction. It runs before **Scale** and before the bidirectional test, so the test is made against the mirrored vector. The node reading the field carries a second **Invert** of its own, in **Tensor Sampling Settings**, acting once on everything the pin composited; switching both on returns the answer to where it started.

bBidirectional.tooltip: If enabled, perform a dot product with the direction of the input transform and the resuting sample. If that dot product is < 0, the sampled direction and size is reversed.
bBidirectional.semantics: The comparison is made against the direction as **Invert** and **Scale** have already left it, not against the raw reading, so a scale that flattens an axis can decide the outcome. This is the only entry in the block that rewrites the reported rotation as well as the direction, and it does so only on the points where the test came out negative, so one tensor can hand back two kinds of rotation across one dataset.
bBidirectional.trap: The rotation it substitutes is not the sampled rotation turned round. The expression building it uses the Y component twice and never reads Z, so what comes out describes no orientation the field gave and is generally not unit length. It reaches a reader through **Tensors Transform** and **Tensors : Extrude** in their `Absolute` and `Relative` modes, both of which ship on `Align`, which reads the direction.

BidirectionalAxisReference.tooltip: Local axis from input transform used to test if the sampled direction should be inverted
BidirectionalAxisReference.semantics: The axis is taken from the transform the field is being asked about, which is not always the point a reader has in mind. On **Tensors : Extrude** it is the extrusion head as it travels, and the head's own rotation is rewritten every step while **Transform Rotation** is on, so the reference turns with the path it is producing. On **Heuristics : Tensor** the transform is built from the edge being scored, so the reference is that edge's direction. On **Tensors Transform**, **Probe : Tensor** and **Filter : Tensor Dot** it is the point's own rotation.

Scale.tooltip: If enabled, applies a scale factor to the direction and size. This is handy for "flattening" tensors (scale by 1,1,0)
Scale.semantics: The three components multiply the direction in world space, so `1,1,0` lays the tensor flat on the ground plane whatever the point is facing. It runs second, before the bidirectional test, so on a tensor with **Bidirectional** switched on, flattening an axis changes which way the test comes out as well as which way the tensor points.

hints.text: This block is authored on the tensor. The node reading the field carries a separate one, **Tensor Sampling Settings**, holding its own **Invert** and its own scale, and that one runs once over everything the pin composited rather than per tensor.

FPCGExTopologyDetails.name: Topology Details
FPCGExTopologyDetails.purpose: Everything the topology nodes decide about the mesh once its triangles exist. The nodes differ in what they turn into a surface, a cluster, a path or a scatter, and they all hand the result the same treatment: a material, vertex colours, UVs, normals, and the cleanup passes that turn raw triangulation into something usable. What each of those means is stated here once.
FPCGExTopologyDetails.situation: A surface that triangulated correctly and still needs shading, coordinates and normals before anything can render it.

mechanism.text: The triangulation arrives, and this block decides what is attached to it and what is repaired. Materials and vertex colours are assigned, UV channels are read from the settings under them, and the geometry passes run in a fixed order: edges are welded before normals are computed, so welding changes what the normals are computed across. Flipping happens last and is a straight reversal of whatever was produced. `Coordinate Space` decides what the vertex positions are relative to.
steps: Triangulation is appended to the mesh under the primitive and triangulation options.
Edges are welded when enabled, which changes what the following pass sees.
Normals are computed, then flipped if asked.

Material.tooltip: Default material assigned to the mesh

DefaultVertexColor.tooltip: Default vertex color used for the points. Will use point color when available.
DefaultVertexColor.semantics: A fallback rather than an override: where the points carry a colour, theirs is used, and this fills in only where none exists. Setting it does not repaint a mesh whose source points already have colours.

fields.name: UVs
fields.tooltip: List of UV channels

PrimitiveOptions.tooltip: Default primitive options. Applied when triangulation is appended to the dynamic mesh.

TriangulationOptions.tooltip: Triangulation options. Applied when triangulation is appended to the dynamic mesh.

bQuietTriangulationError.tooltip: If enabled, will not throw an error in case Geometry Script complain about bad triangulation. If it shows, something went wrong but it's impossible to know exactly why. Look for structural anomalies, overlapping points, ...
bQuietTriangulationError.semantics: Silences the error that comes back when the triangulation library rejects a shape. Worth reaching for only once the failing shapes are understood to be acceptable, since the alternative is a mesh silently missing the parts that failed.

WeldEdgesOptions.semantics: How coincident vertices at triangle boundaries are joined, while welding is enabled above. Welding is what turns a set of separate triangles into a continuous surface, and it runs before normals are computed, so it also decides whether a shared edge produces one smooth normal or two facing different ways.
WeldEdgesOptions.trap: With welding off and normals on, every seam shades faceted. That reads as a triangulation problem rather than as a setting.

NormalsOptions.semantics: How normals are calculated, while the computation is enabled above. It ships enabled, since a mesh without normals shades as though it were flat. What the pass produces depends on whether edges were welded first, so the two are read together rather than independently.

bFlipNormals.semantics: Reverses whatever the normals pass produced. It is the setting to reach for when a surface renders inside out, which happens when the source winding runs the other way round from what the triangulation expected.
