fields.tooltip: Whether to sort hash components or not.

OutputName.tooltip: Name to output the hash to (written on @Data domain)
OutputName.semantics: Names both outputs at once: the `@Data` attribute and the tag, which is written as the name and the value joined by a colon.

bOutputToTags.tooltip: Whether to add the hash as a tag

bOutputToAttribute.tooltip: Whether to add the hash as an attribute

hints.text: The hash lives on the dataset, not on the points. It is one value in the `@Data` domain, so reading it per point returns the same number for every point in that dataset, and splitting the dataset gives each half its own hash.

UPCGExAttributeRemapSettings.name: Attribute Remap
UPCGExAttributeRemapSettings.purpose: Rescales one numeric attribute or point property into a different range, with the input range taken from the data rather than guessed. That is the part worth having: leave `In Min` and `In Max` alone and the node finds the real spread of the values before remapping them, so a normalisation stays correct when the data changes. A curve, an output scale, an offset, snapping and truncation all sit on the same rule, and vector types can give each of their first four components a rule of its own.
UPCGExAttributeRemapSettings.situation: A value with an unknown spread has to become a 0 to 1 weight, or a driver whose response should not be linear.

mechanism.text: Points in, the same points in the same order out. One attribute or property is read per point, converted to double per component, and written back to the target; nothing else on the point is touched. The pass over the data happens twice, and that is what makes the automatic range work: the first pass measures the spread, the second remaps every value against it, so the result depends on the whole dataset and not on the point alone. Splitting one dataset in two therefore gives different numbers than remapping it whole. Only the first four components of a value take part, which is every type except Transform.

off_label.claim: With `In Min` and `In Max` both fixed and a flat curve, the node is a clamp-and-rescale on a point property such as `$Density` or `$Steepness`, which is otherwise awkward to reach.
off_label.grounded_in: the source selector is captured as a property proxy when it names one, and FPCGExRemapDetails::GetRemappedValue runs the same way for properties and attributes

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points carrying the value to remap.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The same points, with the target attribute written.

fields.name: Source
fields.tooltip: Attribute to read on input

fields.name: Target
fields.tooltip: Attribute to write on output, if different from input

bAutoCastIntegerToDouble.tooltip: If enabled, will auto-cast integer to double.

BaseRemap.tooltip: The default remap rule, used for single component values, or first component (X), or all components if no individual override is specified.
BaseRemap.semantics: Governs the first component and every component with no override of its own. Its `Clamp Input` bounds the automatic range rather than the values: the numbers that reach the curve are the raw input, so a clamp narrows what `In Min` and `In Max` resolve to and nothing else. `Clamp Output` does bound the written value.
BaseRemap.trap: `Use Absolute Range` and `Preserve Sign` do not compose as their names suggest. With both off, the input is still folded to its absolute value before remapping, so negative values come out positive.

Component2RemapOverride.tooltip: Remap rule used for second (Y) value component.
Component2RemapOverride.semantics: Each override carries a complete rule, including its own automatic range. Left off, the component follows the base rule but still measures its own range, so the components of a vector never share one span unless you fix `In Min` and `In Max`.

Component3RemapOverride.tooltip: Remap rule used for third (Z) value component.

Component4RemapOverride.tooltip: Remap rule used for fourth (W) value component.

hints.text: The automatic range is per component and per dataset, never across datasets. Several point collections on the input pin are each measured and remapped on their own, so a value at the top of one comes out the same as a value at the top of another. Merge first when one shared scale is what you want.
A Transform source is remapped on its first four components only, because the node caps itself at four and a Transform reports nine. Remap `$Position`, `$Rotation` or `$Scale` instead.

UPCGExAttributeRollingSettings.name: Path : Attribute Rolling
UPCGExAttributeRollingSettings.purpose: Walks a path from one end to the other carrying a state, and writes down what that state was at every point. Filters decide where a stretch begins and where it ends, and the six optional attributes record which stretch each point belongs to, whether it is inside one at all, whether it is a boundary, and how far into it that point sits. Wiring a Blend Op on top makes the walk do work as well as record it: each point inside a stretch takes values from a reference point that travels with the walk, so a value can be dragged forward along the run rather than recomputed per point.
UPCGExAttributeRollingSettings.situation: A path that has to be cut into named stretches by a condition on its points, whether or not anything is blended along them.

mechanism.text: One execution takes paths and returns the same points in the same order. Nothing is added, removed or reordered; only attribute values change. The walk carries one boolean, inside a range or outside it, and a reference index that the blend reads from. Filters flip the boolean, and the six range attributes are written at every point whatever the boolean is, so a point outside every range still receives values rather than keeping the attribute defaults. Closed paths are walked exactly as open ones: the walk starts at an end and stops at the other, and nothing wraps.

off_label.claim: Leave the Blend Ops pin empty and the node blends nothing at all, which leaves it as a pure marker: the six attributes still get written, so it is the cheapest way to number the stretches of a path against a condition and hand those numbers to a filter or a partition downstream.
off_label.grounded_in: The blend manager is only built when blend op factories are present, and the range attribute writes sit above the blending branch

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to walk.

inputs.label: Toggle Conditions
inputs.note: Every point that passes flips the state, so the same condition both opens and closes stretches. Left empty nothing flips and the whole path stays at whatever `Initial Value` said.
inputs.condition: present, and optional, while Range Control is Toggle

inputs.label: Start Conditions
inputs.note: Points that pass open a stretch.
inputs.condition: present and required while Range Control is Start/Stop

inputs.label: Stop Conditions
inputs.note: Points that pass close the stretch, and are tested before the start conditions, so a point passing both closes rather than opens.
inputs.condition: present and required while Range Control is Start/Stop

inputs.label: Pin Conditions
inputs.note: Points that pass become the reference the blend reads from, and it stays that point until another one passes.
inputs.condition: present and required while Value Control is Pin

inputs.label: Blend Ops
inputs.note: Blend Op sub-nodes naming what is carried from the reference point onto each point the walk covers. Left empty the node records ranges and changes no values.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The same points in the same order, carrying whichever range attributes are enabled.

RangeControl.semantics: Which shape the condition takes. `Toggle`, which ships, uses one filter set and flips on every point that passes, so stretches alternate and a condition that fires on a boundary is enough. `Start/Stop` uses two, which is what you need when the thing that opens a stretch is not the thing that closes it, and it also lets a stretch be reopened without ever having been closed.

ValueControl.semantics: Which point the blend reads from. `Previous`, which ships, reads the point one step back so values chain forward and accumulate along the run. `Range Start` reads the point that opened the current stretch, so every point in a stretch is measured against the same reference. `Pin` hands that choice to its own filter, and the reference then survives across stretch boundaries because nothing resets it.

InitialValueMode.tooltip: How the initial rolling value is determined.
InitialValueMode.semantics: What the state is before the first point is tested. `From Point` runs the start or toggle filter on the first point and takes its verdict, and it errors out when there are no filters to run.
InitialValueMode.trap: `Constant (Preserve)` is read nowhere and behaves exactly as `Constant` does. Its description of not switching when the first value already matches is not implemented.

bInitialValue.semantics: Ships true, so a node dropped in with nothing on its condition pins treats the entire path as one open stretch running from the first point to the last.

bReverseRolling.semantics: Walks from the last point to the first, so the stretches are numbered from the other end. Everything the walk consults moves with it: **Pin Conditions** is tested on the point being written, and `Previous` keeps meaning the point already visited, which is the one nearer the end of the array.

bBlendOutsideRange.tooltip: Enable blend operations to be processed outside the rolling range. This can be useful in some cases.
bBlendOutsideRange.semantics: Runs the blend on every point rather than on the ones inside a stretch, which turns the whole thing into an unbroken carry along the path with the stretch attributes still recorded alongside.

bBlendStopElement.tooltip: Include the stop element in blending.
bBlendStopElement.semantics: The point that closes a stretch is outside it by the time it is written, so it is normally left unblended and the stretch's values stop one point short of its own end. This includes it.

RangeStartAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'bool' attribute to write range start to.

RangeStopAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'bool' attribute to write range stop to.

RangePoleAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'bool' attribute to write range pole to. A pole is either start or stop.
RangePoleAttributeName.semantics: True on any point where the state changed, so it is the union of the start and the stop marks. The path's first point always counts as a pole whether or not anything changed there.

RangeIndexAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write range index to.
RangeIndexAttributeName.semantics: A counter that increments each time a stretch opens, written to every point whether or not it is in a stretch. A point between two stretches therefore carries the index of the one that just closed, and `Is Inside Range` is what tells the two cases apart.
RangeIndexAttributeName.trap: The attribute's own default of -1 never survives, because every point is written. Points before the first stretch carry the offset itself.

RangeIndexOffset.tooltip: Let you add an offset to the range index value. Since it's an index, its default value is -1, and the first index is 0; a default value of 0 or above may be more desirable for some usecases.
RangeIndexOffset.semantics: Added to the counter before the walk starts, so the first stretch comes out at the offset plus one. Set it to -1 to have the first stretch read as 0.

IsInsideRangeAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'bool' attribute to write whether a point is inside the range or not.

IndexInsideRangeAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write range index to.
IndexInsideRangeAttributeName.semantics: Counts from 0 at the point that opened the current stretch and keeps counting through the points between stretches, since it is only reset when a stretch opens. Outside a stretch it therefore reads as the distance since the last one started rather than as zero.

bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.tooltip: If enabled, collections that have less than 2 points won't be processed and be omitted from the output.
bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.semantics: Honoured in the off position: a path of fewer than two points is forwarded untouched and carries none of the range attributes, since it was never walked.

hints.text: With `Range Control` on `Toggle` and nothing wired to **Toggle Conditions**, the state never flips. The whole path comes out as one stretch, or as none, decided entirely by `Initial Value`.

UPCGExAttributeStatsSettings.name: Attribute Stats
UPCGExAttributeStatsSettings.purpose: Measures every attribute on the input and reports what it found: extremes, average, how many distinct values there are, how many occur exactly once, and how many points never moved off the attribute's default. It runs over every attribute at once by default, not one you name, so it doubles as a way to see what a dataset is actually carrying. The numbers come out as attribute sets you can branch on, and can also be written back onto the source data or onto its tags.
UPCGExAttributeStatsSettings.situation: A value is behaving strangely and you need to know its real spread, or a graph has to branch on whether an attribute was ever written to.

mechanism.text: The points pass through unchanged and every measurement is per dataset, per attribute. Which attributes take part is settled once, across all inputs, from a name filter; each one gets an attribute set on the **Stats** pin, tagged with its name, carrying one row per input dataset in input order. An attribute missing from one of those datasets still has its row, reporting only that it was not valid. Which points are measured is the **Filters** pin, and the sample count reports how many passed rather than how many there were.

off_label.claim: Has Only Default Values is the cheapest test for whether an attribute has ever been written to, since an attribute created but never set reports every point at its default.
off_label.grounded_in: DefaultValuesNum counts strict equality against the attribute's default value key, and HasOnlyDefaultValues compares it to the sample count

off_label.claim: The per-unique-values output is a histogram: one row per distinct value with its occurrence count, which is what a partition or a weighted pick needs and what Partition by Values does not report.
off_label.grounded_in: the UniqueValues param data is filled from the ValuesCount map, one entry per pair, with the value and count columns

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to measure. Each dataset is measured on its own.

inputs.label: Filters
inputs.note: Point filters deciding which points contribute. Points that fail are excluded from every number, the sample count included.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The input, forwarded. It is only copied when the stats are being written back onto it.

outputs.label: Stats
outputs.note: One attribute set per analysed attribute, tagged with that attribute's name, one row per input dataset in input order.

outputs.label: UniqueValues
outputs.note: One attribute set per input dataset per attribute, with a value column and a count column, tagged with the attribute name and with the source identifier.
outputs.condition: when Output Per Unique Values Stats is on

fields.name: FilterMode
fields.tooltip: How the names are processed.

fields.name: Matches
fields.tooltip: List of matches that will be checked. Any success is a pass.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNames
fields.tooltip: A list of names separated by a comma, for easy overrides. The limitation is that they all use the same shared filter mode.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNameFilter
fields.tooltip: Unique filter mode applied to comma separated names

fields.name: bPreservePCGExData
fields.tooltip: If enabled, PCGEx attributes & tags won't be affected.  Cluster-related nodes rely on these to work!

Filters.semantics: Chooses attributes by name, and it is not the **Filters** pin, which chooses points. `All` takes everything. Two things are removed regardless: attributes carrying the PCGEx prefix, and container or extended types, which have no arithmetic and are reported with a warning. Names are gathered across every input, so an attribute present on one dataset gets a column for all of them.

bOutputPerUniqueValuesStats.tooltip: Output a separate data collection for each unique value with occurrence counts.

OutputToPoints.tooltip: How stats are written to point attributes (None, Prefix, or Suffix to attribute name).
OutputToPoints.semantics: Writes the same values onto the source data in the `@Data` domain, one per dataset, named by joining the stat's name and the attribute's name in the order chosen. Turning it on is also what makes the node copy its input instead of forwarding it.

OutputToTags.semantics: The same values as tags, composed the same way, and independent of the point output: both can run at once. A tag carries the stat's value after a colon, so a downstream match rule can read it without the data being opened.

IdentifierAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the unique identifier.
IdentifierAttributeName.semantics: Holds a string built from the source data's unique id rather than anything authored. Its job is joining a **UniqueValues** set back to the dataset it came from, which is otherwise ambiguous once several datasets are in play, and it is written as a tag on that dataset too.

DefaultValueAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the default value.

MinValueAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the minimum value.

MaxValueAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the maximum value.

SetMinValueAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the non-default minimum value.
SetMinValueAttributeName.semantics: Set here means not equal to the attribute's default value. This pair reports the extremes among the points that hold something other than the default, so an attribute where most points were never written reports a plain minimum of the default and a non-default minimum of the real lowest written value.

SetMaxValueAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the non-default maximum value.

AverageValueAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the average value.

UniqueValuesNumAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the unique values count.
UniqueValuesNumAttributeName.semantics: Counts values that occur exactly once, which is a different question from how many distinct values there are. A dataset of a hundred points holding three values reports zero here and three under Different Values Num.

UniqueSetValuesNumAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the unique non-default values count.

DifferentValuesNumAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the different values count.
DifferentValuesNumAttributeName.semantics: Counts distinct values, however often each occurs. Its non-default counterpart counts distinct values among the points that hold something other than the default.

DifferentSetValuesNumAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the different non-default values count.

DefaultValuesNumAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the default values count.

HasOnlyDefaultValuesAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the all-default-values flag.

HasOnlySetValuesAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the no-default-values flag.

HasOnlyUniqueValuesAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the all-unique-values flag.
HasOnlyUniqueValuesAttributeName.semantics: Compares the sample count against the count of distinct non-default values, so a dataset where every point is distinct still reports false if any of them holds the attribute's default value.
HasOnlyUniqueValuesAttributeName.trap: It reads the Unique Set Values Num measurement, which is only taken while that output is enabled. Turning Unique Set Values Num off leaves this flag reading zero, so it reports false on every non-empty dataset.

SamplesAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the sample count.
SamplesAttributeName.semantics: Counts the points that passed the **Filters** pin, not the points in the dataset. It is also the denominator the average is divided by and the count the two Has Only flags compare against.

IsValidAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the validity flag.
IsValidAttributeName.semantics: False when the attribute could not be read on this dataset, which covers both the case of it being absent and the case of two inputs declaring the same name at different types, where the first type found wins and the others fail. Every other stat on such a row is left at its declared default, so this is the flag to test before trusting the rest of the row.

UniqueValueAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the unique value column in per-value stats output.

bOmitDefaultValue.tooltip: Exclude the default value from unique values output.
bOmitDefaultValue.semantics: Drops the default value's row from the per-unique-values output, which is usually what you want when most points were never written and that one row would dominate the histogram.

ValueCountAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the occurrence count in per-value stats output.

bQuietTypeMismatchWarning.tooltip: Suppress warnings when attribute type doesn't support stats computation.

bFeedbackLoopFailsafe.tooltip: Prevent feedback loops when stats output is used as input.
bFeedbackLoopFailsafe.semantics: Drops any attribute whose name starts or ends with the name of an enabled output, which is what keeps a second run from measuring the first run's results. It matches on the raw affix, so an attribute genuinely called `MinHeight` disappears from the analysis while `Min` is an enabled output name.

hints.text: Two stat outputs sharing an attribute name is an error at startup, not a silent overwrite, and the check runs over the enabled outputs only. Renaming one output onto another's name works until both are enabled.
Types that support no arithmetic still get a row. Strings, names and asset paths report their extremes and counts as usual, with the average being the most frequent value rather than a mean.

UPCGExAttributesToTagsSettings.name: Promote Attributes
UPCGExAttributesToTagsSettings.purpose: Lifts a value off one row of a dataset and attaches it to the dataset as a whole. `Action` decides the shape that takes: a data tag reading `Name:Value`, a `@Data` attribute on a copy of the input, or a standalone attribute set carrying nothing but the promoted values. `Resolution` decides which dataset supplies the value, and `Selection` decides which of its rows, so a value can come from the data itself or from a separate reference pin.
UPCGExAttributesToTagsSettings.situation: A per-element value that later nodes need to match, sort or branch on at the dataset level, where reading it per element is the wrong granularity.

mechanism.text: One input, one output each, in input order. For every input the node resolves a source dataset, resolves one or more row indices in it, and reads the listed attributes at those rows. In tag mode the input is forwarded untouched and the promoted values are unioned into its tags. In the other two modes the values become `@Data` attributes, typed like their sources, either on a duplicate of the input or on a fresh attribute set that carries nothing else. A `@Data`-domain source is read once per dataset and never per row.

off_label.claim: `Collection to Collection` refuses a count mismatch outright, so a node in that mode doubles as an assertion that two branches of the graph still produce the same number of datasets.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExAttributesToTagsElement::Boot errors with Number of input collections don't match the number of sources and stops the node

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The data to be processed. Points and attribute sets both work.

inputs.label: Tags Source
inputs.note: The dataset or datasets the values are read from.
inputs.condition: when Resolution is not Self

inputs.label: Pickers
inputs.note: The picker sub-nodes deciding which rows are read.
inputs.condition: when Selection is Picker, Picker (First) or Picker (Last)

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: One output per input: the original data with tags added, or a duplicate carrying the promoted `@Data` attributes.
outputs.condition: when Action is Promote to Tags or Promote to @Data

outputs.label: Tags
outputs.note: One attribute set per input, holding the promoted values and nothing else. The input itself is not forwarded in this mode.
outputs.condition: when Action is Promote to Attribute Set

pins.dynamic: In the two forwarding actions the output mirrors the input's type, so points come out as points and attribute sets as attribute sets. Promote to Attribute Set has a fixed param output instead.

Action.semantics: Tag mode forwards the original data and unions the new tags into its existing ones. The other two write `@Data` attributes, which are typed and so survive a round trip that a tag string does not.
Action.trap: The two attribute actions delete and recreate each attribute per picked row, so a `Picker` selection that resolves several rows leaves only the last one. Several rows survive as several tags in tag mode alone.

Resolution.semantics: `Self` reads each input from itself and needs no second pin. `Entry to Collection` points every input at the first non-empty **Tags Source** and warns, once, when more than one arrived. `Collection to Collection` pairs the two pins one for one in order and stops the node when the counts differ.

Selection.semantics: `Picker` promotes every index the pickers resolve, ascending and de-duplicated; the other five resolve exactly one row. `Random Entry` seeds from the input's own position on the pin, so the pick is stable across runs and differs between inputs.
Selection.trap: The row greys out under `Entry to Collection`, and the value it greyed out on is still the one that runs. A node switched to that resolution keeps reading whichever row `Selection` was last left pointing at.

bPrefixWithAttributeName.tooltip: If enabled, prefix the attribute value with the attribute name
bPrefixWithAttributeName.semantics: Booleans ignore it either way: a true value tags as the bare attribute name and a false value tags nothing at all. Everything else is a value string, prefixed or not, and an empty string is skipped.

AttributeMappings.tooltip: Attributes whose value is promoted, each with an optional source->target output-name remap. Leave the target empty to keep the source's resolved name (the pre-remapping behavior).

fields.name: Source
fields.tooltip: Attribute to read on input

fields.name: Target
fields.tooltip: Attribute to write on output, if different from input

AttributeMappings.semantics: Leave a row's target empty and the output keeps the source's resolved name, which is what a graph saved before remapping existed migrates to. A source aimed at the `@Data` domain is read once for the whole dataset, so `Selection` has no bearing on it.

CommaSeparatedAttributeSelectors.tooltip: A list of selectors separated by a comma, for easy overrides. Will be appended to the existing array.
CommaSeparatedAttributeSelectors.semantics: Tokens land beside the mapping rows and are never remapped: each token is both the source and the output name.

IncludedSchemas.tooltip: Schema assets whose property names are appended to the selectors above.
IncludedSchemas.semantics: Every property a schema resolves to, recursively, becomes a source under its own name. Like the comma-separated tokens, these carry no remap, so renaming one means adding an explicit mapping row for it.

bQuietTooManyCollectionsWarning.tooltip: Suppress warning when source has more collections than target.

UPCGExAutoTangents.name: Auto
UPCGExAutoTangents.purpose: Splits the tangent length between arrive and leave according to where the point sits between its two neighbours. Direction comes from the straight line joining those neighbours, the same line **Catmull-Rom** works from; the split is what Auto adds, so the side with the nearer neighbour gets the shorter vector. It is the rule a newly placed **Path : Write Tangents** starts on.
UPCGExAutoTangents.situation: Points along the path are unevenly spaced and a curve built from equal-length tangents swings wide over the short gaps.

mechanism.text: The point is projected onto the straight line joining its two neighbours. Both vectors run along that line in path order: arrive as long as the run from the previous neighbour to the projection, leave as long as the run from the projection to the next neighbour, so the two together always measure the full distance between the neighbours. Each is then multiplied by its own scale. An open path's first and last point never reach this rule, and take the base's answer instead.

hints.text: The projection is clamped to the span between the two neighbours. Where the path doubles back sharply enough that the point projects past one of them, the projection lands on that neighbour, the run to it measures nothing, and that side's vector comes out zero-length however the scales are set.

UPCGExBatchActionsSettings.name: Batch Actions
UPCGExBatchActionsSettings.purpose: Runs a stack of Action sub-nodes over one set of points, so several filter-driven writes happen in one pass instead of one node each. Every action carries its own conditions and its own pair of consequences; this node supplies the points, orders the stack, and gives it somewhere to write. A separate pin declares the attributes that should exist on every point whether or not an action reached it.
UPCGExBatchActionsSettings.situation: Several independent per-point tests that each need to write something, where splitting and re-merging the points once per test would be the alternative.

mechanism.text: The points are duplicated, then every attribute declared on the Default Values data is created on that copy, inheriting whatever the points already carried. Each point is then visited once and every action in the stack is run against it in turn, in ascending Priority, so an action can see and overwrite what an earlier one wrote. Point count and order are untouched; the only thing that changes is attribute values. With nothing on the Actions pin the node forwards its input and stops.

off_label.claim: Wiring only the Default Values pin and no actions at all still forwards the input untouched, so the pin cannot be used on its own to seed attributes: the seeding happens inside the per-dataset pass that an empty action stack skips.
off_label.grounded_in: an empty factory list takes the early-exit branch before any processor is built, and the default-attribute writers are created inside the processor

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to process. The output is a duplicate of these.

inputs.label: Actions
inputs.note: Action factories from Action sub-nodes. Sorted by Priority before running. Leaving it empty is legal and makes the node a pass-through.

inputs.label: Default values
inputs.note: An attribute set declaring attributes that should exist on every output point, with the values they take where no action wrote. Its rows are not read.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The same points, in the same order, carrying whatever the stack wrote.

DefaultAttributesFilter.semantics: Narrows which of the attributes present on the Default Values data are created, by name. It does not reach the actions' own attribute lists, which each action filters for itself.

fields.name: FilterMode
fields.tooltip: How the names are processed.

fields.name: Matches
fields.tooltip: List of matches that will be checked. Any success is a pass.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNames
fields.tooltip: A list of names separated by a comma, for easy overrides. The limitation is that they all use the same shared filter mode.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNameFilter
fields.tooltip: Unique filter mode applied to comma separated names

fields.name: bPreservePCGExData
fields.tooltip: If enabled, PCGEx attributes & tags won't be affected.  Cluster-related nodes rely on these to work!

ConsumeProcessedAttributes.semantics: Names attributes to delete from the output once the stack has finished. Only attributes the run actually touched are candidates, and PCGEx-prefixed ones are never removed.
ConsumeProcessedAttributes.trap: This deletes attributes the points arrived with, not attributes the actions created, so it is a way to consume an input marker rather than to clean up after the writes.

hints.text: Two actions naming the same attribute with different types fail the whole node with a type-mismatch error rather than the offending action being skipped.
Every action sees every point. A stack is a sequence of passes over the same points, not a partition of them, so ordering by Priority is how one action's output becomes another's input.

UPCGExBevelPathSettings.name: Path : Bevel
UPCGExBevelPathSettings.purpose: Cuts a corner off and puts a profile in its place. Every point the **Bevel Conditions** pin admits is replaced by a pair, one backing up along the segment that arrives and one running out along the segment that leaves, and `Type` decides what fills the span between them: a straight chord, an arc through where the corner used to be, or a shape you hand it on the **Profile** pin. Width can be read per point, so one node can round some corners hard and others barely. Four flag attributes mark which output points came from which part of a bevel.
UPCGExBevelPathSettings.situation: A path of hard corners that has to read as rounded, or as chamfered, before anything is built along it.

mechanism.text: One execution takes paths and returns them with more points. A bevelled corner leaves two points behind, the arrive and the leave, plus whatever the profile put between them; every point that does not bevel passes through untouched, so the output count is the input count plus one per bevelled corner plus that corner's profile points. On an open path the first and last points never bevel however the conditions are set, because a bevel needs a segment on both sides; on a closed path every point is eligible, the seam included. Each point a bevel produces inherits the corner's attributes verbatim and gets a fresh seed from its own position, so no blending happens anywhere in this node. A path of exactly two points has no corner to work on and comes back as it went in, carrying whichever flag attributes are enabled at false.
steps: Each corner resolves a width from `Width`, `Width Measure` and `Mode`, before any neighbour is consulted.
`Limit` then cuts that width down against the segments and against the bevels on either side, which is why two adjacent corners can each end up narrower than either asked for.
The arrive and leave points are placed at the surviving width, and only then does the profile fill the span between them.

off_label.claim: Enable Flag Poles alone and the node doubles as a corner detector. The flag is written only on points a bevel produced, so a width small enough to be invisible still marks every corner the conditions admitted, and the geometry comes back looking untouched.
off_label.grounded_in: WriteFlags is called only for indices that built a bevel, and writes at the bevel's own start and end output indices

off_label.claim: A two-point path on the Profile pin contributes no interior points at all, because the first and last profile positions are anchors rather than content. Every admitted corner is then cut to a plain chord, which is the shortest route to chamfering a whole path from data rather than from settings.
off_label.grounded_in: SubdivideCustom takes ProfilePositions.Num() minus 2 as its count, and TryBuildCustomProfile accepts any profile of two points or more

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to bevel.

inputs.label: Bevel Conditions
inputs.note: Points that pass are bevelled. Left empty every point is a candidate, which is the opposite of how a pin whose name ends in Conditions usually behaves, so an unfiltered node bevels the whole path.

inputs.label: Profile
inputs.note: A single path read as the shape each bevel is cut to. Its first and last points are the anchors that land on the arrive and leave positions; everything between them becomes the profile. It must hold at least two points and its ends must not sit on top of each other.
inputs.condition: when Type is Custom

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The same paths with each admitted corner replaced by its bevel.

Mode.semantics: How the width is turned into a distance along the two segments. `Distance` uses it as that distance directly. `Radius` divides it by the sine of half the corner's angle, so the sharper the corner the further back the bevel starts, which is what keeps a rounded corner at a constant distance from the corner point rather than at a constant distance along the path.

WidthMeasure.semantics: What the number in `Width` is counted in. `Relative`, which is what ships, multiplies it by the shorter of the two segments meeting at that corner, so 0.1 is a tenth of the shorter one and the bevel scales with the path. `Discrete` reads it as world units.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

Width.semantics: Read once per corner, from the corner's own point. An attribute source therefore varies the bevel from corner to corner, and it is also the number `Limit` weighs when two neighbouring bevels compete for the segment between them: the wider request keeps the larger share.

Limit.semantics: What stops a bevel running past its neighbours. `None` leaves the width alone, so a width larger than the segments produces a path that folds back on itself. `Closest neighbor` caps it at the shorter of the two adjoining segments. `Balanced`, which ships selected, does that and then splits each shared segment between the two bevels at its ends in proportion to what each one asked for, so a wide corner next to a narrow one takes more of the space between them.

bSlideAlongPath.tooltip: When enabled, bevels can extend past non-beveled points, limited only by neighboring bevels or path endpoints. Bevel endpoints will traverse along the path geometry, and intermediate non-beveled points will be removed.
bSlideAlongPath.semantics: Lets a bevel keep going past points that are not themselves bevelled, following the path's geometry instead of the straight run to the immediate neighbour. Its limit becomes the whole distance to the next bevel or to the path's end.
bSlideAlongPath.trap: Points a sliding bevel passes over are deleted, so this is the one setting on the node that can make the output shorter than the input rather than longer.

Type.semantics: What fills the span between the arrive and the leave point. `Line` is a straight chord, `Arc` is a circular arc through the original corner, `Custom` is the shape on the **Profile** pin.
Type.trap: `Arc` produces nothing on its own. The arc is only ever sampled by subdivision, so with `Subdivide` off an arc bevel is two points and a straight chord between them, identical in every way to `Line`.

bKeepCornerPoint.tooltip: Whether to keep the corner point or not. If enabled, subdivision is ignored.
bKeepCornerPoint.semantics: Puts the original corner position back as a third point between the arrive and the leave, turning a cut corner into a mitred one.
bKeepCornerPoint.trap: It overrides the whole `Settings|Subdivision` block rather than adding to it. With this on, a `Line` bevel is exactly three points however the subdivision settings are configured.

MainAxisScaling.tooltip: Define how the custom profile will be scaled on the main axis.
MainAxisScaling.semantics: How the custom profile's lateral offsets are sized. `Uniform` scales them by the straight distance between the arrive and leave points, which keeps the profile's proportions; `Scale` multiplies the bevel's depth, the perpendicular distance from the corner to that straight line; `Distance` ignores both and uses the value as world units.

MainAxisScale.tooltip: Scale or Distance value for the main axis.

CrossAxisScaling.tooltip: Define how the custom profile will be scaled on the cross axis.
CrossAxisScaling.semantics: The same three choices for the axis that leaves the plane the corner sits in, which is the only way a custom profile lifts the path out of that plane.

CrossAxisScale.tooltip: Scale or Distance value for the cross axis.

bSubdivide.semantics: Adds points along the profile between the arrive and the leave. It is hidden under `Custom`, where the profile's own points decide the count instead.

SubdivideMethod.semantics: `Count` adds that many points to every bevel whatever its size; `Distance` divides the profile's own length by the value, so a tight corner gets fewer points than a wide one. `Manhattan` steps between the arrive and the leave one axis at a time, which turns the bevel into a staircase rather than a curve.

SubdivisionDistance.edit_condition: bSubdivide && Type != EPCGExBevelProfileType::Custom && SubdivideMethod == EPCGExSubdivideMode::Distance && SubdivisionAmountInput == EPCGExInputValueType::Constant
SubdivisionDistance.semantics: Measured along the profile being cut, which for `Arc` is the arc length and not the chord, so the same value produces more points on a sharp corner than on a shallow one.

SubdivisionCount.edit_condition: bSubdivide && Type != EPCGExBevelProfileType::Custom && SubdivideMethod == EPCGExSubdivideMode::Count && SubdivisionAmountInput == EPCGExInputValueType::Constant

SubdivisionAmount.edit_condition: bSubdivide && Type != EPCGExBevelProfileType::Custom && SubdivideMethod != EPCGExSubdivideMode::Manhattan && SubdivisionAmountInput != EPCGExInputValueType::Constant

PoleFlagName.tooltip: Name of the boolean flag to write whether the point is a Bevel endpoint or not (Either start or end)
PoleFlagName.semantics: Written true on both ends of every bevel, so it marks twice as many points as there were corners. `Bevel Start` and `Bevel End` split the same set in two if the two ends need telling apart.

StartPointFlagName.tooltip: Name of the boolean flag to write whether the point is a Bevel start point or not

EndPointFlagName.tooltip: Name of the boolean flag to write whether the point is a Bevel end point or not

SubdivisionFlagName.tooltip: Name of the boolean flag to write whether the point is a subdivision point or not
SubdivisionFlagName.semantics: Marks the points between the two ends of a bevel, which is also the point `Keep Corner Point` puts back. A corner kept rather than cut is therefore flagged as a subdivision.

bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.tooltip: If enabled, collections that have less than 2 points won't be processed and be omitted from the output.
bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.semantics: Reaches inputs of fewer than two points only. A path of exactly two is duplicated and comes back whatever this says, because two points make one segment and no corner.

hints.text: An empty **Bevel Conditions** pin bevels every point on the path. The pin narrows the set rather than opening it, which is the reverse of how the Conditions pins on **Path : Shrink** and **Path : Fuse Collinear** behave.

UPCGExBFSDepthSettings.name: Cluster : BFS Depth
UPCGExBFSDepthSettings.purpose: Answers how far every Vtx sits from the nearest seed, counted in edges crossed. Depth is that hop count and it is the only thing this node ranks by; the other outputs describe the route the hop count found, its length in world units, which seed it came from, and how many marked Vtx it passed on the way. A normalized 0 to 1 form of the depth is available for driving anything that wants a gradient running outward from the seeds.
UPCGExBFSDepthSettings.situation: Seed points sit somewhere on or near a cluster, and everything downstream needs to know how many steps away each Vtx is.

mechanism.text: Each seed point claims the Vtx nearest to it, and the traversal expands outward from all claimed Vtx at once, one ring of neighbours at a time, so a Vtx is reached at the fewest hops any seed can reach it in. Vtx in, the same Vtx out with the enabled attributes written on them; the Edges pass through untouched unless the edge direction output is on. Every Vtx of a connected component is reachable once one seed lands in it, and a component no seed reached is skipped with a warning rather than written with defaults.

off_label.claim: Set Trigger Count's filters to something every Vtx passes and its Initial Value to a per-seed attribute, and the count becomes a plain copy of the depth offset by that starting number, which is a per-seed depth origin the Depth output itself has no setting for.
off_label.grounded_in: RunBFS seeds TriggerCounts from GetInitialValue on the seed point and adds one per hop when every Vtx passes IsNodePassingFilters

off_label.claim: With every output off except the edge direction, the node stops being a measurement and becomes an orientation pass: every edge the traversal crossed ends up pointing away from the seeds, which is what a spline or mesh built along the edges needs.
off_label.grounded_in: GetEdgeOutputInitMode makes the Edges writable only when the direction output is on, and WriteFromNodeDepths orients each edge from its shallower endpoint to its deeper one

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The Vtx half of every cluster to traverse, and where the depth attributes are written.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The Edges half. Every Edges dataset that finds its Vtx is one cluster and one traversal.

inputs.label: Seeds
inputs.note: Where the traversal starts. One dataset, and its point indices are what Seed Index reports.

inputs.label: TriggerFilters
inputs.note: Which Vtx count as triggers. Vtx filters, point filters and filter groups are accepted here.
inputs.condition: appears and is required when Trigger Count is enabled

inputs.label: Direction Sorting
inputs.note: Sorting rules the edge direction fallback uses to decide which endpoint of an edge is its start.
inputs.condition: appears and is required when the edge direction output is on and its fallback Direction Method is Endpoints Sort

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: The same Vtx, carrying whichever outputs were enabled.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: Forwarded unchanged, or carrying the traversal direction when that output is on.

SeedPicking.tooltip: How seed points select their starting node in the cluster.
SeedPicking.semantics: A seed claims one Vtx and only one, so seeds are start points rather than a region. Closest edge finds the nearest edge first and then takes one of its endpoints, which lands differently from Closest vtx when a seed sits beside a long edge. Max Distance is a hard cut at 200 by default: a seed further than that from anything claims nothing, and a cluster left with no seed at all is dropped from the output with a warning.
SeedPicking.trap: Two seeds resolving to the same Vtx do not both take it. One claims it and the other is discarded, and which of the two wins is not fixed between runs, so Seed Index and any forwarded seed attribute can change there without the graph changing.

DepthAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write depth to.
DepthAttributeName.semantics: The value is the number of edges crossed on the shortest route from the nearest seed, so a seed's own Vtx is 0 and each ring outward is one more. It is the value every other output is derived from.
DepthAttributeName.trap: The attribute is inherited when one of this name already exists on the Vtx, so a Vtx this run does not reach keeps whatever the earlier run left there instead of falling back to the minus one that a fresh attribute starts at.

DistanceAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'double' attribute to write distance to.
DistanceAttributeName.semantics: The value is the summed straight-line length of the edges along the route the depth found, which is the route with the fewest hops. A cluster whose edges vary in length has cheaper routes than that one, and this output will not find them: it measures the fewest-hop route, not the shortest one.

SeedIndexAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write seed index to.
SeedIndexAttributeName.semantics: The point index, in the Seeds dataset, of the seed whose expansion arrived first. Nearest here means fewest hops, not nearest in space, and a Vtx equidistant in hops from two seeds goes to whichever of them sits earlier in the Seeds dataset.

NormalizedDepthAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'double' attribute to write normalized depth to.
NormalizedDepthAttributeName.semantics: Rebuilt from scratch on every run rather than inherited, so a Vtx this run does not reach is written rather than left alone. It is written 0, and so is a Vtx no seed could reach at all, which under `Global` is also the value the seeds themselves carry. Depth marks unreached Vtx with minus one and is the output to read when the two have to be told apart.
NormalizedDepthAttributeName.trap: The value is bounded to 0 and 1 per cluster, and every cluster gets its own range, so two clusters of very different size come out looking alike. Nothing in this attribute says how many hops a given fraction stands for.

NormalizedDepthMode.tooltip: How to normalize the depth values.
NormalizedDepthMode.semantics: Global divides each depth by the deepest one found in the cluster, giving one gradient that runs 0 at the seeds to 1 at the furthest Vtx, so a short branch only ever covers the low end of the range. Cascade instead gives every branch the full range: it starts at 1 at the seeds and walks back from each tip, and where a short branch leaves a longer one it inherits the value at that fork and falls to 0 over its own remaining length. Cascade is the mode for a falloff that reads the same on a stub as on a trunk; Global is the mode for a true distance ramp.
NormalizedDepthMode.trap: The two run in opposite directions. Global puts 1 at the far end, Cascade puts 1 at the seeds.

EdgeDirectionOutput.tooltip: Output the BFS traversal direction onto each edge, in propagation order (away from the seed).
EdgeDirectionOutput.semantics: Writes a vector on the Edges rather than on the Vtx, and turning it on is what makes the Edges dataset writable at all; left off the Edges are forwarded as they came in. An edge whose two endpoints were reached at different depths points from the shallower toward the deeper one, which is away from the seed. Everything else, an edge between two Vtx at the same depth or an edge the traversal never crossed, falls back to the Edge Direction Settings inside the block, the same rule Cluster : Edge Properties uses.
EdgeDirectionOutput.trap: The fallback is not a weaker version of the depth rule, it is a different rule with its own sign convention: it points the vector at whichever endpoint its method calls the start, which on a cluster with equal-depth edges leaves some vectors aimed back toward the seed.

TriggerCount.tooltip: Output a running count of "trigger" vtx (those passing the Vtx Filters) crossed along the BFS path. Adds a required Vtx Filters input.

fields.name: bOutputTriggerCount
fields.tooltip: Output the running trigger count. Requires Vtx Filters to be connected (they define what a "trigger" is).

fields.name: TriggerCountAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write the trigger count to.

fields.name: InitialValue
fields.tooltip: Starting value for each seed -- a constant, or read per-seed from a seed attribute.

fields.name: bCountTriggerItself
fields.tooltip: If enabled, a trigger vtx itself receives the incremented value (counts on entry); otherwise only vtx reached after it are incremented.

TriggerCount.semantics: A running tally carried along the route rather than a per-Vtx test: each Vtx takes its parent's count and adds one where a trigger was crossed, so the value says how many marked Vtx stand between this Vtx and its seed. Initial Value is read from the seed point, so different seeds can start their branches at different numbers. Count Trigger Itself decides whether a trigger's own Vtx carries the increment or whether it lands on the first Vtx past it.
TriggerCount.trap: Vtx the traversal never reached hold 0 here, which is also a legitimate answer for a Vtx one hop from its seed with nothing in between. Read it alongside Depth, whose unreached value is distinguishable.

SeedForwarding.tooltip: Which Seed attributes to forward on the vtx they reached (each vtx receives values from its owning seed). Disabled by default.

fields.name: FilterMode
fields.tooltip: How the names are processed.

fields.name: Matches
fields.tooltip: List of matches that will be checked. Any success is a pass.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNames
fields.tooltip: A list of names separated by a comma, for easy overrides. The limitation is that they all use the same shared filter mode.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNameFilter
fields.tooltip: Unique filter mode applied to comma separated names

fields.name: bPreservePCGExData
fields.tooltip: If enabled, PCGEx attributes & tags won't be affected.  Cluster-related nodes rely on these to work!

fields.name: bEnabled
fields.tooltip: Is forwarding enabled.

fields.name: bPreserveAttributesDefaultValue
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will preserve the initial attribute default value.

SeedForwarding.semantics: Copies attribute values from the claiming seed onto every Vtx it reached, which is the same claim Seed Index reports. A Vtx no seed reached is not written at all, so whatever it already carried under those names survives.

bUseOctreeSearch.tooltip: Whether to use an octree for closest node search. Depending on your dataset, this may be faster or slower.

hints.text: Depth, Distance and Seed Index inherit an attribute of the same name when one is already on the Vtx, so re-running with a narrower set of seeds leaves the previous run's values on every Vtx the new one misses. Only a name that does not exist yet gets the minus one that marks unreached.

UPCGExBinPacking3DSettings.name: Bin Packing 3D (Q4RealBPP)
UPCGExBinPacking3DSettings.purpose: Packs items into bins under the constraints real loading has: weight limits, things that must not sit on each other, and nothing left floating in mid-air. **Bin Packing** solves the geometry alone; this one adds the physical rules and scores its candidate placements against several goals at once rather than taking the first fit. That makes it the node for arrangements meant to look loaded rather than merely fitted.
UPCGExBinPacking3DSettings.situation: Crates, props or cargo that should stack the way real ones would, with heavy things low and nothing hovering.

mechanism.text: Items are ordered, then each is offered every legal placement and rotation, and the placements are scored rather than accepted on sight. The score combines several goals whose weights are set in the panel, and the constraints act as gates before scoring: an item that would break a weight limit, sit on something too light, or float without support is not a low-scoring candidate but an illegal one. Whatever fits nowhere legal leaves on the Discarded pin.
steps: Items are ordered, by volume when that is enabled and by the sorting rules otherwise.
Each candidate placement is gated by the active physical constraints.
Surviving candidates are scored against the objective weights and the best is taken.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The items to place. Their bounds are what has to fit, and their attributes can supply weight and category.

inputs.label: Bins
inputs.note: The containers. Each input collection expects a matching collection of bins, and per-bin values like the weight limit are read from the bin points.

inputs.label: Sorting Rules
inputs.note: The order items are considered in, when the volume sort is not doing that job.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The items that were placed, moved and rotated into their bins.

outputs.label: Bins
outputs.note: The bins that came in, carrying statistics about what ended up in them.

outputs.label: Discarded
outputs.note: Items that found no legal placement, whether for lack of room or because a constraint refused every candidate.

SortDirection.tooltip: Controls the order in which points will be sorted, when using sorting rules. Uses largest-first by default for best-fit decreasing.

bSortByVolume.tooltip: If enabled, items will be sorted by volume (largest first) before packing. This is the classic BFD approach.
bSortByVolume.semantics: Ships on and orders items largest first, which is the classic approach and the reason the shipped sort direction is descending. It takes precedence as the ordering strategy, so wiring sorting rules matters mainly once this is off.

SeedMode.tooltip: Per-bin seed. Represent a bound-relative location to start packing from.

RotationMode.tooltip: Rotation testing mode. More rotations = better fit but slower. Paper6 uses the paper's symmetry-reduced orientations.
RotationMode.semantics: How many orientations each item is tried in. More orientations find better fits and cost proportionally more, since every candidate placement is evaluated per orientation. The shipped mode uses a symmetry-reduced set rather than every rotation, which avoids testing orientations that would produce the same occupied volume.

bGlobalBestFit.tooltip: If enabled, will evaluate all bins for each item to find the globally best placement.
bGlobalBestFit.semantics: Evaluates every bin for each item rather than filling one before moving on. It produces better overall use of the bins and costs more, because each item's candidate list grows with the number of bins.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

LoadBearingThreshold.semantics: How much heavier than its support an item may be, read per item, while the load-bearing constraint is on. It is a ratio rather than a limit, so it says nothing about absolute mass, and it reads the same weight value the bin weight cap uses.

MinSupportRatio.tooltip: Per-item minimum fraction of base area that must be supported (0 = any contact, 1 = full base).

MinSupportRatio.semantics: How much of an item's base has to rest on something, read per item, while the support requirement above it is on. A small value accepts a corner resting on an edge; a large one demands the base be nearly covered. The requirement ships enabled, which is what keeps items from hovering.
MinSupportRatio.trap: Turning the requirement off does not merely relax the arrangement: items become free to occupy any legal empty volume, so a bin can end up with objects suspended above gaps.

ObjectiveWeightBinUsage.tooltip: Weight for bin-usage objective (o1, Paper Eq. 1). Higher fill-ratio bins are preferred.
ObjectiveWeightBinUsage.semantics: One of the goals the placement score balances, alongside height, load balance and surface contact. They are relative to each other rather than absolute, so what matters is their proportions: raising all four equally changes nothing.
ObjectiveWeightBinUsage.trap: The goals genuinely conflict. Favouring bin usage packs tightly wherever there is room, favouring height keeps the load low, and a graph that turns both up gets a compromise rather than either.

ObjectiveWeightHeight.tooltip: Weight for height objective (o2, Paper Eq. 2). Lower placement Z is preferred (floor-up packing).

ObjectiveWeightLoadBalance.tooltip: Weight for load-balance objective (o3, Paper Eq. 3). Placement closer to bin center-of-mass is preferred.

ObjectiveWeightContact.tooltip: Weight for surface-contact objective. Items touching more surfaces (walls/other items) are preferred for visual stability.

bEnableWeightConstraint.tooltip: Enable maximum weight per bin constraint (Paper Eq. 23).
bEnableWeightConstraint.semantics: Caps the total weight a bin may hold, with the cap read from the bin points rather than set here. It is the constraint most likely to send items to Discarded on data that would otherwise fit, because it has nothing to do with whether there is room.

ItemWeight.tooltip: Per-item weight/mass value. Shared by the weight constraint (Paper Eq. 23) and load bearing (Paper Eq. 26, mass comparison).

UPCGExBinPackingSettings.name: Bin Packing
UPCGExBinPackingSettings.purpose: Fits points into containers by moving them, so that their bounds stop overlapping and stay inside the bin. The input points are the items, a second set supplies the bins, and what comes out is the items repositioned plus the ones that would not fit. It is a placement solver rather than a scatter: nothing is randomised, and an item that has no room is reported rather than squeezed in.
UPCGExBinPackingSettings.situation: Objects of assorted sizes that have to be arranged inside authored volumes without intersecting.

mechanism.text: Each bin starts as one free space. Items are taken in sorted order and each is placed against the free space that best suits it, after which the space it did not fill is cut into new free spaces. `Split Mode` decides how that cut is made, and every later placement chooses among whatever those cuts left. Because the free spaces available to an item are the residue of the placements before it, the order items are considered in changes the result more than any single placement rule.
steps: Items are ordered by the sorting rules, or by input order when none are wired.
Each item takes a free space, favoured by the placement rule.
The remainder of that space is cut into new free spaces for the items that follow.

off_label.claim: The Discarded pin makes it usable as a capacity test: run it, and the count arriving on Discarded says how much of the input the bins could not hold, without anything downstream having to measure volumes.
off_label.grounded_in: Points that could not fit into any bin are routed to the discarded output rather than dropped or forced.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The items to place. Their bounds are what has to fit; their positions are replaced.

inputs.label: Bins
inputs.note: The containers. Each input collection expects a matching collection of bins, so bins and items are paired rather than pooled.

inputs.label: Sorting Rules
inputs.note: The order items are considered in, which is the single largest influence on how well they pack.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The items that were placed, moved to their positions inside a bin.

outputs.label: Bins
outputs.note: The bins that came in, carrying statistics about what ended up in them.

outputs.label: Discarded
outputs.note: Items that fitted in no bin. They are reported rather than forced, so an over-subscribed set does not silently overlap.

SortDirection.tooltip: Controls the order in which points will be sorted, when using sorting rules.
SortDirection.semantics: Read alongside the Sorting Rules pin, and together they decide the order of consideration. Packing quality follows from that order more than from any other setting here, because each placement removes options from everything after it. Largest-first is the usual starting point, since a big item placed late is the one most likely to be discarded.

SeedMode.tooltip: Per-bin seed. Represent a bound-relative location to start packing from.
SeedMode.semantics: Where packing starts inside each bin, given as a bound-relative location. It anchors the arrangement, so items accumulate outward from that corner or face rather than from the bin's centre by default.

bInferSplitAxisFromSeed.tooltip: Will attempt to infer the split axis from relative seed positioning, and fall back to selected axis if it can't find one.

SplitAxis.tooltip: The main stacking axis is the axis that will generate the smallest free space for further insertion.

SplitMode.tooltip: How the space left around a placed item is cut into new free partitions.
SplitMode.semantics: How the leftover room around a placed item becomes new free spaces. It is the setting that decides whether the residue stays as a few large usable regions or becomes many small ones, so it governs what the next items can still fit into rather than where the current one goes.

bAvoidWastedSpace.tooltip: If enabled, fitting will try to avoid wasted space by not creating free spaces that are below a certain threshold.
bAvoidWastedSpace.semantics: Stops the splitting from producing free spaces too small to ever hold anything. Those slivers cost time to carry and consider, so discarding them keeps the candidate list to spaces that could still be used.

PlacementFavor.tooltip: If enabled, fitting will try to avoid wasted space by not creating free spaces that are below a certain threshold.
PlacementFavor.semantics: Which candidate free space an item prefers when several would hold it. It shapes the arrangement's character, whether items cluster toward the seed or spread across the bin, without changing which items fit.

UPCGExBitmaskCollection.name: Bitmask Collection
UPCGExBitmaskCollection.purpose: A named vocabulary of bit patterns, held in one asset instead of typed into every node. Each entry pairs an identifier with a bitmask and a direction, and any setting carrying a `Compositions` list pulls one entry by name. The direction-keyed consumers, **State : Bitmask Adjacency** and **G-Probe : Bitmasks**, can also take a whole collection at once and get one direction-and-mask pair per entry. Change what a name means and every graph referencing it follows.
UPCGExBitmaskCollection.situation: Several graphs that have to agree on what a given bit means, where the meaning is still moving.

mechanism.text: The asset is authored in the Content Browser and read when a graph runs. On first use it bakes each entry down to a plain int64 and a unit-length direction, then answers every lookup from that bake; editing the asset drops it, so the next run picks the change up. A consumer either names one entry through a row of its own, which carries the operation to apply, or takes the whole collection with one operation covering every entry in the order they are listed.

off_label.claim: One collection can serve both kinds of consumer at once: the adjacency and probe nodes read an entry's direction alongside its mask, while a plain composition row on a filter or on **Bitmask** reads the same entry and never looks at the direction.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExBitmaskRef::Mutate resolves through the mask-only TryGetBitmask overload, while TryGetAdjacencyInfos returns the cached direction as well

Entries.tooltip: Named bitmask entries in this collection.
Entries.semantics: Each row is an identifier, a full bitmask block, and a direction. The direction is normalised when it is read, so its length carries nothing and a zero vector matches nothing on the consumers that test directions. Lookup is by name, and the name map holds one row per name.
Entries.trap: Two rows sharing an `Identifier` are not refused. Both stay in the asset and both appear in the identifier dropdown, but a row naming that identifier resolves to the later of the two, while a consumer taking the whole collection still gets both.

hints.text: An entry's `Bitmask` is the same block the **Bitmask** node carries, `Compositions` included, so an entry can be assembled from entries in other collections. The editor refuses a reference that would close a cycle and clears the offending row, logging which asset it was preventing from nesting inside which.

UPCGExBitmaskFilterProviderSettings.name: Filter : Bitmask
UPCGExBitmaskFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Reads a 64-bit integer attribute as a set of flags and asks how it stands against a mask: whether the two share any bit, whether the flags carry every bit of the mask, whether they are identical, or the negations of the first two. The mask is a literal integer, typed in or read per element, and entries from a Bitmask Library asset can be folded into it before the test. Point the flags name at a `@Data.` attribute, with a constant or `@Data.` mask beside it, and the filter answers once per dataset instead of once per element, which is what lets Uber Filter (Data) route whole collections on a flag.
UPCGExBitmaskFilterProviderSettings.situation: Several boolean states are packed into one integer attribute, and the next node should act only on the elements carrying a particular combination of them.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this filter once per element, and the filter reads no data of its own and writes nothing. Two 64-bit integers decide the verdict: the flags read from the element, and a mask. The mask starts as the constant, or as the value read from the mask attribute, and each Compositions entry then applies its own bitwise operation to it in list order, so the comparison sees the composed result rather than the number sitting in the field. The chosen comparison is applied with the flags on the left and the composed mask on the right.

off_label.claim: Set the mask to Attribute and the comparison to Match (strict) and the node becomes an equality test between two 64-bit integer attributes, at full width. Filter : Compare (Numeric) reads both of its operands as doubles, so it stops distinguishing integers once they pass the range a double can hold exactly.
off_label.grounded_in: EPCGExBitflagComparison::MatchStrict resolving to Flags == Mask over the int64 readers built in FBitmaskFilter::Init, against the double broadcasters used by the numeric compare filter

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter passport, so it is accepted on every filter pin, Vtx Filters and Edge Filters included.

UPCGExBitmaskMergeSettings.name: Bitmask Merge
UPCGExBitmaskMergeSettings.purpose: Folds several masks arriving on one pin into a single mask. It reads every int64 an attribute set carries, so a fan of **Bitmask** nodes, a pair of state bitmask pins and a hand-built attribute set all merge the same way. The operation decides what the fold means: a union under `OR`, an intersection under `AND`, a difference under `NOT`.
UPCGExBitmaskMergeSettings.situation: A mask assembled from parts that different branches of the graph decide independently.

mechanism.text: Every attribute set on the input pin is walked, and inside each one every int64 attribute is read as a mask, in pin order and then in attribute order. The first mask found becomes the running result as-is; each one after it is combined into that result by the chosen operation. Output is a single attribute set with one entry and one int64 named Bitmask, and it is emitted whether or not anything usable was found.

off_label.claim: The output is emitted even when the input pin held nothing an int64 could be read from, carrying 0, so a downstream consumer always receives a value rather than an empty pin.
off_label.grounded_in: The param data is created and staged after the input loop unconditionally in FPCGExBitmaskMergeElement::AdvanceWork

inputs.label: Bitmasks
inputs.note: Any number of attribute sets. Each one contributes every int64 attribute it carries.

outputs.label: Bitmask
outputs.note: An attribute set with one entry and one int64 attribute, also named Bitmask.

Operation.tooltip: Bitwise operation to apply when merging input bitmasks.
Operation.semantics: Applied to the running result and each mask after the first, never to the first. That makes `=` a last-one-wins pick rather than a merge, and `NOT` a running subtraction where every later mask clears its own bits from the result.
Operation.trap: Every int64 attribute on every input is treated as a mask, not one per attribute set, so a set that happens to carry a second int64 beside its bitmask joins the fold without any warning.

UPCGExBitmaskSettings.name: Bitmask
UPCGExBitmaskSettings.purpose: Builds one 64-bit mask in the graph and hands it out as data. The value can be typed as a number, ticked bit by bit, or assembled from entries in one or more **Bitmask Collection** assets, and it leaves on a single param pin ready to override a mask setting on any node downstream. It exists so that a mask several nodes share is authored once, in a place the graph shows.
UPCGExBitmaskSettings.situation: A mask that more than one node has to agree on, or one that a graph parameter needs to be able to override.

mechanism.text: No inputs, one execution, one output: an attribute set holding a single int64 named Bitmask. The value is resolved once from the settings, so nothing about the input data can change it. The node's subtitle shows that value, or the names of the referenced collection entries when there are any, which makes the mask readable from the graph without opening the panel.

off_label.claim: What leaves the pin is an ordinary attribute set carrying one int64, so anything that reads an int64 from a param input takes it, bitmask node or not.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExBitmaskElement::AdvanceWork stages a UPCGParamData with CreateAttribute<int64>(FName(Bitmask), value) and one entry

outputs.label: Bitmask
outputs.note: An attribute set with one entry and one int64 attribute, also named Bitmask.

Bitmask.tooltip: Operations executed on the flag if all filters pass

fields.name: Mode
fields.tooltip: How the bitmask value is constructed. Direct uses raw value, Mutations applies per-bit operations.

fields.name: Bitmask
fields.tooltip: Base 64-bit mask value. In Direct mode, used as-is. In Mutations mode, modified by operations.

fields.name: Mutations

UPCGExBitwiseOperationSettings.name: Bitmask Operation
UPCGExBitwiseOperationSettings.purpose: Applies one bitwise operation to an int64 attribute on every point. The mask can be a constant, so the whole dataset moves together, or read per point from another attribute, so each point gets its own. It is the editing half of the bitmask family: **Write States** builds a mask from conditions, this changes one that already exists.
UPCGExBitwiseOperationSettings.situation: A flag attribute that needs a bit added, cleared or flipped after the pass that created it.

mechanism.text: Points in, the same points out, with one int64 attribute rewritten in place. Each point's current value is combined with that point's mask by the chosen operation and written back; point count, order and every other attribute are untouched. An attribute of that name already on the points is read and modified, and a name nothing carries is created at zero first, so the operation runs against zero on every point.

off_label.claim: With the operation on `=` and the mask read from an attribute, the node is a typed copy: it moves an int64 from one attribute to another, creating the target when it does not exist.
off_label.grounded_in: PCGExBitmask::Do's Set branch assigns the mask outright, and the writable is opened with EBufferInit::Inherit, which creates the attribute at 0 when it is new

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points whose flag attribute is edited.

outputs.label: Out

FlagAttribute.tooltip: Attribute to apply the bitmask operation to. Must be int64.
FlagAttribute.semantics: Names the int64 the operation reads and writes back. It is both the operand and the destination, so this node never adds a second attribute alongside the one it edits.
FlagAttribute.trap: It ships blank, and a blank name fails validation, so a freshly placed node errors out until a name is typed.

Operation.semantics: Declared without an initial value, so a freshly placed node sits on `=` and replaces the attribute outright rather than folding into it. That also makes the first placement destructive on a mask built upstream, which `OR` is the usual intent for.

Mask.tooltip: Constant bitmask value to apply. Must be int64 when read from an attribute.

Mask.semantics: Switch its input to an attribute and the mask becomes per point, which is what lets one node set different bits on different points.

UPCGExBlendAttributesSettings.name: Uber Blend
UPCGExBlendAttributesSettings.purpose: Blending with no second dataset and no geometry involved: a point's attributes against each other, in place. Everything this node does is decided on its **Blend Ops** pin, so it exists to give that pin somewhere to run when no sampler, fuser or smoother is the reason for the blend. It is the node to reach for when the operation is arithmetic on attributes and the alternative is a chain of stock metadata nodes.
UPCGExBlendAttributesSettings.situation: An attribute needs to become some expression of the other attributes on the same point.

mechanism.text: Points in, the same points in the same order out, with whatever the operations wrote. Nothing is added or removed and no second dataset is involved: both operands are read from the working copy this node is writing to, so an operation later in `Priority` order sees what an earlier one left. Each operation reads its own `Weight` per point, through its own curve, because there is no distance here to derive one from. The **Point Filters** pin decides which points are touched at all; a point that fails is skipped by every operation and keeps the values it arrived with.

off_label.claim: With one operation set to Copy (Source), Operand A on an existing attribute and a New output, the node is an attribute copy with a type change, which is one node instead of a rename plus a cast.
off_label.grounded_in: the BlendOp Copy modes dispatch to CopyA and honour Output Type; the node itself imposes nothing on the operation

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to blend.

inputs.label: Filters
inputs.note: Point filters deciding which points the operations touch. Points that fail keep their values.

inputs.label: Blend Ops
inputs.note: The operations. This node has no other configuration, so an empty pin fails it.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The same points in the same order, carrying whatever the operations wrote.

hints.text: The **Blend Ops** pin is required, and an empty one is an error rather than a node that passes its points through. That is particular to this node: several other consumers of the same pin treat it as optional so operations can be supplied from outside a subgraph.

This is the family where a blend op's own `Weight` is read. On a sampler or a fuser the consumer computes the weight from distance and the op's value is ignored; here, and on **Path : Attribute Rolling**, **Cluster : Flood Fill** and **Cluster : Diffuse**, there is no distance and the op's own value is what arrives.

UPCGExBlendOpFactory.name: Blend Op Factory
UPCGExBlendOpFactory.purpose: The object a **Blend Ops** pin actually carries, and the contract every consumer of that pin reads it through. Two nodes emit one: **BlendOp**, which carries a single fixed configuration, and **BlendOp : Blend All**, which carries a monolithic block and works out its configurations from the data at run time. A consumer never distinguishes them; it asks each factory on its pin for operations and gets one back, or many.
UPCGExBlendOpFactory.situation: Working out why a mix of BlendOp and BlendOp : Blend All nodes on one pin produced fewer operations than nodes wired, or why one of them had no effect.

mechanism.text: Factories arriving on a pin are sorted by `Priority`, lowest first, ties keeping wiring order.
