The consumer then makes one pass to collect the output names the single-configuration factories claim, and a second pass asking every factory to expand: a single-configuration one hands back its one operation, a monolithic one reads the source data's metadata and hands back one operation per admitted attribute and enabled point property, skipping every name already claimed. Each operation binds its operands and its destination against the actual data, and an operation that cannot bind removes itself if it came from a monolithic factory and fails the node if it did not. What survives runs in that same order for every element the consumer blends.

outputs.label: Blend Op
outputs.note: What both blending sub-nodes emit. Ordinary parameter data, so reroutes carry it and one output feeds as many consumer pins as you wire it to.

hints.text: The two shapes differ in when they decide, not in what they produce. A single-configuration factory settles its attribute, mode and destination in the details panel and carries them unchanged; a monolithic one carries a rule and resolves it against whatever data the consumer hands it, which is why the same node produces a different number of operations on different inputs, and why an attribute absent from the data costs nothing.

The tolerance for a failed binding is not the same on both. A single-configuration operation naming an attribute that is not there fails the consuming node outright; the equivalent operation from a monolithic block drops itself and the node continues. A misspelt attribute name is therefore loud on one and silent on the other.

The two constant pins are read once, when the factory is prepared, and only if something is wired to them. That data becomes a dependency of the factory, so a graph feeding a BlendOp from an attribute set will not run the blend before the set exists.

Operand A and Operand B are registered as consumable attributes, so a consuming node with `Cleanup Consumable Attributes` on deletes them from its output once the blend is done. The `Protected Attributes` list on that node is what keeps one.

UPCGExBlendOpFactoryProviderSettings.name: BlendOp
UPCGExBlendOpFactoryProviderSettings.purpose: One attribute, one blend mode, one destination. This is the sub-node every **Blend Ops** pin consumes, and its whole configuration is an Operand A, an optional Operand B, the mode that combines them, and where the answer lands: back over A, back over B, in a new attribute, or in a transient one that exists only for the duration of the pass and is discarded after. Several ops on one pin run in `Priority` order, lowest first, and a later op can name an earlier one's output through `#Previous` or `#N`, which is what lets multi-step arithmetic run without leaving scratch attributes on the data. Its counterpart is **BlendOp : Blend All**, which starts from everything the data carries instead of naming one attribute.
UPCGExBlendOpFactoryProviderSettings.situation: A node offers blending and only one attribute should move, on terms you want to state exactly.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs the op once per element it is blending, handing it a source row, a target row and a weight. Operand A and Operand B are read from whichever two datasets the consumer nominates as its sides, which on a node blending inside one dataset are the same dataset; with `Use Operand B` off, Operand A stands in for both. The mode combines the two values and the result is written at the target row, to the selector the output mode names. Where the weight comes from is the consumer's business: samplers and fusers derive one from distance and never read the op's own `Weight`, while **Uber Blend**, **Path : Attribute Rolling**, **Cluster : Flood Fill** and **Cluster : Diffuse** have no distance and do read it. The weight curve always applies, remapping whatever number arrived.

off_label.claim: Copy (Source) with no Operand B, a New output and `Output Type` set to Custom is an attribute copy that changes type on the way, which is a rename and a cast in one op.
off_label.grounded_in: EPCGExABBlendingType::CopyTarget dispatches to CopyA; EPCGExBlendOpOutputMode::New plus EPCGExOperandAuthority::Custom sets RealTypeC from CustomType in FPCGExBlendOperation::PrepareForData

off_label.claim: Wire an attribute set into the A pin and Operand A stops reading the data being blended: the value comes from the first element of that set instead, which turns a Multiply or a Subtract op into arithmetic against a graph-level constant.
off_label.grounded_in: UPCGExBlendOpFactory::Prepare fills ConstantA from the A pin, and PrepareForData builds descriptor A from ConstantA whenever it is set

inputs.label: A
inputs.note: Data to read Operand A's value from, taken from its first element, in place of the data being blended. Sits among the advanced pins.

inputs.label: B
inputs.note: The same for Operand B. Advanced, and only read when Use Operand B is on.
inputs.condition: the pin exists only when Use Operand B is on

outputs.label: Blend Op
outputs.note: The configured operation, for any **Blend Ops** pin. Ordinary parameter data, so one output reaches as many consumers as you wire it to.

Priority.semantics: Sorts the ops on one **Blend Ops** pin before any of them runs, lowest first, with ties keeping the order they were wired in. That order is the only thing `#Previous` and `#N` can count on: an op referencing its own position or a later one is a hard error, not a silent misread.

Config.semantics: Everything below configures one operation on one attribute. Two attributes means two of these nodes on the pin.

hints.text: The blend mode matters as much as the wiring. `Average` ignores the weight it is handed and divides by the contributor count instead, so any falloff the consumer computed is discarded and every contributor counts the same. `Weight` is the mode that honours it.

A composite property and its components cannot both be written by the ops on one pin. `$Transform` alongside any of `$Position`, `$Rotation` or `$Scale`, or `$Extents` alongside `$BoundsMin` or `$BoundsMax`, fails the consuming node with an error naming both, because the result would depend on which op ran last.
Project settings carry a per-type default blend mode. It reaches the monolithic surface only; a BlendOp's `Blend Mode` is read as written.

UPCGExBlendOpMonolithicProviderSettings.name: BlendOp : Blend All
UPCGExBlendOpMonolithicProviderSettings.purpose: The other half of the **Blend Ops** pin: instead of naming one attribute, it takes everything the data carries and gives it all the same treatment. The block it holds is the same inline blending block the fuse and union family carries, so what you configure is a `Default Blending` mode, a name filter deciding which attributes are admitted, and two override layers for the cases that need something else. It is the answer when the list of attributes is not known at authoring time, or is long enough that wiring one **BlendOp** per attribute stops being reasonable.
UPCGExBlendOpMonolithicProviderSettings.situation: Everything on the points should carry across a blend, with two or three exceptions.

mechanism.text: The factory resolves nothing at authoring time. When the consumer runs, it reads the metadata of the data being blended and expands into one ordinary blend operation per admitted attribute, plus one for each of the nine point properties, each configured with Operand A and Operand B pointing at the same name and the result written back over it. The mode each operation gets is settled per attribute: a name listed in `Attributes Overrides` wins, then the project settings' default for that value's type, then `Default Blending`; attributes carrying the PCGEx prefix are forced to `Copy` regardless, and anything landing on `None` produces no operation at all. Point properties skip the project-settings layer, taking their own override or `Default Blending`. An operation whose attribute is missing from the data is dropped rather than failing the node.

off_label.claim: Wired alongside individual BlendOp nodes it works as a catch-all: each individual op claims its own output name, and the expansion skips every name already claimed, so the block covers the remainder without a filter list.
off_label.grounded_in: FBlendOpsManager::Init builds SupersedeNames from every non-monolithic factory output name and passes it to ResolveConfigs, which skips those names

off_label.claim: Set `Default Blending` to None and the block admits nothing, which reduces it to whatever the per-attribute overrides list says. It becomes an allow-list rather than a blanket.
off_label.grounded_in: GetBlendingParam and the Param.Blending == EPCGExABBlendingType::None continue in UPCGExBlendOpMonolithicFactory::ResolveConfigs

outputs.label: Blend Op
outputs.note: The same factory type an individual **BlendOp** emits, so the two mix freely on one **Blend Ops** pin.

Priority.semantics: Sorts against every other op on the pin, lowest first. It has no effect inside the expansion: the operations this factory produces are all created at its position, in the order the source metadata reports its attributes.

hints.text: Where an individual **BlendOp** and this block both claim one attribute, the individual op wins and the block skips that name. Mixing the two on one pin is the intended shape, not a conflict.

`Seed` is a blendable point property and `Default Blending` covers it. Left on `Average`, merged points end up with the integer mean of their sources' seeds, which is deterministic, meaningless, and prone to collisions that quietly break every downstream node randomising from it. Set its override wherever points merge.

UPCGExBlendPathSettings.name: Path : Blend
UPCGExBlendPathSettings.purpose: Rewrites every point of a path from its own two ends. The first and the last point are the only sources, and each point in between takes a mix of the two decided by how far along it sits, so a value authored once at each end spreads across the whole run. `Blend Over` is what position means: distance travelled, position in the order, or a number you supply per point. What actually gets rewritten is named by the **Blend Ops** pin, which is required, so the node does nothing at all until something on it says what to write.
UPCGExBlendPathSettings.situation: A run whose values have to ramp from one end to the other, where the two ends are already carrying what the ramp should start and finish at.

mechanism.text: One execution takes paths and returns the same points in the same order, in the same places unless a Blend Op was pointed at their positions. Nothing is added or removed. Every point is written from the same pair, the point at index 0 and the point at the last index, so the sources never change along the run and a closed path is treated exactly as an open one, with its seam ignored. The two end points are left out of the rewrite by default, which is what keeps the sources intact.

off_label.claim: Turn on both Blend First Point and Blend Last Point and the sources overwrite themselves, which under a mode that ignores the weight, Average among them, collapses the whole path to a single value at every point.
off_label.grounded_in: The two toggles remove the guards that skip index 0 and the last index, so both source points are also written from the pair they belong to

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to blend along.

inputs.label: Blend Ops
inputs.note: Blend Op sub-nodes naming what is written and how it is mixed. This is where every value the node touches is chosen, and the pin is required.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The same points, carrying whatever the Blend Ops rewrote.

BlendOver.semantics: What decides each point's share of the two ends. `Distance` uses how far along the run the point sits, so a long gap moves the mix further than a short one. `Index` uses position in the order, so every gap counts the same however long it is. `Fixed` ignores position altogether and takes the number from `Lerp`, which is what makes a per-point attribute drive the mix directly.
BlendOver.trap: `Index` divides by the point count rather than by the last index, so the final point sits fractionally short of a full 1 rather than on it. `Distance` reaches 1 exactly.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

Lerp.semantics: Read per point under `Fixed`, so an attribute source turns this into an arbitrary ramp rather than a uniform one: any curve, mask or noise already on the points becomes the mix. As a constant it gives every point the same mix, which is a uniform shift toward one end.

bBlendFirstPoint.tooltip: If enabled, will apply blending to othe first point. Can be useful with some blendmodes.
bBlendFirstPoint.semantics: The first point is one of the two sources, so writing it changes what every other point is blended from. Under a mode that consumes the weight it is written at 0 and comes back as itself; under one that ignores the weight it does not.

bBlendLastPoint.tooltip: If enabled, will apply blending to the last  point. Can be useful with some blendmodes.
bBlendLastPoint.semantics: The same for the other source, at the far end of the range.

bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.tooltip: If enabled, collections that have less than 2 points won't be processed and be omitted from the output.
bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.semantics: Honoured in the off position: a path of fewer than two points has no pair of ends to blend between, and is forwarded untouched rather than processed.

hints.text: The sources are the first and last points of the array, not the two ends of a shape. On a closed path that pair sits either side of the seam, so the ramp runs the long way round the loop and meets itself at the seam.

UPCGExBooleanCompareFilterProviderSettin.name: Filter : Bool Compare
UPCGExBooleanCompareFilterProviderSettin.purpose: Tests a boolean read on the element against a second one, either a typed true or false or another attribute on that same element. The two operators are each other's inverse, so this filter carries no Invert toggle and needs none. Point both selectors at `@Data.` attributes and it answers once per dataset instead of once per element, which is what Uber Branch and Break require of any filter handed to them, and what lets Uber Filter (Data) judge each dataset directly instead of counting how many of its elements passed.
UPCGExBooleanCompareFilterProviderSettin.situation: A flag already written onto the elements, and the next node should act only where it is set.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this filter once per element and decides what the answer means; the filter reads no data of its own and writes nothing. Operand A is read on the element being tested, Operand B is either the typed constant or a second attribute read on that same element, and both arrive as booleans whatever type they are stored as. The verdict is equality or inequality between the two.

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter passport, so it is accepted on every filter pin, Vtx Filters and Edge Filters included.

fields.name: OperandA
fields.tooltip: Operand A for testing -- Will be translated to `bool` under the hood (numeric values read true when > 0).

fields.name: Comparison
fields.tooltip: Comparison

fields.name: CompareAgainst
fields.tooltip: Type of OperandB

fields.name: OperandB
fields.tooltip: Operand B for testing -- Will be translated to `bool` under the hood.

fields.name: OperandBConstant
fields.tooltip: Operand B for testing

UPCGExBoundsAxisToPointsSettings.name: Bounds Axis To Points
UPCGExBoundsAxisToPointsSettings.purpose: Picks one axis of each point's bounds and produces the pair of points at its ends. Which axis gets picked is the whole subject: the choice starts from the box's proportions and is then shifted by where the axis points and how long it is. The output is a two-point segment per input, which is what makes this the node for turning boxes into something with a direction.
UPCGExBoundsAxisToPointsSettings.situation: Boxes of varying proportion and orientation that each need to yield a spanning segment, chosen by a rule rather than by hand.

mechanism.text: Each point's bounds give three axes. `Priority` names the first choice by length, and the two constraints can then move the selection to a different axis: one on whether the axis points toward or away from a reference direction, the other on whether it is longer or shorter than a threshold. `Constraints Order` settles which of the two gets the last word, because they routinely disagree. Whatever axis survives that produces two points at its extremes, offset by `U`.
steps: Priority picks an axis by length.
The direction and size constraints each propose a shift, resolved in the order the sorting setting names.
Two points are emitted at the chosen axis's ends.

bGeneratePerPointData.tooltip: Generates a point collections per generated point

BoundsReference.tooltip: Which point property to use for bounds calculation.

Priority.tooltip: Which initial direction should initially picked.
Priority.semantics: The starting choice, by the box's own proportions: shortest, longest, or the one that is neither. It is a first preference rather than a decision, since either constraint can move the selection off it.

DirectionConstraint.tooltip: Shifts the axis selection based on whether the selected axis points toward or away from a static direction.
DirectionConstraint.semantics: Shifts the selection by how the candidate axis is oriented relative to a fixed direction, so it is what keeps a set of differently rotated boxes from each choosing a differently aimed axis. It moves the choice rather than rejecting it: there is always an axis at the end.

Direction.tooltip: Reference direction for the direction constraint.

SizeConstraint.tooltip: Shifts the axis selection based on whether its size is greater or smaller than a given threshold.
SizeConstraint.semantics: Shifts the selection by whether the axis is longer or shorter than `Size Threshold`. On boxes where every axis is on the same side of the threshold there is nothing to shift to, so the constraint quietly does nothing.

SizeThreshold.tooltip: Size threshold for the size constraint.

ConstraintsOrder.tooltip: In which order shifting should be processed, as one is likely to override the other.
ConstraintsOrder.semantics: The setting that makes the other two predictable. The direction and size constraints frequently want different axes, and this decides which is applied last and therefore wins. Without reading it the selection looks arbitrary on any data where both constraints are active.

U.tooltip: Extent factor at which the points will be created on the selected world-align axis
U.semantics: How far along the chosen axis the two points sit, as a factor of its extent. The shipped 1 puts them at the ends of the bounds; smaller values pull them inward, which is how the segment can be made to sit inside the box rather than spanning it.

Extents.tooltip: Set the output point' extent to this value

Scale.tooltip: Set the output point' scale to this value

PointAttributesToOutputTags.tooltip: Copy source point attributes as tags on output collections.

hints.text: With both constraints active the result depends on this ordering and not only on the constraints themselves. Points whose chosen axis looks wrong are usually a case of the other constraint having applied last.

UPCGExBoundsFilterProviderSettings.name: Filter : Inclusion (Bounds)
UPCGExBoundsFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Tests each element against the bounds of other points. The reference points arrive on the Bounds pin and every one of them contributes an oriented box, sized by its own bounds and turned by its own rotation; the node produces a filter on its Filter pin, which any node carrying a filter pin runs once per element. The element being tested brings a box of its own, so the question is box against box: overlapping, fully contained, or contained with a boundary allowance. The palette carries the four checks as separate drop-in entries, Intersects (Bounds), Is Inside (Bounds), Is Inside or On (Bounds) and Is Inside or Intersects (Bounds).
UPCGExBoundsFilterProviderSettings.situation: A second point set marks out regions through its point bounds, and an element survives by landing inside one of them.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this filter once per element: a box is built for the element being tested, checked against the reference boxes, and the first reference box that satisfies the check decides a match. Every dataset on the Bounds pin is searched as one pool, so adding a second reference dataset can only make a match more likely, and `Ignore Self` and `Data Matching` are the two ways to take datasets back out of that pool. Under `Per Point Bounds` both sides are oriented boxes taking their own point's rotation, one built from the tested element through `Bounds Source` and one per reference point through `Bounds Target`. The reference boxes are indexed once, on this node, and every consumer wired to its Filter pin shares that index.

off_label.claim: Set `Bounds Source` to `Center` and `Test Mode` to `Expanded Sphere`, and the filter becomes a proximity test whose reach is set per reference point: an element passes when it comes within `Expansion` of a reference point's own bounding sphere, so large reference points claim more ground than small ones. Filter : Distance cannot express that, because its threshold is one number for every target.
off_label.grounded_in: the ExpandedSphere branch of PCGExMath::OBB::TestOverlap, which compares centre distance against the two bounding-sphere radii plus Expansion, with the tested radius driven to near zero by EPCGExPointBoundsSource::Center

inputs.label: Bounds
inputs.note: The reference points. Each one contributes one oriented box, and several datasets are accepted and searched as one pool.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match rules deciding which reference datasets each tested dataset is allowed to see. The pin is always present, sitting among the advanced pins until Data Matching is switched on.
inputs.condition: when Data Matching Mode is All or Any

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node produces. It carries the point-filter type, so every filter pin accepts it, Vtx and Edge pins included.

hints.text: An empty Bounds pin does not stop the node: it is the failure that routes through Missing Data Policy, which defaults to Fail. Downstream the symptom is an empty result with nothing in the log to explain it, and under Error the node reports the missing input and cancels instead.

Ignore Self is off out of the box. Wire one dataset into both the consumer and the Bounds pin without turning it on and each element meets the box it contributed, which satisfies all four checks, so the filter passes everything.

An attribute set carries no positions, so a consumer filtering one hands every row to this filter as a default point at the world origin, with no rotation and default bounds. Every row then tests the same box in the same place, the whole set takes one answer, and nothing is logged.
The node subtitle reads back the check type, with an inversion flag when Invert is on, so a graph carrying several of these can be read without selecting them one at a time.

UPCGExBoundsPathIntersectionSettings.name: Path × Bounds Intersection
UPCGExBoundsPathIntersectionSettings.purpose: Finds where a path passes through the volumes of a set of points and puts a point at each of those places. The volumes are the target points' own bounds, oriented by their rotation, so a turned box carries a turned volume. Each new point can record whether the path was going in or coming out, which surface it met, which target it belonged to, and whatever attributes that target carried.
UPCGExBoundsPathIntersectionSettings.situation: A path runs through a scattering of volumes and something has to happen exactly at the borders: a marker, a split later on, or a value taken from whichever volume was crossed.

mechanism.text: Points are inserted, never removed, and the path is never cut: one path in, one path out, longer. Each segment is tested against every target volume matched to it and the crossings it found are sorted along the segment and inserted in order between its two ends. Targets are read and nothing is written back to them. A new point's transform and attributes come from blending the two points bracketing the segment it landed on, so its values sit between theirs, and the intersection attributes are written on top of that afterwards.

off_label.claim: It is also a containment test for path points that were already there. With the cut type written, a path point sitting inside a volume can be told from one outside it, because the crossings either side of it were classified going in and coming out.
off_label.grounded_in: the cut type is written per intersection from the OBB classification, so the entry and exit pair bracketing an original point identifies the stretch that was inside

off_label.claim: With the bound index written, the inserted points spell out the sequence of volumes the path went through, in the order it met them, so reading that attribute along the path recovers the route as a list of targets.
off_label.grounded_in: the bound index is written per intersection from the target point that produced the cut, and the cuts on a segment are sorted along it before insertion

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to cut into. Each is handled on its own.

inputs.label: Bounds
inputs.note: The points whose bounds become the volumes. They are read only and never come out of this node.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match-rule factories deciding which volumes each path is tested against. With none, every path is tested against every target.
inputs.condition: required while Data Matching has a mode set; an advanced pin otherwise

inputs.label: Blend Ops
inputs.note: Declared and gathered, and read by nothing: no blender is built from what arrives here, and the node logs a warning as soon as anything is wired to it. What decides an inserted point's values is the `Blending` dropdown in the details panel.

inputs.label: Overrides : Blending
inputs.note: An attribute set whose names are matched against the picked `Blending` sub-node's own settings.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: One path per input, with the crossings inserted. A path that met nothing still comes out, tagged accordingly.

outputs.label: Unmatched
outputs.note: Paths that matched no target volume at all.
outputs.condition: when Data Matching is set to split unmatched data out; an advanced pin otherwise

DataMatching.tooltip: If enabled, allows you to filter out which targets get sampled by which data

Blending.tooltip: Blending applied on intersecting points along the path prev and next point. This is different from inheriting from external properties.
Blending.semantics: It decides what an inserted point inherits from the two path points bracketing the segment it landed on, and the several crossings on one segment are handed over together so they interpolate across the whole gap rather than one at a time.

OutputSettings.tooltip: Output settings for intersection points and attributes.

fields.name: BoundsSource
fields.tooltip: Bounds type.

fields.name: IsIntersectionAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to write point intersection boolean to.

fields.name: CutTypeAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to write point toward inside boolean to.

fields.name: CutTypeValueMapping
fields.tooltip: Pick which value will be written for each cut type.

fields.name: NormalAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to write point intersection normal to.

fields.name: BoundIndexAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Attribute name for the intersecting bounds index.

fields.name: IntersectionForwarding
fields.tooltip: Forward attributes from intersecting bounds to intersection points.

OutputSettings.semantics: The whole intersection payload lives in this block, and its bounds picker is read once when the volumes are built rather than per path, so it describes the targets and not the paths. Its attributes are created after the blender has taken stock of what it may touch, so nothing here is blended into the neighbouring points.
OutputSettings.trap: A path that met nothing still gets these attributes, written at their default values across every point, so their presence downstream says nothing about whether an intersection happened. The cut type's own zero-valued row is the reading for a point that is not an intersection. The bound index has a second catch: it is the target's index within its own dataset and the dataset is not recorded anywhere, so with several datasets on the **Bounds** pin the same index means different points.

HasCutsTag.tooltip: Tag to apply to paths with intersection cuts.
HasCutsTag.semantics: Applied to the whole dataset, so it says a path was cut somewhere and never where. It is the pairing of this with the uncut tag that makes the two useful: exactly one of them lands on every output.

UncutTag.tooltip: Tag to apply to uncut paths.
UncutTag.semantics: Off by default while the cut tag is on, so out of the box uncut paths arrive carrying nothing to distinguish them and are told apart by the absence of the other tag.

bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.tooltip: If enabled, collections that have less than 2 points won't be processed and be omitted from the output.
bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.semantics: This is one of the nodes that acts on the off position, and it does not act on it by forwarding. A path under two points is duplicated and stamped with the intersection attributes at their defaults, so what comes back carries this node's attributes with none of its work behind them. It forwards untouched only when nothing was going to be written anyway.

hints.text: The **Blend Ops** pin is visible, accepts sub-nodes and is read by nothing. Wiring blend operations here changes no value on any output point, and the node logs a warning saying as much.
A closed loop is tested as a loop: the segment from its last point back to its first is included, so a crossing there is found and inserted at the end of the point list.

UPCGExBoundsToPointsSettings.name: Bounds To Points
UPCGExBoundsToPointsSettings.purpose: Puts a new point somewhere on each existing point's bounds. The position is named in normalised coordinates, so one setting means the same corner or face on points of any size, and the result is a fresh point set derived from where the originals sit rather than a modification of them. It is the generator counterpart to **Move Pivot**, which relocates an origin instead of producing a point.
UPCGExBoundsToPointsSettings.situation: Points that need a companion at their base, their top face, or a chosen corner, produced consistently across a set of varied sizes.

mechanism.text: For each input point a new point is placed at the normalised position within its bounds. `Symmetry Axis` produces the mirrored position as well, so one setting can yield the pair on opposite faces. The generated point takes its extents and scale from the source unless those are switched off, and `Generate Per Point Data` decides whether the results arrive as one dataset or as one dataset per generated point.

off_label.claim: A symmetry axis with the coordinate at a face gives both faces at once, which is the cheapest way to get a matched pair per point for measuring across them or connecting them.
off_label.grounded_in: The symmetry axis emits the mirrored coordinate alongside the authored one for each input point.

bGeneratePerPointData.tooltip: Generates a point collections per generated point
bGeneratePerPointData.semantics: Decides the shape of the output rather than its content: one dataset holding every generated point, or one dataset per generated point. The per-point form is what downstream nodes that operate per dataset need, and it multiplies the number of datasets by the number of points.

SymmetryAxis.semantics: Emits the mirrored position on the named axis as well as the authored one, doubling the output. It is a second point per input rather than a choice between two, so the count leaving the node changes with it.

UVW.tooltip: UVW coordinates for point placement on bounds.
UVW.semantics: Normalised across the bounds rather than measured in world units, so 0 is one face, 1 is the opposite and 0.5 is the middle on each axis. The same setting therefore lands on the same relative spot across points of different sizes, which is what makes it usable on a varied scatter.

Extents.tooltip: Extents to set on the generated point.

bMultiplyExtents.semantics: Scales the source's extents onto the generated point instead of copying them, which is how a point can be produced at a face with a fraction of the original's size rather than the whole of it.

Scale.tooltip: Scale to set on the generated point.

PointAttributesToOutputTags.tooltip: Copy source point attributes as tags on output collections.

hints.text: Per-point data on a large input produces one dataset per point, which multiplies the work of everything downstream that iterates datasets. It is the right shape only when something later genuinely needs each generated point isolated.

UPCGExBoxFittingRelax.name: Box Fitting
UPCGExBoxFittingRelax.purpose: The fitting rule that takes its collision shape from the points themselves. Each Vtx is given the bounds its point already carries, padded and run through that point's transform, so rotation and scale are both in the box and there is nothing to author or wire up to make it work. Any two Vtx whose boxes intersect are pushed apart; the springs holding edge lengths, the target lengths themselves and the step size all reach it from **Abstract Fitting**.
UPCGExBoxFittingRelax.situation: Vtx standing for something with a real footprint that the points' own bounds already describe, packed tightly enough that the footprints intersect.

mechanism.text: This rule contributes the middle turn of the fitting cycle, the separation. At the start of every iteration it rebuilds one box per Vtx: the point's bounds, padded, then run through the Vtx's current transform, which means a rotated box becomes the upright box that contains it. Every pair of Vtx is then tested, and where two boxes intersect a push is added along the line between the two Vtx, with each axis of that push scaled by how deep the two boxes overlap on that axis. The push therefore leans toward the axes on which the overlap runs deepest.

off_label.claim: Padding is applied before the transform, so a per-point scale attribute doubles as a per-Vtx spacing multiplier on a rule that otherwise offers one padding value for the whole cluster.
off_label.grounded_in: PrepareNextStep builds each box as the point's local bounds expanded by Padding and then transformed by the Vtx transform, so the point's scale multiplies the padding along with the bounds

Padding.tooltip: A padding value added to the box bounds to attempt to reduce overlap or add more spacing between boxes.
Padding.semantics: Added to the point's bounds before the transform is applied, so it lives in the point's local space and the point's scale multiplies it: at a scale of 2, a padding of 10 opens the box by 20. It grows the box on every side and both boxes of a pair carry it, so the clear space it asks for between two Vtx is twice the value. It also decides when a pair counts as overlapping at all, so raising it starts the separation earlier as well as making it stronger.
Padding.trap: This is not the same kind of value as `Padding` on **Box Fitting v2**, which is added in world units to an extents value and never sees the point's scale.

UPCGExBoxFittingRelax2.name: Box Fitting v2
UPCGExBoxFittingRelax2.purpose: The fitting rule whose collision box you author instead of inherit. `Extents` reads a half-size per Vtx, from an attribute or one constant, and the box is built upright around the Vtx position from that value alone, so the point's own bounds, rotation and scale reach it only through whatever the value carries. What it adds over **Box Fitting** is `Separation Mode`, three different answers to the question of which way an overlapping pair should move. The springs holding edge lengths, the target lengths and the step size all reach it from **Abstract Fitting**.
UPCGExBoxFittingRelax2.situation: Vtx standing for footprints whose size lives in an attribute, or a cluster where the direction overlapping pairs move matters as much as the fact that they move.

mechanism.text: This rule contributes the middle turn of the fitting cycle, the separation. Every pair of Vtx is tested for box intersection, and where two boxes intersect the overlap is measured on each axis and then turned into one direction and one distance by `Separation Mode`. That push is scaled by `Repulsion Constant` and lands in the same accumulator as the spring half, so what the pair ends up doing is the sum of both.

off_label.claim: Nothing checks the Extents value against the point it belongs to, so an attribute that has nothing to do with size works just as well: drive it from a per-Vtx importance or weight and the rule spaces the cluster by that instead, giving the Vtx that matter more room around them.
off_label.grounded_in: Step2 reads the extents buffer per Vtx and uses the value directly as the box half-size, with no reference to the point's bounds

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

ExtentsValue.semantics: A half-size in world units, added to and subtracted from the Vtx position on every axis to make the box. Nothing else feeds that box: the point's rotation and scale contribute only through whatever the value itself carries, and the box is always centred on the Vtx, so a value describing bounds that sit off their pivot describes a volume in the wrong place. The shipped setting reads `$Extents` per point, so with nothing changed the size comes from the point's own bounds.

SeparationMode.tooltip: How to determine separation direction when boxes overlap
SeparationMode.semantics: Minimum Penetration finds the axis on which the two boxes overlap least and moves the pair apart along that axis alone, by that overlap, which is the shortest travel that would clear them. It is the shipped default, and it is the only mode whose push lands on a world axis rather than on the line between the two Vtx. Edge Direction moves a pair that shares an edge along the line between them, by the smallest of the three overlap depths, and hands every pair that shares no edge to Minimum Penetration, which in most clusters is nearly every pair. Centroid moves every overlapping pair along the line between them by that same smallest depth, and it is the only mode that does anything at all with two Vtx at identical positions, separating them along X.

Padding.semantics: Added to the `Extents` value on every axis before the box is built, in world units, so the point's scale never touches it. Both boxes of a pair carry it, which makes the clear space it asks for between two Vtx twice the value.

bUseOrientedBounds.tooltip: Whether to consider rotation when computing bounds (more expensive)
bUseOrientedBounds.semantics: Nothing reads this value. The box is built upright from `Extents` in every separation mode and the point's rotation never enters, so moving the toggle changes neither the result nor the time the run takes.
bUseOrientedBounds.trap: The tooltip promises rotation-aware bounds and a higher cost for them, and neither happens. **Box Fitting** is the rule whose box follows the point's rotation.

hints.text: Edge Direction asks, for every overlapping pair it finds, whether those two Vtx share an edge, and it answers by walking the Edges dataset until it finds one. One separation turn therefore costs the number of overlapping pairs multiplied by the edge count, which on a crowded cluster is far more than the other two modes ask for.

UPCGExBranchOnDataAttributeSettings.name: Branch on Data
UPCGExBranchOnDataAttributeSettings.purpose: Routes whole datasets down named pins by reading one @Data value off each of them. The branches are authored as a list of comparisons, each owning the pin it feeds, or generated from an enum so the pins carry the enum's own names. What arrives is forwarded untouched; only which pin it leaves on changes.
UPCGExBranchOnDataAttributeSettings.situation: Datasets that were stamped with a kind, a state or an enum value upstream, and now need to take different routes without being merged and re-split.

mechanism.text: The attribute named by Branch Source is read from each input dataset's @Data domain and converted to both a number and a string. Branches are then tested in the order they are listed, and the first one whose comparison passes claims the dataset, which is re-pinned to that branch's label. A dataset that matches nothing, or whose attribute is missing, goes to the default pin. Branch pins that claimed nothing are deactivated, so the nodes hanging off them are culled; the default pin is never deactivated.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: Any data carrying the branch attribute in its @Data domain. Forwarded by reference.

outputs.label: Default
outputs.note: Datasets that matched no branch, plus every dataset whose branch attribute could not be found. Renamed by Default Pin Name.

outputs.label: One pin per branch
outputs.note: Labelled by each branch's own Label. A branch that claimed nothing this run is deactivated.

pins.dynamic: The output pin set is rebuilt from the branch list, and every data pin accepts and mirrors any type.

BranchSource.semantics: Read from the @Data domain, so it is one value per dataset rather than per point. A dataset that does not carry it is reported as an invalid attribute and sent to the default pin rather than dropped.

SelectionMode.tooltip: Determines the type of value to be used to select an output.
SelectionMode.semantics: User Defined evaluates the Branches list as authored. Enum Integer and Enum Name instead build one branch per visible value of the picked enum, comparing the attribute against the enum's numeric value or against its display name; both name their pins after the display name.

Branches.tooltip: User-defined branch conditions and output pins.
Branches.semantics: Order is precedence, since testing stops at the first branch that passes. Each entry owns the pin it feeds, so two entries sharing a Label collapse into one pin.
Branches.trap: The pin set and the comparisons the element runs are both taken from a copy of this list that is rebuilt only when a property changes in the details panel. Overriding Branches at execution time therefore changes nothing.

EnumPicker.tooltip: Determines which Enum be used. Enum selection is ignored here, it's only using the class value internally.

DefaultPinName.tooltip: Name of the default/fallback output pin. This is exposed because to allow easy disambiguation when 'default' is a valid switch.
DefaultPinName.semantics: Exists so the fallback pin can be moved out of the way when one of the branch labels is itself Default.

hints.text: The value is read once per dataset. To branch on something that varies point by point, narrow with filters first and let the split produce separate datasets, or promote the per-point value to @Data before this node.

UPCGExBreakClustersToPathsSettings.name: Cluster : Break to Paths
UPCGExBreakClustersToPathsSettings.purpose: Reads a cluster back out as paths, so everything phrased in terms of order becomes available again: resampling, offsetting, sweeping a mesh along a run. A path can only hold binary Vtx, so the cluster has to be cut where it stops being one, and the node cuts it at every leaf and at every Vtx holding more than two edges. `Operate On` offers a coarser answer as well: set to Edges, every edge comes back as its own two-point path.
UPCGExBreakClustersToPathsSettings.situation: A cluster has been generated and refined down to the connections that were meant, and the runs between its junctions now have to be treated as ordered geometry.

mechanism.text: In Paths mode the cluster is cut into chains and each chain becomes one path. A chain is a run of Vtx that each hold exactly two edges, bounded at either end by a Vtx that does not: a leaf, or a Vtx with more than two edges. That bounding Vtx belongs to every chain reaching it, so its point is copied into each resulting path as an endpoint, and a Vtx holding three edges comes out as the first or last point of three separate paths. A chain that closes on itself is tagged as a closed loop. In Edges mode chains are not built at all and every edge becomes its own two-point path. Either way the result is plain point data: the cluster role tags and both cluster attributes are stripped, and neither input dataset is forwarded.

off_label.claim: Because a junction Vtx is copied into every path that meets it, feeding these paths straight back through **Path : To Clusters** with fusing on rebuilds the same connectivity. That makes the pair a way to run path operations over a cluster's runs and get a cluster back, rather than a one-way extraction.
off_label.grounded_in: One chain is seeded per edge at every non-binary Vtx, so that Vtx's point index is an endpoint of every chain incident to it, and the coincident copies re-weld on the fuse pass.

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The cluster's Vtx dataset. Its points are what the output paths are made of.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The cluster's Edges datasets, one per cluster. Each is broken independently.

inputs.label: Break Conditions
inputs.note: Vtx that pass become extra cut points, splitting a chain that would otherwise run through them. Unconnected, nothing is a break and the cuts land only where the topology forces them.

inputs.label: EdgeFilters
inputs.note: Judges whole chains rather than trimming them: the edges of each chain are tested and `Edge Filter Mode` decides how many have to pass for that chain to be emitted.
inputs.condition: when Operate On is Paths

inputs.label: Direction Sorting
inputs.note: The sorting rules that decide endpoint order, and required once they are the method in use.
inputs.condition: when Direction Settings uses the Endpoints Sort direction method

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: One dataset per chain, or one per edge in Edges mode, each carrying the closed-loop tag when the chain closed on itself.

LeavesHandling.semantics: A chain counts as a leaf chain when a leaf sits at either of its ends, so **Exclude Leaves** drops the dangling runs and keeps the interior, and **Only Leaves** keeps the dangling runs alone. A closed loop is never a leaf chain and survives **Exclude Leaves**.

OperateOn.semantics: **Paths** builds chains and is what the rest of the panel is written for. **Edges** skips chain building entirely and emits one two-point path per edge, which costs one output dataset per edge and is why the tooltip calls it expensive.
OperateOn.trap: Edges mode leaves most of the panel inert. `Leaves Handling`, `Winding`, the point-count limits and the **Break Conditions** pin are all read only on the chain path, and the **EdgeFilters** pin is not declared at all. Only `Direction Settings` still applies, deciding which endpoint of each edge becomes point 0.

DirectionSettings.tooltip: Defines the direction in which points will be ordered to form the final paths.
DirectionSettings.semantics: Decides which end of a chain becomes point 0, and it is the only ordering rule that also applies in Edges mode. The Endpoints Sort method is what makes the **Direction Sorting** pin appear, and it is required rather than optional once selected.

Winding.tooltip: Enforce a winding order for paths.
Winding.semantics: Enforced on a 2D projection of the path, so `Projection Details` decides the plane the answer is measured in and a loop viewed edge-on has no reliable winding to correct. The test reads the order that will actually ship, reversal included, so `Winding` has the last word on every path it judges and `Direction Settings` decides the orientation only of the ones it leaves alone: open chains while `Wind Only Closed Loops` is on, and every path in Edges mode.

bWindOnlyClosedLoops.tooltip: Whether to apply winding on closed loops only or all paths.
bWindOnlyClosedLoops.semantics: Off, open chains are wound too, using the signed area of the polyline as though its two ends were joined. That is well defined for a chain that curls back on itself and arbitrary for one that runs roughly straight.

ProjectionDetails.tooltip: Projection settings. Winding is computed on a 2D plane.

MinPointCount.tooltip: Do not output paths that have less points that this value
MinPointCount.semantics: Counted in points, so a chain of a single edge is 2 and the default lets it through. Raising it to 3 removes every chain that is one edge long, which on a dense cluster is most of what runs between adjacent junctions.

MaxPointCount.tooltip: Do not output paths that have more points that this value
MaxPointCount.semantics: The cap is not a split: a chain longer than this is dropped whole, not cut into pieces that fit. Use **Break Conditions** where the long runs still have to come through.

EdgeFilterMode.tooltip: When edge filters are connected, how many of a chain's edges must pass for that chain to be output as a path. Inert if no edge filters are connected.
EdgeFilterMode.semantics: The verdict is per chain and it decides emission, never trimming: **All** needs every edge of the chain to pass, **Any** needs one, **Partial** needs the ratio below. A closed loop counts its closing edge in both the pass count and the total.
EdgeFilterMode.trap: The mode is live in the panel whether or not anything is wired to **EdgeFilters**, and with that pin empty no chain is ever tested, so **All** does not silently reject everything.

EdgeFilterPassRatio.tooltip: Minimum ratio (0-1) of a chain's edges that must pass the edge filters when using Partial mode.

hints.text: A Vtx that ends several chains is copied into each of them, so a cluster of C chains meeting at one junction hands back C paths that each own a separate copy of that junction point. Anything written per point downstream is written once per copy, and merging the paths back into one dataset gives you C coincident points at every junction.

UPCGExBuildAssetCollectionSettings.name: Build Asset Collection
UPCGExBuildAssetCollectionSettings.purpose: Every other route into staging starts from a collection someone authored and saved. This one builds a collection while the graph runs, from an attribute set whose rows name asset paths, and hands out that collection's asset path for Staging : Distribute to stage from through its Source Collection Constant override. It is the inverse of Asset Collection to Set.
UPCGExBuildAssetCollectionSettings.situation: The list of assets to stage from is decided by the graph, from a data table or a filtered set of paths, so no saved collection can name it up front.

mechanism.text: One attribute set in, one attribute set out: a single row carrying the built collection's asset path under Output Attribute Name. Each row of the input becomes one entry in input order, and a row whose path attribute is missing, empty, or of a type other than soft object path or string is dropped. The collection is transient and owned by the PCG component that ran the graph, so it never appears in the Content Browser and its path resolves only while that component holds it. Staging is baked during the build, so a downstream node reads bounds and sockets from it exactly as it would from a saved collection. Re-running with the same settings over the same input data hands back the collection already on the component instead of building a second one, which is what keeps the path stable across regenerations.

off_label.claim: Paired with Get Collection Data it turns a saved collection into something the graph can edit: read the collection out as an attribute set, drop rows, rewrite weights or categories, merge two sets, then rebuild and stage from the result. The saved asset is never written to, so the edit reaches only what this graph stages.
off_label.grounded_in: Get Collection Data emits AssetPath, Weight and Category attributes, the exact columns FPCGExAssetAttributeSetDetails maps back into a built collection

inputs.label: AttributeSet
inputs.note: The entry list, one row per entry, carrying an asset path and optionally a weight and a category. The first attribute set on the pin is the one read; further connections are ignored.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: One attribute set holding a single row: the built collection's asset path under Output Attribute Name. It is typed as a soft object path, so it drops straight onto Staging : Distribute's Source Collection Constant override pin. A run that could not build still emits the row, carrying an empty path.

AttributeSetDetails.tooltip: Which collection type to build, and which attributes hold the asset path / weight / category.

fields.name: AssetPathSourceAttribute
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute on the AttributeSet that contains the asset path to be staged

fields.name: WeightSourceAttribute
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute on the AttributeSet that contains the asset weight, if any.

fields.name: CategorySourceAttribute
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute on the AttributeSet that contains the asset category, if any.

fields.name: AssetCollectionType
fields.tooltip: Defines what type of temp collection to build from input attribute set

AttributeSetDetails.semantics: The collection type decides how bounds get baked, not only what an entry holds. Mesh and Skinned Mesh read bounds and sockets from the asset and work wherever the graph runs; Actor and Level entries need an editor world to spawn a temporary instance into, and bake nothing anywhere else. Weight and Category are optional, and leaving either unset gives every entry weight 1 and no category. The weight attribute is read as an integer and the category as a name, so an attribute of any other type is not found and the entries take those defaults with no warning. A weight that is read is floored at 1, so a row cannot be switched off by writing 0 the way an authored entry can.
AttributeSetDetails.trap: The type picker offers Omni Collection and Variant Collection, and neither can be built this way: their rows carry no typed payload until one is authored, so no entry is ever filled and the node reports that the build failed.

OutputAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the output FSoftObjectPath attribute carrying the built collection's soft path.

hints.text: Baking staging loads every asset the list names, on the game thread. This is the one point in staging where content is loaded before anything spawns, so a long list is a visible stall on the first build; unchanged inputs keep later regenerations off that path.

Without an owning PCG component there is nowhere to anchor the collection's lifetime, so the node warns and emits an empty path rather than a dangling one. The failure only becomes an error downstream, where Staging : Distribute reports an empty Source Collection.

UPCGExBuildCellDiagramSettings.name: Cluster : Cell Diagram
UPCGExBuildCellDiagramSettings.purpose: Reads the closed cells of a cluster and hands back a second cluster made of them: one Vtx at the middle of each cell, joined to the cells it shares a side with. What was a question about regions becomes a question about neighbours, which is what the rest of the cluster tools know how to answer. The subdivision settings then let the result be more than one point per cell: connections can be routed through the midpoints of the shared sides, cells can spoke out to their own corners, and `Extract Skeleton` collapses the run-of-the-mill cells so what remains is the branching structure of the region layout. The input cluster is consumed rather than forwarded.
UPCGExBuildCellDiagramSettings.situation: A layout of rooms, plots or districts exists as the closed cells of a cluster and the next step is about which of them touch.

mechanism.text: One cluster in, one cluster out, sharing no rows with it. Every closed cell is found from a flattened view of the input, narrowed by `Constraints`, and each survivor becomes one Vtx at the average of its own corner positions, carrying the cell's bounds and its attributes blended from the corners. Two of those Vtx are joined when their cells share a side. The subdivision settings add further Vtx, corners and side midpoints, and reroute the connections through them, so a cell can end up standing for more than one point. Fewer than two surviving cells produces nothing.

off_label.claim: Turn every write on at once, `Write Area`, `Write Compactness`, `Write Num Nodes` and `Write Vtx Type`, and take only the **Vtx** pin: it is a per-cell measurement table with positions, which filters and sorters read like any other point data. The connections are then a way of asking about neighbours later rather than the reason to run the node.
off_label.grounded_in: FProcessor::ProcessRange writes AreaWriter, CompactnessWriter and NumNodesWriter on centroid rows from Cell->Data, alongside the blended transform, before OnRangeProcessingComplete builds any connection.

off_label.claim: `Extract Skeleton` on a cluster of corridor-shaped cells gives back the corridor centreline: the two-neighbour cells drop out and their side midpoints chain together, so a run of cells collapses into a run of points down the middle of it.
off_label.grounded_in: The skeleton branch of FProcessor::OnRangeProcessingComplete emits no centroid-to-midpoint connection for a cell with a neighbour count of two and instead bridges its two incident side midpoints, leaving that centroid unconnected so the cluster output step prunes it.

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The Vtx half of every cluster to process. Their positions define the cells, and their attributes are what the centroids blend.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The Edges half. Every Edges dataset that finds its Vtx is one cluster and one run of the node, and each run yields one new cluster.

inputs.label: Holes
inputs.note: A single point dataset. Any cell containing one of these points is dropped, which takes its Vtx and its adjacencies out of the result.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: New points: one per surviving cell, plus corner and side-midpoint points when the subdivision settings ask for them. The input Vtx are not forwarded.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One point per connection, one dataset per connected component of the finished cluster.

Constraints.tooltip: Cell constraints for filtering which cells become graph nodes
Constraints.semantics: Which cells become Vtx. The outer face wrapping the whole cluster is detected as such and dropped unless this block says to keep it, and any cell the block rejects takes its adjacencies with it, so filtering changes connectivity rather than only thinning the point set. Two neighbours that shared only a rejected cell between them come out unconnected.
Constraints.trap: `Area` and `Compactness` are measured on the flattened view rather than on the cell as it sits in space, so a cell on a steep slope reads smaller than it is and the thresholds cut it sooner. `Area` also carries a hundredfold reduction: the value compared against is the flattened area divided by a hundred.

ProjectionDetails.semantics: The flattening the cells are found from, and the plane their area, winding and compactness are measured in. `Normal` uses one direction for every cluster on the pin; `Best Fit` works out its own plane per cluster, which is what suits a batch of clusters lying at different angles.
ProjectionDetails.trap: `3D Surface` is offered in the dropdown and this node does not support it: the method falls back to `Best Fit` when the projection is set up, with no message. Only `Normal` and `Best Fit` do what they say here.

bExtractSkeleton.tooltip: Extract a topological "cell skeleton": a cell with exactly two neighbors drops its centroid and bridges its two shared-side midpoints with a single edge, while one-neighbor (leaf) and three-or-more-neighbor (junction) cells keep their centroid. Forces shared-midpoint routing internally and re-scopes Spoke Mode to leaf cells' unshared corners.
bExtractSkeleton.semantics: Turns the diagram into the branching structure of the layout. Side-midpoint routing is forced on and the panel hides the switch for it, then each cell is judged by how many sides it shares: two and its centroid is dropped and its two side midpoints are wired straight to each other, one or three-or-more and the centroid stays and connects to its side midpoints as usual. A run of two-sided cells therefore collapses into a chain down the middle of the run, and only the ends and the junctions keep a point of their own.
bExtractSkeleton.trap: It also re-scopes `Spoke Mode`. Spokes are emitted from single-neighbour cells only, and only to corners no other surviving cell shares, so a setting that reached every cell without it now touches the tips alone.

SpokeMode.tooltip: How to emit additional edges connecting each cell centroid to its corner vertices. Corners are shared between adjacent cells. When Extract Skeleton is on, this is re-scoped to leaf (single-neighbor) cells and their unshared corners only: None = no spokes, All Corners = every unshared corner, Longest/Shortest = the single farthest/nearest unshared corner.
SpokeMode.semantics: Adds a Vtx at cell corners and connects cells out to them, on top of whatever the cell-to-cell connections are doing. `None` adds nothing. `All Corners` activates every corner of every surviving cell, and a corner shared by several cells is one Vtx that all of them connect to, so shared corners become hubs. `Longest Spoke` and `Shortest Spoke` activate one corner per cell, the furthest or nearest from that cell's own centre, measured in space rather than on the flattened view.
SpokeMode.trap: Corner Vtx are copies of the input cluster's own Vtx, at the same positions, so the result overlaps the input geometry point for point wherever a corner is activated. Under `All Corners` on a dense cluster that is most of the input coming back inside the new cluster.

bConnectSharedSelectedCorners.tooltip: In a single-spoke mode, also connect every other cell that shares an elected corner to that corner (in addition to its own spoke), turning the corner into a shared hub. A cell may then emit multiple spokes.
bConnectSharedSelectedCorners.semantics: Only reachable in one of the two single-spoke modes and not while `Extract Skeleton` is on. Without it, a cell connects to the corner it elected and to nothing else, so a corner elected by two cells still gets one connection from each of them and no more. With it, every cell touching an elected corner connects to it, whether or not that cell elected it, so a single popular corner can gather spokes from all around while its neighbours contribute none.

bSplitCellEdgesAtSharedMidpoint.display: Split Cell Edges At Shared Midpoint
bSplitCellEdgesAtSharedMidpoint.tooltip: Replace each centroid-to-centroid adjacency edge with two edges routed through a new vertex at the midpoint of the shared cell segment (centroid -> midpoint -> centroid). Forced on internally when Extract Skeleton is enabled.
bSplitCellEdgesAtSharedMidpoint.semantics: Puts a Vtx at the middle of each shared side and routes the adjacency through it, so a connection between two cells becomes two connections and the count of Vtx grows by one per shared side. Every cell centre then reaches its neighbours through a point that sits on the boundary between them, which is what makes the result usable as a road layout rather than as a bare adjacency web. `Extract Skeleton` forces this on and hides the switch.

AreaAttributeName.semantics: The flattened area of the cell divided by a hundred, written on centroid Vtx only. Corner and side-midpoint Vtx keep the default of zero, which is worth knowing before filtering on it.

CompactnessAttributeName.semantics: How near the flattened cell is to a circle, one for a circle and falling away as the outline gets longer for the area it encloses. Written on centroid Vtx only, so corner and side-midpoint Vtx read zero.

NumNodesAttributeName.semantics: How many corners the cell has, which is also how many input Vtx were blended into this centroid. Written on centroid Vtx only, so corner and side-midpoint Vtx read zero.

VtxTypeAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the vertex type tag
VtxTypeAttributeName.semantics: Which of the three kinds each output Vtx is: 0 for a cell centre, 1 for a corner, 2 for a side midpoint. With any subdivision setting on, this is the only way to tell them apart downstream, and it is what the cell measurements have to be read against, since those are written on kind 0 alone.

EdgeTypeAttributeName.tooltip: Attribute name for the edge type tag
EdgeTypeAttributeName.semantics: Which of the four kinds each connection is: 0 for a plain cell-to-cell adjacency, 1 for one half of an adjacency split at a side midpoint, 2 for a corner spoke, 3 for a skeleton bridge running midpoint to midpoint. The kinds that can appear follow the subdivision settings, so a run with no subdivision writes 0 everywhere.

BlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how cell vertex properties and attributes are blended to the centroid.
BlendingDetails.semantics: How the input cluster's Vtx attributes reach the output. The sources differ by kind: a cell centre blends every corner of its cell at equal weight, a side midpoint blends the two ends of that side, and a corner Vtx has one source and copies it. It starts at `Average` for attributes, so unlike the other nodes in this family this one carries data across without being asked.

CarryOverDetails.tooltip: Meta filter settings for attribute carry-over.

fields.name: bPreserveAttributesDefaultValue
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will preserve the initial attribute default value.

fields.name: Attributes
fields.tooltip: Attributes to carry over.

fields.name: bDataDomainToElements
fields.tooltip: If enabled, data domain attributes are promoted to the elements domain (the single @Data value is broadcast to every point). Off by default; Merge Points is the node that enables it. Not used by all nodes.

fields.name: Scope
fields.tooltip: Scope

fields.name: Tags
fields.tooltip: Tags to carry over.

fields.name: bTestTagsWithValues
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

hints.text: A cluster whose cells the flattening cannot resolve produces nothing rather than a partial result, and so does one that comes out with fewer than two cells after `Constraints`. The symptom is a run that stages no cluster at all for that input while its neighbours on the same pin come through.

UPCGExBuildConvexHull2DSettings.name: Cluster : Convex Hull 2D
UPCGExBuildConvexHull2DSettings.purpose: Finds the outer boundary of a point set as seen from one direction and gives it back in order, as a closed path and as a cluster ring. The points that come out are input points with their attributes, only the boundary ones, at their original positions; everything inside the boundary is dropped. What comes back is a single closed ring, which is what separates this from **Cluster : Convex Hull 3D**, where a shell point can carry many connections and some of them cut through the middle. `Output Clusters` decides whether the cluster halves are produced at all, and the **Paths** pin is there either way.
UPCGExBuildConvexHull2DSettings.situation: A scatter needs the outline that encloses it, as an ordered loop rather than as a set.

mechanism.text: One point dataset in, a closed path out and, unless it is switched off, a cluster too. The boundary is computed from the points as the projection sees them, the ones on it are kept in boundary order with their attributes, and the rest are discarded. The path is marked closed and the cluster is the same loop wired end to end, one component in which each Vtx joins the two boundary points either side of it. A dataset of fewer than three points is skipped with a warning, and neither output moves a point: the projection decides the boundary and nothing else.

off_label.claim: With `Output Clusters` off the node collapses to one pin and becomes a boundary extractor for plain point data: an ordered, closed path of the outermost points, with no cluster bookkeeping to carry downstream.
off_label.grounded_in: UPCGExBuildConvexHull2DSettings::OutputPinProperties returns a fresh list holding only the Paths pin when bOutputClusters is false, and FProcessor::Process then skips the graph builder entirely.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to enclose. Each dataset is handled on its own; datasets under three points are skipped and reported together in one warning.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: The boundary points, with their attributes, carrying the cluster's endpoint data.
outputs.condition: Output Clusters is on, which is the default

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One point per connection around the ring.
outputs.condition: Output Clusters is on, which is the default

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The boundary points as one closed path, in boundary order. Always present, and the only pin on the node when Output Clusters is off.

bOutputClusters.tooltip: Output the hull as a cluster (vtx + edges) instead of paths.
bOutputClusters.semantics: Off removes the **Vtx** and **Edges** pins from the node rather than leaving them empty, so a wire dropped on either of them breaks when this is cleared. The **Paths** pin carries the same points in the same order in both positions.

ProjectionDetails.semantics: The direction the boundary is worked out from, and the plane the winding is measured in. It never moves the points, so the path follows the surface the points sit on.
ProjectionDetails.trap: `3D Surface` is offered in the dropdown and this node does not support it: the method falls back to `Best Fit` when the projection is set up, with no message. Only `Normal` and `Best Fit` do what they say here.

Winding.semantics: Decides which way round the boundary is walked, measured on the projected shape, and it sets the order of both the path and the ring of connections. The two outputs are ordered from the same decision, so the path's direction and the ring's always agree.

hints.text: The node's own description calls it deprecated as of 5.4 and points at Find Convex Hull 2D. Nothing by that name ships in the plugin, and this node is neither hidden nor stripped, so it remains the way to get a convex boundary from loose points. The only other node with Hull in its name is **Pathfinding : Find Cluster Hull**, and that one takes a cluster rather than points.

UPCGExBuildConvexHullSettings.name: Cluster : Convex Hull 3D
UPCGExBuildConvexHullSettings.purpose: Keeps the points that sit on the outside of a cloud and throws the rest away, wiring what survives into a cluster. The Vtx are input points, with their attributes, and there is no setting to change that: the only choice on the node is what the cluster output step does with the result. Its 2D sibling, **Cluster : Convex Hull 2D**, walks a boundary in order and gives back a ring; this one works on the whole shell at once and the connections it keeps are the ones the tetrahedralisation found between shell points.
UPCGExBuildConvexHullSettings.situation: A point cloud needs its outer shell isolated, either as a cage to build on or to get rid of everything buried inside it.

mechanism.text: One point dataset in, one cluster out. The points are tetrahedralised, every point that touches the outer boundary is kept, and every other point is discarded along with anything that only connected to it. A connection survives when both of its endpoints were kept, which is a test on the endpoints rather than on the surface, so the result traces the shell and can also carry connections running straight through the inside between two shell points. A dataset of fewer than four points is skipped with a warning, and one whose points all lie on a plane produces nothing at all, with a log line pointing at **Cluster : Convex Hull 2D**.

off_label.claim: Take the **Vtx** pin on its own and the node is an outer-shell filter for point clouds: interior points are gone, the survivors keep every attribute they arrived with, and nothing has to be measured or thresholded to get there.
off_label.grounded_in: FProcessor::Process initialises the output as EIOInit::Duplicate and FProcessor::ProcessRange marks every non-hull node invalid, after which FGraphBuilder::Compile drops invalid and unconnected nodes from the staged Vtx dataset.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to wrap. Each dataset is handled on its own and produces its own cluster; datasets under four points are skipped and reported together in one warning.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: The input points that landed on the shell, with their attributes. Interior points are absent.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One point per surviving connection, one dataset per connected component of the finished cluster.

hints.text: The shell is convex, so a dent in the cloud is bridged rather than followed and the points inside the dent are treated as interior. Nothing here traces a concave boundary.
Coplanar input is the common failure and it is silent in the graph: the node logs a warning and stages nothing, so the downstream cluster nodes report missing inputs rather than flat geometry.

UPCGExBuildCustomGraphSettings.name: Cluster : Build Custom Graph
UPCGExBuildCustomGraphSettings.purpose: Builds a cluster from Blueprint rather than from a rule. The other cluster generators derive connections from what the points look like; this hands the decision to a builder object you write, which is what makes it the route for connectivity that comes from somewhere the graph cannot see, like a level's own structure or an external description.
UPCGExBuildCustomGraphSettings.situation: Connectivity that already exists somewhere outside PCG and has to be reproduced rather than inferred.

mechanism.text: A builder instance is asked to produce the Vtx and the edges between them, and the node turns what it returns into a cluster. `Mode` decides which actors are handed to the builder as context, so the builder can read components and data off them rather than being given only points. Everything about which points connect is the builder's decision; the node contributes the surrounding machinery and the graph output settings.

Mode.tooltip: Actor fetching mode. These actors will be forwarded to the builder so it can fetch components and data from there during its initialization.
Mode.semantics: Which actors reach the builder as context. The shipped owner mode hands it the component's own actor; the reference mode reads a per-point attribute instead, which is how one execution can build from many actors.

Builder.semantics: The instance that does the work. Without one the node has nothing to build from, and since the connectivity logic lives entirely in it, two graphs using this node have nothing in common beyond the wiring.

GraphBuilderDetails.semantics: The shared cluster output settings, applied to whatever the builder produced. They govern how the result is cleaned up and emitted rather than how it was decided, so they behave here as they do on any cluster generator.

bQuietUnprocessedSettingsWarning.tooltip: Suppress warnings when graph settings remain unprocessed.

bQuietFailedBuildGraphWarning.tooltip: Suppress warnings when BuildGraph returns false.
bQuietFailedBuildGraphWarning.semantics: Silences the warning raised when the builder reports failure. Worth reaching for only where failure is an expected outcome for some inputs, since otherwise it hides the one signal that the builder ran and declined.

hints.text: This is an extension point rather than a node with behaviour of its own. What it produces is defined by the Blueprint builder assigned to it, so its page can describe the contract and not the result.

UPCGExBuildDelaunayGraph2DSettings.name: Cluster : Delaunay 2D
UPCGExBuildDelaunayGraph2DSettings.purpose: Triangulates a point set as it looks from one direction, and hands back the same points as Vtx with connections between them. The Vtx are the input points themselves, all of them, at their original positions, so a triangulation of scattered points on terrain drapes over the terrain rather than flattening it. The `Projection Details` block is what decides the viewing direction, and it is the whole difference from **Cluster : Delaunay 3D**, which connects through the volume and stops on flat input. `Urquhart` thins the result, and `Output Sites` adds a second dataset with one point per triangle.
UPCGExBuildDelaunayGraph2DSettings.situation: A scattered set of points needs connectivity across a surface, a ground plane or a facade rather than through the space between them.

mechanism.text: One point dataset in, one cluster out. The Vtx are that dataset duplicated whole, so every position and attribute survives, and the Edges carry one point for each pair of Vtx that share a triangle. The projection decides which triangles form and nothing else: the points are never moved, and two points sitting one above the other along the projection direction land on top of each other for the purpose of the triangulation. A dataset of fewer than three points is skipped with a warning, and `Output Sites` adds a separate dataset alongside the cluster, one point per triangle, which is neither of the cluster's two halves.

off_label.claim: Because the triangulation is projected while the Vtx are not, the same points can be triangulated twice along two directions and the results overlaid: each pass gives a different connection set over identical Vtx positions, which is a way of getting two independent connectivity readings of one surface.
off_label.grounded_in: FProcessor::Process projects a copy of the positions into TDelaunay2::Process while initialising the output as EIOInit::Duplicate, so the projection never reaches the staged Vtx transforms.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to triangulate. Each dataset is handled on its own and produces its own cluster; datasets under three points are skipped and reported together in one warning.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: The input points, duplicated at their original positions, carrying the cluster's endpoint data.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One point per connection, one dataset per connected component of the finished cluster.

outputs.label: Sites
outputs.note: One point per triangle, at the average of its three corners. Not one of the cluster's halves.
