outputs.condition: Output Sites is on

bUrquhart.tooltip: Output the Urquhart graph of the Delaunay triangulation (removes the longest edge of each Delaunay cell)
bUrquhart.semantics: Each triangle elects its longest connection and that connection is dropped. A connection shared by two triangles is elected by both and removed once, so fewer connections go than there are triangles. The length is measured between the points where they actually sit, in three dimensions, while the triangles themselves were decided on the projected view, so on anything other than flat input the connection that goes is not always the one that looks longest from the projection direction.

bOutputSites.semantics: A site sits at the average of its triangle's three corner positions, taken in three dimensions, and it inherits every other point property and attribute from one of those three corners rather than from all of them. The pin only exists while this is on.
bOutputSites.trap: The site is the middle of the triangle, not its circumcentre, so the sites are not the corners of a Voronoi diagram. **Cluster : Voronoi 2D** is the node that builds those.

SiteHullAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute to output the Hull boolean to. True if point is on the hull, otherwise false.
SiteHullAttributeName.semantics: True for a site whose triangle has fewer than three neighbours, which is the outer ring of the triangulation. Under a merge mode the flag is true for a merged site when any triangle in its group qualified.

UrquhartSitesMerge.tooltip: Merge adjacent sites into a single point
UrquhartSitesMerge.semantics: Available only with both `Urquhart` and `Output Sites` on, and it changes the site count as well as the positions: triangles that the thinning joined by removing the connection between them collapse into one site each. `Merge Sites` puts that site at the average of every corner of every triangle in the group. `Merge Edges` puts it at the average of the midpoints of the connections that were removed to form the group, which pulls it towards the seams rather than towards the bulk. `None` leaves one site per triangle.

HullAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute to output the Hull boolean to. True if point is on the hull, otherwise false.
HullAttributeName.semantics: The boundary is the convex hull of the projected positions, not of the points where they sit, so a point that looks interior from any other direction can still come out flagged.

ProjectionDetails.semantics: The direction the triangulation is computed from. It never moves the Vtx, so changing it rewires the cluster over an unchanged set of points.
ProjectionDetails.trap: `3D Surface` is offered in the dropdown and this node does not support it: the method falls back to `Best Fit` when the projection is set up, with no message. Only `Normal` and `Best Fit` do what they say here.

hints.text: Two points that share a spot when viewed along the projection direction are two coincident points to the triangulation, and a whole column of them is worse. The connections that come back are then decided by tie-breaking rather than by the shape you can see, which is the usual reason a Delaunay over stacked or vertically layered points comes out tangled.

UPCGExBuildDelaunayGraphSettings.name: Cluster : Delaunay 3D
UPCGExBuildDelaunayGraphSettings.purpose: Turns a loose point cloud into a dense cluster by tetrahedralising it: every point keeps its place and gains connections to the neighbours it shares a tetrahedron with. The Vtx are the input points themselves, all of them, with their attributes intact, which makes this the usual first step when a scattered set needs connectivity and there is no other rule for what should join what. It works through the volume and refuses input that is flat; the sibling **Cluster : Delaunay 2D** triangulates the same points as seen from one direction instead. `Urquhart` thins the result, and `Output Sites` adds a second dataset with one point at the middle of each tetrahedron.
UPCGExBuildDelaunayGraphSettings.situation: A scattered point cloud has to become a connected cluster and nothing in the data says which points belong together.

mechanism.text: One point dataset in, one cluster out. The Vtx are that dataset duplicated whole, so every position and attribute survives, and the Edges carry one point for each pair of Vtx that share a tetrahedron. A dataset of fewer than four points is skipped with a warning, and one whose points all lie on a plane produces nothing at all, with a log line pointing at **Cluster : Delaunay 2D**. `Output Sites` adds a separate dataset alongside the cluster, one point per tetrahedron, which is neither of the cluster's two halves.

off_label.claim: `Output Sites` is a volumetric scatter in its own right: one point at the centre of every tetrahedron, so the sites come out denser wherever the input points crowd together and sparser where they spread. Discard the cluster and keep only that pin when what you wanted was a second point set that follows the first one's density.
off_label.grounded_in: FOutputDelaunaySites::ExecuteTask writes one point per Delaunay->Sites entry at the average of the tetrahedron's four vertex locations, into a PointIO staged on the Sites pin independently of the graph builder's outputs.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to tetrahedralise. Each dataset is handled on its own and produces its own cluster; datasets under four points are skipped and reported together in one warning.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: The input points, duplicated, carrying the cluster's endpoint data.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One point per connection, one dataset per connected component of the finished cluster.

outputs.label: Sites
outputs.note: One point per tetrahedron, at the average of its four corners. Not one of the cluster's halves.
outputs.condition: Output Sites is on

bUrquhart.tooltip: Output the Urquhart graph of the Delaunay triangulation (removes the longest edge of each Delaunay cell)
bUrquhart.semantics: Each tetrahedron elects its longest connection and that connection is dropped. A connection shared by several tetrahedra is elected by each of them and removed once, so far fewer connections go than there are tetrahedra, and the thinning is uneven across the cluster. Every Vtx stays: this takes connections away, never points.

bOutputSites.semantics: A site sits at the average of its tetrahedron's four corner positions, and it inherits every other point property and attribute from one of those four corners rather than from all of them. The pin only exists while this is on.
bOutputSites.trap: The site is the middle of the tetrahedron, not its circumcentre, so the sites are not the vertices of a Voronoi diagram. **Cluster : Voronoi 3D** is the node that builds those.

SiteHullAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute to output the Hull boolean to. True if point is on the hull, otherwise false.
SiteHullAttributeName.semantics: True for a site whose tetrahedron has at least one face on the outside of the tetrahedralisation. Those are the tetrahedra that stretch out to cover the empty space around a concave point cloud, which is why the hull sites are the ones most often thrown away.

HullAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute to output the Hull boolean to. True if point is on the hull, otherwise false.

hints.text: Coplanar input is the common failure and it is silent in the graph: the node logs a warning and stages nothing, so the downstream cluster nodes report missing inputs rather than flat geometry. Points on a shared plane, on a grid, or projected before they arrive all land here.

UPCGExBuildDualGraphSettings.name: Cluster : Edge Dual Graph
UPCGExBuildDualGraphSettings.purpose: Swaps the two halves of a cluster over: every connection becomes a Vtx, and the new connections join the ones that sat next to each other around a shared endpoint. What comes out is a cluster whose Vtx sit at the midpoints of the old connections, so a dense web turns into a web offset half a step from it, and questions about which connections neighbour which become ordinary neighbour questions. The input cluster is consumed rather than forwarded, and the new Vtx start empty: the two blending blocks are the only route by which anything the original carried reaches the result.
UPCGExBuildDualGraphSettings.situation: A question is about the connections of a cluster rather than its vertices, and the tools available all work on vertices.

mechanism.text: One cluster in, one cluster out, sharing no rows with it. Every valid connection of the input becomes one Vtx placed at its midpoint, and two of those Vtx are joined when their original connections met at the same endpoint and were next to each other in the turn around it. Which connections count as next to each other is decided from a flattened view of the cluster, so a Vtx of the original with several connections contributes one new connection per neighbouring pair in that turn rather than joining all of them to each other. A cluster with fewer than two connections, or one the flattening cannot resolve, is skipped and produces nothing.

off_label.claim: The Vtx output alone is a midpoint sampler for a cluster: one point per connection, at the centre of it, with the original connection's attributes copied across as soon as the first blending block is set to anything other than `None`. **Cluster : Edge Properties** annotates the existing edge points in place; this gives a plain point set instead, with no cluster pairing to keep track of.
off_label.grounded_in: FProcessor::Process writes each dual Vtx transform to the midpoint of Cluster->VtxTransforms at the edge's two endpoints, and VtxBlender blends from a single source, the original edge, at weight 1.

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The Vtx half of every cluster to process. Its points are read for positions and, when edge blending is set up, for the attributes handed to the new connections.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The Edges half. Every Edges dataset that finds its Vtx is one cluster and one run of the node, and each run yields one new cluster.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: New points, one per connection of the input cluster, at its midpoint. The input Vtx are not forwarded.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One point per connection between two neighbouring original connections, one dataset per connected component of the finished cluster.

ProjectionDetails.semantics: The flattening the turn around each endpoint is read from, which is what decides the order the connections are considered to be in. A cluster standing on a wall or draped over a curved surface is the case that needs it set: read from the wrong direction, the turns come out tangled and the new connections join the wrong pairs.
ProjectionDetails.trap: `3D Surface` is offered in the dropdown and this node does not support it: the method falls back to `Best Fit` when the projection is set up, with no message. Only `Normal` and `Best Fit` do what they say here.

VtxBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how original edge attributes are blended to new vertices.
VtxBlendingDetails.semantics: Attributes of the original connections, arriving on the new Vtx. Each new Vtx has one source, the connection it stands for, so this is a carry-over switch rather than a real choice of how values combine. It starts at `None`, which is why the Vtx come out bare unless it is changed.

EdgeBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how original vertex attributes are blended to new edges (from shared endpoint).
EdgeBlendingDetails.semantics: Attributes of the original Vtx, arriving on the new connections. The source is the single endpoint the two original connections met at, so a new connection inherits from the vertex that produced it. It starts at `None`.

VtxCarryOverDetails.tooltip: Meta filter settings for attribute carry-over.

hints.text: The result is one dual Vtx per **valid** connection of the input, so anything that invalidated connections upstream is baked into the count before this node runs. A cluster whose halves are out of step gives a dual that is quietly missing pieces rather than one that fails.

UPCGExBuildVoronoiGraph2DSettings.name: Cluster : Voronoi 2D
UPCGExBuildVoronoiGraph2DSettings.purpose: Reads the input points as cell seeds, viewed from one direction, and builds the cell walls between them: the Vtx are cell corners and the connections run along the boundaries. The input points do not come out as Vtx. They come back on the separate **Sites** pin instead, still carrying their attributes, moved to the middle of the cell they own and optionally annotated with how large that cell is. `Metric` is a second, larger switch than it looks: Euclidean gives the classic diagram, while Manhattan and Chebyshev bend every wall and add Vtx that are not cell corners at all. **Cluster : Delaunay 2D** is the node that keeps the input points and connects them to each other.
UPCGExBuildVoronoiGraph2DSettings.situation: A set of seed positions has to become the walls, plots or districts that divide the space between them, with the seeds coming back as plot centres.

mechanism.text: One point dataset in, two datasets out that share no rows: a cluster of cell corners, and the seeds again on the **Sites** pin. The seeds are triangulated as seen along the projection, one cell corner is placed per triangle at a position chosen by `Method`, and two corners are connected when their triangles neighbour each other. Every Vtx is a fresh point with no attribute carried over and a seed recomputed from its position, while a site is the original point moved to the average of the corners around it. A dataset of fewer than three points is skipped with a warning.

off_label.claim: Turn `Output Sites` on and ignore the cluster entirely and the node becomes a relaxation step: every seed moves to the middle of its own cell, which is one round of Lloyd's algorithm. Feeding the Sites pin back into the node spreads a clumped point set out over a few passes.
off_label.grounded_in: The OutputSites sub-loop in FProcessor::BuildOutputs sets each site's location to SitesOutputDetails.Locations divided by its influence count, which FPCGExVoronoiSitesOutputDetails::AddInfluence accumulated from the cell centres of every triangle containing that seed.

off_label.claim: `Write Max Radius` on its own is a crowding measure: it is the distance from a seed to the furthest corner of its cell, so it grows wherever the input is sparse. Sorting or filtering on it separates the isolated seeds from the packed ones without any neighbour search.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExVoronoiSitesOutputDetails::AddInfluence measures FVector::Distance from the cell centre to the seed's own untouched input transform and keeps the running maximum.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The cell seeds. Each dataset is handled on its own; datasets under three points are skipped and reported together in one warning.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: New points, one per triangle of the seeds under Euclidean, plus one bend point per wall under the other two metrics. Nothing is carried over from the input.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One point per wall segment between two cells, one dataset per connected component of the finished cluster.

outputs.label: Sites
outputs.note: The input points, duplicated with their attributes, each moved to the middle of its own cell. Not one of the cluster's halves, though it is tagged as though it were.
outputs.condition: Output Sites is on, which is the default

Metric.tooltip: Distance metric used for the Voronoi diagram. Euclidean produces classic Voronoi, Manhattan/Chebyshev produce axis-aligned edge structures.
Metric.semantics: `Euclidean (L2)` gives one Vtx per triangle and one connection per wall, and every connection is a straight run between two corners. `Manhattan (L1)` and `Chebyshev (L-Inf)` measure distance along axes instead, which makes each wall a two-part bend rather than a straight line: the node inserts an extra Vtx at the bend and splits the connection in two. Under either of those the Vtx dataset holds the cell corners first and the bend points after them, so the Vtx count is larger than the triangle count and not every Vtx is a corner.
Metric.trap: Manhattan and Chebyshev put many segments on the same axes, so two walls can come out lying on top of each other. That is a duplicate connection between different Vtx rather than the same pair twice, which the cluster output step does not deduplicate, and it is enough to confuse the face and cell nodes downstream. **Cluster : Fuse** merges the coincident geometry back into clean topology.

Method.tooltip: Method used to find Voronoi cell location
Method.semantics: `Canon (Circumcenter)` is the position that makes the result a true Voronoi diagram, and it is also the one that flies off: a thin sliver triangle has a circumcentre far outside itself, so a few corners can land a long way from anything. `Centroid`, the default, keeps every corner inside its own triangle and gives up on the walls being where the diagram says they are. `Balanced` takes the circumcentre where it lands inside the input bounds grown by `Expand Bounds`, and the centroid where it does not. All three are computed on the projected view and then brought back, so a corner sits at the height of the triangle it came from rather than on a flat plane.

ExpandBounds.tooltip: Bounds used for point pruning & balanced centroid.
ExpandBounds.semantics: The input dataset's own bounds grown by this many units, read by three separate things: `Balanced` compares each circumcentre against it to decide which position to take, `Prune Out Of Bounds` uses it as the cut on the cluster, and a corner falling outside it makes every seed around that corner count as open. That last reading runs whatever `Method` and `Prune Out Of Bounds` are set to, so the box reaches the **Sites** pin even when nothing on the cluster reads it.

bPruneOutOfBounds.semantics: Only reachable under `Canon (Circumcenter)`, because it exists for the runaway corners that mode produces. A corner outside the box is dropped along with every connection that touched it, so the cluster can come apart into several components. It cuts the cluster alone: which seeds leave on the **Sites** pin is `Prune Open Sites`.

ProjectionDetails.semantics: The direction the cells are worked out from. Corners are computed flat and then brought back to where the seeds are, so the cluster follows the seeds' own surface rather than sitting on a plane.
ProjectionDetails.trap: `3D Surface` is offered in the dropdown and this node does not support it: the method falls back to `Best Fit` when the projection is set up, with no message. Only `Normal` and `Best Fit` do what they say here.

bOutputSites.semantics: On by default, which is the difference from every other node in this family. A site is the input point with its attributes, moved to the average of the cell corners around it, each corner weighted by how many neighbouring cells its own triangle has. A seed that ended up touching no such corner keeps its original position.

bPruneOpenSites.tooltip: If enabled, sites whose cell is open -- on the hull, or dropped as out-of-bounds -- are removed from the output.
bPruneOpenSites.semantics: On by default, so the **Sites** pin normally comes back shorter than the input. A seed counts as open on either of two grounds: it sits on the outer ring of the triangulation, or one of the cell corners around it landed outside the bounds grown by `Expand Bounds`. The second ground is measured whether or not `Prune Out Of Bounds` is on, so widening that box is what keeps border seeds when the ring is not the reason they are going.

OpenSiteFlag.tooltip: Flag sites belonging to an open cell with a boolean attribute.
OpenSiteFlag.semantics: The alternative to dropping the open seeds: keep every seed and mark them instead, true for an open cell. It appears only with `Prune Open Sites` cleared, and that is not the default, so the flag is reachable only once the dropping is turned off.

SitesOutputDetails.tooltip: Additional data to output for each Voronoi site.

hints.text: Attributes reach the **Sites** pin and nothing else. The Vtx that come out are new points that were never the seeds, so anything the seeds were carrying has to travel through Sites or be sampled back on afterwards.

The **Sites** dataset leaves the node carrying the cluster's own tags, the pair tag and the Vtx role tag among them. Anything that sorts datasets into clusters by tag therefore reads it as a second Vtx dataset for the same pair, so keep it on its own branch rather than letting it reach a cluster consumer alongside the real Vtx.

UPCGExBuildVoronoiGraphSettings.name: Cluster : Voronoi 3D
UPCGExBuildVoronoiGraphSettings.purpose: Reads the input points as cell seeds and builds the skeleton between the cells: the Vtx are the corners where cells meet, and each connection runs along a shared cell wall. The input points do not come out. They are consumed to decide where the cells are, and the cluster that arrives on the pins is made of new points with no attributes and no relationship to the input rows, which is the single fact that decides whether this is the node you want. **Cluster : Delaunay 3D** is the one that keeps the input points and connects them to each other.
UPCGExBuildVoronoiGraphSettings.situation: A set of seed positions has to become the lattice of walls or struts that separates them, rather than a web joining them.

mechanism.text: One point dataset in, one cluster out, and the two have no rows in common. The input points are tetrahedralised, one Vtx is made for each tetrahedron at a position chosen by `Method`, and two Vtx are connected when their tetrahedra share a face. The Vtx count therefore follows the number of tetrahedra rather than the number of input points, and every Vtx is a fresh point: no attribute survives the crossing, and seeds are recomputed from the new positions. A dataset of fewer than four points is skipped with a warning, and one whose points all lie on a plane produces nothing at all, with a log line pointing at **Cluster : Voronoi 2D**.

off_label.claim: With `Method` on `Centroid` the node stops being a Voronoi builder and becomes a tetrahedron-centre scatter with connectivity: the same points **Cluster : Delaunay 3D** emits on its Sites pin, but wired up into a cluster instead of loose. Reach for it when what you want is the connected dual of a point cloud rather than the correct cell geometry.
off_label.grounded_in: The Centroid branch in FProcessor::Process writes Voronoi->Centroids, which TVoronoi3::Process fills with GetCentroid over each tetrahedron's four vertices, the same average FOutputDelaunaySites computes for the Delaunay Sites pin.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The cell seeds. Each dataset is handled on its own and produces its own cluster; datasets under four points are skipped and reported together in one warning.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: New points, one per tetrahedron of the seeds, holding nothing carried over from the input.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One point per connection between two cell corners, one dataset per connected component of the finished cluster.

Method.tooltip: Method used to find Voronoi cell location
Method.semantics: `Canon (Circumcenter)` is the position that makes the result a true Voronoi diagram, and it is also the one that flies off: a thin sliver tetrahedron has a circumcentre far outside itself, so a few corners can land hundreds of units away from anything. `Centroid`, the default, keeps every corner inside its own tetrahedron and gives up on the diagram being correct. `Balanced` takes the circumcentre where it lands inside the input bounds grown by `Expand Bounds`, and the centroid where it does not, which keeps the correct geometry through the middle of the cloud and tames the outer shell.

ExpandBounds.tooltip: Bounds used for point pruning & balanced centroid.
ExpandBounds.semantics: The input dataset's own bounds grown by this many units, and the box is used by two different settings: `Balanced` compares each circumcentre against it to decide which position to take, and `Prune Out Of Bounds` uses it as the cut. It does nothing at all under `Canon (Circumcenter)` with pruning off, or under `Centroid`.

bPruneOutOfBounds.semantics: Only reachable under `Canon (Circumcenter)`, because it exists for the runaway corners that mode produces. A corner outside the box is dropped along with every connection that touched it, so the cluster loses both points and connections, and what is left can come apart into several components.

hints.text: Attributes do not cross this node. Anything the seeds were carrying has to be sampled back onto the result afterwards, or kept on a separate branch of the graph, because the Vtx that come out are new points that were never the seeds.
There is no Sites output here. **Cluster : Voronoi 2D** has one, carrying the seeds back out with per-cell measurements written on them; the 3D node emits the cluster and nothing else.

UPCGExCatmullRomTangents.name: Catmull-Rom
UPCGExCatmullRomTangents.purpose: Both vectors get half the straight-line vector from the previous point to the next, the uniform Catmull-Rom tangent. That makes each point's tangent proportional to how far apart its neighbours are. The point's own position is never read, so the rule describes the run through the neighbourhood rather than the point itself. **From Neighbors** reaches the same vector by a different route, so the two are interchangeable.
UPCGExCatmullRomTangents.situation: A path of reasonably even spacing is on its way to a spline and should read as one continuous curve, with no point treated as special.

mechanism.text: Both vectors get half the vector running from the previous point to the next, each then multiplied by its own scale. The current point's position is not read at all, so moving a point off the line between its neighbours changes their tangents and not its own. An open path's first and last point never reach this rule; they take the base's answer, which for evenly spaced points comes out the same length this rule would have given.

hints.text: Tangent length follows the distance between the two neighbours, not the two segment lengths separately, which is what the uniform formulation means. Where one segment is much shorter than its partner, the tangent is long relative to the short one and the curve swings out past the point on that side. This implementation carries no chordal or centripetal option to damp that.

**From Neighbors** computes the same vector. It averages the run back to the previous neighbour with the run on to the next, and at full length that average reduces to the same half-difference, so the two rules match at every point, on open and closed paths alike.

UPCGExCherryPickPointsSettings.name: Cherry Pick Points
UPCGExCherryPickPointsSettings.purpose: Keeps the points a picker named and drops the rest. It is the plainest consumer of the picker family: the Pickers pin decides which indices, and this node acts on them. Invert turns the same selection into a removal, which is how a handful of points are taken out of a dataset by position.
UPCGExCherryPickPointsSettings.situation: A dataset where the points to keep, or the points to remove, are known by their position rather than by anything they carry.

mechanism.text: Each input dataset is handled on its own. Every picker on the Pickers pin is asked for its indices against that dataset point count, and the answers are pooled into one set. Points whose index is in the set are kept and the rest are dropped, or the other way round with Invert on. The survivors come out in their original order, whatever order the pickers named them in, and the point count changes while nothing else about the points does.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The datasets to cherry pick from. Each one is picked over separately.

inputs.label: Pickers
inputs.note: The picker sub-nodes naming the indices. Several stack, and their picks are pooled into one selection.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The points that survived the selection.

outputs.label: Discarded
outputs.note: Intended for the points the selection dropped.
outputs.condition: when Output Discarded Points is on

bInvert.tooltip: Whether to invert the picking (picked indices will be discarded instead or kept)
bInvert.semantics: It decides what an empty selection means, which is where this node is least forgiving. A picker that names nothing, an index past the end of a short dataset with Safety on Ignore being the usual cause, discards the whole dataset with Invert off and passes it through untouched with Invert on.

bOutputDiscardedPoints.tooltip: Whether to output discard points to their own dataset
bOutputDiscardedPoints.semantics: It adds the Discarded output pin. Where every point was discarded and nothing was picked, the whole dataset is forwarded down that pin intact, which is the one path through this setting that behaves as the label reads.

bAllowEmptyOutputs.tooltip: Whether to output discard points collections to be empty
bAllowEmptyOutputs.semantics: It applies to the dataset being picked over, so a dataset the selection emptied still comes out as an empty dataset instead of disappearing from the stream. Turn it on where a downstream node counts datasets and needs the count to survive.

hints.text: Output Discarded Points is broken for any selection that picked something. The discarded points are written over the start of the kept output instead of into the new dataset, so Out comes back holding the discarded points followed by whatever picked points ran past their count, and the Discarded pin receives an empty dataset. Only the all-discarded case routes correctly. Until this is fixed, take the remainder with a second Cherry Pick Points carrying the same pickers and Invert on.

UPCGExClipper2BooleanSettings.name: Clipper2 : Boolean
UPCGExClipper2BooleanSettings.purpose: Combines closed shapes by area: keeping what they share, what either covers, what one covers and the other does not, or what exactly one of them covers. Which of the four it does is a single setting, and the palette carries a preconfigured entry per operation so the node can be dropped in already set, its title showing the operation rather than the family name. Three of the four take a second set of shapes on their own pin; a union merges whatever it is given.
UPCGExClipper2BooleanSettings.situation: Two sets of closed outlines overlap and only the overlap, the merger, or the remainder is wanted, as real geometry rather than as a selection.

mechanism.text: Each group is solved once, and what comes back is one dataset per contour of the result, so the count follows the geometry rather than the inputs. Where two outlines cross, a point is created at the crossing and takes its values from the four source points bounding the two segments that met there; a point that passed through untouched keeps its original transform outright, so it comes back exactly where it started rather than at a grid position. Holes are contours in their own right, arriving on the same pin as their outer shape and told apart by their tag or their winding.

off_label.claim: A union of one group with no operands is a self-cleaning pass: overlapping outlines merge, self-crossings resolve into separate contours, and what comes back is the same footprint with a well-behaved outline.
off_label.grounded_in: the union branch requires no operand set and the solver resolves subject-against-subject overlap the same way it resolves subject against clip

off_label.claim: Naming the intersection flag turns the operation into a crossing detector as well: every point the solve invented carries the flag, so a union of several outlines comes back with a mark at each place two of them met.
off_label.grounded_in: the shared Z callback stamps every solver-created vertex, and the flag is written from that marker rather than from anything operation-specific

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The subjects. How many are solved together is the grouping policy's decision, not the wire order.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match-rule factories splitting the subjects into pre-groups.
inputs.condition: required while Main Data Matching has a mode set; an advanced pin otherwise

inputs.label: Operands
inputs.note: The shapes the operation works against. They must be closed: open operands are dropped on the way in whatever `Skip Open Paths` says.
inputs.condition: required on every operation except Union, where it is required only while Use Operand Pin is on

inputs.label: Match Rules (Ops)
inputs.note: Match-rule factories pairing operands with each subject group.
inputs.condition: required while Operands Data Matching has a mode set and the operand pin is in use

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: One dataset per contour of the result, holes included. Open results land here too unless `Open Paths Output` sends them elsewhere.

outputs.label: Open Paths
outputs.note: Open results, moved off the main pin.
outputs.condition: Open Paths Output is Output (Pin)

Operation.semantics: `Union` treats everything it is given as one set and merges it, which is why it alone needs no second set. The other three are asymmetric: `Intersection` keeps what subjects and operands both cover, `Difference` removes the operands from the subjects, and `XOR` keeps what exactly one side covers. Swapping which set is wired where changes the result of `Difference` and of nothing else.

FillRule.semantics: How the solver decides which enclosed regions are solid before the operation runs, which settles what a self-crossing outline or a ring inside a ring means. `Non Zero`, the default, fills anything enclosed however many times it is wound, so nested rings come back filled. `Even Odd` alternates with each enclosure, so a ring inside a ring reads as a hole whichever way either is wound. `Positive` and `Negative` fill by winding direction, which makes an outline's own authored direction decide whether it is solid.

bUseOperandPin.tooltip: Display operand pin as a separate pin. Union is the only operation that does not already need one.
bUseOperandPin.semantics: It exists to give a union a second set of shapes to merge with, and the panel shows it under `Union` alone because the other three already require the operand pin. Turning it on promotes that pin from an advanced one nothing reads to a required one, and turns on the operand match rules along with it.

hints.text: The node's title in the graph reads as the operation rather than as the family, so a graph holding all four is readable without opening any of them. The four palette entries set that operation and nothing else, so any of them can be switched to another operation afterwards.

Open input is accepted on the subject side and is not made into a closed area first. An open subject is carried through the solve as a run and comes back as a run, so a union of two open paths is not the outline of the shape they seem to enclose. `Skip Open Paths` is how a graph declines them at the door.

UPCGExClipper2DecomposeSettings.name: Clipper2 : Decompose
UPCGExClipper2DecomposeSettings.purpose: Cuts a closed footprint into convex cells and hands the result back as a cluster. The footprint is flattened, triangulated, and its triangles are greedily merged into the largest convex pieces they can form, after which every side of every piece becomes an edge. Convexity is the reason to reach for it: a downstream step that assumes a cell has no reflex corner gets that guarantee here and cannot get it from a footprint alone. **Clipper2 : Volume** runs the same three stages over the same settings and emits volume actors instead.
UPCGExClipper2DecomposeSettings.situation: A closed path outlines an area that has to be worked with as a set of convex cells rather than as one outline.

mechanism.text: Closed paths in, one cluster out per group. The footprint is flattened onto a plane, triangulated under `Fill Rule`, and its triangles merged into convex pieces; every side of every surviving piece becomes an Edge, and a side two pieces share becomes one. The Vtx are the deduplicated corners those pieces stand on, which is the footprint's own points plus whatever Clipper created where paths crossed. Nothing on the output records which edges bounded which piece: the pieces survive only as the edges around them. A path not flagged as a closed loop is skipped, because a decomposition needs a closed footprint.

off_label.claim: Turn `Merge Convex Pieces` off and the cluster is the constrained-Delaunay triangulation of the footprint, every triangle side included, which is a mesh-free way to get a triangulated interior as cluster data.
off_label.grounded_in: FDecomposeParams::bUseDelaunay is fixed true and MergeIntoConvexPieces is the only step the toggle skips, so the piece list stays as the triangle list Clipper produced

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The closed footprints to decompose. Several may be wired, and how they are grouped is the grouping policy's decision.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Rules pairing main inputs into pre-groups before the grouping policy runs inside each. Required once Main Data Matching is switched on, advanced and unread otherwise.
inputs.condition: when Main Data Matching is enabled

inputs.label: Operands
inputs.note: Declared by the shared Clipper2 base for the boolean nodes. This node reads nothing from it and the editor marks it unused.

inputs.label: Match Rules (Ops)
inputs.note: The operand half of the same matching mechanism, inert here for the same reason.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: One dataset per group that decomposed, holding the deduplicated footprint corners.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: The piece sides, one dataset per connected component.

ProjectionDetails.tooltip: Projection settings used to flatten the path into a 2D footprint before decomposition.
ProjectionDetails.semantics: The plane the footprint is flattened onto before triangulation, so it decides the shape of the result and not, for the most part, where the Vtx end up: a Vtx standing on an input point comes back at that point's own transform.
ProjectionDetails.trap: A Vtx that Clipper created where two paths crossed has no input point behind it, so it is placed by unprojecting its flat position, which lands it on the projection plane through the world origin rather than at the footprint's own height.

FillRule.tooltip: Fill rule used when triangulating the footprint. Even-Odd treats nested rings as holes (donut footprints).
FillRule.semantics: Decides which enclosed regions count as filled, which is what makes a ring inside another a hole or a solid. `Even Odd` alternates, so nesting always cuts a hole regardless of how the rings were wound. The three winding rules read the direction each ring was authored in, so a ring wound the same way as the one containing it fills solid under `Non Zero` and the donut closes up.

bMergeConvexPieces.tooltip: Greedily merge triangles into larger convex pieces (Hertel-Mehlhorn); disable to keep the raw triangulation (every triangle edge).
bMergeConvexPieces.semantics: On, adjacent triangles are merged as far as convexity allows, and the diagonals no longer needed to keep a piece convex are gone from the edge set. Off, the raw triangulation stands and every triangle side becomes an edge, so the same footprint yields a much denser cluster.
bMergeConvexPieces.trap: The piece cap is compared after this step, so turning the merge off compares the triangle count against it instead of the merged count. A footprint of a few hundred triangles then trips the default cap of 256 and is skipped whole.

MaxConvexPieces.tooltip: Safety cap on convex pieces per footprint. Footprints exceeding this are skipped with a warning.
MaxConvexPieces.semantics: A footprint over the cap yields no cluster at all rather than a partial one, and the warning names the count it reached, which is the number to raise this to.

bQuietWarnings.tooltip: Suppress per-group warnings about degenerate footprints / failed triangulation.

MainInputGroupingPolicy.tooltip: How main inputs are grouped. With data matching enabled this applies *within* each matched pre-group; otherwise it applies across all main inputs.
MainInputGroupingPolicy.semantics: `Auto` groups the inputs by spatial nesting, so an outer footprint and the rings inside it become one group and those rings become holes; `Separate` gives one cluster per path and no holes at all; `Merged` puts every input into a single group.
MainInputGroupingPolicy.trap: The shared Clipper2 block declares `Merged` as its own default, and this node overrides it to `Auto` in its constructor, so a fresh node is on `Auto`.

Precision.tooltip: Decimal precision Clipper2 Uses int64 under the hood to preserve extreme precision, so we scale floating point values then back.
Precision.semantics: Coordinates are scaled by this before the triangulator sees them, and the vertex dedup key reads the low 32 bits of each scaled coordinate, so the range over which two corners stay distinct shrinks as the number rises: roughly 215 km from the origin at the default of 100, roughly 2 km at 10000. Past that, distinct corners can weld into one Vtx.

HoleTag.tooltip: Write this tag on paths that are holes

hints.text: Attributes carry from one input path only. A Vtx that came from the group's first path keeps that point's attributes; every other Vtx, which is any vertex from a nested hole ring and any vertex Clipper created, takes the first path's point 0 values instead. The positions are right in every case; the attributes are not.

A path that is not flagged as a closed loop is dropped with no message of its own, and the node only speaks up when nothing survived, reporting that no valid path was found in the main input. So a path built upstream by something that never set the flag surfaces here as a missing-input report.

`Precision` and the grouping controls are the shared Clipper2 rows that reach this node. The path-output rows below them, blending, carry over, open-path output, simplify and arc tolerance, are hidden here because the output is a cluster and not paths.
The hole, intersection and joint tagging rows stay visible and do nothing on this node. They are written while path data is being assembled, which is a step this node never takes.

UPCGExClipper2OffsetSettings.name: Clipper2 : Offset
UPCGExClipper2OffsetSettings.purpose: Grows or shrinks a shape by a distance, solving the whole outline at once so corners round or square off cleanly and self-overlap is resolved rather than left folded. A negative distance pulls inward, and the offset can be read per point, so a single shape can swell unevenly. Asking for several iterations gives a set of concentric outlines from one run rather than a single one.
UPCGExClipper2OffsetSettings.situation: A footprint needs a border, an inset, or a nest of rings at even spacing, and the corners have to survive the operation.

mechanism.text: Each group is offset as one shape, and what comes back is one dataset per resulting outline, so the count follows the geometry rather than the input. Iterations do not stack: every iteration re-offsets the original by its own multiple of the distance, so iteration three sits three offsets out from the input and not three offsets out from iteration two. This is the one Clipper2 node whose points have all moved, so every output position is unprojected from the solve grid rather than restored from a source point. Corner and end shaping is the offset solver's own, which is why the join, end and collinear settings are read here and nowhere else.

off_label.claim: A distance of zero with a positive iteration count still produces output, and each iteration is then a re-tracing of the input at grid precision. It is a way to see what the quantisation is doing to a shape before an operation that depends on it.
off_label.grounded_in: the iteration loop runs on NumIterations alone and never tests the resolved offset, and OutputPaths64 unprojects every point whatever the delta was

off_label.claim: Reading the offset from a per-point attribute turns this into a variable-width outline rather than a uniform one: the delta callback resolves a value for the point behind each vertex, so a distance authored along the input varies around the result.
off_label.grounded_in: CreateDeltaCallback decodes the source point index from the vertex Z and reads OffsetValues for that point rather than a single group value

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The shapes to offset. How many are solved together is the grouping policy's decision.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match-rule factories splitting the inputs into pre-groups.
inputs.condition: required while Main Data Matching has a mode set; an advanced pin otherwise

inputs.label: Operands
inputs.note: Declared by the shared base and never read here. This node takes no operands.

inputs.label: Match Rules (Ops)
inputs.note: The operand side's match rules, inert here for the same reason.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: One dataset per resulting outline, per iteration. Ten inputs solved as one shape with three iterations can come back as any number of datasets.

outputs.label: Open Paths
outputs.note: Open results moved off the main pin.
outputs.condition: Open Paths Output is Output (Pin)

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute name to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

Iterations.semantics: Read once per input dataset as a data value rather than per point. Each iteration is a fresh solve on the original input at that multiple of the distance, which is what makes the rings evenly spaced.
Iterations.trap: Successive rings are not offsets of each other, so a shape whose detail is erased at one distance comes back at the next: iteration two is solved from the original, not from what iteration one produced.

IterationConsolidation.tooltip: How to determine final iteration count when iteration attribute from multiple source differ
IterationConsolidation.semantics: A group is solved as one shape and therefore gets one iteration count, so this decides which of the group's inputs wins when they disagree. It never applies within one input.

MinIterations.semantics: A floor applied after consolidation, so a group whose attribute resolved to zero still runs this many times. Its default of 1 is why the node produces output even with the iterations attribute missing or zero.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

Offset.semantics: Positive grows the shape, negative shrinks it. The value is resolved for the source point behind each vertex rather than once per shape, so an attribute gives a width that varies around the outline, and the iteration multiplier is applied on top of whatever it resolved to.

OffsetScale.tooltip: Offset Scale (mostly useful when using attributes)
OffsetScale.semantics: A plain multiplier on whatever the offset resolved to, iteration multiplier included. It exists so an attribute authored in some other unit can be brought to world units without rewriting the attribute.

JoinType.semantics: `Round` is the default and the only value that builds arcs, so it is the only one for which `Arc Tolerance` means anything.

MiterLimit.tooltip: Miter limit (only used with Miter join type)
MiterLimit.semantics: Read whatever the join type is, and acted on by `Miter` alone. It caps how far a sharp corner is allowed to extend before the solver squares it off, as a multiple of the offset distance.

EndTypeClosed.semantics: What the solver does with closed input. `Polygon` is the offset every other setting assumes, and the other values treat the closed shape as a run with two ends, which turns a filled outline into a band around the original line.

EndTypeOpen.semantics: Only reachable while open input is being accepted, which is why it disappears with `Skip Open Paths` on. `Polygon` here closes the run before offsetting it, so an open input comes back as a filled outline rather than a band.

IterationAttributeName.tooltip: Write the iteration index to a data attribute
IterationAttributeName.semantics: Written to the data domain of every output of that iteration, zero-based, so the first ring reads 0. It is the only thing distinguishing the rings once they are all sitting on the same pin.

IterationTag.tooltip: Write the iteration index to a tag
IterationTag.semantics: A key-value tag, so the tag carries the zero-based iteration index as its value rather than being a bare presence flag.

hints.text: Every output point here is unprojected from the solve grid, this node's points having all moved. `Precision` therefore sets the resolution of every position in the result and not just of the invented ones, and lowering it to widen the addressable window is paid for in visible stepping.

UPCGExClipper2ProcessorSettings.name: Clipper2 Processor
UPCGExClipper2ProcessorSettings.purpose: The shared surface behind the nodes that hand their paths to the Clipper2 library. **Clipper2 : Boolean**, **Clipper2 : Offset**, **Clipper2 : Rect Clip**, **Clipper2 : Triangulate**, **Clipper2 : Decompose** and **Clipper2 : Volume** all work in two dimensions on a flattened, quantised copy of the input and hand back fresh geometry, so this block owns the round trip: which inputs are solved together, how fine the quantisation is, what happens to paths that are not closed, and where the output points get their values. It sits on the path processor base, so the two-point floor and `Omit Invalid Paths Outputs` apply here too.
UPCGExClipper2ProcessorSettings.situation: Several path datasets were wired into a Clipper2 node, and the question is whether they were solved as one shape or as several, and where the output points took their attributes from.

mechanism.text: Inputs are flattened onto a plane and every coordinate rounded onto an integer grid, `Precision` setting how many steps there are per world unit. The solve returns contours, and the node writes one output dataset per contour of two points or more, so nothing about the input shape survives: point counts, dataset counts and ordering are all decided by the geometry. Each output point is traced back to the source points behind it, one where a point passed through and four where a crossing invented it, and its transform and attributes are built from those. Which inputs are solved together is the grouping policy's call, and every group is solved on its own, its results carrying the tags of the inputs that fed it.

off_label.claim: Flagging intersections turns a Clipper2 node into a crossing detector. The flag marks the points the solve invented, so a union of several paths in one group comes back as their outline with a flag on every point where two of them crossed.
off_label.grounded_in: The Z callback in FProcessingGroup::CreateZCallback stamps every solver-created vertex with the intersection marker, and OutputPaths64 writes IntersectionFlagName from that marker rather than from any node-specific state.

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The subjects of the operation, inherited from the path processor base. Several datasets are accepted and how they are partitioned is the grouping policy's decision, not the wire order.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match-rule factories splitting the main inputs into pre-groups before the grouping policy runs inside each.
inputs.condition: required while Main Data Matching has a mode set; an advanced pin otherwise

inputs.label: Operands
inputs.note: The second set of paths an operation works against, or on **Clipper2 : Rect Clip** the paths whose bounds become the clipping rectangle. On the nodes that want no operands the pin is declared advanced and the node never reads it.
inputs.condition: required on Clipper2 : Boolean unless the operation is a Union with its operand pin switched off, and on Clipper2 : Rect Clip while Bounds Source is Operand

inputs.label: Match Rules (Ops)
inputs.note: Match-rule factories pairing operands with each main group. On a node that wants no operands the mode is forced off before the pin is declared, so it can never be required there.
inputs.condition: required while Operands Data Matching has a mode set on a node that takes operands; advanced otherwise

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: Closed results always, and open ones too unless `Open Paths Output` sends them elsewhere. One dataset per contour, so the count bears no relation to the number of inputs.

outputs.label: Open Paths
outputs.note: Open results, moved off the main pin.
outputs.condition: Open Paths Output is Output (Pin)

MainDataMatching.tooltip: If enabled, matches main inputs into pre-groups (by tags / @Data) before the grouping policy below is applied within each. If disabled, the grouping policy alone partitions the inputs.
MainDataMatching.semantics: Matching runs first and splits the main inputs into pre-groups; the grouping policy then applies inside each pre-group. The two settings multiply: with the policy left at `Merged` each match becomes one shape, and at `Separate` a match is refined back into its individual inputs.

MainInputGroupingPolicy.tooltip: How main inputs are grouped. With data matching enabled this applies *within* each matched pre-group; otherwise it applies across all main inputs.
MainInputGroupingPolicy.semantics: `Merged` is the default, so out of the box everything on **Paths** is one shape and a boolean or an offset sees the union of the lot. `Separate` gives each input its own solve. `Auto` partitions by spatial nesting, so an outer contour and the rings inside it become one footprint with holes, while unrelated footprints stay apart.
MainInputGroupingPolicy.trap: `Auto` is offered everywhere and acted on only where nesting is supported. **Clipper2 : Decompose** and **Clipper2 : Volume** support nesting; on **Clipper2 : Boolean**, **Clipper2 : Offset**, **Clipper2 : Rect Clip** and **Clipper2 : Triangulate** it falls back to `Separate` with nothing said.

OperandsDataMatching.tooltip: If enabled, lets you to pick which are matched with which main data. The match is done against every single data within a group and then consolidated; this means if you have a [A,B,C] group, ABC will be executed against operands for A, B and C individually.
OperandsDataMatching.semantics: The rules are evaluated against every input in a main group and the results consolidated, so a group of three main inputs collects the operands that matched any of the three.
OperandsDataMatching.trap: A main group whose operand match comes back empty is removed from the run. It produces no output at all, rather than passing through unoperated.

bSkipOpenPaths.semantics: It drops open paths on the way in, before the solve, and it governs the main input alone. The nodes that take operands decide the operand side for themselves: **Clipper2 : Boolean** always drops open operands, and **Clipper2 : Rect Clip** always keeps them, since it reads only their bounds. Where open results go is a separate decision, made by `Open Paths Output`.
bSkipOpenPaths.trap: Three nodes refuse open input outright and never consult this. **Clipper2 : Decompose** and **Clipper2 : Volume** hide it along with the rest of the output block; **Clipper2 : Triangulate** shows it and ignores it.

Precision.tooltip: Decimal precision Clipper2 Uses int64 under the hood to preserve extreme precision, so we scale floating point values then back.
Precision.semantics: A multiplier, despite the name. Coordinates are rounded onto a grid of one over this value, so the default of 100 quantises to a hundredth of a world unit and raising it buys a finer grid. `Arc Tolerance` is converted by it on the way to the solver, so that setting stays in world units whatever this is set to.
Precision.trap: The crossing bookkeeping keeps only the low 32 bits of each scaled coordinate, which addresses a window of some 215 kilometres either side of the projection origin at the default of 100, shrinking in step with the value: some 2 kilometres at 10000. Two crossings one window apart on both axes share an entry and the later one wins, so a point takes another crossing's blended attributes, and on **Clipper2 : Offset** and **Clipper2 : Rect Clip** its height along the projection axis with them.

bSimplifyPaths.semantics: It runs on each result after the solve, at a fixed tolerance of half a world unit that tracks `Precision` so it stays there. There is no tolerance to set. Closed and open results are simplified as closed and open respectively, so an open result keeps its two endpoints.
bSimplifyPaths.trap: A result simplified below two points is dropped, so this can cost whole paths and not only points.

bPreserveCollinear.tooltip: Keep collinear points in the output instead of simplifying them.
bPreserveCollinear.semantics: Read by **Clipper2 : Offset** alone, where it is handed to the offset solver. It is visible and inert on **Clipper2 : Boolean**, **Clipper2 : Rect Clip** and **Clipper2 : Triangulate**, and hidden on the other two.

ArcTolerance.tooltip: Tolerance for arc approximation when generating curved offsets. Higher values = fewer points.
ArcTolerance.semantics: Arcs exist where a round join or a round end is being built, which is **Clipper2 : Offset** alone; the setting shows on the other Clipper2 nodes and none of them reads it. The value is in world units and multiplied by `Precision` on the way to the solver, so a given tolerance means the same thing at any precision.

CarryOverDetails.tooltip: Filter in/out which attributes get carried over from inputs to outputs.

fields.name: bPreserveAttributesDefaultValue
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will preserve the initial attribute default value.

fields.name: Attributes
fields.tooltip: Attributes to carry over.

fields.name: bDataDomainToElements
fields.tooltip: If enabled, data domain attributes are promoted to the elements domain (the single @Data value is broadcast to every point). Off by default; Merge Points is the node that enables it. Not used by all nodes.

fields.name: Scope
fields.tooltip: Scope

fields.name: Tags
fields.tooltip: Tags to carry over.

fields.name: bTestTagsWithValues
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

CarryOverDetails.semantics: It filters attributes and tags both. Tags are pruned once on the group as a whole and again on each finished path, and a path collects the tags of only the inputs that actually put a point into it, so a merged group does not stamp every result with every tag.
CarryOverDetails.trap: `IsClosed` and `IsHole` are excluded by name, because the node writes those itself. An attribute of your own carrying either name never reaches the output.

BlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how source point properties and attributes are blended together for fused output points.
BlendingDetails.semantics: It decides what a point invented at a crossing inherits from the up-to-four source points behind it. Every point resolves through it, a passed-through point included, with a single source to blend from. `Position` ships as `None` because positions come from the solve, and giving it any other mode moves points off the geometry the operation returned.

OpenPathsOutput.tooltip: How to handle open paths in the output (ignore, output to main pin, or separate pin).
OpenPathsOutput.semantics: `Output`, the default, puts open and closed results on the same **Paths** pin, where the only thing telling them apart downstream is `@Data.IsClosed`. `Output (Pin)` adds the **Open Paths** pin and moves them there. `Ignore` discards them.
OpenPathsOutput.trap: It decides where open results go, never whether open input is accepted. That is `Skip Open Paths`, and on the nodes refusing open input there is never an open result to route.

HoleTag.tooltip: Write this tag on paths that are holes
HoleTag.semantics: A hole is decided by winding: a closed result whose contour runs counter-clockwise in the projected plane. Open results are never tested, so the tag never lands on one.

IntersectionFlagName.tooltip: Name of the boolean attribute for intersection points
IntersectionFlagName.semantics: The flag marks the points the solve invented at a crossing, which are the same points whose values came from blending four sources instead of one. It is the fastest way to check whether a suspect value sits on an invented point or on one that passed through.

JointFlagName.tooltip: Name of the int32 attribute for joint type
JointFlagName.semantics: Only points tracing back to the first or last point of an open source path are classified, and within each unbroken run of them only the boundary points are written. An offset cap arc therefore gets a value at each end and nothing in between, and a run of a single point is written as a start.

JointTypeValueMapping.tooltip: Pick which value will be written for each joint type.
JointTypeValueMapping.semantics: Fixed size with read-only keys, holding `None`, `Start` and `End` at 0, 1 and 2. Only `Start` and `End` are ever written; the `None` row is the value the attribute is created with, so it is what every unclassified point keeps.

bUnionGroupBeforeOperation.tooltip: (DEBUG) If enabled, performs a union of all paths in the group before proceeding to the operation
bUnionGroupBeforeOperation.semantics: Marked DEBUG in source. Only the closed subject paths of a group are unioned, so overlapping inputs stop being separate contours going in. It does nothing to a group holding one path.

bUnionOperandsBeforeOperation.tooltip: (DEBUG) If enabled, performs a union of all paths in the operand group before proceeding to the operation
bUnionOperandsBeforeOperation.semantics: Marked DEBUG in source, and the operand-side twin of the setting above. It does nothing to an operand set holding one path.

hints.text: Each input dataset is projected on its own. Left at `Normal`, the node projection method puts them all on the same plane, but `Best Fit` computes a plane per dataset and `3D Surface` drops the shared plane altogether, so a group holding several datasets is then solved on planes that disagree and the result matches none of them.

Boolean results keep the original transform of every point that passed through, so those points come back where they started rather than back through the grid. **Clipper2 : Offset** unprojects instead, because its points have moved, and there the quantisation shows on every point. **Clipper2 : Rect Clip** unprojects on its ordinary branch but not under `Invert Clip`, which calls the same output path without the unprojection and restores passed-through points from source.

UPCGExClipper2RectClipSettings.name: Clipper2 : Rect Clip
UPCGExClipper2RectClipSettings.purpose: Cuts paths to a rectangle, taking that rectangle either from the bounds of whatever is wired to the operand pin or from a box typed into the panel. It is the same job an intersection against a four-cornered shape would do, at a fraction of the work, and it can be inverted to keep the outside instead. Closed shapes can be clipped as areas or sliced open as lines, which is the difference between a trimmed footprint and a set of cut runs.
UPCGExClipper2RectClipSettings.situation: Paths have to be trimmed to a tile, a cell, or the extent of some other dataset, and the boundary is a box.

mechanism.text: The rectangle is axis-aligned in the projected plane and derived once per group, so the projection settings decide which way it is turned relative to the world. Each group is clipped in one pass and comes back as one dataset per resulting contour. Where a path meets the border a point is created, and it takes its values by interpolating along the input segment it was cut from. Points that were already inside are recognised as the source points they came from and keep those points' rotation, scale and attributes.

off_label.claim: Wiring the same dataset to both the subject and the operand pin and giving the padding a negative value clips a shape to its own bounding rectangle brought inward, which is a crude inset that costs nothing next to a real offset solve.
off_label.grounded_in: the rectangle is measured from the operand data's own bounds with nothing preventing the same data on both pins, and ApplyPadding moves each side inward for a negative value

off_label.claim: Feeding a single point dataset to the operand pin makes the rectangle that point's own bounds, so a box point becomes a movable cutter that a graph can drive per instance.
off_label.grounded_in: ComputeCombinedBounds accumulates the data bounds of every operand in the group without a minimum count, and open or single-element operands are accepted because only their bounds are read

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to cut. How many are clipped together is the grouping policy's decision, though the rectangle is the same for the whole group either way.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match-rule factories splitting the inputs into pre-groups, each of which then gets its own rectangle.
inputs.condition: required while Main Data Matching has a mode set; an advanced pin otherwise

inputs.label: Operands
inputs.note: Whatever the rectangle is measured from. Only the bounds are read, so open paths and single points are accepted here and the shape itself is never clipped against.
inputs.condition: required while Bounds Source is Operand Bounds

inputs.label: Match Rules (Ops)
inputs.note: Match-rule factories pairing operands with each group, which is how one run can cut different groups to different rectangles.
inputs.condition: required while Operands Data Matching has a mode set

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: One dataset per resulting contour. Open results land here too unless `Open Paths Output` sends them elsewhere.

outputs.label: Open Paths
outputs.note: Open results, moved off the main pin. `Clip As Lines` sends every cut closed shape here.
outputs.condition: Open Paths Output is Output (Pin)

ProjectionDetails.semantics: The rectangle is axis-aligned in this plane and not in the world, so turning the projection turns the cutter. It also decides the direction along which everything is flattened, which is the axis the rectangle ignores entirely.

BoundsSource.tooltip: Source for the clipping rectangle bounds
BoundsSource.semantics: `Operand Bounds` reads the data bounds of every operand matched to the group and takes their union, so several operands give one rectangle covering all of them rather than one rectangle each. `Manual` uses the box below and drops the operand pin's requirement.
BoundsSource.trap: A group left with no operands has no bounds to measure, and it is skipped with a warning rather than passed through, so its paths produce nothing at all.

ManualBounds.tooltip: Manual rectangle bounds in world space (used when BoundsSource is Manual). Note: Only X and Y are used after projection.
ManualBounds.semantics: Authored in world space and in three dimensions, then reduced: all eight corners are projected and the rectangle is their extent in the projected plane. A box that is not aligned with the projection therefore yields a rectangle larger than any of its faces.

BoundsPadding.tooltip: Uniform padding to apply to the bounds (can be negative to shrink)
BoundsPadding.semantics: World units applied to all four sides, and negative values shrink the rectangle. It is applied after the rectangle is rounded outward to whole grid steps, so it moves the border rather than trimming the rounding.

BoundsPaddingScale.semantics: A per-axis multiplier on the padding in the projected plane, so a value of one and zero pads sideways and leaves the other axis alone. With the padding itself at zero it does nothing whatever it is set to.

bClipOpenPathsAsLines.tooltip: If true, clips open paths using RectClipLines (preserves them as open paths). If false, treats open paths as closed polygons for clipping.
bClipOpenPathsAsLines.semantics: The open-input twin of the setting above. On, an open path stays a run and comes back as the pieces of it that were inside; off, it is treated as though its two ends were joined and comes back as an area. It is only reachable while open input is being accepted at all.

bClipAsLines.tooltip: If true, clips closed paths as lines (outputs will be open paths). Useful when you want to cut through paths rather than get polygon intersections.
bClipAsLines.semantics: It changes what a closed input means: as an area, a clipped shape comes back closed with the border making up its missing side; as lines, the shape is cut into the runs that were inside and every one of them comes back open. A closed shape sitting entirely inside the rectangle is passed through untouched either way.
bClipAsLines.trap: It disappears while `Invert Clip` is on, and inverting takes a different route entirely: the inverted result is always areas, so there is no way to slice a closed shape into runs outside the rectangle.

bInvertClip.tooltip: If enabled, inverts the clip region (uses boolean difference with the rectangle instead)
bInvertClip.semantics: Keeps what falls outside the rectangle instead of inside, by taking a boolean difference against it rather than by clipping.
bInvertClip.trap: That is a different solve, and it restores positions differently: inverted, a point that was already outside comes back at its own original position, while the ordinary clip takes every position off the projection grid. Switching the toggle therefore moves points that were nowhere near the border.

Precision.tooltip: Decimal precision Clipper2 Uses int64 under the hood to preserve extreme precision, so we scale floating point values then back.
Precision.semantics: It does more here than on the other Clipper2 nodes. Beyond the shared crossing bookkeeping, the ordinary clip identifies which output points were already source points by looking them up on their coordinates, keeping only the low 32 bits of each; that window is some 215 kilometres either side of the projection origin at the default of 100 and shrinks in step with the value.
Precision.trap: Two source points a window apart on both axes share an entry, and an output point landing on one of them is then restored as the other: it inherits that point's rotation, scale, height and attributes while staying where it is. The same key can also make a genuine border point look like a source point and skip the interpolation it needed. Inverting the clip takes the other route and is not subject to this lookup.

hints.text: Nothing here is oriented. The cutter is a rectangle aligned to the projected plane's own axes, so a box wired to the operand pin contributes its extent and never its rotation. A rotated cutter is an intersection against the rotated shape on **Clipper2 : Boolean**, not this node.

UPCGExClipper2TriangulateSettings.name: Clipper2 : Triangulate
UPCGExClipper2TriangulateSettings.purpose: Fills closed paths into a mesh, and unlike the other filling nodes it says what to do when the outlines overlap. A fill rule decides which enclosed regions count as inside, which is what makes it the node for shapes with holes, shapes cut out of each other, and outlines that cross. **Topology : Path Surface** fills a simple outline with no such question to answer.
UPCGExClipper2TriangulateSettings.situation: Outlines with holes or overlaps, where which parts should be solid is a decision rather than an accident.

mechanism.text: The paths are projected flat, and every region their boundaries enclose is classified by the fill rule before anything is triangulated. `Even Odd` alternates solid and hollow with each boundary crossed, which is what turns a ring inside a ring into a hole. The winding rules instead count boundary directions, so a path's own direction decides whether it adds material or removes it. What survives is triangulated into one dynamic mesh.
steps: Paths are projected and their enclosed regions identified.
The fill rule decides which regions are solid.
The solid regions are triangulated and appended to the mesh.

off_label.claim: Under the winding rules, reversing a path is a boolean operation with no second node: the same outline that added material cuts it away instead, which makes hole authoring a matter of path direction.
off_label.grounded_in: The Positive and Negative rules classify regions by signed winding count, which reverses with the path's own direction.

outputs.label: Mesh
outputs.note: The dynamic mesh, triangulated from whatever the fill rule left solid.

ProjectionDetails.semantics: The plane the regions are classified on. Everything about inside and outside is decided there, so paths at different heights that overlap in the projection interact as though they were coplanar.

FillRule.semantics: Decides which enclosed regions are solid, and the two families answer differently. `Even Odd` counts crossings and ignores direction, so nested outlines alternate solid and hollow whichever way they were authored. The winding rules count direction, so `Positive` and `Negative` are opposites of each other and a reversed path changes what it contributes rather than only where.

bUseDelaunay.tooltip: Use Delaunay optimization for better triangle quality
bUseDelaunay.semantics: Changes how the solid regions are cut into triangles without changing which regions they are. It matters for the shape of the triangles rather than the shape of the surface, which is what shading and later subdivision are sensitive to.

bAttemptRepair.tooltip: Attempt to repair degenerate geometry after triangulation
bAttemptRepair.semantics: Tries to fix triangles with no real area, with `Repair Degenerate` deciding how far it goes. Overlapping outlines produce more of these than simple ones, which is why the repair pass matters more on this node than on the simpler filling nodes.

Topology.tooltip: Topology settings. Some settings will be ignored based on selected output mode.

hints.text: The rule is applied to every input together, not per path. Outlines that were never meant to interact still interact if they overlap in the projection, which usually shows up as unexpected holes where two unrelated shapes cross.

UPCGExClipper2VolumeSettings.name: Clipper2 : Volume
UPCGExClipper2VolumeSettings.purpose: Turns a closed path into a spawned actor with real collision matching its footprint, extruded upward. The footprint may be concave and may have holes, because it is triangulated and rebuilt as a set of convex prisms rather than as one hull. Output Mode picks what the actor is: a Volume, which is what a trigger or post-process volume needs, or a Primitive, a hidden static-mesh collider for cases where an actor of that class is not wanted. Either way the collision is convex geometry rather than BSP, so it behaves the same in the editor and in a cooked build.
UPCGExClipper2VolumeSettings.situation: A region drawn as a path in the graph that has to exist in the level as something gameplay or rendering can query.

mechanism.text: Each footprint is flattened to two dimensions by the projection, triangulated under the fill rule, and its triangles merged into convex pieces. Every piece becomes a vertical prism: its floor comes from the Z of its own points and its height is read per point from the Height input, taking the tallest point of that piece. One actor is spawned per footprint, positioned at the footprint's centre on its base plane and oriented by the projection, and the node emits one spatial data per spawned actor carrying the actor's own reference in its @Data domain. Open paths are not footprints and are dropped before any of this.

off_label.claim: The output data carries the source path's @Data attributes alongside the actor reference, so a downstream matching rule can pair each spawned volume back with the path that made it without any extra bookkeeping.
off_label.grounded_in: the spawn pass runs a data-forward handler per source facade onto each volume's @Data domain, alongside the actor reference attribute

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The closed paths to extrude. Open paths are excluded before processing, and a run left with nothing valid warns and stops.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Rules that pre-group the inputs before the grouping policy is applied within each group.

inputs.label: Operands
inputs.note: Present but unused by this node, which performs no boolean operation.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: One spatial data per spawned actor: volume data under Volume, primitive data under Primitive. Nothing else is emitted, so the source paths do not pass through.

OutputMode.tooltip: Whether each footprint becomes an AVolume (UPCGVolumeData) or a simple static-mesh collider (UPCGPrimitiveData).
OutputMode.semantics: Volume spawns an actor of the chosen AVolume subclass and emits volume data. Primitive spawns a plain actor carrying a hidden static-mesh component whose simple collision is the convex pieces, and emits primitive data. The choice changes which class field, which collision field and which output data type apply, so the two halves of the panel are mutually exclusive.

ProjectionDetails.tooltip: Projection settings used to flatten the path into a 2D footprint and to orient the extrusion.
ProjectionDetails.semantics: Does two jobs: it fixes the plane the footprint is flattened onto, and it orients the extrusion, which is the axis the prisms rise along. The first path in a group supplies the frame for the whole volume, so paths grouped together should share a plane.

FillRule.tooltip: Fill rule used when triangulating the footprint. Even-Odd treats nested rings as holes (donut volumes).
FillRule.semantics: Even-Odd is what makes a ring inside another ring a hole rather than a solid, which is the behaviour Auto grouping is built around.

VolumeClass.tooltip: Volume actor class to spawn (Volume mode). Must derive from AVolume (e.g. ATriggerVolume, APostProcessVolume, a custom gameplay volume).
VolumeClass.semantics: Any AVolume subclass, which is where the volume's actual behaviour comes from: a trigger volume triggers, a post-process volume grades. The node only supplies the shape.

PrimitiveActorClass.tooltip: Actor class spawned as the collider host (Primitive mode). A UStaticMeshComponent carrying the convex simple collision is attached to it -- and made the root component when the chosen class has none.
PrimitiveActorClass.semantics: The host for the collider component. A class with no root component of its own gets the mesh component as its root and is then placed; a class that brings its own root keeps the transform it was spawned with.

Height.tooltip: Extrusion height applied above the footprint base plane. Constant, per-point attribute, or property (e.g. $Extent).

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.
