PriorityThreshold.tooltip: For Priority mode: minimum average weight for a box to be extracted in the first pass. Compared against the raw attribute average, so a weight on a larger scale clears it everywhere and collapses the two passes.

PreferredMinVolume.tooltip: Soft preference for minimum box volume (in voxels). 0 = no minimum preference.
PreferredMinVolume.semantics: Counted in voxels, so the number moves with `Voxel Size`, and under `Edge Inferred` it moves with the cluster. A box under this is scored down by how far short it falls, and the preference is soft throughout: nothing stops an undersized box from being claimed when it is the only candidate left.

PreferredMaxVolume.tooltip: Soft preference for maximum box volume (in voxels). 0 = no maximum preference.
PreferredMaxVolume.semantics: Counted in voxels like `Preferred Min Volume`, and equally soft: it scores an oversized box down rather than preventing it. `Max Cell Size` is the hard limit, and it is the one that actually cuts a box up.

VolumePreferenceWeight.tooltip: How strongly the volume preference affects scoring.
VolumePreferenceWeight.semantics: The band's penalty is raised to this before multiplying into the score. At 0 the preference is dropped outright even with a band set on both sides.

bUseHeuristicMergeGating.tooltip: Enable heuristic-based merge control. When enabled, the Heuristics input pin is required.
bUseHeuristicMergeGating.semantics: Turning this on is what makes the consumer's Heuristics pin required, so the node errors out until a stack is wired rather than carrying on ungated. The gate only speaks where the cluster does: two touching groups with no edge running between them merge whatever the heuristics say.

MergeScoreThreshold.tooltip: Boundary edge score above which merging is discouraged. 0 = only merge if all boundary edges score 0 (very strict). 1 = merge freely regardless of edge scores (effectively disabled).
MergeScoreThreshold.semantics: The test is against the average score of the edges running between the two groups, so one expensive edge is diluted by every cheap one beside it and a wide boundary is easier to merge across than a narrow one.

UPCGExDecompositionInstancedFactory.name: Decomposition Factory
UPCGExDecompositionInstancedFactory.purpose: The shared base of the decomposition rules that Cluster : Decomposition picks from. It carries no settings, and it never appears in the palette on its own. What it fixes is the contract every rule answers to: one group per Vtx, a count of the groups made, and a size for each group whether or not the rule has a box of its own. It also carries the one declaration that reaches outside the rule's own panel, which is whether the rule needs heuristics.
UPCGExDecompositionInstancedFactory.situation: Reading any of the Decompose sub-nodes and needing to know what all seven guarantee about the grouping they hand back.

mechanism.text: **Cluster : Decomposition** creates one of these per cluster and asks it, once, for a grouping of that cluster's Vtx. What comes back is a group number for every Vtx plus the number of groups made, and a Vtx the rule chose not to place comes back unplaced, which the consumer writes as -1. When cell sizes have been asked for, a rule that works in boxes hands back its own boxes and every other rule has the bounding box of its members' positions filled in on its behalf, so that attribute is never left empty whichever rule is selected. A rule also declares whether it needs heuristics, and that single answer is what turns the consumer's Heuristics pin from an advanced pin into a required one.

UPCGExDecompSpectral.name: Decompose : Spectral
UPCGExDecompSpectral.purpose: The one rule of the seven that decides on connectivity. It bisects the cluster at its weakest boundary, then bisects the halves, so Vtx that are strongly connected stay together even when they sit far apart. Every edge carries a strength, and that strength is whatever the heuristics stack charges for crossing it, which is why the consumer's Heuristics pin becomes required the moment this rule is selected. The heuristics are the control surface here: anything you can write onto the Vtx or the Edges and score can decide where the cluster comes apart.
UPCGExDecompSpectral.situation: Cutting a cluster where its structure is thin, so the pieces are held together by their own connections instead of by proximity.

mechanism.text: The cluster is split in two where the connections crossing the boundary are weakest, and each half is split again until the requested number of pieces is reached or the structure runs out of boundaries to cut. Strength comes from the heuristics: each edge is scored in both directions and the two are averaged, and the split settles where the total strength crossing it is lowest. `Partition Mode` decides what happens on a piece with no clear boundary left. Every Vtx is placed, and a piece is a set of Vtx with no spatial meaning at all.

off_label.claim: With `Num Partitions` at two and `Natural`, the two groups are the two sides of the cluster's single weakest boundary, so the edges whose endpoints hold different ids are that boundary: the decomposition doubles as a bottleneck finder.
off_label.grounded_in: the Natural branch cutting a single subset at the Fiedler sign

PartitionMode.tooltip: How the requested partition count is reconciled with the graph's natural spectral cuts.

NumPartitions.tooltip: Target number of partitions to produce. Whether it is met exactly depends on Partition Mode and graph connectivity (Exact reaches it when the cluster has at least that many valid nodes; Natural may fall short on degenerate cuts).
NumPartitions.semantics: The count is chased down the tree: the first half of a split gets half the request, and the second half gets whatever the first did not spend, so an odd number is met by an uneven tree instead of being rounded away. `Natural` still falls short wherever the structure offers no further boundary, and `Exact` makes up the difference afterwards by splitting the largest piece again.

MaxIterations.tooltip: Maximum iterations for power iteration convergence.

ConvergenceTolerance.semantics: Measured on how much the estimate moved between two rounds, and the search stops at whichever arrives first, this or `Max Iterations`. Running out of rounds is not an error and is not reported: the best estimate so far is used as though it had settled, so a cut that looks arbitrary on a large cluster is worth retesting with more iterations before blaming the mode.

hints.text: The heuristic score enters as connection strength, so the edges the stack charges most for are the ones the cut avoids, and the cheap edges are what gets severed. To make the boundary fall where cost is high, invert the heuristic.

UPCGExDecompThreshold.name: Decompose : Threshold
UPCGExDecompThreshold.purpose: Groups the Vtx by a number they already carry. Nothing spatial and nothing structural: one numeric attribute is read off the Vtx and its range is cut into bands, so two Vtx at opposite ends of the cluster share a group whenever their values are close. `Binning Mode` picks between bands of equal width and bands of equal population.
UPCGExDecompThreshold.situation: A value already written onto the Vtx, a height or a density or a sampled field, that has to become discrete groups the rest of the graph can act on.

mechanism.text: The named value is read from every Vtx of the cluster, and the group is decided by where that value falls among the values of that cluster. The range is measured per cluster, so the same number can land in different bands in two clusters of one execution. Bands that catch nothing are closed up, so the number of groups is `Num Bins` at most and often fewer. Every Vtx is placed, and the edges are never read, so a group is a band of values and not a connected piece of the cluster.

off_label.claim: With `Num Bins` at its minimum of two and `Uniform` binning, the split falls at the midpoint of whatever range that cluster happens to span, which gives an above-or-below marker for a value whose range you do not know in advance and cannot write into a fixed-threshold filter.
off_label.grounded_in: the Uniform branch measuring min and max from the cluster's own values before cutting

off_label.claim: In `Quantile`, setting `Num Bins` to the cluster's Vtx count gives every Vtx its own group numbered in ascending order of the value, so the cell id becomes a per-cluster rank.
off_label.grounded_in: the Quantile branch computing nodes per bin as the total divided by the bin count, floored at one

AttributeSelector.tooltip: The numeric attribute to read values from.
AttributeSelector.semantics: The whole selection is read, so a single component of a vector and a point property both resolve as readily as a plain numeric attribute does. Values are read from the Vtx dataset, one per Vtx.
AttributeSelector.trap: When the selection resolves to nothing readable the rule places nothing for the whole cluster. The node warns, and every Vtx of that cluster comes out at the unplaced id with the cell count attribute at zero and the cell size attribute at zero.

NumBins.semantics: A ceiling, not a count. Bands that catch no Vtx are closed up, and in `Quantile` a cluster holding fewer Vtx than bins gives one group per Vtx, so the number of groups written is only ever this or fewer. A cluster whose values are all the same comes back as a single group in `Uniform`, whatever this is set to.

BinningMode.semantics: `Quantile` cuts the sorted list by position, not by value, so a run of identical values can be split across two groups. The last group also takes the remainder of the division and can end up noticeably larger than the rest.

UPCGExDefaultActorContentFilter.name: Default Actor Content Filter
UPCGExDefaultActorContentFilter.purpose: Decides which actors in a level count when something reads that level. A Level Collection consults it while baking an entry's bounds, and a level data exporter consults it while choosing what to export, so one object answers what matters in a level for both. A new collection or exporter arrives with an instance already in the slot: the class named by Default Content Filter Class in the project's Collections settings, falling back to Default Actor Content Filter, whose tag and class include and exclude lists are its whole panel. The slot is Blueprintable, so a project with its own idea of what counts writes a subclass and assigns that instead.
UPCGExDefaultActorContentFilter.situation: A level being read into a collection is full of gameplay volumes, spawn markers and helper actors that should not count toward what that level is.

mechanism.text: One actor in, kept or rejected out, asked once per actor while an editor-time walk reads a level. Two rejections happen before whatever sits in the slot is consulted at all: an actor tagged StaticIgnore, and a socket-provider actor set to strip itself from export. Leave the slot empty and the built-in rejection of engine infrastructure is the entire remaining answer. Default Actor Content Filter runs that same infrastructure rejection as the first thing in its own implementation, then narrows what survives through its four lists.

off_label.claim: Additional System Actor Classes in the project's Collections settings is matched against an actor's own instance name as well as its class name, so naming one placed actor there suppresses that single actor across every level read, without editing any collection.
off_label.grounded_in: UPCGExActorContentFilter::IsInfrastructureActor tests both the actor's class FName and the actor's own FName against the combined system-actor name set

IncludeTags.tooltip: If non-empty, only actors with at least one of these tags pass.
IncludeTags.semantics: The four lists are four independent conditions and an actor has to clear all of them, so a tag listed here does not rescue an actor that a non-empty Include Classes fails to match, and an exclude entry outranks any include entry. All four narrow what the infrastructure rejection already allowed, so nothing listed here brings back a hidden actor, an editor-only actor or a registered system actor.

ExcludeTags.tooltip: Actors with any of these tags are rejected.

IncludeClasses.tooltip: If non-empty, only actors of these classes (or subclasses) pass.
IncludeClasses.semantics: Both class lists resolve their rows against what is already in memory and never load a class to answer, so a row pointing at a Blueprint class the editor has not loaded is skipped. A row naming a compiled class always resolves.
IncludeClasses.trap: A skipped row withholds a match here and withholds a rejection on Exclude Classes, so the same collection can bake different bounds depending on what the editor happened to have loaded when the rebuild ran.

ExcludeClasses.tooltip: Actors of these classes (or subclasses) are rejected.

hints.text: A Blueprint subclass that overrides Passes Filter replaces the infrastructure rejection rather than adding to it. Hidden actors, editor-only actors, main-world-only actors, level script actors, Info actors, non-volume brushes, navigation data and registered system actor classes all start counting again unless the subclass rejects them itself. Default Actor Content Filter keeps them out because its own implementation runs that rejection first.

A Blueprint override receives the owning collection and the entry index as context, and both are empty when the call comes from a level data exporter rather than from a collection entry: the collection is null and the index is -1. Logic that branches on either has to handle that case.

UPCGExDefaultActorMeshClassificator.name: Default Actor Mesh Classificator
UPCGExDefaultActorMeshClassificator.purpose: Decides which actors a level export opens up. Exporting a level sorts every actor it keeps into one of two shapes, a mesh container harvested for its static mesh components or an actor reference carrying the class and its property delta, and this object answers which. The exporter holds one instance in its Mesh Classificator slot, minted from whichever class the plugin's collection settings name as the default, and the shipped default answers from class and tag lists. The base is Blueprintable, so a project whose scenery does not live on Static Mesh Actors writes a subclass rather than reworking the export.
UPCGExDefaultActorMeshClassificator.situation: A level export came back with hand-placed scenery as actor references when those actors should have arrived as staged meshes.

mechanism.text: An instance lives on the level exporter, which asks it about every actor that survived the exporter's content filter, during the staging rebuild of a level-sourced PCGDataAsset row. Level instances referencing a world are settled before the question is asked, so they are never offered. Approval is a precondition and not a verdict: an approved actor exports as a mesh container only when it also owns a static mesh component holding a valid mesh, with at least one instance when that component is instanced, and it exports as an actor reference otherwise. The two outcomes are exclusive and carry different payloads: a mesh container contributes one staged point per mesh component, one per instance where that component is instanced, and keeps nothing of itself but its name, while an actor reference contributes a single point carrying its class and its captured property delta.

off_label.claim: Adding a blueprint class to the include list flattens it: the export harvests the meshes inside it and stops spawning the blueprint, which turns a logic-bearing prop into plain geometry in the shared mesh collection.
off_label.grounded_in: ClassifyActor routes approved actors into the mesh extraction pass, which walks every static mesh component and keeps nothing of the actor beyond its ActorName attribute.

IncludeClasses.tooltip: Actors of these classes (or subclasses) are treated as mesh containers and will be parsed for static/instanced mesh components. Defaults to AStaticMeshActor.
IncludeClasses.semantics: The two include lists are alternatives and either one is enough: matching a class or carrying a tag makes an actor a candidate. Empty both and nothing in the level is ever opened up, so the export comes back as actor references only, each one spawning its whole blueprint instead of the meshes inside it.

IncludeTags.tooltip: Actors with any of these tags are treated as mesh containers.

ExcludeClasses.tooltip: Actors of these classes (or subclasses) are never treated as mesh containers, even if they match include rules.
ExcludeClasses.semantics: Excluding is not skipping. A rejected actor still exports, as an actor reference carrying its class and property delta, so everything the mesh harvest would have dropped survives instead. Removing an actor from the export altogether is the Content Filter's job, not this one's.

ExcludeTags.tooltip: Actors with any of these tags are never treated as mesh containers.

hints.text: A Blueprint subclass that leaves Should Classify As Mesh unimplemented inherits the base answer, which is no. The export still succeeds, and the level comes back as actor references with no mesh points in it at all.

UPCGExDefaultBoundsEvaluator.name: Default Bounds Evaluator
UPCGExDefaultBoundsEvaluator.purpose: Decides what counts as an actor's size when a staging rebuild measures one. Three surfaces bake bounds from live actors, an Actor Collection entry, a Level Collection entry and the level data exporter, and none of them measures anything itself: each hands the actor to whatever evaluator sits in its Bounds Evaluator slot. The shipped Default Bounds Evaluator unions the world-space boxes of the actor's primitive components, with four toggles for the components that usually should not count. Subclassing the base in Blueprint is how a project answers what counts in an actor once, for every collection that asks.
UPCGExDefaultBoundsEvaluator.situation: An entry bakes bounds far larger than anything visible on the actor, and every point staged from it fits against the wrong box.

mechanism.text: A staging rebuild hands the evaluator one live actor and takes back one box. The default gathers that actor's primitive components, drops the ones its toggles reject, and unions what survives into a world-space box; an actor left with nothing yields an invalid box, which reads downstream as no bounds. What the host does with that box differs: an Actor Collection entry keeps it as its staged bounds, a Level Collection entry folds it into a union across every actor its Content Filter kept, and the level data exporter writes it as that actor's own bounds beside its transform. The abstract base is what a Blueprint subclasses, and it measures every registered primitive component with no exclusions at all, so an override that defers to the parent gets the unfiltered box.

off_label.claim: A Blueprint evaluator that answers with an invalid box for an actor drops that actor out of a Level Collection entry's union without changing it, which turns the measuring slot into a second per-actor gate sitting behind the Content Filter.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExLevelCollectionEntry::UpdateStaging folds each evaluated box into the entry union with FBox::operator+=, which leaves the union unchanged when the incoming box is invalid

bOnlyCollidingComponents.tooltip: When true, only components with collision enabled contribute to bounds.
bOnlyCollidingComponents.semantics: The test is per component, not per actor, so the box narrows to the collision shell of whatever geometry has collision and ignores the rest of the actor entirely. An actor whose components all sit on No Collision contributes nothing, and on a Level Collection that actor disappears from the entry's union while still passing the Content Filter.

bIgnoreLightComponents.tooltip: When true, light components are excluded from bounds computation.
bIgnoreLightComponents.semantics: Only components carrying geometry are gathered, and light components are not among them, so nothing that reaches this test is ever a light. Ignore Editor Only Components is the exclusion that actually keeps a light actor from inflating an entry, by dropping the sprite and arrow visualizers a light carries in an editor world.
bIgnoreLightComponents.trap: Toggling this changes no measurement in either direction. An actor still measuring larger than its geometry is being inflated by something else, most often a visualizer that survives because the editor-only exclusion is off.

bIgnoreEditorOnlyComponents.tooltip: When true, editor-only components (billboard sprites, arrow visualizers, etc.) are excluded. Disabling this re-introduces the inflated bounds those visualizers add.

bIncludeFromChildActors.tooltip: When true, child actor components are included in bounds computation.
bIncludeFromChildActors.semantics: Off, only components the actor owns directly are gathered, so a blueprint that builds its shape out of child actor components measures as though it were empty. On, those components join the gather and then face the same collision and editor-only tests as everything else.
bIncludeFromChildActors.trap: An Actor Collection entry pointing at a blueprint whose geometry lives entirely in child actors bakes empty bounds with this off, and empty bounds are indistinguishable downstream from an entry that failed to measure at all.

hints.text: The evaluator is handed the owning collection and the entry index as context, and the level data exporter passes neither. A Blueprint that varies its answer by entry works on a collection and silently falls back to its no-context branch when the exporter runs it.

The class exposes a second overridable event, Evaluate Actor Local Bounds, which accumulates the same qualifying components in the actor's own frame with actor scale left out. Nothing in the plugin calls it: both collection types and the level data exporter read Evaluate Actor Bounds, so overriding the local variant alone changes no baked bounds.

UPCGExDefaultLevelDataExporter.name: Default Level Data Exporter
UPCGExDefaultLevelDataExporter.purpose: The exporter that runs when a PCG Data Asset Collection captures a level and nothing else is assigned. It reads the level once and splits what it finds three ways: mesh components become one point each, actors become one point each carrying their class and the differences from its defaults, and nested level instances become one point each pointing at the world they reference. Which actors count, which of them are mesh containers, and what an actor's bounds are, are three separate objects assigned on it, so most of what a project wants to change here is a setting rather than a subclass. Classification and a post-export step are the two C++ overrides for the rest.
UPCGExDefaultLevelDataExporter.situation: A level was dressed by hand, and the capture has to keep its meshes, its configured actors and its nested level instances apart.

mechanism.text: One run reads the world's persistent level and sorts every actor the content filter admits into three kinds: nested level instances, mesh containers, and everything else. Each kind becomes its own point dataset on the generated asset, Meshes, Actors and Levels: one point per mesh component and one per instance of an instanced component, one point per actor, one point per level instance. Mesh points sit at their component's transform and carry the mesh's own bounds; actor and level points sit at the actor's transform and carry what the bounds evaluator returns. Identical things collapse into one entry whose weight is how many points stand behind it: meshes match on mesh asset and component settings, actors on class and captured configuration, levels on the world they reference. A level where nothing is admitted produces no data, and the row stages nothing.

off_label.claim: Every generated entry's weight is the number of points standing behind it, so a capture doubles as a frequency census of the level: anything picking from the resulting entries at random reproduces how often that level used each mesh, each configured class and each nested level.
off_label.grounded_in: In the collection-generation phase, mesh entry weight is set to the bucket's total contributing point count, and actor and level entry weights to their bucket's actor count.

ContentFilter.tooltip: Actor content filter. Defaults to UPCGExDefaultActorContentFilter.
ContentFilter.default:
Cast<UPCGExActorContentFilter>(
		ObjectInitializer.CreateDefaultSubobject(this, TEXT("ContentFilter"),
		                                         UPCGExActorContentFilter::StaticClass(), FilterClass, false, false))
ContentFilter.semantics: Membership only: it decides which actors reach the export, never which kind they come out as. Two rejections happen before it is consulted and nothing assigned here admits them back: actors tagged `StaticIgnore`, and socket-provider actors that ask to be stripped from content scans, so a socket marker that opts out never becomes a point. The shipped one rejects infrastructure first (hidden, editor-only and main-world-only actors, level script actors, Info actors, brushes that are not volumes, navigation data, and registered system actor classes), then narrows what is left by its own tag and class lists.

MeshClassificator.tooltip: Determines which actors are treated as mesh containers (parsed for static/instanced mesh components). Defaults to UPCGExDefaultActorMeshClassificator.
MeshClassificator.semantics: Approval is necessary and not sufficient: an approved actor still has to own a static mesh component, or a subclass of one, holding a valid mesh, and an instanced component with no instances does not count. Level instances are decided before this is consulted, so an actor referencing a world is never a mesh container whatever the rules say. The shipped one approves Static Mesh Actors and nothing else until its own include lists are widened by class or by tag, with excludes taking precedence over includes.
MeshClassificator.trap: A Blueprint actor built around static mesh components is exported as an actor by default, and the two kinds are exclusive: its components contribute no mesh points and no mesh entries. Widening this is what turns a kit of Blueprint props into mesh picks.

BoundsEvaluator.default:
Cast<UPCGExBoundsEvaluator>(
		ObjectInitializer.CreateDefaultSubobject(this, TEXT("BoundsEvaluator"),
		                                         UPCGExBoundsEvaluator::StaticClass(), EvalClass, false, false))
BoundsEvaluator.semantics: It answers for actor points and level points. Mesh points never consult it: they carry the source mesh's own bounding box, which is what keeps every instance of one mesh identically sized whatever actor it came from. What it returns is in world space, and the point stores it relative to its actor's transform. The shipped one accumulates registered primitive components and can be told to ignore editor-only components, light components, and anything without collision.

bGenerateCollections.tooltip: When true, the exporter builds embedded mesh/actor collections and writes collection entry hashes instead of raw metadata.
bGenerateCollections.semantics: On, an actor collection is built inline from the actor entries and the actor points get their pick hashes here, while the mesh and nested-level entries are reported to the collection, which pools them across rows and writes those hashes afterwards. Off, no entries are built and no hashes are written: mesh points carry a `Mesh` asset path, actor points an `ActorClass` path, level points a `LevelAsset` path, and none of that is something the staging routes resolve. `ActorName` is written either way. Material capture, property deltas and the schema policy all hang off this being on.
bGenerateCollections.trap: Off, a level-sourced row still stages successfully. It stages an asset whose points carry asset paths instead of picks, so the failure surfaces downstream, where a spawn route finds nothing to resolve.

bCaptureMaterialOverrides.tooltip: When true, material overrides from source components will be captured and stored as material variants on the mesh collection entries.
bCaptureMaterialOverrides.semantics: Component settings decide which mesh points share an entry, and override materials are deliberately left out of that comparison, so components differing only in their materials always land in the same entry. This decides what becomes of those materials. On, each distinct combination becomes one equally weighted variant on the entry, the entry's own descriptor is stripped of materials so the variants are the only source, and a component that overrode nothing records no variant and keeps the mesh's own materials. Off, the first component to reach the entry donates its overrides to the descriptor.
bCaptureMaterialOverrides.trap: Off does not mean no material overrides. One arbitrary contributor's materials become the entry's, and every point of that entry spawns with them, including points whose source component had different ones or none.

bCapturePropertyDeltas.tooltip: When true and bGenerateCollections is enabled, capture per-instance property deltas (CDO diff) on actor collection entries. Only applies to "Actor"-classified actors.
bCapturePropertyDeltas.semantics: The captured difference is also part of what makes two actors the same entry, so this decides how finely one class splits: on, a class placed in three distinct configurations becomes three entries, each spawning as its instances were configured; off, it becomes one entry that spawns as the class defaults. Mesh-classified actors sit outside this entirely, since they contribute no actor entry to carry a delta.

SchemaMergePolicy.tooltip: Policy used when merging actor-component schemas into the generated embedded actor collection's CollectionProperties + per-entry PropertyOverrides. Forwarded to UPCGExActorCollection::RebuildPropertiesFromActorComponents and also mirrored onto the embedded collection's own SchemaMergePolicy field so manual rebuilds stay consistent.
SchemaMergePolicy.semantics: The scan behind it reads one representative actor per generated entry, the first of its bucket, rather than every actor that contributed to the entry.
SchemaMergePolicy.trap: With property deltas off, a bucket is an entire class, so whichever of its actors was met first supplies the property values that class ships with.

ValueTagMode.tooltip: Controls how actor tags in the form Name:Value are handled. Parse: plain tags → bool=true attributes; Name:Value tags → typed attributes; tag string not written. ParseAndKeep: same as Parse, but the name-part of each value tag is also included in the tag string. NoParsing: all tags are treated as plain strings (original behavior).
ValueTagMode.semantics: Tag names become attribute names, and the first actor to declare a name fixes that attribute's type for the whole export: a later actor giving the same name a different type has its value discarded with a warning. Tags are parsed for mesh and level points too, from their source actor, not only for actor points. The mode also decides which tags reach the generated actor entries, and only tags carried by every actor behind an entry survive, so a tag placed on some instances of a class is dropped from it. Under Parse the name part of a `Name:Value` tag is not among the tags considered, under Parse and Keep it is, and under No Parsing the actor's raw tags are.

InstanceTagsAttributeName.tooltip: Output attribute name for the joined per-actor tag string.

hints.text:
## An actor is one kind or the other

An actor treated as a mesh container contributes only mesh points, so its class and its configuration are recorded nowhere. An actor treated as an actor contributes one point at its own transform and no mesh points, even when it owns mesh components. Nothing in the level comes out as both.

UPCGExDestroyActorSettings.name: Destroy Actor
UPCGExDestroyActorSettings.purpose: Destroys named actors, but only ones the PCG component running this graph spawned itself. It reads an attribute of actor references off whatever data it is given, matches them against the component's own record of what it spawned, and destroys the matches. Anything it did not spawn is untouchable, which is what makes it safe to point at a list of references gathered from the level.
UPCGExDestroyActorSettings.situation: Spawned actors that have to go before the rest of a generation continues, selected by a reference list the graph has already built.

mechanism.text: Actor references are collected from every input, deduplicated, and matched against the executing component's record of the actors it spawned, comparing stored paths rather than resolving them. A match that is currently loaded is destroyed and struck from that record; a match that is not loaded stays on it and survives. Every input is forwarded to the output untouched whatever happens, including when the attribute yields no references at all, which warns instead of failing. The whole node runs on the game thread in a single pass.

off_label.claim: Because a destroyed actor is also struck from the component's spawn record, this node can be used to hand an actor over: the actor survives if it is unloaded at the time, and in either case the component stops considering it its own to clean up on the next regeneration.
off_label.grounded_in: matched entries are removed from the managed actor resource's generated list before the destroy pass, and only resolved actors are destroyed

inputs.label: Targets
inputs.note: Any data carrying the actor reference attribute. Every input is scanned, so the references can be spread across several datasets.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: Every input, forwarded by reference and unmodified. The reference attribute still holds the paths of the actors that were just destroyed.

pins.dynamic: The output mirrors whatever type the input carried, so points in gives points out.

ActorReferenceAttribute.tooltip: Attribute holding the actor references to destroy. FString-typed attributes are parsed as soft object paths.
ActorReferenceAttribute.semantics: Read from every input dataset, and from any domain the attribute happens to live in. An input that does not carry it contributes nothing and is still forwarded.
ActorReferenceAttribute.trap: A misspelled name looks exactly like having nothing to destroy: the node warns that it found no references and passes the data through.

hints.text: The node does nothing when the graph is not executing on a PCG component, because there is then no spawn record to match against.

UPCGExDiscardByOverlapSettings.name: Discard By Overlap
UPCGExDiscardByOverlapSettings.purpose: Resolves conflicts between whole datasets by throwing some of them away. It measures the same overlap **Sample : Overlap Stats** reports, then keeps removing whichever dataset scores worst until nothing conflicts. The unit is the dataset, so nothing is ever partly kept: a layer either survives intact or leaves entirely.
UPCGExDiscardByOverlapSettings.situation: Several candidate layouts scattered over the same ground, where only the ones that do not fight each other should survive.

mechanism.text: Every dataset is scored against every other for how much they overlap, and the scores are combined by the weighting block into one number per dataset. The worst-scoring dataset is discarded, the scores are reconsidered, and it repeats until the survivors no longer conflict. `Logic` decides which end of the scale counts as worst. Because removal is iterative rather than a single pass, discarding one dataset can save another that was only in conflict with it.
steps: Pairwise overlap is measured under the test mode and the threshold.
Scores are combined by the weighting block into one figure per dataset.
The worst dataset is removed and the remaining scores are re-evaluated, until no conflict is left.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: Every candidate dataset. A single dataset conflicts with nothing and always survives.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The datasets that survived. Removal is whole-dataset, so no partial data reaches this pin.

TestMode.semantics: Trades exactness for cost, and the source is candid about which way each errs. `Fast` compares only the datasets' overall bounds, so two layers whose bounding boxes touch conflict even when no points do. `Box` can miss overlaps, and `Sphere` reports some that are not real.
TestMode.trap: Under `Fast` a large sparse dataset conflicts with everything its bounds reach, which usually makes it the first thing discarded regardless of whether any of its points were in the way.

BoundsSource.tooltip: Point bounds to be used to compute overlaps

Expansion.tooltip: Expand bounds by that amount to account for a margin of error due to multiple layers of transformation and lack of OBB

fields.name: DynamicBalance
fields.tooltip: How much of the dynamic weights to account for vs. static ones

fields.name: OverlapCount
fields.tooltip: Overlap count weight (how many sets overlap)

fields.name: OverlapSubCount
fields.tooltip: Overlap Sub-Count weight (how many points overlap)

fields.name: OverlapVolume
fields.tooltip: Overlap volume weight (cumulative volume overlap). Each sub point adds its own intersection volume whether or not it occupies an already computed volume in space.

fields.name: OverlapVolumeDensity
fields.tooltip: Overlap volume density weight (cumulative volume overlap / number of overlapping points)

fields.name: StaticBalance
fields.tooltip: How much of the static weights to account for vs. dynamic ones

fields.name: NumPoints
fields.tooltip: Number of points weight (points in a given set)

fields.name: Volume
fields.tooltip: Volume weight. Each sub point adds its own intersection volume whether or not it occupies an already computed volume in space.

fields.name: VolumeDensity
fields.tooltip: Volume density.

fields.name: CustomTagWeight
fields.tooltip: Weight of custom tags scores, if any.

fields.name: TagScores
fields.tooltip: Lets you add custom 'score' by tags. If the tag is found on the collection, its score will be added to the computation, letting you have more granular control.

fields.name: DataScoreWeight
fields.tooltip: Weight of custom tags scores, if any.

fields.name: DataScores
fields.tooltip: Lets you add extra custom 'score' using @Data attributes.

Weighting.semantics: How the several overlap measurements are folded into the one number the pruning order uses. This is where a graph decides whether sheer overlap count matters more than overlapped volume, and it is the setting that most changes which datasets survive.

Logic.semantics: Decides which end of the combined score is pruned first. It does not decide what a good score is, only which direction the node reads it in, so it has to be set alongside the weighting block rather than independently of it.

MinThreshold.tooltip: The minimum amount two sub-points must overlap to be added to the comparison.  The higher, the more "overlap" there must be.
MinThreshold.semantics: How much two points must overlap before the pair counts toward a score. `Threshold Measure` decides whether the figure is a world distance or a fraction of average point size, and the shipped configuration is the fraction.

ThresholdMeasure.tooltip: How to interpret the min overlap value.  Discrete means distance in world space  Relative means uses percentage (0-1) of the averaged radius.

bIncludeFilteredInMetrics.tooltip: If enabled, points that are filtered out from overlap detection are still accounted for in static metrics/maths. i.e they still participate to the overall bounds shape etc instead of being thoroughly ignored.
bIncludeFilteredInMetrics.semantics: Decides whether points excluded from overlap detection still count toward the totals the scores are measured against. Left on, a dataset's score reflects its full size even when only part of it was tested, which keeps scores comparable between datasets that were filtered differently.

hints.text: Pruning is iterative and order-dependent, so the survivors are not the set with the least overlap overall. Removing the worst dataset can clear the only conflict another one had, which then survives on a score it would not have won in a single pass.

UPCGExDiscardByPointCountSettings.name: Discard By Point Count
UPCGExDiscardByPointCountSettings.purpose: Splits datasets by how many points they hold. A dataset whose count falls outside the band leaves on Discarded instead of Out; nothing is deleted and no points are touched. It exists because a generator that emits one dataset per island or per cell routinely produces a tail of two-point and one-point results that are not worth carrying further.
UPCGExDiscardByPointCountSettings.situation: A pin carrying many datasets of wildly different sizes, where the small ones, the huge ones, or both are noise for what comes next.

mechanism.text: Each input dataset is measured once and kept when its point count sits inside the band, inclusive at both ends. Datasets outside it are re-pinned to Discarded rather than dropped, so the two pins together always carry everything that came in. Both bounds are optional and default to open, so with neither enabled every dataset is kept. Whichever of the two pins received nothing is deactivated, which culls the nodes hanging off it.

off_label.claim: With both bounds set to the same value, Discarded carries every dataset except those of exactly that size, which turns the node into an exact-count gate.
off_label.grounded_in: the keep test is an inclusive range check against the resolved minimum and maximum

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The point datasets to measure. Forwarded, never duplicated.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: Datasets inside the band. Deactivated when every input was discarded.

outputs.label: Discarded
outputs.note: Datasets outside it, whole and unmodified. Deactivated when nothing was discarded.

MinPointCount.tooltip: Discarded if point count is less than
MinPointCount.semantics: Inclusive: a dataset holding exactly this many points is kept. A negative value disables the lower bound as surely as clearing the toggle does.

MaxPointCount.tooltip: Discarded if point count is more than
MaxPointCount.semantics: Inclusive as well, so a dataset of exactly this size is kept rather than discarded. This was not always true, and older graphs may have been authored around the off-by-one.

bAllowEmptyOutputs.tooltip: Whether or not to allow empty outputs (either discarded or not)
bAllowEmptyOutputs.semantics: Applies to both pins. Left off, a dataset with no points at all is emitted on neither pin, which is why an empty dataset can vanish rather than appear under Discarded.

hints.text: This measures datasets, not points. To remove points from within a dataset, use a filter and one of the filtering nodes.

UPCGExDiscardSameSettings.name: Discard Same
UPCGExDiscardSameSettings.purpose: Finds datasets that are duplicates of each other and routes all but one of each family to Discarded. Sameness is decided by up to four cheap comparisons run over the whole dataset: its bounds, its point count, the set of positions it occupies, and hashes of chosen attributes. Nothing is deleted; the duplicates leave on the second pin, so the split is inspectable.
UPCGExDiscardSameSettings.situation: A pin carrying datasets that several upstream branches produced independently, where the same shape has arrived more than once.

mechanism.text: Every dataset is reduced to a small set of values first: a point count, a bounds hash quantised by its tolerance, a hash of the sorted set of quantised point positions, and one hash per configured attribute. Each dataset is then compared against every other, and Test Mode decides whether all the enabled comparisons have to agree or any one of them is enough. A dataset with at least one twin is then kept or discarded according to Mode. Discarded datasets are re-pinned rather than dropped, so Out and Discarded together carry everything that came in.

off_label.claim: The position test hashes the set of occupied positions rather than the ordered list, so two datasets holding the same points in different order compare equal. Turning off the point count test as well makes it a test for occupying the same space, which is what identifies a dataset that was merely reordered or partially re-emitted.
off_label.grounded_in: the position hash is built from a TSet of quantised position hashes, sorted before hashing, with point count carried by a separate test

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The point datasets to compare against each other. Forwarded, never duplicated.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The datasets that survived.

outputs.label: Discarded
outputs.note: Duplicates, whole and unmodified.

Mode.tooltip: Which duplicate to keep when matches are found.
Mode.semantics: Names which end of the arrival order leaves first, not which one is kept. FIFO discards the earliest of each family, so the last arrival survives; LIFO discards the later ones, so the first survives; All discards every dataset that has a twin, keeping none of them.
Mode.trap: Order here is the order the datasets arrived on the pin, which is upstream wiring order and not something this node controls.

TestMode.tooltip: How to combine multiple test conditions.
TestMode.semantics: And requires every enabled comparison to agree before two datasets count as the same, which is the strict reading. Or calls them the same as soon as one comparison agrees, so with bounds and point count both on, two unrelated datasets that merely share a size are duplicates.

TestBoundsTolerance.tooltip: Test collection bounds equality, within tolerance
TestBoundsTolerance.semantics: Quantises the bounds corners before hashing, so it is a grid size rather than a distance: two datasets agree when their corners land in the same cell of that grid, which means a pair straddling a cell edge can differ by less than the tolerance and still not match.

TestPointCountTolerance.tooltip: Test collection point count equality, within tolerance
TestPointCountTolerance.semantics: Compared as a near-equality on the counts, so a tolerance of two makes datasets of 100 and 101 points the same size.

TestPositionTolerance.tooltip: Test point positions equality, within tolerance. It computes space occupation, and does not account for point count.
TestPositionTolerance.semantics: Quantises each position before it enters the set, with the same grid caveat as the bounds tolerance. The comparison ignores how many points sit at each spot, so a dataset with duplicated coincident points matches one without them.

TestAttributesHash.semantics: None skips attribute comparison entirely. Single uses the one overridable config below. List uses the array, optionally appending the single config as well.
TestAttributesHash.trap: Under And, the attribute hashes are compared whether or not this is set to None; with no hashes configured that comparison trivially passes, so it never blocks a match. Under Or it only contributes when this is not None.

AttributeHashConfigs.tooltip: Build a hash from a single attribute and test it against the others.

fields.name: SourceAttribute
fields.tooltip: Which attribute should be used to generate the hash

fields.name: Scope
fields.tooltip: Which values will be combined to a hash

fields.name: Sorting
fields.tooltip: Whether to sort hash components or not.

AttributeHashConfigs.semantics: Order matters: the hashes are compared position by position, so two datasets configured with the same attributes in a different order would not be comparable. In practice every dataset in one run shares this node's configuration, so the ordering is only a concern when a hash fails to bind on one dataset and not another.

bIncludeSingleAttribute.tooltip: Also include the single overridable attribute config below.
bIncludeSingleAttribute.semantics: Puts the single config at the head of the list, ahead of the array entries.

AttributeHashConfig.tooltip: Build a hash from a single attribute and test it against the others.

fields.name: SourceAttribute
fields.tooltip: Which attribute should be used to generate the hash

fields.name: Scope
fields.tooltip: Which values will be combined to a hash

fields.name: Sorting
fields.tooltip: Whether to sort hash components or not.

hints.text: A comparison that is switched off does not merely stop mattering: each dataset falls back to its own position in the input for that value, which can never equal another dataset's. Under Or that is harmless, and under And it means the enabled comparisons alone decide.

UPCGExDispatchSubgraphSettings.name: Dispatch Subgraphs
UPCGExDispatchSubgraphSettings.purpose: Runs a subgraph chosen by the data rather than by the wiring. Each row of the Drivers input names a graph as an asset path and can carry values that are written into that graph's user parameters before it runs, so one node stands in for a fan of subgraph nodes that would otherwise have to be authored by hand. Rows that resolve to the same graph with the same parameter values are collapsed, so the count of executions follows the distinct configurations rather than the row count. It accepts graph instances as well as graphs, using the instance's presets as the base the overrides are written over.
UPCGExDispatchSubgraphSettings.situation: A table of work where each row names which graph should process it and with what settings, and the set of graphs is not known when the parent graph is authored.

mechanism.text: Every row of every Drivers input is read for the Graph Path Attribute; empty values are skipped in silence. For each resolved graph the node works out which of the row's values map onto that graph's user parameters, then groups rows by graph identity plus those values, comparing them value by value rather than trusting a hash. One dynamic subgraph is scheduled per group, fed the graph's own defaults with the group's overrides written in, plus whichever declared Custom Input Pins the graph has matching inputs for. The node then parks until every dispatch finishes and routes their outputs by pin label. A graph that is or contains the running graph is refused, as is one whose Required input pins are not all declared here, each warned about once.

off_label.claim: With no override sources at all, the node degenerates into a deduplicating runner: a thousand rows naming ten graphs schedule ten executions, which makes it a way to run a set of graphs named by data exactly once each.
off_label.grounded_in: the group key is graph identity plus the applied override list, which is empty when no driver attribute matches a user parameter

off_label.claim: Attributes To Tags stamps the driver row's values onto every output of the dispatch that row produced, which is what lets a downstream matching rule tie results back to the row that asked for them.
off_label.grounded_in: the per-group tag set is built from the first contributing entry and appended to every gathered output in GatherDispatchOutputs

inputs.label: Drivers
inputs.note: Points or attribute sets. Each point or row is one candidate dispatch. Never forwarded into the dispatched graphs. Renamed by Drivers Pin Label.

inputs.label: One pin per Custom Input Pins entry
inputs.note: Declared by the user and forwarded identically to every dispatch, matched to the subgraph's own input pins by exact label. A subgraph that does not declare that label never sees the data.

outputs.label: One pin per Custom Output Pins entry
outputs.note: Receives subgraph outputs whose pin label matches exactly.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: Everything the dispatched graphs emitted that matched no declared output pin. Renamed by Output Pin Label.

GraphPathAttribute.tooltip: Attribute on the Drivers input holding the subgraph reference as a soft object path. Empty values are ignored (no warning).
GraphPathAttribute.semantics: Read per row as a soft object path. A row whose value is empty is skipped without a warning, which makes an empty path the intended way to say this row dispatches nothing. A value that names something that is not a graph or graph instance does warn.

bAutoMatchByName.tooltip: If enabled, any driver attribute whose name exactly matches a subgraph user-parameter is applied as an override.
bAutoMatchByName.semantics: Turns every driver attribute whose name is exactly a user-parameter name into an override. Convenient, and worth turning off when the drivers carry bookkeeping attributes that happen to collide with parameter names.

OverrideRemap.tooltip: Explicit source -> target-parameter remaps, for when the driver source name differs from the parameter name. Takes precedence over auto-match. The source may be an attribute name or a point-property selector ($Transform, $Density, $Position, ...); point-property sources apply only to point drivers.
OverrideRemap.semantics: Maps a driver source onto a differently named parameter, and wins over auto-match for that parameter. The source side may be a point property selector rather than an attribute name, which only resolves on point drivers; on an attribute set the override is skipped.

DriversPinLabel.tooltip: Label of the required Drivers input pin. Rename it if a dispatched subgraph declares an input pin with the same label (custom pins colliding with this label are never forwarded). Renaming breaks existing edges on that pin.
DriversPinLabel.semantics: Worth changing when a dispatched subgraph declares an input pin called Drivers, because a Custom Input Pin colliding with this label is excluded from forwarding and cannot satisfy a required input either.
DriversPinLabel.trap: Renaming breaks the wires already on the pin.

OutputPinLabel.tooltip: Label of the default output pin (receives subgraph outputs that match no custom output pin). Rename it if it collides with a subgraph output you want routed to a custom pin. Renaming breaks existing edges on that pin.
OutputPinLabel.semantics: Worth changing when a subgraph output is called Out and should reach a custom pin instead of the catch-all.
OutputPinLabel.trap: Renaming breaks the wires already on the pin.

CustomInputPins.tooltip: User-declared input pins, forwarded identically to every dispatched subgraph and matched to the subgraph's inputs by name.
CustomInputPins.semantics: The only route data reaches a dispatched graph. Forwarded whole to every dispatch, so the same data feeds each one; the graph picks up only the pins whose labels it declares.
CustomInputPins.trap: A subgraph with a Required input pin that is not declared here is skipped entirely, with one warning per graph, rather than running with that input empty.

CustomOutputPins.tooltip: User-declared output pins. Subgraph outputs are routed here by exact name; anything unmatched goes to the default Out pin.
CustomOutputPins.semantics: Routing is by exact label. A subgraph output whose label is not declared here is not lost, it lands on the catch-all output pin along with everything else unmatched.

AttributesToTags.tooltip: Driver attributes promoted to tags on every output of the dispatched subgraph, tying outputs back to their source entry. Entries deduplicated into a shared dispatch tag with the FIRST entry's values (the index tag uses that entry's row index within its driver data).
AttributesToTags.semantics: Reads from the driver row, not from the subgraph output.
AttributesToTags.trap: Deduplication happens before tagging, so a group formed from several identical rows is tagged with the first row's values alone, and the index tag names that row's position.

hints.text: The node parks while its dispatches run and is never cached, so it re-dispatches on every execution of the parent graph.

Struct-valued and other extended-typed overrides are compared only within one driver input. Identical struct values arriving on two separate driver datasets dispatch separately, which costs executions but never produces a wrong result.

UPCGExDistanceFilterProviderSettings.name: Filter : Distance
UPCGExDistanceFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Answers how close each element sits to a set of reference points, and turns that into a pass or fail. The reference points arrive on the Targets pin; the node produces a filter on its Filter pin, which any node carrying a filter pin runs once per element. Only the nearest target counts, so the question is always a proximity one, measured against a threshold that is either a constant or read per element. Both ends of the measurement are configurable, so it can run location to location, or surface to surface using each point's own bounds.
UPCGExDistanceFilterProviderSettings.situation: A second point set is on hand, and whether an element survives depends on how near it sits to that set.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this filter once per element: the distance to the nearest target is measured, compared against the threshold, and that single comparison is the verdict. Every dataset on the Targets pin is searched as one pool, so adding a second target dataset can only bring the nearest target closer. An element is never measured against itself, so the same dataset can safely feed both a consumer and this node's Targets pin. Target data is indexed once, on this node, and every consumer wired to its Filter pin shares that index; two identically configured copies of the node build the same index twice.

off_label.claim: Feed one dataset into both the consumer and the Targets pin and the filter becomes a self-spacing test: each element measures to its nearest neighbour within its own set, because the search skips the probe element itself while keeping the rest of the data.
off_label.grounded_in: the bSelf plus matching-index skip inside PCGExMatching::FTargetsHandler::FindClosestTarget, which excludes only the probe element, and IgnoreList carrying the whole dataset only when bIgnoreSelf is set

off_label.claim: Leave the Source end of Distance Details on Center, set the Target end to a bounds mode, keep Overlap Is Zero on, and compare with `<=` against a threshold of zero. An element sitting inside a target's bounds then measures zero, so the filter answers containment rather than proximity.
off_label.grounded_in: the BoxBounds clamp in PCGExMath::GetSpatializedCenter, which returns the probe location itself once it is inside the box, and the bOverlap dot-product test in TDistancesBase::GetDistSquared whose result FTargetsHandler::FindClosestTarget substitutes zero for

inputs.label: Targets
inputs.note: The reference points distances are measured against. Several datasets are accepted and searched as one pool, and the same data wired twice is counted once. The threshold is read on the data being tested, never here.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match rules deciding which target datasets each tested dataset is allowed to see. The pin is always present, sitting among the advanced pins until Data Matching is switched on.
inputs.condition: when Data Matching Mode is All or Any

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node produces. It carries the point-filter type, so every filter pin accepts it, Vtx and Edge pins included.

hints.text: An empty Targets pin does not stop the node. Taking a data input is what makes Missing Data Policy live here, and it defaults to Fail, so the node still emits a filter and that filter rejects every element. Under Pass and Fail the node says nothing, since the policy is what answers the missing input, and the symptom downstream is an empty result with no explanation. Only Error logs it, and Error cancels the node.

An attribute set carries no positions, so a consumer filtering one hands every row to this filter as a default point at the world origin. The nearest target is then the same one for every row, the verdict comes back uniform, and nothing is logged.

The node subtitle reads back the comparison and the threshold, so a graph carrying several distance filters can be read without selecting them one at a time. With Compare Against set to Attribute, the attribute name takes the place of the number.

UPCGExDistributeTupleSettings.name: Tuple : Distribute
UPCGExDistributeTupleSettings.purpose: Hands each point one whole row of a table authored on the node. Composition names the columns, each column being one output attribute with a type; Values holds the rows, each carrying a weight and one value per column. Every point gets a row picked for it and that row's values written as attributes, so the values stay in the combinations they were authored in; a column holding a Collection Entry lands as a staged pick, with the Collection Map it resolves against emitted on a second pin. Tuple emits the same table as an attribute set; this node puts it on points.
UPCGExDistributeTupleSettings.situation: Several attributes have to vary together in fixed combinations, and each point should receive one whole combination.

mechanism.text: One point in, one point out, in the order they arrived; nothing is added, removed or reordered. Each column of the Composition becomes one attribute named after that column, and a point receives the values of its picked row. A column the picked row has disabled writes nothing, so the point keeps whatever that attribute already held, or the column's own value from the Composition when the attribute is new. Distribution is the single thing that decides which row a point gets. A node with no columns or no rows passes its input straight through.

off_label.claim: Name the columns after attributes the points already carry and the node becomes a weighted partial overwrite: a picked row rewrites the columns it has enabled and leaves the rest of the point's incoming values in place.
off_label.grounded_in: the per-type InitializeOutput opens the column buffer with EBufferInit::Inherit, and the point loop skips any column whose RowSources entry is null because IsOverrideEnabled was false for that row.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to receive row values. Several datasets can be wired, and each is picked over on its own.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The same points, carrying one attribute per column of the Composition.

outputs.label: Map
outputs.note: The Collection Map for the picks this node wrote: one row per collection, carrying its index and its asset path, with every sub-collection reachable from it listed too.
outputs.condition: when Output Map is on and an enabled cell holds a collection pick; the pin sits collapsed as an advanced pin otherwise

Composition.tooltip: Tuple composition defines the columns (property types and names).

fields.name: Schemas
fields.tooltip: Schema array (locals -- always take precedence over imported entries with matching names)

fields.name: ImportedSchemas
fields.tooltip: Imported schema assets, resolved in array order after locals. Hard refs -- assets stay loaded as long as the owning collection exists. Recursion through imported assets' own ImportedSchemas is supported with cycle detection.

fields.name: ImportOverrides
fields.tooltip: Per-entry value overrides for imported entries. EditAnywhere is required so the detail panel's GetChildHandle can reach this property's children -- the registered FPCGExPropertySchemaCollectionCustomization takes over rendering entirely (CustomizeChildren controls every visible row), so this never appears as a top-level array editor in the inspector. The array is kept parallel with the imports-only schema via ReconcileImportOverrides (which delegates to FPCGExPropertyOverrides::SyncToSchema). UE per-instance UPROPERTY delta serialization handles three-layer composition: asset default -> template (collection on CDO) -> instance (collection on actor instance). Each layer overrides the previous via bEnabled toggles on individual entries. Locals do not appear here -- they are edited in-place on Schemas.

Composition.semantics: A column's Name is the attribute name written to the points, one attribute per column. Columns come from the schemas authored here and from any imported Property Schema assets, locals first, so a shared schema can define the table shape for several nodes at once and a local column of the same name overrides the imported one. A Float Curve column has no attribute form and is skipped, writing nothing for any row.
Composition.trap: Two local columns sharing a name is an execution error, and the message reports that duplicates exist without naming which.

Values.tooltip: Weighted tuple values. Toggle 'Enabled' per column to include/exclude values. Rows auto-sync with composition changes.

fields.name: Overrides
fields.tooltip: Overrides array - parallel with schema (same size, same order)

fields.name: Weight
fields.tooltip: Weight for this row in distribution (higher = more likely to be picked)

Values.semantics: A disabled column leaves the point's incoming attribute value untouched; when the attribute is new to the points, the column's own value from the Composition is what stays there instead. Weight is per row and is used raw, with no offset applied.
Values.trap: A row at weight 0 drops out of the Weighted random pool but stays in the table, so Index and Random still land on it.

Distribution.tooltip: How to distribute rows across points
Distribution.semantics: Index reads the point's position in its own dataset, so it takes no seed and the seed settings disappear with it. Random rolls evenly across every row and ignores the weights entirely. Weighted random rolls against the summed weights, and falls back to an even roll across every row when every weight is 0.

IndexSafety.tooltip: Index safety mode when Distribution is Index and point count exceeds row count
IndexSafety.semantics: Tile, Clamp and Yoyo each map an out-of-range point index onto a real row, so every point still gets one. Ignore skips the point outright.
IndexSafety.trap: Under Ignore a skipped point is written nothing at all, so it leaves carrying its incoming attribute values or the Composition defaults, looking identical to a point that was given a row.

SeedComponents.tooltip: Which components contribute to seed generation
SeedComponents.semantics: Local and Settings are both on by default, so the node's own Seed property folds into every roll and changing it re-rolls every point. The staging selectors ship with all components off, where the point's own seed is the only thing that counts, so a table set up by habit from that side will behave differently here.

RowIndexAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute to write the picked row index to

WeightAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute to write the picked row's weight to
WeightAttributeName.semantics: The value written is the row's authored Weight, unchanged and unnormalized. It is written in every distribution mode, including Index and Random, where the weight took no part in the pick.

bOutputMap.tooltip: Emit the "Map" attribute set describing external resources referenced by written values (e.g. Collection Entry picks).
bOutputMap.semantics: A Collection Entry column writes its pick under the staging-layer name PCGEx/CollectionEntry followed by the column name, and the pick is meaningless on its own: this is the toggle that emits the Map it resolves against. The Map gathers the collections of every enabled Collection Entry cell across all input datasets, so a table holding no picks emits nothing on the pin however the toggle is set.
bOutputMap.trap: The column name is the staging layer, so a consumer left on the default layer will not see the pick at all; its Staging Layer has to be set to the column name.

hints.text: An empty Composition or an empty Values list makes the node a pass-through, silently and with no warning. A half-configured node produces exactly the points it received, which reads as a downstream problem.

A Collection Entry cell whose collection is missing, or whose entry has since been deleted from it, writes a pick of zero, which every downstream consumer reads as no pick. Nothing is reported: the attribute is written either way, and the points look the same as points carrying valid picks.

UPCGExDotFilterProviderSettings.name: Filter : Dot
UPCGExDotFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Compares two directions per element and turns how closely they agree into a pass or fail. Operand A is read off the element being tested and Operand B is either a fixed vector, world Up out of the box, or a second per-element value; you name both, which is the whole difference from Filter : Angle, where the two directions come from neighbouring positions instead. Either operand can be negated, and either can be rotated by the element's own transform, which is how a direction authored in local space meets one that lives in world space. Fed entirely from the `@Data` domain with both transform toggles off, the same filter also answers once per dataset, so the consumers that judge whole datasets accept it.
UPCGExDotFilterProviderSettings.situation: A direction is already on the elements, and what survives depends on how closely it agrees with another direction.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this filter once per element: two vectors are read, both normalised, and the dot product of that pair against the threshold is the verdict. Only direction counts on either side, so the length of whatever Operand A reads never moves the result. A transform toggle rotates its operand by the element's transform, rotation only, with scale left out. The dataset-level path does the same arithmetic once per dataset, reading one value per operand, applying the same negations, and handing every element of that dataset the same verdict.

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter passport, so every filter pin accepts it, Vtx Filters and Edge Filters included.

hints.text: The dataset-level path needs all four conditions at once: Operand A on a `@Data` attribute, Operand B constant or on a `@Data` attribute, the threshold constant or on a `@Data` attribute, and both transform toggles off. Miss one and **Uber Branch** and **Break** skip the filter with a warning, while **Uber Filter (Data)** falls back to testing elements and counting how many passed.

UPCGExDrawAttributesSettings.name: Draw Attributes
UPCGExDrawAttributesSettings.purpose: Draws attribute values in the viewport so they can be looked at rather than inferred. Most of what a PCGEx graph computes is invisible: directions, weights, indices and flags exist only as numbers, and this is the node that puts them on screen where the geometry is.
UPCGExDrawAttributesSettings.situation: A graph producing the wrong result for a reason that would be obvious if the intermediate values could be seen.

mechanism.text: Each entry in the list names an attribute and how to draw it, and the node draws one of those per point as persistent debug geometry. Nothing about the data changes: points pass through untouched, so the node can sit anywhere in a chain without altering what follows it. The drawing persists until something clears it, which is what **Flush Debug** is for.

fields.name: Selector
fields.tooltip: Attribute or $Property.

fields.name: bEnabled
fields.tooltip: Enable or disable this debug group.

fields.name: ExpressedAs
fields.tooltip: How the attribute value is interpreted for debug visualization.

fields.name: bAsOffset
fields.tooltip: Treat the value as an offset from the point rather than absolute.

fields.name: bNormalizeBeforeSizing
fields.tooltip: Normalize direction vectors before applying size multiplier.

fields.name: Thickness
fields.tooltip: Draw line thickness.

fields.name: Size
fields.tooltip: Draw size. What it means depends on the selected debug type.

fields.name: LocalSizeAttribute
fields.tooltip: Fetch the size from a local attribute. The regular Size parameter then act as a scale.

fields.name: Color
fields.tooltip: Draw color for the debug visualization.

fields.name: SecondaryColor
fields.tooltip: Secondary color used for boolean false values.

fields.name: LocalColorAttribute
fields.tooltip: Fetch the color from a local attribute.

fields.name: bColorIsLinear
fields.tooltip: Basically divides input values by 255

fields.name: DepthPriority
fields.tooltip: Depth priority.

DebugList.semantics: One entry per attribute to draw, each with its own presentation. Several entries draw together, so a single node can show a direction and the weight behind it at once.

bPCGExDebug.tooltip: Debug drawing toggle. Exposed to have more control on debug draw in sub-graph.
bPCGExDebug.semantics: The master switch, and the one to use rather than disabling the node. Turning the node off leaves whatever it already drew on screen, because nothing then runs to clear it.

hints.text: Disable the drawing here before disabling the node. A disabled node draws nothing and also clears nothing, so its last output stays in the viewport until **Flush Debug** removes it. The node's own description says as much.

UPCGExDynamicMeshToClustersSettings.name: Dynamic Mesh to Clusters
UPCGExDynamicMeshToClustersSettings.purpose: Reads dynamic mesh data off a wire and hands back its topology as a cluster, one per input mesh. `Graph Output Type` decides what that structure is: the mesh's own vertices joined by its triangle sides, the dual made of triangle centroids, a hollow version joining centroids to their corners, or the open border of a surface that is not closed. **Mesh to Clusters** is the sibling for static mesh assets, which it names by reference and places once per target point; this one takes the geometry it is handed and adds no placement of its own.
UPCGExDynamicMeshToClustersSettings.situation: A dynamic mesh built earlier in the graph carries the connectivity wanted, and the next step needs it as cluster data.

mechanism.text: One or more dynamic meshes in, one cluster out per usable mesh. Vtx land on the mesh's vertex positions as the mesh stores them, so there is no placement step and nothing to aim. Before any of that the raw vertices are welded by position, which is what puts back together the split copies a mesh keeps at hard edges and UV seams, and `Graph Output Type` alone then decides what becomes a Vtx and what becomes an Edge. Each input's tags travel onto its Vtx dataset. Inputs that are not dynamic mesh data are skipped, and a run where none of them is usable stops with an error.

inputs.label: Mesh
inputs.note: The dynamic meshes to read. Several may be wired, and each one yields its own cluster.

inputs.label: UV Imports
inputs.note: Attribute sets pairing a name with a channel index, adding to the mappings authored inline.
inputs.condition: when Import Details has Import UVs on

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: One dataset per usable input mesh, carrying that input's tags.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One dataset per connected component of each mesh's result.

GraphOutputType.semantics: `Raw Triangles` maps the mesh's vertices onto Vtx and each triangle's three sides onto Edges, with a side shared by two triangles arriving as one edge; triangles themselves are not carried, so a quad reads as four sides plus the diagonal that split it. `Dual Graph` replaces all of that: one Vtx per triangle, sitting at its centroid, and an Edge wherever two triangles share a side, so the mesh's own vertices are gone. `Hollow Graph` keeps the mesh vertices and adds the centroids, joining each centroid to its triangle's three corners and dropping the triangle sides, so the result is a fan per triangle and no closed triangle outline. `Boundaries` keeps only the vertices sitting on a side that belongs to a single triangle, joined by those sides.
GraphOutputType.trap: `Boundaries` reads the open border of a surface rather than a silhouette or an outer shell, so a closed mesh has no such side and produces no cluster at all.

ImportDetails.tooltip: Which data should be imported from the dynamic mesh onto the generated points

bIgnoreMeshWarnings.tooltip: Skip invalid meshes & do not throw warning about them.
bIgnoreMeshWarnings.semantics: An input that is not dynamic mesh data is dropped and contributes no cluster; this decides whether that is announced, never whether it happens. When it drops every input the node errors either way.

VertexMergeHashTolerance.tooltip: Set tolerance for merging vertices, such as those found at split vertices along hard edges or UV seams. The value is clamped to be no less than a small positive value to prevent division by zero errors.
VertexMergeHashTolerance.semantics: The cell size of the grid that decides which of the mesh's raw vertices are the same Vtx. A mesh splits its vertices at hard edges and UV seams, so the raw count sits above the visible one, and this is what puts them back together. Too large and distinct vertices weld into one, which shows up as edges that were never in the mesh; the value is held above zero, so some merging always happens.

bPreciseVertexMerge.tooltip: Use two overlapping spatial hashes to detect vertex proximity. More accurate, but slightly slower and uses slightly more memory during processing.
bPreciseVertexMerge.semantics: Adds a second lookup half a cell offset from the first, so two vertices inside the tolerance of each other but on opposite sides of a cell boundary still land on one Vtx. Off, which is how this node ships, that pair comes through as two.

GraphBuilderDetails.semantics: Judged per input mesh, so a component discarded for its size is missing from that mesh's cluster and no other input is touched.

hints.text: Only the Vtx half inherits the input mesh's tags. The Edges datasets carry the cluster pair tag and nothing from the source, so a downstream match written against a tag the mesh arrived with finds the Vtx and misses its Edges.

UPCGExEdgeEndpointsCheckFilterProviderSe.name: Edge Filter : Endpoints Check
UPCGExEdgeEndpointsCheckFilterProviderSe.purpose: Turns a condition about Vtx into a condition about edges. You wire a filter set into the **Vtx Filters** pin, the node runs it at the two Vtx an edge connects, and `Mode` says which combination of the two answers makes the edge pass. `Two Filter Sets` opens a second pin for the other shape of the question: one end matching the first set, the other matching the second. The verdict leaves on the **Edge Filter** pin, so this is the adapter that lets any Vtx or point filter gate an **Edge Filters** pin.
UPCGExEdgeEndpointsCheckFilterProviderSe.situation: A condition that is natural to write about a Vtx, and the node downstream takes edges.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per edge; the filter reads no data of its own and writes nothing. The wired filter set is evaluated at the two Vtx the edge connects, and each endpoint's answer is matched against `Comparison`. With one set, `Mode` folds that pair of matches into the edge's verdict. With `Two Filter Sets`, the second set is evaluated at the endpoints as well and the edge passes when one end matches the first set's expectation and the other matches the second's, in either orientation unless `Respect Edge Direction` binds set A to the Start endpoint.

off_label.claim: `SeeSaw` compares the two endpoint answers to each other, so a filter that marks out a region turns the node into a border finder: the edges that pass are the ones with one end inside the region and one end outside it.
off_label.grounded_in: EPCGExEdgeEndpointsCheckMode::SeeSaw testing StartResult against EndResult instead of against Expects

inputs.label: Vtx Filters
