fields.name: bTestTagsWithValues
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

bQuietAttributeMismatchWarning.tooltip: Suppress warning about attribute type mismatches during merging.

hints.text: Under `Merged` the results carry attributes reconciled across inputs, so a value that existed on only some of them may not survive. The per-point form is the one that keeps each result's own attributes untouched.

UPCGExFittingRelaxBase.name: Abstract Fitting
UPCGExFittingRelaxBase.purpose: The shared half of the fitting relaxations: Box Fitting, Box Fitting v2 and Radius Fitting. All are picked from the `Relaxing` dropdown on **Cluster : Relax**, and all inherit the settings on this page unchanged, so what `Edge Fitting`, `Spring Constant`, `Repulsion Constant` and `Time Step` mean is stated once here. Each adds only its own overlap test, which is what decides whether two Vtx count as colliding. The remaining relaxations, **Force Directed**, **Laplacian (Poisson)** and **Verlet (Gravity)**, share none of this and carry their own settings.
UPCGExFittingRelaxBase.situation: Reading Box Fitting, Box Fitting v2 or Radius Fitting and needing to know what the four settings they all have in common actually do.

mechanism.text: When **Cluster : Relax** runs one iteration, this half contributes two of the three turns and the fitting rule contributes the middle one. Every edge adds a push to both of its Vtx, proportional to how far the edge's current length sits from the target length it was given, and pointing along the edge. The fitting rule then adds a separating push between any two Vtx it finds overlapping. Each Vtx is finally moved by the sum of everything pushed at it, scaled by `Time Step`. Every push in an iteration is measured against the positions as they stood when that iteration began, so the two forces are summed and compete on equal footing.

RepulsionConstant.tooltip: Amount of translation for a single step. Relative to other parameters.
RepulsionConstant.semantics: Scales the separating push, and does nothing by itself: which Vtx overlap, and by how much, is entirely the fitting rule's answer. Raise it against `Spring Constant` to favour clearing overlap over holding edge lengths.

EdgeFitting.tooltip: Which edge length should the computation attempt to preserve.
EdgeFitting.semantics: Ignore removes the spring entirely: no edge is consulted, nothing holds connected Vtx together, and only the fitting rule's separating push moves anything, so the cluster keeps spreading until no pair overlaps. Fixed gives every edge one target, `Desired Edge Length`, taken verbatim. Existing gives each edge the length it had on the incoming Vtx positions, measured once before the first iteration and never measured again, so the targets do not follow the cluster as it moves. Attribute reads a target per edge from the Edges dataset.
EdgeFitting.trap: Existing does not preserve the existing length on its own. `Scale` multiplies the target and ships at 2, so the default of this mode asks every edge to reach twice the length it arrived with, and the cluster expands.

DesiredEdgeLength.tooltip: The desired edge length. Low priority in the algorithm, but help keep edge topology more consistent.
DesiredEdgeLength.semantics: Taken verbatim as the target for every edge in the cluster, so the relaxation drives toward uniform spacing regardless of how the edges came in.
DesiredEdgeLength.trap: `Scale` is forced to 1 in this mode. It is hidden from the panel here, so the only way to notice is through the overrides pin, where a Scale value pushed onto the rule is accepted and then discarded.

DesiredEdgeLengthAttribute.semantics: Read once per edge from the Edges dataset, then multiplied by `Scale`. Because it is per edge rather than per Vtx, one region of a cluster can be told to open up while another holds its spacing, without any filter involved.
DesiredEdgeLengthAttribute.trap: The attribute has to exist on the Edges data. When the selector resolves to nothing the node reports the missing attribute as an error and the relaxation does not run; there is no fallback to the edge's own length.

Scale.tooltip: Scale factor applied to the edge length.
Scale.semantics: Multiplies the target length in Existing and Attribute modes, and ships at 2. It is applied once, when the targets are captured, so it changes the length an edge aims for and never the strength of the pull toward it.

SpringConstant.tooltip: Stiffness of the edges. Lower values yield better placement (less overlap), but edge topology may be affected.
SpringConstant.semantics: Scales a corrective push proportional to the gap between an edge's current length and its target, so a badly stretched edge pulls harder than a nearly correct one. Both endpoints receive the same push in opposite directions, which means a Vtx collects one push per edge it carries and a complex Vtx is pulled harder than a leaf. This lands in the same accumulator as the fitting rule's separating push, so the balance between this and `Repulsion Constant` is what decides whether edge length or clear space wins.

TimeStep.tooltip: If this was a physic simulation, represent the time advance each iteration
TimeStep.semantics: Multiplies the whole accumulated push at the end of each iteration, springs and separation alike, so it is the size of one step and never a balance between the two. Halving it and doubling `Iterations` on Cluster : Relax reaches a similar place for more work.
TimeStep.trap: Leaving it large enough that a Vtx overshoots its target on every iteration makes the layout oscillate instead of settling, and more iterations then make it worse rather than better.

hints.text: All three fitting rules test every Vtx against every other Vtx in the cluster on the separation turn, so that turn grows with the square of the Vtx count and the iteration count on Cluster : Relax multiplies that. A cluster of a few thousand Vtx at a high iteration count is a long wait.

UPCGExFlagNodesSettings.name: Cluster : Write States
UPCGExFlagNodesSettings.purpose: Turns a stack of named conditions into one number on every Vtx. Each **State :** sub-node on the **States** pin decides per Vtx whether it holds, then applies its own bit operation to a shared int64, and what comes out is a flag mask saying which conditions were true there. Two kinds of state feed it: **State : Cluster**, which wraps a filter stack, and **State : Bitmask Adjacency**, which keys its bits to the directions the Vtx's edges leave in.
UPCGExFlagNodesSettings.situation: A cluster whose Vtx have to be classified once, several ways at a time, so everything downstream can select on the classification instead of recomputing it.

mechanism.text: Vtx in, the same Vtx out, carrying one extra int64 attribute. Every Edges dataset passes through untouched and no state is ever asked about an edge. Each Vtx starts at `Initial Flags`, and every state on the pin is asked whether it holds there, in ascending `Priority` order; a state that holds applies its pass operation to that Vtx's number, one that does not applies its fail operation. States never name an attribute and never create one. The mask belongs to this node, and mutating it is the only thing a state can do.

off_label.claim: One state setting one bit turns the node into a way to mark Vtx that pass a cluster-aware test, because a state's own filter stack accepts Vtx filters as well as point filters, and the result lands as a plain attribute that ordinary point nodes can read.
off_label.grounded_in: UPCGExStateFactoryProviderSettings::CreateFactory collects the state's internal filters against PCGExFactories::ClusterNodeFilters, which includes the Vtx filter type

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The Vtx half of every cluster to classify. This is the only half that gets written.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The Edges half. Every Edges dataset that finds its Vtx is one cluster and one run.

inputs.label: States
inputs.note: The **State :** sub-nodes whose bit operations build the mask. Required: the node does not run without at least one.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: The same Vtx, carrying the flag attribute.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: Forwarded unchanged.

FlagAttribute.semantics: One int64 per Vtx, and the only thing this node writes. It is the same shape the point-level **Write States** produces, so the bitmask filters and the bitmask nodes read either of them without needing to know which made it.

InitialFlags.semantics: The value every Vtx starts from before any state runs, which only applies when the named attribute is new. Point the node at an int64 attribute the Vtx already carry and their incoming values are the starting point instead, which is what lets a second **Cluster : Write States** add bits to a mask an earlier one wrote.
InitialFlags.trap: The corollary is that this row goes quiet the moment the named attribute exists upstream. A mask that will not reset is usually a Flag Attribute already carried in from an earlier pass, not a value typed here.

hints.text: The **States** pin advertises the wider point-state type and narrows to cluster states when the node starts, so a **State : Point** connects, logs an invalid-input warning and is dropped. If it was the only thing wired there, the now-empty required pin raises a missing-input error naming **States**, which reads as nothing being connected. The two states this pin keeps are **State : Cluster** and **State : Bitmask Adjacency**.

UPCGExFlatProjectionSettings.name: Flat Projection
UPCGExFlatProjectionSettings.purpose: Flattens points onto a plane, and can put them back afterwards. A great many operations are simpler in two dimensions, so the usual shape is to project, do the work flat, then restore the heights that were set aside. The restore half is what makes this a round trip rather than a destructive flatten.
UPCGExFlatProjectionSettings.situation: Work that only makes sense in plan view, on points that still need their original heights when it is done.

mechanism.text: Each point's transform is replaced by its projection onto the plane, and the original is stored on the point under an attribute prefix so a later pass can find it. Restoring reads those stored values back, and the component masks decide how much of the original transform returns: a graph can bring back the height and keep the flattened rotation, or bring back everything. The pairing is by attribute name, so the two passes have to agree on the prefix.
steps: Projecting writes the original transform to attributes and flattens the point.
Restoring reads those attributes back, applying only the components its masks name.

off_label.claim: Restoring only the position components brings points back to their heights while keeping whatever orientation the flat work gave them, which is how a set relaxed or sorted in plan view returns to terrain without losing the alignment it just gained.
off_label.grounded_in: The restore path applies the stored transform per component through the position, rotation and scale masks rather than wholesale.

bRestorePreviousProjection.tooltip: Whether this is a new projection or an old one
bRestorePreviousProjection.semantics: Switches the node between the two halves of the round trip. Projecting stores and flattens; restoring reads back. The same node does both, so a graph doing a flat detour uses it twice with this cleared and then set.

AttributePrefix.tooltip: The name of the attribute to write its index to.
AttributePrefix.semantics: How the two passes find each other. The stored transform is written under this prefix and the restore pass looks for the same one, so a mismatch is not an error that reports itself: the restore finds nothing and the points stay flat.
AttributePrefix.trap: Two flat detours nested inside one another need different prefixes, or the inner projection overwrites what the outer one stored and the outer restore brings back the wrong transform.

TransformPosition.tooltip: Which position components from the stored transform should be applied to the point.
TransformPosition.semantics: Chooses which position components the restore pass brings back, per axis. Restoring the vertical alone is the common case: the points return to their heights while keeping whatever the flat work did to them in plan.

TransformRotation.tooltip: Which rotation components from the stored transform should be applied to the point.

TransformScale.tooltip: Which scale components from the stored transform should be applied to the point.

bSaveAttributeForRestore.tooltip: Whether this is a new projection or an old one
bSaveAttributeForRestore.semantics: Decides whether the projecting pass stores anything at all. Cleared, the flatten is one-way and no later restore can undo it, which is what to use when the heights are genuinely not wanted back.

bAlignLocalTransform.tooltip: Whether this is a new projection or an old one

ProjectionDetails.tooltip: Projection settings for flattening points to the XY plane.

hints.text: The stored transform travels as ordinary attributes on the points, so anything that drops or renames attributes between the two passes breaks the restore. Nodes that rebuild point data rather than pass it through are the usual culprits.

UPCGExFlattenSettings.name: Flatten
UPCGExFlattenSettings.purpose: Hands back a copy of each input that owns every attribute it carries, with no reference back to the data it came from. PCG metadata is normally parented, which is cheap and fine inside one graph and unsafe once another component wants to read the result while the producing graph is still running. Flattening cuts that link, and it is the thing to put in front of any output that another component will fetch.
UPCGExFlattenSettings.situation: Data another PCG component will read across the component boundary, most often the output of a graph that Wait for PCG Data is watching.

mechanism.text: Each input is duplicated, and the duplicate's metadata is collapsed so every attribute it exposes is stored locally instead of inherited. The originals are left alone and the duplicates take their place on the output, carrying the same tags. Nothing about the data changes: same points, same attributes, same values, same order. There are no settings, and the node always copies.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: Any data. Each input is handled independently.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: One owned, flattened duplicate per input, carrying that input's tags.

pins.dynamic: Both pins accept any data type and the output mirrors the input.

hints.text: This always duplicates, so it costs memory proportional to what passes through it. Put it at the boundary where the data leaves the graph rather than partway through a chain.

UPCGExForceDirectedRelax.name: Force Directed
UPCGExForceDirectedRelax.purpose: Spreads a cluster out under two competing forces, one pulling along the edges and one pushing everything apart. Every edge pulls its two Vtx together, and every Vtx pushes every other Vtx in the cluster away, whether they share an edge or not. The spacing it heads toward comes out of the ratio between `Spring Constant` and `Electrostatic Constant`, it is the same everywhere in the cluster, and it owes nothing to the lengths the edges arrived with. That makes it the rule for a cluster whose incoming positions carry nothing worth keeping and whose layout should come from connectivity alone.
UPCGExForceDirectedRelax.situation: A cluster generated somewhere the positions were incidental, where what the layout should show is which Vtx connect to which.

mechanism.text: One turn over the Vtx per iteration. Each Vtx collects a pull toward every neighbour it shares an edge with, growing with that edge's current length, plus a push away from every other Vtx in the cluster, falling off with the square of the distance between them. The sum is added straight onto the position as a distance in world units, with no step size in between, so the size of the two constants is also the size of the move. The pull has no length it is aiming for, so the two terms balance at one distance: the cube root of `Electrostatic Constant` divided by `Spring Constant`, which is a little over 21 units at the shipped values.

off_label.claim: Set Spring Constant to 0 and nothing pulls back. The rule becomes a blanket de-clumper that keeps opening the cluster out for as long as it runs, carrying the connections along without ever consulting them.
off_label.grounded_in: CalculateAttractiveForce multiplies its whole contribution by SpringConstant, so at zero only the electrostatic term reaches the force Step1 applies

SpringConstant.tooltip: Strength of the attraction pulling connected Vtx together. Grows with edge length, like a spring.
SpringConstant.semantics: The pull grows with the edge's whole current length and not with any departure from a target, so there is no length an edge is trying to reach and on its own this would collapse the cluster onto a point. What stops it is the repulsion term. Because the force is applied as a displacement with no step size in between, the value doubles as the fraction of an edge's length travelled per iteration: at the shipped 0.1 a Vtx a thousand units from its neighbour is moved a hundred units toward it in one go.

ElectrostaticConstant.tooltip: Strength of the repulsion pushing every Vtx pair apart. Falls off with squared distance, and is capped at the pair's own distance so near-coincident Vtx cannot be thrown apart.
ElectrostaticConstant.semantics: The push reaches every other Vtx in the cluster, sharing an edge or not. Set against `Spring Constant` it is what fixes the spacing the layout heads toward, at the cube root of one divided by the other, so raising both by the same factor leaves that spacing alone and only makes each iteration travel further. The cap the tooltip names binds below the cube root of this value on its own, which is 10 units at the shipped 1000, and so never reaches the balance distance sitting above it.
ElectrostaticConstant.trap: Two Vtx at identical positions are the one case that produces no push at all, because there is no direction to push along. A stacked pair stays stacked however long the run is, and the cap cannot help there.

hints.text: The repulsion term pairs every Vtx with every other one, so one iteration grows with the square of the Vtx count and the iteration count on Cluster : Relax multiplies that. A cluster of a few thousand Vtx at a high iteration count is a long wait.

UPCGExFormatAttributesSettings.name: Format Attributes
UPCGExFormatAttributesSettings.purpose: String templating over attributes: name a literal token, point it at another attribute, and every occurrence of that token inside the chosen `FName` and `FString` attributes becomes that attribute's value. The replacement source can be the row being processed or an external dataset wired to a pin the rule names, and a rule's source can be any type at all, because values are converted to text on the way in. It works the same on points and on attribute sets, which is what makes it usable for building asset paths, display names and tags from data.
UPCGExFormatAttributesSettings.situation: A name or path attribute has to be assembled per row from values that live in other attributes.

mechanism.text: Every dataset on the input pin comes out, duplicated, with the same rows and the same tags. For each dataset, each rule resolves its token and its replacement once, then each target attribute is read as text, rewritten and written back. Rules apply in the order they are listed. A rule whose token or replacement cannot be read is dropped for that dataset only, so a rule that fails on one input still runs on the next. A target attribute that is missing, or that is not `FName` or `FString`, is skipped with a warning and left alone. Matching is case sensitive.

off_label.claim: Point a rule's token at an attribute rather than a constant and the token itself becomes per-row, so one rule can strip a different substring from every row.
off_label.grounded_in: the Token value is an input shorthand read through ReadSourceIntoValue when it is not a constant, producing a per-row token array

off_label.claim: A rule with an empty token is a no-op rather than an insert-everywhere, so rules can be parked in the list without being deleted.
off_label.grounded_in: both ApplyRulesSequential and ApplyRulesSinglePass skip a rule whose resolved token is empty

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The data whose text attributes get rewritten. Points or attribute sets.

inputs.label: One pin per external source name
inputs.note: A rule set to External adds a pin named by its `External Pin` field, defaulting to Format Source. Distinct names get distinct pins; rules sharing a name share the pin.
inputs.condition: a pin exists for each distinct External Pin name among the rules set to External

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The same data, duplicated, with the rewritten attributes and the original tags.

pins.dynamic: The input and output pins accept any data, and the external source pins are computed from the rules, so the node's pin set changes as rules are added and their pin names edited.

WriteMode.tooltip: Whether to overwrite the source attribute or write the result to a new one.

NewAttributeSuffix.tooltip: Suffix appended to each target attribute name when WriteMode is NewAttribute.
NewAttributeSuffix.semantics: Appended to each target's own name, so formatting three targets under `New Attribute` writes three new attributes rather than one. The new attribute keeps the original's kind, `FName` staying `FName`. A suffix that makes the derived name invalid skips that target with a warning.

ReplacementMode.tooltip: How rule replacements compose with each other.
ReplacementMode.semantics: The difference shows when a replacement value contains text another rule would match. `Sequential` will match it, because each rule runs over the previous rule's result; `Single Pass` will not, because inserted text is never re-scanned. Sequential is the one that can loop a value through several substitutions, and the one that can expand something unintentionally.

TargetAttributes.tooltip: Attributes the rules will operate on. Each must resolve to a FName or FString attribute; others are skipped with a warning.
TargetAttributes.semantics: Only `FName` and `FString` attributes are eligible. Anything else named here is skipped with a warning rather than converted, so a numeric attribute cannot be formatted in place; copy it into a string attribute first.

CommaSeparatedAttributeSelectors.tooltip: A list of selectors separated by a comma, for easy overrides. Will be appended to the existing array.
CommaSeparatedAttributeSelectors.semantics: Appended to the list above, not a replacement for it, and the two are merged with duplicates dropped. This is the overridable half, so a parent graph can extend the target list without touching the array.

Rules.tooltip: Rules applied in order, top to bottom.
Rules.semantics: Order is the rule's only priority, top to bottom, and it decides two different things: under `Sequential` a later rule sees the earlier rules' output, and under `Single Pass` the earliest rule whose token matches at a position wins. A rule's `Target Attributes` list scopes it to particular targets and an empty list means every target. Its `Fallback` covers the replacement only: a rule whose token cannot be read is dropped whether or not a fallback is set.
Rules.trap: An external source with one row broadcasts that row to everything, and so does an external source whose row count differs from the target's. Row-by-row pairing happens only on an exact match above one row, and the mismatch is silent.

bQuietMissingSourceWarning.tooltip: Suppress warnings when a rule's source attribute can't be read and the rule has no fallback.

hints.text: Setting a rule's fallback also silences the warning for that rule's unreadable source, an empty fallback string included. A rule that quietly does nothing is usually a fallback left on with nothing behind it.

UPCGExFromNeighborsTangents.name: From Neighbors
UPCGExFromNeighborsTangents.purpose: Builds each point's tangent from the two runs leading away from it, one back to the previous point and one on to the next, averaged at half weight. The runs are averaged at their real lengths rather than as directions, so a long segment on one side outweighs a short one on the other. Written out, that average is half the run from the previous point to the next, which is what **Catmull-Rom** computes, so the two rules produce the same vector at every point and the choice between them comes down to which description fits how you are thinking about the path.
UPCGExFromNeighborsTangents.situation: A path is on its way to a spline and needs an even, neighbour-driven tangent at every interior point.

mechanism.text: The run from the point back to its previous neighbour is flipped so both runs point forward, then the two are averaged at half weight, and the result goes to arrive and leave alike, each times its own scale. Because they are averaged at full length rather than normalised first, the point's own position cancels out of the average and what is left is half the run from the previous neighbour to the next. An open path's first and last point never reach this rule, and take the base's answer instead.

hints.text: Because the two runs carry their real lengths into the average, the result is not the bisector of the corner at the point. A long segment on one side pulls the average towards itself and a short one has correspondingly little say, so a right-angle corner between segments of different lengths does not come out at 45 degrees.

UPCGExFromTransformTangents.name: From Transform
UPCGExFromTransformTangents.purpose: The one rule that ignores the path: each point's tangent comes from its own rotation, so order and spacing change nothing. It is also one of only two rules that answers for the first and last point of an open path, which makes it the pick for `Start Override` and `End Override` when a curve should enter and leave along an authored direction. As the main rule it is for paths where something upstream has already decided which way each point faces, **Path : Orient** most often.
UPCGExFromTransformTangents.situation: Point rotations already carry the direction the curve should take, and the tangents should follow them rather than the point positions.

mechanism.text: The chosen local axis of the point's own rotation is handed to arrive and leave alike, each times its own scale. The vector is one unit long before scaling, which is where this rule parts company with the other four: they take their length from the distance between neighbours, and this one takes no length from the path at all. It answers for the first and last point of an open path as well as for the interior ones, so nothing falls through to the base.

Axis.tooltip: Which axis of the point transform to use for the tangent direction.
Axis.semantics: A local axis of the point rather than a world direction, and the same vector reaches arrive and leave, so this one setting decides which way the curve leans through every point at once. It has to agree with whatever wrote the rotations: **Path : Orient** aims the axis named in its own `Orient Axis` along the path, so a path oriented on `Forward` wants `Forward` here for its tangents to run with it and `Backward` for them to run against it.

hints.text: One unit is nothing beside normal point spacing, so at the default scale of one this rule writes tangents that are effectively nothing next to what the other four produce. Scale it to something on the order of the gap between points before judging the result.

UPCGExFuseClustersSettings.name: Cluster : Fuse
UPCGExFuseClustersSettings.purpose: Merges every cluster on its inputs into one, welding Vtx that land in the same place and optionally resolving the places where the geometry meets without sharing a point. It is the node for combining clusters that came from different sources, because nothing else joins clusters that arrived on separate Vtx datasets. **Cluster : Connect** is the neighbour it gets mistaken for, and it does the other job: inserting edges between the components of one Vtx dataset, without touching a single Vtx.
UPCGExFuseClustersSettings.situation: Modular cluster pieces, or a pathfinding result converted back, have to become one network at the seams where they overlap.

mechanism.text: Every cluster on the input pins is drawn into one union, whatever Vtx dataset each arrived on. Vtx closer together than the fuse distance become a single Vtx whose attributes blend, edges that resolve to the same pair of surviving Vtx collapse into one, and an edge whose two ends welded together is dropped instead of becoming a connection from a Vtx to itself. What comes out is a new cluster rather than an edited one: the Vtx pin carries a dataset no input owned, and the Edges pin carries one dataset per connected component of it. Inputs that never came within the fuse distance of one another therefore come back as separate components of a single cluster.
steps: Vtx within the fuse distance collapse into one, and every edge that named them follows.
Point/Edge intersections split an edge wherever a Vtx sits along it, which is what turns a T contact into a junction.
Edge/Edge intersections add a Vtx wherever two edges cross and split both, including edges the previous stage created.

off_label.claim: With both intersection stages off and the fuse distance left small, this is the way to gather several clusters onto one Vtx dataset without changing what connects to what. Anything downstream that consumes a single cluster pair then sees all of them at once.
off_label.grounded_in: The union is built over every input regardless of the intersection toggles, and points that weld to nothing are still emitted as Vtx of the new cluster with their edges intact.

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: Every Vtx dataset to be merged. Unlike most cluster nodes, several unrelated pairs on these pins are the point rather than a mistake.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The Edges datasets, matched to their Vtx by the pair tag as usual.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: One dataset for the whole merge, built fresh. No input Vtx dataset is forwarded.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One dataset per connected component of the merged cluster.

PointPointIntersectionDetails.semantics: The fuse distance inside this block is the whole of the welding decision, measured in world units between point locations and never against their bounds. It is also where the union metadata lives, which is what records how many original points went into each surviving Vtx.
PointPointIntersectionDetails.trap: The distance applies inside a single input cluster as readily as between two. Set it wider than the shortest edge of any input and that input loses Vtx to itself, taking the edges between them with them.

fields.name: bEnableSelfIntersection
fields.tooltip: If disabled, points will only check edges they aren't mapped to.

fields.name: FuseDetails
fields.tooltip: Fuse Settings

fields.name: bSnapOnEdge
fields.tooltip: When enabled, point will be moved exactly on the edge.

fields.name: IsIntersectorAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to flag point as intersector (result of an Point/Edge intersection)

PointEdgeIntersectionDetails.semantics: The stage that handles one cluster ending against the middle of another's edge rather than at one of its Vtx. Without it that Vtx welds to nothing, and the two clusters stay separate components however close the contact looks.

EdgeEdgeIntersectionDetails.semantics: Crossings become new Vtx, so two clusters that pass through each other come out joined at a degree-four Vtx. The angle limits inside the block narrow which crossings count, which is how a near-parallel overlap can be left alone while a genuine crossing is split.

DefaultPointsBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged together for fused points.
DefaultPointsBlendingDetails.semantics: Governs what a welded Vtx inherits from the several points that became it, and it also supplies the values for the Vtx that the two intersection stages invent, which correspond to no input point at all.

DefaultEdgesBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged together for fused edges.
DefaultEdgesBlendingDetails.semantics: Governs the edge points, which have their own values to reconcile: several input edges collapsing onto one surviving pair, and the halves an intersection split an edge into.

CustomPointEdgeBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged together for Point/Edge intersections.

CustomEdgeEdgeBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged together for Edge/Edge intersections (Crossings).
CustomEdgeEdgeBlendingDetails.semantics: One toggle, two defaults displaced. The Vtx a crossing creates are blended by this block in place of `Default Points Blending`, and every edge point of the merged cluster is blended by it in place of `Default Edges Blending`. Turning it on to shape crossings therefore also rewrites how the ordinary edge points are built.

fields.name: bDataDomainToElements
fields.tooltip: If enabled, data domain attributes are promoted to the elements domain (the single @Data value is broadcast to every point). Off by default; Merge Points is the node that enables it. Not used by all nodes.

fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

VtxCarryOverDetails.semantics: Decides which attributes and tags of the input Vtx datasets reach the merged one. The output belongs to no input, so anything not admitted here is gone rather than merely renamed.

fields.tooltip: If enabled, will preserve the initial attribute default value.

fields.tooltip: Attributes to carry over.

fields.tooltip: If enabled, data domain attributes are promoted to the elements domain (the single @Data value is broadcast to every point). Off by default; Merge Points is the node that enables it. Not used by all nodes.

fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

GraphBuilderDetails.semantics: The last thing that can drop a result. The small and big cluster limits are measured per connected component of the merge, so inputs that failed to weld and stayed small can be discarded here rather than by the fusing.

hints.text: The merge is total. Every cluster reaching these pins ends up in the same output cluster whether or not it touched anything, so a graph that wanted only some of its clusters fused has to keep the rest off this node rather than expect them back unchanged.

UPCGExFuseCollinearSettings.name: Path : Fuse Collinear
UPCGExFuseCollinearSettings.purpose: Drops the points that were not doing anything. A point whose run in and run out are within `Threshold` degrees of each other adds no shape, so it goes and the two segments either side become one. Inverting the threshold flips which points are the redundant ones, and the collocation test removes points sitting on top of each other whatever the angle says. The **Keep Conditions** pin protects points from removal, and the optional blending folds the removed points' values into the point that absorbed them.
UPCGExFuseCollinearSettings.situation: A path that came out of an operation with far more points than its shape needs, a boolean result or a dense conversion being the usual sources.

mechanism.text: One execution takes paths and returns them with fewer points, in the same order, in the same places. Nothing is moved and nothing is invented; the survivors are a subset of the input. Each point is measured against the last point that was kept rather than against its immediate neighbour, so a gentle arc accumulates deviation and eventually keeps a point rather than collapsing to a straight line. The first point is always kept, and so is the last unless the path is closed, in which case the first point can still be removed once the wrap is measured. A path reduced below two points is dropped rather than emitted short.

off_label.claim: Turning on Invert Threshold with a high angle keeps only the straight stretches and removes every corner, which reads as a crude smoothing pass: the run comes out cutting across its own bends rather than following them.
off_label.grounded_in: bInvertThreshold flips the comparison against the dot threshold, so the points removed are the ones whose turn exceeds it

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to fuse.

inputs.label: Keep Conditions
inputs.note: Points that pass survive whatever the angle test says, and each one also resets the measurement, so protecting a point changes which of its neighbours are judged redundant. Left empty nothing is protected and the angle test decides everything.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The fused paths. One reduced below two points is not emitted at all.

Threshold.semantics: The largest turn a point may make and still count as redundant, in degrees, measured between the direction from the last kept point and the direction on to the next one. Larger values remove more.
Threshold.trap: At 0 nothing is removed, not even a perfectly straight run, because the test is strictly greater than the threshold and a straight run sits exactly on it. Any value above 0 is what starts fusing.

bInvertThreshold.tooltip: Fuse points that are not collinear (Smooth-like).
bInvertThreshold.semantics: Swaps which side of the threshold is redundant, so the points removed become the ones that turn more than it rather than less. What survives is the straight stretches and the run cuts across its own corners.

bFuseCollocated.tooltip: If enabled, will consider collocated points as collinear
bFuseCollocated.semantics: Ships on, and runs before the angle test, so a point close enough to the last kept one is removed whether or not it turned. It is what keeps a path from carrying stacked duplicates through the node.

FuseDistance.tooltip: Distance used to consider point to be overlapping.
FuseDistance.semantics: Measured against the last point that was kept rather than the immediate previous point, so a run of points each within the distance of the one before it collapses to a single point rather than to a chain of pairs.

BlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged together into the first point of a collinear chain.
BlendingDetails.semantics: Folds the removed points into the point that absorbed them, which is otherwise untouched: without it a survivor keeps only its own values and everything the removed points carried is lost. Every point in a removed run is weighted the same, so `Average` gives their mean and `Copy (Target)` takes the last of them.

fields.name: IsUnionAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to mark point as union or not

fields.name: UnionSizeAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to mark the number of fused point held

UnionDetails.semantics: Records what was absorbed rather than changing it. The size it writes counts the survivor itself, so a point that absorbed nothing carries 1, and the flag is what separates the two cases without arithmetic.

bOmitInvalidPathsFromOutput.tooltip: Drop paths that arrive with fewer than 2 points. Separate from the inherited Omit Invalid Paths Outputs, which judges the result: both must be off for a short input to reach the output.

bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.tooltip: If enabled, collections that have less than 2 points won't be processed and be omitted from the output.
bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.semantics: It judges what the node produced, so it catches a path the fusing itself reduced below two points as well as a short input the node's own toggle let through.

UPCGExFusePointsSettings.name: Fuse Points
UPCGExFusePointsSettings.purpose: Merges points that sit close enough together into one. Where **Collocation Count** only reports coincident points and a filter only removes them, this combines them: a cluster within the fusing distance leaves as a single point carrying what the group added up to. That is the difference between deduplicating and consolidating.
UPCGExFusePointsSettings.situation: Points arriving from several sources that land near enough to each other to be the same thing, and should be treated as one.

mechanism.text: Points within the fusing distance of each other form a group, and each group leaves as one point. `Mode` decides whether that point is a blend of the group or the existing member nearest its middle, which is the difference between a synthesised point and a real one. `Fused Bounds Mode` can grow the survivor's bounds to cover everything that went into it, so the merged point occupies the space its group did rather than only its own.

off_label.claim: Keep Most Central with no bounds override is a sampling-free way to thin a set down to real members: nothing is synthesised, so attributes and references that only make sense on an authored point survive intact.
off_label.grounded_in: The Keep Most Central mode selects an existing point from the group rather than blending a new one.

Mode.semantics: `Blend` produces a new point whose attributes are the group's blended values, which is right when the attributes are quantities. `Keep Most Central` keeps one of the original points untouched, which is right when they carry things a blend would corrupt, like an asset path or an index into something else.

bPreserveOrder.tooltip: Preserve the order of input points
bPreserveOrder.semantics: Keeps the output in the input's order rather than in whatever order fusing resolved. It matters wherever something downstream pairs by index, and it is on by default.

FusedBoundsMode.tooltip: Override the bounds of each fused point to encompass all the points that were merged into it.
FusedBoundsMode.semantics: Decides whether the survivor's bounds still describe one point or the whole group it replaced. Left at `None` the merged point keeps its own size, so a wide group collapses to something much smaller than it occupied. `OBB` fits the group's own orientation and overrides the point's rotation to do it, which is a change to the transform and not only to the bounds.

BoundsSource.tooltip: Which point bounds should be used

MinBoundsExtent.tooltip: Minimum extent for fused bounds on each axis. Prevents degenerate (flat) bounds.
MinBoundsExtent.semantics: Stops a group that is flat in one axis from producing bounds with no thickness there. A degenerate box passes most spatial tests as though it were nothing, so this is a floor rather than a padding.

fields.name: bDataDomainToElements
fields.tooltip: If enabled, data domain attributes are promoted to the elements domain (the single @Data value is broadcast to every point). Off by default; Merge Points is the node that enables it. Not used by all nodes.

fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

hints.text: Fusing changes the point count, so anything downstream pairing by index against the original data no longer lines up. `Preserve Order` keeps the survivors in their original relative order but does not keep their indices.

UPCGExGameplayTagsFilterProviderSettings.name: Filter : GameplayTags
UPCGExGameplayTagsFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Answers a question about an actor in the level rather than about the element in front of it. Each element carries a reference to an actor, and the node resolves that actor, walks a property path to a gameplay tag container on it, and runs an Unreal gameplay tag query against what it finds. Actor-side state stays where it lives: nothing has to be copied onto the points for a graph to react to what the level already knows about them.
UPCGExGameplayTagsFilterProviderSettings.situation: Points were built from actors already placed in the level, and which of them the next node touches depends on the tags those actors carry.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this filter once per element, and the filter reads no data of its own and writes nothing. The actor reference read from the element resolves against actors already in memory, the property path is walked from that actor as its root, and the tag container it lands on is handed to the query, whose verdict becomes the filter's. Each of the two ways that lookup can fail has its own fixed verdict rather than an error, so a level that is half streamed out still produces a full set of answers. PCG's own data tags are a separate system and are never consulted here.

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter passport, so it is accepted on every filter pin, Vtx Filters and Edge Filters included.

UPCGExGetCollectionDataSettings.name: Get Collection Data
UPCGExGetCollectionDataSettings.purpose: Turns a collection into rows. One row per entry, carrying the Symbol, per-axis Size and Scalable flag that vanilla PCG subdivision consumes, next to weight, category, bounds, nesting depth and any custom properties asked for. Every row also carries the entry hash under the same attribute staged points use, so one output feeds the subdivision grammar and, once the structure is subdivided, the staging spawn routes. It also reads back: pointed at an upstream Collection Map, it takes entry hashes that name sub-collections and expands one level deeper, which is how a hierarchical grammar falls out of collection nesting instead of a dedicated asset type.
UPCGExGetCollectionDataSettings.situation: A collection has to be read out as subdivision modules, or a module that resolved to a sub-collection has to be opened one level further.

mechanism.text: One execution reads collections and emits attribute sets of rows, one row per entry, with the collection's nesting already flattened away. Source Mode decides where the collections come from, Source Shape how an input row names one, and Fanout how many attribute sets those become. Every row carries the entry hash, and the Map output carries a row for every collection the walk reached, including sub-collections, so the emitted set is grammar data and staged data at once. An attribute set that ends up with no rows is still emitted, tagged empty, so the output count keeps matching what was asked for.

off_label.claim: In From Inputs, Annotate Sources with Per Entry fanout stamps every source row with the index of the collection it resolved to. Ignore the Data output and the node becomes a labeller: staged points come out carrying which collection and which nesting context their pick belongs to, without the collection contents entering the graph.
off_label.grounded_in: AnnotateSources duplicates each Sources input and writes RootCollectionIndex / CollectionIndex / CollectionHash on the element domain whenever Fanout is not Per Input Data.

off_label.claim: Turn Omit Invalid and Empty off and rows that resolved to nothing survive carrying only their root identity, so a single execution reports which sources failed to resolve alongside the ones that did.
off_label.grounded_in: the root and collection identity attributes are written before the null-entry early-out in the row loop, and the placeholder row is added by the AddNone path in ProcessEntry.

inputs.label: Sources
inputs.note: Points or attribute sets carrying the collection reference on the Source Attribute. Several datasets are accepted, and each row of each of them names one collection.
inputs.condition: when Source Mode is From Inputs, where the pin only exists

inputs.label: Map
inputs.note: The upstream Collection Map the entry hashes resolve against. A Map that rebuilds no valid mapping is an execution error.
inputs.condition: when Source Mode is From Inputs and Source Shape is Entry Id + Map, where the pin only exists

outputs.label: Annotated Sources
outputs.note: One copy of each Sources input with the enabled identity attributes added. With none of them enabled the inputs are forwarded untouched rather than withheld.
outputs.condition: when Source Mode is From Inputs and Annotate Sources is on

outputs.label: Data
outputs.note: The rows. How many attribute sets arrive here is Fanout's answer.

outputs.label: Map
outputs.note: The Collection Map that keeps the emitted entry hashes resolvable, one row per collection the walk reached, sub-collections included. Emitted in every mode. Collections that a Collection Entry property output points at are appended to the same set, so one Map answers for every pick the rows carry.

pins.dynamic: The pin set is only dynamic in From Inputs with Annotate Sources on, and only Annotated Sources moves: it mirrors whatever Sources carries, so points in gives points out and an attribute set in gives an attribute set out. Data and Map stay attribute sets whatever the input shape is.

SourceMode.tooltip: Where collections come from: a single asset on this node, or resolved from input data.
SourceMode.semantics: Collection takes the pin set down to outputs alone and emits exactly one attribute set per execution; the asset is a hard reference, so it loads whenever the graph does. From Inputs adds the Sources pin and hands the count question to Fanout, and the collections named there are loaded on execution instead.

AssetCollection.tooltip: The asset collection to read from. Hard reference -- the asset is guaranteed loaded by the time this node executes.

SourceShape.tooltip: How the source attribute is interpreted on each input row.
SourceShape.semantics: Soft Object Path reads asset paths, and a path that resolves to nothing leaves that row with an empty attribute set. Entry Id + Map reads pick hashes against the Map, and only a hash naming a sub-collection entry opens: a hash naming a leaf produces an empty attribute set for that row rather than an error, which is what makes the mode safe to run over a mixed staged dataset. That is the recursive case, since the hashes an earlier read emitted are exactly what this mode consumes.

SourceAttribute.tooltip: Name of the attribute holding the collection reference (soft path or entry hash).
SourceAttribute.semantics: This name is not derived from Staging Layer the way the output entry attribute is, so reading hashes written to a named layer means typing that layer's full attribute name here. The default is the default layer's name.
SourceAttribute.trap: In Per Input Data the read is data-domain only, with no fall back to per-element values. Feeding staged points, whose pick lives per element, finds nothing and leaves every slot empty.

Fanout.tooltip: How many outputs to emit per input.
Fanout.semantics: Per Entry emits one attribute set per input row, and each one holds the whole collection that row resolved to, so two rows naming the same collection emit the same contents twice. Per Input Data emits one per input data and reads a single value from the data domain. Merged appends every unique collection into one set, which is the only mode where entries from different sources share an output, and so the only mode where the Duplicates skip and the weight denominators reach past a single source collection and its subtree. It also sets the domain the annotated sources are written on.

bForwardInputTags.tooltip: Forward source input data tags to the corresponding output attribute set.
bForwardInputTags.semantics: In Per Entry and Per Input Data the tags land on the attribute set that row or input produced. In Merged there is one output, so it receives the union of the tags of every input that contributed to it.

bAnnotateSources.tooltip: Forward each input from Sources to an additional 'Annotated Sources' output pin with identity attributes added -- whichever of RootCollectionIndex / CollectionIndex / CollectionHash are enabled below. Attribute names mirror the output-side names. Domain matches Fanout: PerInputData -> @Data (one value per input), PerEntry / Merged -> @Element (one value per row).
bAnnotateSources.semantics: The identity toggles under Annotations decide what gets added; with none of them and no Source Schema Properties configured, the pin forwards the inputs as they are rather than emitting nothing, so wiring it up before choosing an annotation still carries data. The attributes go on the data domain in Per Input Data and per element otherwise.

SubCollectionHandling.tooltip: How sub-collection entries are handled during flattening. Grammar defers to each entry's own SubGrammarMode (Flatten recurses, Inherit/Override emit one row).
SubCollectionHandling.semantics: Grammar is the only setting that reads per entry: an entry whose Grammar Mode is Flatten has its children hoisted into the parent's rows, and Inherit or Override emit the sub-collection as a single row instead. That row carries the sub-collection asset's own path, its category and its grammar, but no weight, bounds or nesting depth, because those are leaf values. Expand always recurses and Ignore drops sub-collections outright; the four pick modes take exactly one entry out of each sub-collection and recurse from there.
SubCollectionHandling.trap: Recursion is guarded against cycles per top-level entry, not per execution, so a shared sub-collection reached from two different top-level entries is walked twice. The Duplicates skip flag is what collapses the repeats.

SkipFlags.tooltip: Row-skip conditions. Default = EmptySymbol (matches the prior bSkipEmptySymbol = true behavior).
SkipFlags.semantics: Empty Symbol and Empty Axes both test a resolved grammar, and a grammar is only resolved when at least one of Symbol, Size, Scalable or Debug Color is enabled and Output Axes is not empty. With no grammar output requested, Empty Symbol drops nothing at all and Empty Axes drops every row. Duplicates acts twice: pointer-identical entries reached through more than one sub-collection path are collapsed during the walk, and rows repeating a Symbol already emitted into the same attribute set are dropped as they are written.
SkipFlags.trap: The default is Empty Symbol on, so a collection read purely for asset paths and weights behaves as if no skip were configured, while the same collection read for grammar silently loses every entry that was never given a Symbol.

bOmitInvalidAndEmpty.tooltip: Drop entries that resolve to invalid / empty data instead of keeping them as placeholders.
bOmitInvalidAndEmpty.semantics: A kept placeholder row has no entry behind it, so only the root, collection and hash identity attributes carry meaning; everything else on the row, the asset path and the entry hash included, stays at its attribute default.

CategoryFilters.tooltip: Optionally include/exclude entries by category name. Tested against both leaf entries and sub-collection containers; excluding a sub-collection skips its descendants entirely.

fields.name: FilterMode
fields.tooltip: How the names are processed.

fields.name: Matches
fields.tooltip: List of matches that will be checked. Any success is a pass.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNames
fields.tooltip: A list of names separated by a comma, for easy overrides. The limitation is that they all use the same shared filter mode.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNameFilter
fields.tooltip: Unique filter mode applied to comma separated names

fields.name: bPreservePCGExData
fields.tooltip: If enabled, PCGEx attributes & tags won't be affected.  Cluster-related nodes rely on these to work!

CategoryFilters.semantics: The test runs on the authored category, before any inheritance is folded in, and it runs on a sub-collection container before the walk descends, which is why excluding a container removes its whole subtree rather than just the container row.

AssetPathAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute the asset path is written to.
AssetPathAttributeName.semantics: One attribute and one type per emitted attribute set, decided from the entries that reached it: a set holding only actor entries gets a soft class path, any other mix gets a soft object path. Sub-collection rows carry the sub-collection asset's own path here, so a single attribute resolves both kinds of row.
AssetPathAttributeName.trap: A host holding both kinds resolves to the soft object path form, so an Omni collection of actors and meshes, or a Merged fanout spanning both, writes no class path anywhere. The actor rows still carry their class path as the string value of that object path attribute.

WeightAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute the asset weight is written to.
WeightAttributeName.semantics: Leaf rows only; a sub-collection row keeps the attribute default.
WeightAttributeName.trap: Entries disabled by a weight of 0 are absent from the read entirely, not written as zero-weight rows, because the collection's validated pool is what gets walked.

WeightNormalization.tooltip: How (and whether) to normalize the weight value. When set to anything other than None, the Weight attribute is written as a float in [0..1] instead of the raw int32.
WeightNormalization.semantics: The denominators are scoped to one emitted attribute set, so in Per Entry and Per Input Data each output normalizes against its own collection while Merged normalizes across everything merged into it. Sub-collection rows contribute nothing to the sums.
WeightNormalization.trap: Per Category buckets by the resolved category, and inheritance is only applied when Category output is enabled, so the same normalization gives different numbers depending on whether a category attribute is being written at all.

CategoryAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute the asset category is written to.

CategoryInheritance.tooltip: How (and whether) to fold parent sub-collection categories down into descendant entries during expansion. Also applies to Per Category weight normalization.
CategoryInheritance.semantics: Inheritance is applied only while the Category output is enabled, and that includes the copy of it that Per Category weight normalization reads.

OutputAxes.tooltip: Which subdivision axes to emit per row. Bits are intersected with each entry's own Axes bitmask at write time, so axes the entry doesn't enable produce no output for that row. When exactly one axis ends up being emitted across all rows, the _X/_Y/_Z suffix is dropped from per-axis attribute names (Size, Scalable) for the legacy single-axis shape -- unless bAlwaysSuffixAxes is set.
OutputAxes.semantics: Requested axes are intersected with each entry's own, so an axis no entry enables produces no attribute at all rather than an empty column. Clearing this switches off every grammar output, Symbol and Debug Color included, because no grammar is resolved when there is nothing to resolve it for.

bAlwaysSuffixAxes.tooltip: Always append _X/_Y/_Z to per-axis attribute names, even when only one axis is emitted. Use this when downstream graphs expect suffixed names regardless of axis count.
bAlwaysSuffixAxes.semantics: The suffix decision is made per emitted attribute set, from the axes that set's own rows turned out to use. In Per Entry and Per Input Data that means one output can carry Size while another carries Size_X, from the same node in the same execution. Turning this on makes the names identical across every output.

NestingDepthAttributeName.semantics: Leaf rows only, so a sub-collection emitted as a single row keeps the attribute default instead of reporting the depth it sits at. Depth counts recursion steps, so under a handling mode that never descends every row reads 0.

CollectionHashAttributeName.semantics: It is a dense index handed out in discovery order within one execution, not a stable identifier: the same collection can receive a different number on the next run if the inputs discovered it in a different order. What it is good for is grouping inside a single output, where every row from the same root, host and depth shares one short token.

SchemaPropertyAnnotations.tooltip: Schema-level properties (CollectionProperties) written as attributes; per-entry overrides ignored. Written to AnnotatedSources (FromInputs) or OutputCollectionData (Collection). Domain: @Data for PerInputData/Collection, @Element for PerEntry/Merged.
SchemaPropertyAnnotations.semantics: Schema-level values, taken from the collection rather than the entry, so per-entry overrides are ignored here. The destination changes with Source Mode: the Data output in Collection, the Annotated Sources output in From Inputs. A Collection Entry declared at collection level reaches the Map the same way an entry-level one does.
SchemaPropertyAnnotations.trap: In From Inputs with Annotate Sources off there is nowhere for these to go and nothing is written, on either output, and nothing of theirs reaches the Map either, without a warning.

StagingLayer.tooltip: Staging layer the entry hash attribute is written to. None = default layer (PCGEx/CollectionEntry); otherwise the layer name is appended (PCGEx/CollectionEntry/<layer>). Downstream consumers must read the same layer.

PropertyOutputSettings.tooltip: Additional custom properties to extract from each collection's CollectionProperties (and per-entry overrides).
PropertyOutputSettings.semantics: The per-row counterpart to Source Schema Properties: entry-level values with per-entry overrides honoured, resolved against the collection that actually owns the entry, so rows hoisted up out of a sub-collection read their own host's values rather than the root's. These always land on the Data output. One type renames its own output: a Collection Entry property writes an int64 pick hash under `PCGEx/CollectionEntry/` followed by the output name, so the row ends up carrying a second pick beside its own entry hash, on a staging layer of its own. The collection that pick names is loaded before the rows are written, and it joins the Map output, so both picks on a row resolve against the one Map.
PropertyOutputSettings.trap: Output Map decides nothing on this node, in this block or in Source Schema Properties. The Map output exists in every mode, and property picks merge into it whether the toggle is set or not.

hints.text: Empty Axes with no grammar output enabled empties the whole output. The flag tests a resolved grammar, and nothing resolves one until `Symbol`, `Size`, `Scalable` or `Debug Color` is on and `Output Axes` names an axis, so every row measures as contributing nothing and every row is dropped.

`Per Input Data` reads the data domain only. The default `Source Attribute` is the staging pick, which lives per element on staged points, so the default pairing finds nothing and every slot comes back empty. Feeding staged points means `Per Entry` or `Merged`.
Reading loads the collections and the sub-collections underneath them, never the assets the entries reference. Bounds, sizes and symbols all come from baked staging data.

UPCGExGetGUIDSettings.name: Get GUID
UPCGExGetGUIDSettings.purpose: Reads the identity of one point instead of stamping every point with its own. Given the same configuration, it produces exactly the value **Write GUID** would have written at that index, and hands it out as data rather than as an attribute. The points themselves come through the node untouched, so it answers a question about the data without changing it.
UPCGExGetGUIDSettings.situation: One value out of a dataset that has to seed or key something else in the graph, taken from a known position rather than from every point.

mechanism.text: Every dataset arriving on the input is read, so several inputs give several results on the output pin, one each. For each one the node resolves `Index` against that dataset's own length, computes the identity of the point it lands on, and emits an attribute set of one entry holding that value. Nothing is written to the points and nothing is forwarded: the output pin carries the results alone.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to read from. Every dataset on the pin is read.

outputs.label: GUID
outputs.note: One attribute set per input dataset, each with a single entry and a single attribute named by `Output Attribute Name`.

Index.semantics: Counted inside each dataset separately, so the same number reaches a different point in each one and a pin carrying several datasets yields several results.

IndexSafety.semantics: `Tile`, `Clamp` and `Yoyo` fold an out-of-range index back into the dataset. It ships on `Ignore`, which does not skip the input.
IndexSafety.trap: Under `Ignore` an out-of-range index resolves to no index at all and the whole node stops with an invalid-index error, taking every other dataset on the pin down with it.

hints.text: The match with **Write GUID** holds only while every setting in the two configuration blocks agrees, this node's own `Index` and `Index Safety` aside. A single flag out of step, or a unique key switched from a constant to an attribute, silently returns a value that belongs to no point.

UPCGExGetPathDataSettings.name: Get Path Data
UPCGExGetPathDataSettings.purpose: Reads spline components straight off selected actors and hands back a path per component, with the actor it came from recorded on the data. The vanilla getter loses that link the moment a spline becomes PCG data, so anything downstream that has to look the actor back up has nothing to look it up by. It also emits the source spline data on a second pin, stamped the same way, and it reads landscape spline components alongside regular ones.
UPCGExGetPathDataSettings.situation: Splines authored on level actors have to become paths, and something further down still needs to know which actor each one belongs to.

mechanism.text: The actor selection is walked component by component, and every spline component that survives the component filter becomes one path: a point per spline vertex, in order, with closure carried on the data. Nothing is resampled, so point positions are the spline's own control vertices and the point count is fixed by the spline. Enabling the second output costs one more dataset per component and nothing else, since both are built from the same component read. Actor reference and forwarded tags land on whichever outputs are enabled.

off_label.claim: With the path output switched off this is a spline getter that remembers its actor, which is the only way to hand vanilla spline data downstream with the source actor still attached to it.
off_label.grounded_in: PrepareActor emits PolyData on the Splines pin through the same StampAndEmit path as the point output, before the bOutputPaths early-out

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: Actors to read, inherited from the vanilla actor getter. The pin only exists while the actor selection is set to take actors from an input.
inputs.condition: when Actor Filter is From Input

inputs.label: Bounding Shape
inputs.note: Inherited from the vanilla actor getter: a shape narrowing which found actors are kept.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: One path per spline component, closure carried on the data.

outputs.label: Splines
outputs.note: The source spline data per component, unchanged apart from the stamp.

pins.dynamic: Both output pins are always declared and never disappear. Switching an output off greys its pin out instead of removing it, so a wire already dropped onto it survives being toggled off and on.

bOutputPaths.tooltip: Output a converted point path per spline (on the Paths pin).

bOutputSplines.tooltip: Output the source spline data per spline on the Splines pin -- "GetSplineData that remembers its actor" when Write Actor Reference is enabled. Built from the same component, so nearly free.

TransformDetails.tooltip: How point transforms inherit from the source spline. Location is always taken.

fields.name: bInheritScale
fields.tooltip: Multiply result scale by the parent's scale.

fields.name: bInheritRotation
fields.tooltip: Rotate result by the parent's rotation.

SampleInputs.tooltip: Which splines to include based on their open/closed state.
SampleInputs.semantics: A component that fails the open or closed test is dropped from both outputs, not just the path one. Components with no segments at all are skipped ahead of this test and never appear either way.

ArriveTangentAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'FVector' attribute to write the arrive tangent to.

LeaveTangentAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'FVector' attribute to write the leave tangent to.

LengthAtPointAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'double' attribute to write the length at point to.

AlphaAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'double' attribute to write the alpha to.

PointTypeAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write the point type to.
PointTypeAttributeName.semantics: Landscape spline components carry no interpolation modes, so the attribute is created only for regular spline components. A path built from a landscape spline comes back without it, with nothing logged.

ActorReferenceAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'FSoftObjectPath' @Data attribute to write the actor reference to.
ActorReferenceAttributeName.semantics: Written to the data domain, so it is one value per output dataset rather than one per point. Leaving the name blank falls back to the engine's own actor-reference attribute name rather than skipping the write.
ActorReferenceAttributeName.trap: Forwarded tags are turned into attributes first and the actor reference is written after, so a source tag carrying this same name is overwritten by the node's stamp rather than the other way round.

bForwardSourceTags.tooltip: Forward the source actor & spline-component tags onto the output data.

TagsToData.tooltip: How key:value tags (from the forwarded actor/component tags) are converted to attributes.

hints.text: This is the vanilla actor getter with a PCGEx element under it, so the actor and component selection blocks behave exactly as they do on the stock node, `Ignore PCG Generated Components` included. What is not inherited is the path processor: no **Paths** input pin, and no `Omit Invalid Paths Outputs`.

UPCGExGetPropertiesDataSettings.name: Get Properties Data
UPCGExGetPropertiesDataSettings.purpose: Turns actor references into attributes. Each row of the input names an actor or a property collection component by soft path; the node resolves it, reads the custom properties that component exposes, and writes their values as per-row attributes on a copy of the input. Resolution never loads anything, so a reference whose target is not already in memory counts as unresolved and is dropped or kept by the filtering toggles. A second output carries the external resources those property values point at.
UPCGExGetPropertiesDataSettings.situation: Points or rows carrying actor references, where the decisions downstream depend on values authored on those actors rather than on anything the graph knows.

mechanism.text: One output per input, same shape and same row order: points come back as points and attribute sets as attribute sets. Rows are dropped from the output by the filtering block, never reordered, and the surviving rows carry one attribute per property that was written. Which properties those are comes from `Output Mode`: every property the resolved components carry, or exactly the ones listed. Rows pointing at the same component share one schema read, so the cost follows the number of distinct components rather than the number of rows.

off_label.claim: Because the output mirrors the input's shape, an attribute set of reference paths comes back as an attribute set of resolved values, which reads a property table off a set of actors without any points being involved.
off_label.grounded_in: HasDynamicPins is true and both pins are PCGEX_PIN_ANY; the stage step routes point data through FPointIO::StageOutput and everything else through a direct TaggedData emplace

inputs.label: Sources
inputs.note: Points or attribute sets carrying the reference attribute.

outputs.label: Sources
outputs.note: One forwarded copy of each input, with the resolved property values written on the surviving rows.

outputs.label: Map
outputs.note: An attribute set describing the external resources the written properties reference, a staged collection pick being the usual case. The pin is always present and sits in the advanced section when nothing will be sent to it.

pins.dynamic: The output pin mirrors the input pin's type rather than declaring one, so the node preserves whatever it was handed.

SourceAttribute.tooltip: Attribute on each input row holding the soft object path of the actor (or the UPCGExPropertyCollectionComponent directly). FString-typed attributes fall back to parsing the string as an FSoftObjectPath.

OutputMode.tooltip: How to pick which properties to write per row.
OutputMode.semantics: `All Found` takes the union of everything the resolved components declare, which means the set of output attributes depends on what happened to resolve rather than on anything typed here. Where several components declare the same property, its output type and default come from the first one encountered, so a mixed batch is typed by whichever component appeared first on the pin.

PropertyOutputSettings.tooltip: Explicit list of properties to output. The Configs entries take precedence; IncludedSchemas contribute any property name they declare.

bOutputMap.tooltip: Emit the "Map" attribute set describing external resources referenced by written properties. Always emitted in AllFound mode (the toggle is hidden there).
bOutputMap.semantics: Reachable in `Explicit` only. `All Found` sends the map regardless, which is why the row disappears there rather than greying out.

bForwardInputTags.tooltip: Forward each input's tags to the corresponding output.

bOmitUnresolvedEntries.tooltip: Drop rows whose soft path didn't resolve to a UPCGExPropertyCollectionComponent.
bOmitUnresolvedEntries.semantics: Turn it off and unresolved rows stay in the output with nothing written for them, so they carry whatever default their output attribute was created with rather than a marker of any kind.

bOmitPartialMatches.tooltip: Drop rows where one or more requested properties could not be located on the resolved component. Has no effect when OutputMode is AllFound.

RequiredSchemas.tooltip: When non-empty, only keep rows whose resolved component imports the listed schema asset(s). The check walks the component's full import tree recursively.
RequiredSchemas.semantics: The check walks each component's import tree, so a schema reached through another schema counts.
RequiredSchemas.trap: A row whose component fails this check is dropped whatever `Omit Unresolved Entries` says. That toggle governs rows that never resolved, not rows that resolved to the wrong thing.

hints.text: Resolution is tentative: the soft path is looked up among what is already loaded, and nothing is ever pulled in for it. A reference that resolves in the editor because the level happens to be open can come back unresolved elsewhere, so anything depending on it needs the asset loaded upstream.

UPCGExGetTextureDataSettings.name: Get Texture Data
UPCGExGetTextureDataSettings.purpose: Turns asset paths carried on points into texture data something can sample. The path can name a texture outright, or name a material whose parameters have to be resolved first, and that choice is what decides whether a **Texture Param** is needed. It is the loading step of the texture route, and the node that produces what **Sample : Texture** requires.
UPCGExGetTextureDataSettings.situation: Points that know which material or texture they belong to, and a graph that needs to read pixels out of it.

mechanism.text: Each point's named attribute is read as an asset path and resolved into texture data on the output pin. Under `Material Path` the path names a material and the Texture Param factories say which parameter inside it to take, so the same points can yield different textures depending on what is wired. Under `Texture Path` the path is the texture and no parameters are involved. The transform and tiling settings decide how the resulting data is laid out for later sampling rather than what is loaded.

inputs.label: Texture Params
inputs.note: Texture Param factories naming which parameter to pull out of each material. Under Texture Path the pin is not declared.
inputs.condition: only when Source Type is Material Path

outputs.label: Texture Data
outputs.note: The loaded texture data, ready for **Sample : Texture**.

pins.dynamic: The Texture Params pin exists only under Material Path, so switching the source type changes the node's wiring rather than just its behaviour.

SourceType.semantics: Decides whether the attribute is a texture or a material, and rewires the node accordingly. `Material Path` adds the required Texture Param pin, because a material holds several textures and something has to name which one. `Texture Path` removes that pin: the path is already the answer.

SourceAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute to read asset path from (material or texture).
SourceAttributeName.semantics: The attribute holding the path, read per point. Points sharing a path resolve to the same texture data rather than to a copy each, so a large point set referencing few assets costs what the assets cost.

bOutputTextureIds.tooltip: If enabled, will write resolved texture paths as per their definitions.

bBuildTextureData.tooltip: If enabled, will build PCG Texture data for each unique texture reference found.

Filter.tooltip: Method used to determine the value for a sample based on the value of nearby texels.

TexelSize.tooltip: The size of one texel in cm, used when calling ToPointData.
TexelSize.semantics: Decides how finely the texture is laid out into data, which sets the resolution anything downstream can read. It is a sampling density rather than a property of the source asset, so a coarse value discards detail the texture still has.

Rotation.tooltip: Rotation to apply when sampling texture.

bUseAdvancedTiling.tooltip: Whether to tile the source or to stretch it to fit target area.

UPCGExGoalPicker.name: Goal Picker : Default
UPCGExGoalPicker.purpose: The base every goal picker inherits, and the choice a node starts on. A picker decides one thing: which goal each seed routes to. Two nodes carry the dropdown, **Pathfinding : Edges** and **Pathfinding : Navmesh**, and both ask their picker before any searching happens. This one pairs by position, seed *n* to goal *n*, with `Index Safety` deciding what a seed gets once its row runs past the end of the Goals data.
UPCGExGoalPicker.situation: Seeds and goals arrive as two datasets whose rows already correspond, and each seed should route to the goal on its own row.

mechanism.text: A picker is handed the whole Seeds and Goals datasets once, then asked about each seed point in turn. It answers with an index into the Goals data, or with a list of them, and every index it hands back becomes one query: one seed, one goal, one path once the search resolves it. An index below zero is dropped rather than corrected, which is how a picker declines a seed outright. Nothing about the cluster or the navmesh is in scope while this happens, so a pairing never depends on whether a route between the two exists. This picker answers with the seed's own row index run through `Index Safety`, and never with more than one goal.
