UPCGExOffsetPathSettings.name: Path : Offset
UPCGExOffsetPathSettings.purpose: Moves every point of a path sideways, to lay a parallel run beside it or to grow and shrink a closed shape. The sideways direction is worked out from the segments meeting at each point, and the distance is a value read at the point, so both can vary along the run. `Direction` can also be handed a per-point vector instead, which takes the path out of the decision entirely.
UPCGExOffsetPathSettings.situation: A path needs a second run holding a fixed distance beside it, or a closed shape needs to be inflated or inset.

mechanism.text: One execution takes paths and returns the same points in the same order, moved. Point count, order, rotations, scales and every attribute come through untouched; only locations change. Each point is moved from the positions as they arrived, so one point's move never feeds another's, and a point the **Filters** pin rejects keeps the location it came in with. Every point moves, the last one on an open path included: it has no segment of its own to read, so it borrows the final segment's. A path of fewer than two points is refused with a warning.

off_label.claim: Set `Direction` to Custom and point it at a vector attribute and the node stops being a path operation: it moves each point along whatever that attribute holds, by a per-point distance, with the path consulted for nothing. A general per-point displace with two independently drivable halves.
off_label.grounded_in: ProcessPoints reads DirectionGetter->Read(Index) in place of the path-derived direction whenever DirectionConstant is Custom, and no path geometry is consulted on that branch

bApplyPointScaleToOffset.semantics: The point's scale multiplies the direction vector component by component, in world axes, before the distance is applied. A uniform scale therefore only changes how far the point travels, and a non-uniform one swings it off the direction that was computed.

Direction.semantics: Read once per point and negated on the way in, the same as the four built-in directions are, so the shipped `$Rotation.Left` selector moves points along their local right. `Invert Direction` cancels that, and a path oriented by **Path : Orient** first is what makes this route predictable.

bInvertDirection.tooltip: Inverts offset direction. Can also be achieved by using negative offset values, but this enable consistent inversion no matter the input.

UpVectorConstant.tooltip: Up vector used to calculate Offset direction.
UpVectorConstant.semantics: The same vector at every point of every path. Where a segment runs close to it the cross product collapses and the direction is resolved arbitrarily, which shows as the offset run flipping sides over a short stretch. Parallel Transport is the only entry that stops consulting it after the first segment.

AdjustmentScale.semantics: The opposite lean to Auto Smooth, which widens tight corners and leaves straight runs alone.
AdjustmentScale.trap: The shipped -0.5 moves points on straight stretches half again as far as `Offset` asks for, holds a right-angle corner where it is, and halves the distance at a doubling back. On an open path the first point is treated as straight whatever its neighbours do, and the last point borrows the corner angle of the point before it.

MitreLimit.semantics: A ceiling on how far the mitre may push a corner out, counted as a multiple of `Offset`. At the shipped 4 it is reached at a corner of about 29 degrees, and everything tighter moves four times `Offset`. The ceiling is on distance alone, so a negative `Offset` caps at the same multiple in the direction it points.

UPCGExOmniCollection.name: Collection | Omni
UPCGExOmniCollection.purpose: Holds entries of every registered type in one weighted list. Mesh, skinned mesh, actor, level and PCG data asset rows sit side by side in one pool, along with any entry type a plugin registers. The entry type is a property of each row, picked when the row is created, so the asset itself carries no single type. Existing typed collections fold in through the merge action, which is also the route for converting one collection.
UPCGExOmniCollection.situation: One weighted library has to draw across asset kinds, or a set of single-type collections needs folding into one pool.

mechanism.text: Each row wraps one entry payload of a concrete type, so adding an entry starts by choosing that type, and a row's settings are the ones its own type declares. A row whose payload is unset is tolerated: it keeps its place in the list and contributes nothing to picking or staging. Collection-level settings that a typed collection carries as plain properties arrive here as **Type Globals** blocks, at most one per entry type, and an entry whose type has no block reads its own local values. Those blocks, and the **Type Machinery** states for types that need cross-entry state, are installed automatically as new entry types appear, seeded from the matching typed collection's defaults, and re-checked at the start of every staging rebuild.

off_label.claim: Cleanup also drops blocks with no type and empty machinery slots whatever the entry list holds, so it doubles as a repair pass on a collection whose Global arrays were edited by hand.
off_label.grounded_in: the two removal branches in EDITOR_CleanupUnusedTypeSetup, which treat a block with no struct and a null state slot as removable without consulting the present entry types

Entries.semantics:
A row's entry type is fixed when the row is created. The add flow asks for the type first; dropping assets from the Content Browser answers by inspection instead, routing static meshes to mesh rows, skinned assets to skinned mesh rows, actor blueprints to actor rows, level assets to level rows and PCG data assets to data asset rows, and skipping any asset a row of that same type already references. An actor row made this way references the blueprint's generated class, not the blueprint asset.

Dropping a collection asset makes a sub-collection row instead, and the row takes the referenced collection's entry type when that collection has one, so clearing its sub-collection flag later reveals that type's asset picker. A source with no single type of its own, another Omni Collection among them, leaves a typeless row that shows no picker at all.

The merge action appends entries from other collections and leaves the sources untouched. Each entry arrives as a row of its exact type with a fresh identity, the source collection's own tags baked onto the copied entry's tags, and sub-collection rows keeping the collection they reference. Category override rows travel only with entries that carry their category, and a category this collection already overrides keeps its existing row. Once the append finishes the property schema is re-derived and staging rebuilt. A Variant Collection has no per-entry payloads to copy, so nothing can be merged out of one; merge its source collections instead.

TypeGlobals.tooltip: Per-type collection-level globals blocks. One block per entry type at most (first struct match wins); entries whose type has no block fall back to entry-local settings. NOTE: raw FInstancedStruct copies are SHALLOW for Instanced subobjects -- cross-asset copies must DuplicateObject them into the destination asset.
TypeGlobals.semantics:
A block is installed with the first entry of its type and seeded from that type's collection defaults, so it starts out matching a freshly created collection of that type rather than empty. Only types that declare collection-level settings get one, which among the shipped types means mesh, skinned mesh, actor, level and PCG data asset.

Merging brings each source's block along. When two merged sources disagree over a type's block, the block is dropped and both sources' entries keep their exact values baked into their own rows. When the disagreement is with a block already on this collection, that block stays and only the incoming entries are baked.
TypeGlobals.trap: A block already on this collection wins a merge conflict, and its collection-wide rules still apply to the entries the merge just baked. A block set to overrule its type's entry-local values silently overrides the values the merge preserved.

TypeStates.tooltip: Per-type machinery state/processor blocks (see UPCGExCollectionTypeState). One instance per present entry type whose registry entry declares a StateClass -- ensured automatically at the start of every editor staging rebuild session. Owns the mutable cross-entry state (e.g. the PCGDataAsset shared collections) and receives the host lifecycle dispatches. Serialized (cooked too -- state may carry runtime subobjects).
TypeStates.semantics: Of the shipped entry types only the PCG data asset type declares machinery, so this array stays empty on a collection holding meshes, actors and levels alone. An existing state always wins: merging a source that carries its own machinery settings leaves the state as it is, and only a state created by that merge adopts the source's settings.
TypeStates.trap: Duplicating an element of this array leaves two states in the same slot, each running the same machinery over the same entries. The collection warns about it on the next staging rebuild; remove the duplicate rather than leaving it in place.

hints.text: Removing the last entry of a type leaves its **Type Globals** block and **Type Machinery** state behind, because either may carry edits. The collection editor's **Cleanup** toolbar button removes the setup no remaining entry needs, and keeps whatever the type registry does not recognise, so a block belonging to an unloaded plugin survives it.

UPCGExOrientAverage.name: Average
UPCGExOrientAverage.purpose: Splits the corner. It takes the direction the path arrives on and the direction it leaves on and hands back the one that sits exactly between them, so a point at a corner meets both of its segments evenly instead of lining up with either. It has no settings at all: the axis the direction lands on, the roll around it and whether the point is turned end for end are **Path : Orient**'s to decide.
UPCGExOrientAverage.situation: A path with corners, where whatever is placed at a corner should straddle it rather than agree with one of its two segments.

mechanism.text: Reads the two segments meeting at the point and returns the midpoint of their two directions. Along a straight run the two are the same direction and the midpoint is that direction. At the first and last point of an open path there is only one segment and both halves of the average resolve to it, so the endpoint takes that segment's direction and there is nothing to split. A closed path gives every point two real segments, the one at the seam included.

UPCGExOrientInstancedFactory.name: Orient Operation
UPCGExOrientInstancedFactory.purpose: The half the three orient rules share, whichever one is picked from the Orientation dropdown on Path : Orient. A rule answers one question, which direction this point should point at, and nothing else: **Path : Orient** owns which local axis carries that direction, what resolves the roll around it, whether the point is flipped, and where the finished rotation is written. It declares no settings of its own, so the axis pair the panel shows under a rule belongs to the node above it and switching rules never disturbs it. What it does settle for every rule is what a neighbour resolves to when there is not one.
UPCGExOrientInstancedFactory.situation: Reading one of the three rules and needing to know which part of the resulting rotation is the rule's doing and which part is the node's.

mechanism.text: A rule is handed the whole path and the point's own data, and returns one transform per point: that point's own location and scale with a new rotation in place of the old one. Positions are read as they arrived and never from rotations the run has already produced, so no point's result feeds another and the order points are visited in changes nothing. Neighbours are resolved by the path itself, and that is where the two ends of an open path are settled: a request for the point before the first, or after the last, comes back as that same point, so the direction to the missing neighbour collapses onto the one segment that does exist. A closed path wraps instead, and every point on it has a real neighbour on both sides.

UPCGExOrientLookAt.name: Look At
UPCGExOrientLookAt.purpose: Aims at a target instead of working one out from the shape of the path. `Look At` picks where that target comes from: the next point, the previous point, a direction read from an attribute, or a world position read from an attribute. The two attribute modes are the reason to reach for this rule, because they take the rotation off the path's own geometry and hand it to whatever wrote the attribute. It is also the rule a fresh **Path : Orient** ships with, set to `Next Point`.
UPCGExOrientLookAt.situation: Points along a path that have to face something the path knows nothing about, a fixed location in the level or a direction an earlier node worked out.

mechanism.text: Returns one direction per point and reads only what the selected mode needs. The two path modes take the direction of the single segment on the chosen side. The two attribute modes read a vector from the point, and they bind that attribute once before any point is processed, so a selector that resolves to nothing stops the whole path rather than failing point by point. Nothing here reads both sides of a point at once, which is what separates it from the other two rules.

off_label.claim: In `Direction` mode the attribute is used as it stands, so writing a constant vector onto every point turns the rule into a fixed world orientation for the whole path, with the path itself contributing nothing.
off_label.grounded_in: LookAtDirection normalises the buffer value and passes it straight to the axis mapping, with no reference to Path

LookAt.semantics: `Next Point` and `Previous Point` differ everywhere except at the two ends of an open path, where the missing side resolves to the point itself and both modes fall back on the one segment that exists: the first point of an open path behaves identically under either mode, and so does the last. `Direction` uses the attribute value as it stands, in world space, without transforming it by the point's own rotation, so a vector authored in the point's own terms has to be transformed before it reaches here. `Position` subtracts the point's location from the attribute value, so the value is read as a world location and the resulting direction differs from point to point even when the attribute holds the same value everywhere.
LookAt.trap: A zero-length direction leaves the rotation with nothing to build from, and the point comes out aligned to the world axes rather than keeping the rotation it arrived with. That covers a zero vector in `Direction` mode and, in `Position` mode, a target sitting exactly on the point.

LookAtAttribute.tooltip: Vector attribute representing either a direction or world position, depending on selected mode.
LookAtAttribute.semantics: Read through a broadcaster, so a source that is not already a vector is converted where a conversion exists. A selector that resolves to nothing warns and leaves that whole path unprocessed, which reaches the graph as a path that came through with the rotations it arrived with rather than as a node-level error.

hints.text: Which axis of the point does the aiming is `Orient Axis` on **Path : Orient**, not something this rule decides. At the shipped `Forward` and `Next Point`, a point's +X ends up pointing at the point after it.

UPCGExOrientSettings.name: Path : Orient
UPCGExOrientSettings.purpose: Sets each point's rotation from the shape of the path around it. The rule doing the pointing is picked from the `Orientation` dropdown, and the node owns everything around it: which local axis carries the result, what resolves the roll, whether a point is turned end for end, and whether the rotation lands on the point or in an attribute. It can also record how sharp the corner at each point is, as a dot product, independently of which rule is selected.
UPCGExOrientSettings.situation: A path whose points came from somewhere that did not care about rotation, and something is about to be placed along it that does.

mechanism.text: One execution takes paths and returns the same points in the same order, with new rotations. Point count, order, locations, scales and every attribute come through untouched, and in `Output to attribute` mode the rotations do too. Each point is handled on its own from the positions as they arrived, so nothing is order dependent and one point's new rotation never feeds another's. A path of fewer than two points is refused with a warning. The rule returns a direction and the node turns it into a rotation, so all three rules land in the same frame and differ only in the direction they hand back.

off_label.claim: Turn on the dot output with `Output` left on `Apply to point` and the node doubles as a corner-sharpness pass: every point gets both its orientation and a number a downstream filter can threshold on to find the turns.
off_label.grounded_in: ProcessPoints writes DotWriter unconditionally on bOutputDot, in the same loop and independently of the Output mode

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to orient.

inputs.label: Flip Conditions
inputs.note: Points that pass have the rule's direction negated. With the pin empty every point takes `Flip Direction` instead.

inputs.label: Overrides : Orient
inputs.note: Attribute set whose entries overwrite the selected rule's own properties by name. Sits under the node's advanced pins.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The same points in the same order, rotated, or unrotated with the result in an attribute.

OrientAxis.tooltip: Which axis of the point transform is aimed along the direction the rule computes.
OrientAxis.semantics: Names which of the point's local axes is laid along the direction the rule computed, so with the shipped `Forward` a point's +X ends up pointing at whatever the rule aimed at. The six entries are three axes taken positively and negatively, which makes `Forward` and `Backward` one axis pointed opposite ways: switching between a pair does exactly what `Flip Direction` does, and doing both cancels.

UpAxis.tooltip: World direction used to resolve the remaining roll. Resolved per point, with no continuity between points.
UpAxis.semantics: Which local axis this ends up constraining follows from `Orient Axis`: the point's Z for the four horizontal entries and the point's Y when `Orient Axis` is `Up` or `Down`. It is the same world vector at every point of every path, so where a path turns to run along the direction chosen here the roll is resolved arbitrarily and whatever is deformed along the path rolls with it. Continuity of that kind lives elsewhere: **Parallel Transport** is a value of `Normal` on **Path : Solidify** and of `Direction` on **Path : Offset**, and this node has no equivalent.

Orientation.semantics: Holds the three rules, and the node's subtitle in the graph names whichever is selected. A fresh node ships with `Look At` selected and set to `Next Point`; emptying the slot stops the node with an error asking for a module. Everything shown under the dropdown belongs to the rule and the axis pair above it does not, so switching rules leaves the frame alone. A rule that has to bind an attribute and cannot, which is `Look At` in its two attribute modes, warns and leaves that path unprocessed rather than falling back, so the path reaches the output with the rotations it arrived with.

bFlipDirection.tooltip: Flip every point's direction. Read only when the filter pin is empty -- wiring filters replaces it entirely.
bFlipDirection.semantics: Negates the direction the rule handed back before the axis is built, which turns the oriented axis end for end.
bFlipDirection.trap: It is the value used when the **Flip Conditions** pin is empty, not a fallback for points the filters do not reach. Wire anything into that pin and every point takes its verdict instead: points that pass are flipped, points that fail are not, and this setting stops applying to any of them.

Output.tooltip: How to use the computed orientation.

OutputAttribute.tooltip: Name of the attribute to output orientation to.
OutputAttribute.semantics: What lands in the attribute is a whole transform, not a rotation: the point's own location and scale with the computed rotation substituted. The point's own rotation is left exactly as it arrived in this mode, so the node's output looks unchanged in the viewport until something reads the attribute.

DotAttribute.tooltip: Name of the attribute the prev/next dot product is written to.
DotAttribute.semantics: The dot product of the direction the path arrives on with the direction it leaves on: 1 along a straight run, 0 at a right angle, -1 where the path doubles back on itself. The node computes it, not the rule, so it reads the same whichever rule is selected, and it is written in both `Output` modes.
DotAttribute.trap: On an open path the first and last point always read 1, because the missing neighbour resolves to the point itself and the two directions collapse onto one segment. An endpoint and a straight run cannot be told apart in this attribute.

UPCGExOrientWeighted.name: Weighted
UPCGExOrientWeighted.purpose: Average with a lean toward the segment the path leaves on. It mixes the same two directions **Average** does, using a factor built from the two segments' lengths, and that factor is symmetric in them: it reads how unequal the two segments are and never which of them is the shorter. Equal segments produce the strongest lean, two parts outgoing to one part incoming, and the more unequal the segments become the closer the result creeps back toward the plain bisector.
UPCGExOrientWeighted.situation: A corner where the bisector reads as lagging behind the turn, and the direction the path leaves on should carry more of the result.

mechanism.text: Mixes the direction the path arrives on with the direction it leaves on, weighting the outgoing one more heavily. The factor is one plus the longer of the two segments' squared lengths divided by the shorter, which is never below two, and the outgoing direction's share of the result runs from two thirds when the segments are equal down toward one half as they diverge. Both directions are the ones **Average** uses, so the result always sits between the bisector and the outgoing segment and never outside them. `Inverse Weight` uses one minus that factor instead, which reverses the result end for end and moves the lean onto the incoming direction. At the two ends of an open path one of the segments has no length to measure, so the weighing is dropped and the one real segment decides alone, pointing forward under the plain factor and backward under `Inverse Weight`.

bInverseWeight.semantics: Turns the factor into one minus itself, which does two things at once: the returned direction points the opposite way, and the lean moves from the outgoing segment to the incoming one. The reversal is the part that shows, and `Flip Direction` on **Path : Orient** cancels it without touching the lean.

UPCGExPackClustersSettings.name: Cluster : Pack
UPCGExPackClustersSettings.purpose: Folds each cluster into one point dataset, so it can go where a pair of pins cannot: into a PCG Data Asset, through a boundary that carries one dataset, into storage. **Cluster : Unpack** is the other half. Inside a running graph there is nothing to gain from it, because the Edges pin already hands you one dataset per cluster and **Find Clusters** already pulls pairs back out of a mixed pile.
UPCGExPackClustersSettings.situation: A cluster has to be written into a PCG Data Asset and read back later.

mechanism.text: Each cluster becomes one dataset on **Packed Clusters**: that cluster's edge points first, then the vertices it actually uses, appended after them, with the edge count recorded on the dataset so the split can be undone. Only the vertices belonging to that cluster travel, so a Vtx dataset shared by four Edges datasets packs into four datasets rather than one. The endpoint ids on both halves are copied across as they are, which is what lets the pairing survive the fold. `Carry Over Settings` prunes the tags that travel.

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The Vtx dataset. Only the vertices a given cluster uses are packed with it.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The Edges datasets, one per cluster. Each one becomes one packed dataset.

outputs.label: Packed Clusters
outputs.note: One dataset per cluster, edge points then Vtx points. This is the node's only output: neither a Vtx nor an Edges pin survives here.

fields.name: bPreserveAttributesDefaultValue
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will preserve the initial attribute default value.

fields.name: Attributes
fields.tooltip: Attributes to carry over.

fields.name: bDataDomainToElements
fields.tooltip: If enabled, data domain attributes are promoted to the elements domain (the single @Data value is broadcast to every point). Off by default; Merge Points is the node that enables it. Not used by all nodes.

fields.name: Scope
fields.tooltip: Scope

fields.name: Tags
fields.tooltip: Tags to carry over.

fields.name: bTestTagsWithValues
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

CarryOverDetails.semantics: Only the tag half of the block is read here. Attributes are not filtered on the way in: every attribute on either half of the cluster lands on the packed dataset.
CarryOverDetails.trap: Filtering tags here can produce packed data that **Cluster : Unpack** cannot open. The pair tag `PCGEx/Cluster` is how Unpack rebuilds the pairing, and it is an ordinary tag as far as this block is concerned, so switching the tag filter to `Include` without naming it strips it. The packed dataset still carries its edge count, so Unpack splits it, warns, and emits both halves with neither the pair tag nor a Vtx or Edges role tag, which leaves nothing downstream able to read them as a cluster. The default, `All`, keeps everything and is safe.

hints.text: The round trip is not shape-preserving. One Vtx dataset paired with four Edges datasets comes back as four separate pairs, each holding only its own vertices, and the vertices come back in cluster order rather than their original row order. The packed dataset is built from the Edges half, so the Vtx dataset's own tags do not travel and both halves come back carrying the Edges dataset's tags. An attribute name carried by both halves survives on the Vtx rows only: the edge rows come back at that attribute's default. The endpoint ids do survive, so the pairing itself is intact.

UPCGExPartitionIdentifierSettings.name: Partition Identifier
UPCGExPartitionIdentifierSettings.purpose: Names the partition cell a position sits in, as a string a graph can key on. A cell is a grid size plus an integer coordinate, and the identifier is a pure function of the two, so the same position always yields the same name regardless of which component asks. It answers two different questions depending on Source: which cell am I generating in, and which cell does each of these points fall in. The Grids list turns one query into several, so the neighbours and the coarser parents of a cell can be named in the same pass.
UPCGExPartitionIdentifierSettings.situation: A partitioned generation that has to address cells by name, whether to key streaming, to build asset identifiers per cell, or to reason about its own neighbours.

mechanism.text: Every entry in the Grids list is one query. It resolves a grid size, decides whether the grid is two or three dimensional, converts the anchor position into an integer cell coordinate at that size, adds the entry's offset, and formats the result as the grid size and the coordinate joined by underscores. The anchor is the executing component's bounds centre under Executing Component, or each point's own position under Input Positions. Cells are laid out from the world origin, which is what makes the names line up with the engine's own partition actors. An empty Grids list produces nothing at all.

off_label.claim: An entry whose only change is a coarser explicit grid names the parent cell containing the anchor, and a second entry a step coarser again names its parent, which turns one node into a way of writing a whole ancestry of cell names onto each point.
off_label.grounded_in: each Grids entry resolves its own grid size independently and shares only the anchor position, with Grid Size Offset stepping the power-of-two ladder

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points whose positions are classified. Non-point data on this pin is skipped and does not reach the output.
inputs.condition: when Source is Input Positions

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: Under Input Positions, a duplicate of each input carrying one id attribute per grid entry. Under Executing Component, one attribute set describing the current cell and its configured relatives.

Source.tooltip: Where the queried position(s) come from.
Source.semantics: Executing Component asks about the cell the current generation belongs to and emits an attribute set; it needs no input and produces one row's worth of description per grid entry. Input Positions asks about points instead, forwarding a copy of them with the ids written per point.
Source.trap: Under Executing Component the answer depends on the component that is generating. A graph running on a non-partitioned component, or with no execution source at all, warns and emits an empty attribute set rather than failing.

PositionSource.tooltip: Position to classify, read per input point. Defaults to the point location.
PositionSource.semantics: Any per-point value that reads as a vector, not only the point location, so a stored destination or a projected position can be classified instead.
PositionSource.trap: Scalar sources are rejected rather than broadcast to all three axes; the input is skipped with a warning.

bOutputPartitionId.tooltip: Write the formatted partition id string.

PartitionIdAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the string attribute receiving the partition id (suffixed per grid entry in Columns layout).
PartitionIdAttributeName.semantics: The base name. In Columns and in Input Positions each grid entry appends its own Suffix to it, so entries sharing a Suffix collide; the duplicate is skipped with a warning rather than overwriting.

IdPrefix.tooltip: Optional prefix prepended to the id. Empty by default -- add your own separator if you want one (e.g. "MyAsset_").
IdPrefix.semantics: Prepended with no separator of its own, so a separator has to be part of the string. Ignored entirely while the engine actor name is being matched, since that supplies its own prefix.

bMatchEnginePartitionActorName.tooltip: Emit the exact engine partition actor name (PCGPartitionGridActor_... or its runtime variant) instead of the size_x_y_z form. Note: editor-only DataLayer/HLOD name suffixes are not reproduced.
bMatchEnginePartitionActorName.semantics: Swaps the prefix for the engine's own partition actor prefix, picking the runtime variant when the generation is a runtime one.
bMatchEnginePartitionActorName.trap: It reproduces the name's shape, not the whole name: the editor-only data layer and HLOD suffixes are not part of it, so the result matches a plain partition actor and not one carrying those.

Layout.tooltip: Columns: one suffixed attribute per grid entry on the @Data domain. Rows: one attribute-set row per grid entry. Input Positions always writes per-point id columns.
Layout.semantics: Columns writes one suffixed attribute per grid entry onto the @Data domain, so the whole answer is one row wide and read by name. Rows writes one row per grid entry with the same attribute names throughout, which is the shape to iterate over. Only Executing Component offers the choice; Input Positions is always columns, per point.

Grids.tooltip: The partitions to emit, relative to the anchor. The default single entry is the cell itself; add entries for neighbors (Offset) or parents (a coarser Explicit grid). An empty array emits nothing.
Grids.semantics: One entry is one cell query. The default single entry describes the cell itself at the component's own grid; an Offset names a neighbour, a coarser Explicit Grid or a positive Grid Size Offset names a parent. Clearing the list is a valid state and emits nothing.
Grids.trap: Under Input Positions only the id and the grid size are written per entry; the structured per-cell outputs are Executing Component only.

bOutputGridSize.tooltip: Write the grid size (cm) as an int attribute, suffixed per grid entry. Available for both sources (written to the @Data domain).

GridSizeAttributeName.semantics: Written to the @Data domain in both sources, since a grid size describes the query rather than any one point. It takes the entry's Suffix like the id does.

Outputs.tooltip: Structured per-cell outputs (Executing Component only): grid coordinate, cell center/bounds, and the Rows-layout label.
Outputs.semantics: The geometric description of each cell: its integer coordinate, its centre, and its two corners, all in world space and all anchored at the world origin. The row label is the entry's Suffix written as a value, which is what identifies a row once Rows layout has removed the suffixes from the names.

hints.text: Grid Size Offset steps the power-of-two ladder rather than scaling the number: minus one halves the cell, plus one doubles it, and the result is clamped to the range the grid dropdown exposes.
In a two-dimensional grid the Z coordinate is always zero and is dropped from the identifier, so the same name is produced for positions at any height and an entry's Z offset does nothing.

UPCGExPartitionVerticesSettings.name: Cluster : Partition Vtx
UPCGExPartitionVerticesSettings.purpose: Gives every Edges dataset a Vtx dataset of its own. One Vtx dataset serving several Edges datasets is the normal shape a generator emits, and it means the Vtx half carries points belonging to components an operation is not looking at. This node cuts that shared pool up: one cluster in, one cluster out, each self-contained. It is the reverse of Cluster : Merge Vtx.
UPCGExPartitionVerticesSettings.situation: A cluster came out of a generator as one Vtx dataset and several Edges datasets, and something downstream has to treat each component as a dataset in its own right.

mechanism.text: Each Edges dataset gets a new Vtx dataset holding only the Vtx its edges name, carrying their attributes across, and the two are stamped as a fresh pair. The incoming Vtx dataset is not part of the output at all, so what leaves the Vtx pin is entirely the new datasets, one per Edges dataset. A Vtx no edge names is in none of them and does not come out anywhere. Edges pass through untouched, still naming the same endpoint ids, which is why the pairing keeps resolving.

off_label.claim: Run it on a single-component cluster and it becomes a pruning pass: the Vtx that no edge names are the ones a refinement left stranded, and they are dropped from the output without any filter being wired.
off_label.grounded_in: The new dataset is sized to the cluster's node count and filled from the node list, which holds only Vtx an edge referenced

off_label.claim: A Vtx named by two different Edges datasets is copied into both partitions, so a cluster whose components genuinely share Vtx comes out with those Vtx duplicated rather than with the components still joined.
off_label.grounded_in: Each processor builds its own output dataset from its own cluster's node list, with no coordination between them

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The shared Vtx dataset to cut up.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The Edges datasets that decide the partitions. One partition comes out per dataset here.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: One new Vtx dataset per Edges dataset, each holding only the Vtx its partner names.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: Forwarded unchanged, re-tagged to point at their new partner.

hints.text: The output Vtx are in the order the edges first named them, which is not the order they arrived in. Anything downstream reading a Vtx by index, an index attribute captured before this node among them, is reading a different point afterwards. Endpoint ids survive the move, so cluster nodes are unaffected.

UPCGExPathCrossingsSettings.name: Path × Path Crossings
UPCGExPathCrossingsSettings.purpose: Finds where path segments cross other path segments, on the pin's other paths or on the same path, and puts a point at each crossing. Nothing is joined and nothing is split: each path keeps its identity and gains points. Which paths are allowed to cut and which are allowed to be cut are separate questions with separate answers, by tag at the dataset level and by filter at the segment level, so the relationship can be made one-way.
UPCGExPathCrossingsSettings.situation: Two sets of paths overlap and the overlap has to become addressable, as points that carry which way the other path was going.

mechanism.text: One path in, one path out, longer: crossings are inserted between the two points of the segment they were found on, in order along it. Both paths of a crossing gain a point at the same place, and they are two separate points in two separate datasets, since each path is cut on its own pass and neither is aware of what the other kept. The crossing point sits where the segments met, and its values are blended from the two points bracketing its own segment; the other path contributes nothing to it unless cross blending is switched on. Everything crosses everything by default, including a path with itself.

off_label.claim: Switched to detect without inserting, this is a whole-dataset overlap test: nothing about the paths changes and the tags alone say which of them met something, which is the cheap way to route overlapping and non-overlapping paths apart before doing real work on either.
off_label.grounded_in: with Create Point At Crossings off the path is forwarded rather than rebuilt, and the has-crossings tag is written from the crossing count found during the search

off_label.claim: The cross direction attribute records the other path's heading at the meeting point, so a crossing point carries information about a path it is not part of. Orienting on it turns each inserted point to face along whatever cut it.
off_label.grounded_in: the crossing's direction is taken from the cutting edge and written to the cross-direction attribute, and the orient toggle builds the point's rotation from that same vector

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: Every path, on one pin. Cutters and cut paths are not separated by wiring but by the tag and filter settings.

inputs.label: Can Cut Conditions
inputs.note: Point filters narrowing which segments of a path are allowed to cut others. Unwired, every segment can cut.

inputs.label: Can Be Cut Conditions
inputs.note: Point filters narrowing which segments of a path are allowed to be cut. Unwired, every segment can be cut.

inputs.label: Overrides : Blending
inputs.note: An attribute set whose names are matched against the picked `Blending` sub-node's own settings.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: One path per input, with crossings inserted. A path that could not be cut comes back only if it is not being omitted.

bSelfIntersectionOnly.tooltip: If enabled, crossings are only computed per path, against themselves only. Note: this ignores the "bEnableSelfIntersection" from details below.
bSelfIntersectionOnly.semantics: Each path is tested against itself and against nothing else, which is what finds the places a single route doubles back over its own line. It overrides the self-intersection toggle inside the intersection block rather than being combined with it.

CanBeCutTag.tooltip: Filter entire dataset. If any tag is found on these paths, they are considered cut-able. Empty or None will ignore filtering.
CanBeCutTag.semantics: A whole-dataset gate, so it says a path is off limits rather than a segment. A path shut out here is never tested and never gains a point, whatever the segment-level conditions say.

bInvertCanBeCutTag.tooltip: If enabled, the absence of the specified tag considers paths as cut-able.

CanCutTag.tooltip: Filter entire dataset. If any tag is found on these paths, they are considered cutters. Empty or None will ignore filtering.
CanCutTag.semantics: The other half of the pair, and setting only this one is what makes the relationship one-way: the tagged paths cut everything and are cut by nothing, so a set of guides can slice a set of routes without picking up any points of their own.

bInvertCanCutTag.tooltip: If enabled, the absence of the specified tag considers paths as cutters.

bCreatePointAtCrossings.tooltip: If enabled, a point will be created at the crossing' location.
bCreatePointAtCrossings.semantics: Off, the search still runs and the tags are still written, but the path is forwarded exactly as it arrived. Every attribute this node offers goes with the insertion, so switching it off leaves the tags as the only evidence.

IntersectionDetails.tooltip: Configuration for how edge intersections are detected and processed.
IntersectionDetails.semantics: Its tolerance is a distance rather than a plane test, so two segments passing near each other in three dimensions count as crossing without ever touching. Its angle limits gate on how the two segments meet, which is how a near-parallel graze can be excluded while a clean crossing is kept.
IntersectionDetails.trap: Its own self-intersection toggle is what allows a path to cut itself in the ordinary mode, and it is bypassed entirely once `Self Intersection Only` is on.

Blending.tooltip: Blending applied on intersecting points along the path prev and next point. This is different from inheriting from external properties.
Blending.semantics: It decides what an inserted point takes from the two points bracketing the segment it landed on, and the several crossings on one segment are handed over together so they interpolate across the whole gap rather than one at a time. It never sees the path that did the cutting.

bDoCrossBlending.semantics: The only route by which the cutting path reaches the crossing point. It blends in the two points of the cutting segment on top of what the sub-node already wrote, so the crossing ends up carrying something of both paths.

CrossingCarryOver.tooltip: If enabled, blend in properties & attributes from external sources.

fields.name: bPreserveAttributesDefaultValue
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will preserve the initial attribute default value.

fields.name: Attributes
fields.tooltip: Attributes to carry over.

fields.name: bDataDomainToElements
fields.tooltip: If enabled, data domain attributes are promoted to the elements domain (the single @Data value is broadcast to every point). Off by default; Merge Points is the node that enables it. Not used by all nodes.

fields.name: Scope
fields.tooltip: Scope

fields.name: Tags
fields.tooltip: Tags to carry over.

fields.name: bTestTagsWithValues
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

CrossingBlending.tooltip: If enabled, blend in properties & attributes from external sources.
CrossingBlending.semantics: It ships blending attributes by `Average` with the point properties on `None`, so out of the box cross blending moves attributes and leaves transforms where the sub-node put them.
CrossingBlending.trap: Switching `Orient Crossing` on forces rotation here to `None` whatever this is set to, because that toggle is what writes the rotation.

CrossingAlphaAttributeName.semantics: Where along its own segment the crossing fell, 0 at the segment's first point and 1 at its second. Points that are not crossings get the default value beside it instead, which ships at -1 so they can be told apart rather than reading as a crossing at the segment start.

CrossingOrientAxis.semantics: Which axis of the inserted point is turned to face along the cutting segment. The rest of the rotation follows from that one constraint, so the point's roll about that axis is not something this decides.

CrossDirectionAttributeName.semantics: The direction of the segment that did the cutting, not of the segment being cut, so it describes the other path. Points that are not crossings get the default beside it.

IsPointCrossingAttributeName.semantics: Separates crossings that landed on an existing point of the other path from crossings that landed partway along one of its segments. It is written on inserted points alone; everything else reads false.

bOmitUncuttableFromOutput.tooltip: If enabled, paths that are only "cutters" (paths that will cut but won't be cut).
bOmitUncuttableFromOutput.semantics: Paths shut out by the cut-able tag or by their filters produce nothing of their own, and this decides whether they still come out. Off, which is the default, they are forwarded untouched, so a set of cutters wired in alongside the routes appears in the output beside them.

hints.text: Both paths of a crossing are cut, and they are cut independently: two points end up at the same location, one in each dataset, with nothing recording that they are the same crossing. Making a crossing into a shared junction is a different job, and **Path : To Clusters** is where it lives.

A path arriving under two points is forwarded here whatever `Omit Invalid Paths Outputs` says, and then dropped when the results are staged while that toggle is on. It comes back without any of this node's attributes, so it is not interchangeable with a path that was tested and found nothing.

UPCGExPathfindingEdgesSettings.name: Pathfinding : Edges
UPCGExPathfindingEdgesSettings.purpose: Routes from seeds to goals across a cluster's edges. The **Goal Picker** decides which goals each seed is paired with, the **Search Algorithm** solves each pair under the heuristics wired in, and every solved pair comes back as its own path. `Output Mode` offers a second answer to the same run: instead of the routes, forward the cluster and write onto each Vtx and each edge how many of those routes crossed it.
UPCGExPathfindingEdgesSettings.situation: A network of connections already exists, and routes have to be traced through it between two sets of points.

mechanism.text: One resolved query is one output path. Each seed point resolves to a Vtx and each goal to its own, the search walks edges between them, and the points that come out are copies of the elements the route ran through, in order, with the cluster tagging stripped so the result is a plain path. The pairing is settled once, against the Seeds and Goals data alone, then attempted against every cluster on the input, so several Edges datasets means the whole pair list is run once per cluster. A query whose two ends land on the same Vtx, or whose search finds nothing, is dropped without a warning.

off_label.claim: Wire the same dataset into Seeds and Goals with the All goal picker and the run becomes an all-pairs reachability probe: what comes back is one path for every pair the cluster can actually connect, and the pairs it cannot are the ones missing from the output.
off_label.grounded_in: ProcessGoals builds the full pair list from the two facades without comparing them, and FPathQuery::FindPath drops a query whose search fails or whose endpoints resolve to the same Vtx

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The Vtx half of every cluster to search.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The Edges half. Each Edges dataset that finds its Vtx is one cluster, and each cluster runs the whole query list on its own.

inputs.label: Seeds
inputs.note: Where routes start. One dataset, resolved to Vtx through Seed Picking.

inputs.label: Goals
inputs.note: Where routes end. One dataset, resolved to Vtx through Goal Picking. Which seed pairs with which goal is the Goal Picker's decision.

inputs.label: Heuristics
inputs.note: The cost model the search minimises. Required, and an empty pin stops the cluster rather than falling back to plain distance.

inputs.label: Overrides : Goal Picker
inputs.note: An attribute set whose names match the selected picker's settings one to one, driving the picker from data.

inputs.label: Overrides : Search
inputs.note: The same arrangement for the selected search algorithm's settings.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: One dataset per resolved query, its points copied from the cluster and its cluster tagging stripped.
outputs.condition: Output Mode is Paths

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: The Vtx forwarded through, carrying the per-Vtx visited count.
outputs.condition: Output Mode is Visited

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: The Edges forwarded through, carrying the per-edge visited count.
outputs.condition: Output Mode is Visited

OutputMode.tooltip: Whether to output paths, or to forward Vtx & Edges with a per-element visited count instead.
OutputMode.semantics: Changes the shape of the node, not only what it writes. `Paths` gives the node a single Paths output and hides the whole tagging, forwarding and path-output surface behind it. `Visited` replaces that pin with the forwarded Vtx and Edges, so switching an existing graph over drops the downstream wire.

GoalPicker.semantics: Runs once per seed before any cluster is touched, and every index it returns becomes a query. It is what decides how many searches the node performs, which makes it the first place to look when a run is slower or emptier than expected.

bAddSeedToPath.tooltip: Add seed point at the beginning of the path
bAddSeedToPath.semantics: The point prepended is a copy of the seed point itself, from the Seeds data, so it sits at the seed's own location and carries the Seeds attributes. That location is wherever the seed was authored, which is rarely the position of the Vtx the route actually started from.

bAddGoalToPath.tooltip: Add goal point at the end of the path
bAddGoalToPath.semantics: The mirror of the seed case, appended after the last route point and copied from the Goals data with the Goals attributes. Both extras are counted before `Paths Output Settings` tests its limits.

PathComposition.tooltip: What are the paths made of.
PathComposition.semantics: `Vtx` copies the Vtx the route ran through. `Edge` copies the Edges points of the edges it crossed instead, which is one point fewer and puts each point wherever its edge point sits rather than at a vertex. The two also carry different attributes, one set coming from the Vtx dataset and the other from the Edges dataset.
PathComposition.trap: Under `Edge` a route between two adjacent Vtx yields a single point, which clears the node's own floor and is not a usable path downstream.

SeedPicking.tooltip: Drive how a seed selects a node.
SeedPicking.semantics: `Max Distance` defaults to -1 here, meaning no limit, so a seed anywhere in the level still snaps to the nearest Vtx of every cluster on the input. Setting a real distance is what confines a seed to the cluster it was meant for.

GoalPicking.tooltip: Drive how a goal selects a node.
GoalPicking.semantics: Resolved independently of the seed, and a pair whose two ends land on the same Vtx is discarded before the search runs. Two nearby seed and goal points over a coarse cluster therefore produce silence rather than a short path.

HeuristicScoreMode.tooltip: Scoring mode for combining multiple heuristics

SeedAttributesToPathTags.tooltip: Copy seed point attributes as tags on output paths.

SeedForwarding.tooltip: Which Seed attributes to forward on paths.

Statistics.tooltip: Per-element visited counts written onto the forwarded Vtx & Edges.

PathOutputDetails.tooltip: Point-count limits deciding which generated paths are kept. Paths with fewer than 2 points are always dropped.
PathOutputDetails.semantics: Tested against the finished point count, extras included, so turning `Add Seed To Path` and `Add Goal To Path` on lifts every path two points closer to a minimum and two points closer to a maximum.

bUseOctreeSearch.tooltip: Whether or not to search for closest node using an octree. Depending on your dataset, enabling this may be either much faster, or slightly slower.
bUseOctreeSearch.semantics: Only affects how seed and goal points are matched to cluster elements. The search itself is untouched.

bGreedyQueries.tooltip: If disabled, will share memory allocations between queries, forcing them to execute one after another. Much slower, but very conservative for memory.  Using global feedback forces this behavior under the hood.
bGreedyQueries.semantics: Turning it off makes the queries run one after another rather than side by side, which changes results and not only memory once a feedback heuristic is on the pin: each finished route feeds its cost back before the next one starts, so the order they run in becomes part of the answer. A global feedback heuristic forces that behaviour whatever this is set to.

hints.text: Both instanced dropdowns keep their configuration when you switch between them, and each has its own advanced overrides pin. The Heuristics pin is the one that composes: several factories stack there and the node's `Heuristic Score Mode` decides how their answers collapse into the single number the search ranks by.

Seeds and goals are matched against every cluster on the input, so a batch of ten Edges datasets runs the full query list ten times and emits paths from each cluster that could resolve one. Restrict this with `Max Distance` on Seed Picking, or split the clusters upstream.

UPCGExPathfindingGrowPathsSettings.name: Pathfinding : Grow Paths
UPCGExPathfindingGrowPathsSettings.purpose: Walks outward from seeds with no destination in mind. Each seed starts one or more growths, and a growth repeatedly steps to whichever neighbour the heuristics score cheapest, until it runs out of iterations, runs past a distance limit, or reaches a Vtx flagged to stop it. Each finished growth is one path. The rest of the pathfinding family answers where do these two points connect; this one answers how far does this seed get.
UPCGExPathfindingGrowPathsSettings.situation: A structure has to spread out from a handful of starting vertices and the shape it reaches is the answer, with no target to aim at.

mechanism.text: A growth holds one current Vtx and one visited list. Each step it scores every neighbour it has not already taken, moves to the cheapest, and records the edge. There is no lookahead and no backtracking: a growth that walks into a dead end stops there rather than unwinding. Since a growth has no goal, each candidate is scored as if it were its own goal, so any heuristic measuring remaining distance contributes nothing and the steering is entirely the per-edge cost. Every growth that completes writes one path, its points copied from the Vtx in the order they were taken.

off_label.claim: Set `Num Iterations` to 1 and the node collapses to a one-hop probe: every path is two points, the seed Vtx and its cheapest neighbour, which reads the heuristic stack's verdict at each seed without running a search.
off_label.grounded_in: FGrowth::FindNextGrowthNodeIndex refuses once Iteration + 1 exceeds SoftMaxIterations, and the first hop is taken during processor setup before any further growth runs

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The Vtx half of every cluster to grow through.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The Edges half. Each Edges dataset that finds its Vtx is one cluster, and every seed is attempted on each of them.

inputs.label: Seeds
inputs.note: Where growths start. One dataset, resolved to Vtx through Seed Picking.

inputs.label: Heuristics
inputs.note: What decides which neighbour a growth takes next. Drawn as an ordinary pin rather than a required one, and the cluster still stops when it is empty.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: One dataset per completed growth, its points copied from the Vtx it walked, in order, with the Vtx tagging stripped.

SeedPicking.tooltip: Drive how a seed selects a node.
SeedPicking.semantics: `Max Distance` is constructed at 200 here rather than the -1 the shared block shows, so seeds further than 200 units from any Vtx are dropped before growth starts. A seed landing on a Vtx with no edges is dropped too.

HeuristicScoreMode.tooltip: Scoring mode for combining multiple heuristics

GrowthMode.tooltip: Controls how iterative growth is managed.
GrowthMode.semantics: `Parallel` runs each growth to exhaustion before starting the next. `Sequence` advances every growth by one step in turn until none can continue. The two only differ once a feedback heuristic is on the pin, because that is what makes one growth's choices visible to the others.
GrowthMode.trap: The two option tooltips describe the opposite of what each value does. Read the sentence above rather than the dropdown.

NumIterations.tooltip: The maximum number of growth iterations for a given seed.
NumIterations.semantics: Counts steps taken, not points written, so a growth that runs its full budget produces one point more than the number here. A value of zero or less at the seed drops that seed before it starts.

NumIterationsAttribute.tooltip: Num iteration attribute name. (will be translated to int32)

NumIterationsUpdateMode.tooltip: How to update the number of iteration for each seed. Note: No matter what is selected, will never exceed the Max iteration.
NumIterationsUpdateMode.semantics: Only acts under `Vtx Attribute`, where the value is re-read from each Vtx the growth arrives at. `Set Each Iteration` replaces the remaining budget with that Vtx's number and `Add Each Iteration` adds to it, so a cluster carrying the right attribute can extend or cut a growth as it passes through.
NumIterationsUpdateMode.trap: There is no ceiling on the accumulated budget. `Add Each Iteration` over a cluster whose values are all positive grows the budget faster than the growth spends it, and the growth then only ends at a dead end, a distance limit or a stop flag.

SeedNumBranches.tooltip: The maximum number of growth started by a given seed.
SeedNumBranches.semantics: How many growths one seed starts. Each is an independent walk with its own visited list, and none of them knows what the others took.
SeedNumBranches.trap: Without a feedback heuristic on the pin, every branch from one seed scores the neighbours identically and therefore takes the same first step, and the same one after that. Branches above 1 produce duplicate paths until something makes a taken edge more expensive.

SeedNumBranchesMean.tooltip: How the NumBranches value is to be interpreted against the actual number of neighbors.
SeedNumBranchesMean.semantics: `Relative` reads the number as a fraction of the seed Vtx's own edge count, floored at one branch, so a leaf starts one growth while a hub starts several from the same setting.

NumBranchesAttribute.tooltip: Num branches attribute name. (will be translated to int32)

GrowthDirection.tooltip: The maximum number of growth iterations for a given seed.
GrowthDirection.semantics: Read into each growth and updated as it moves, and never consulted for anything. Nothing in the node compares a candidate against it, so the whole Growth Direction group changes no output.
GrowthDirection.trap: To bias growth along an axis, wire a directional heuristic onto the Heuristics pin. This setting cannot do it.

GrowthDirectionAttribute.tooltip: Growth direction attribute name. (will be translated to a FVector)

GrowthDirectionUpdateMode.tooltip: How to update the number of iteration for each seed. Note: No matter what is selected, will never exceed the Max iteration.

GrowthMaxDistance.tooltip: The maximum growth distance for a given seed.
GrowthMaxDistance.semantics: Measured along the route the growth actually walked, summed edge by edge, rather than as a straight line from the seed. The step that crosses the limit is the one that ends the growth, and it is already recorded, so a path can reach slightly past the number.

GrowthMaxDistanceAttribute.tooltip: Max growth distance attribute name. (will be translated to a FVector)

bUseGrowthStop.tooltip: Enable growth stop points that terminate paths when reached.
bUseGrowthStop.semantics: Reads a boolean per Vtx and ends a growth on arrival at a flagged one, keeping that Vtx as the path's last point.
bUseGrowthStop.trap: A name the Vtx data does not carry silently disables the limit. Nothing is logged and the growth runs to its other limits instead.

GrowthStopAttribute.tooltip: An attribute read on the Vtx as a boolean. If true and this node is used in a path, the path stops there.

bUseNoGrowth.tooltip: Enable no-growth points that paths cannot traverse (but can be used as seeds).
bUseNoGrowth.semantics: Refuses flagged Vtx as candidates, so a growth routes around them, and a growth boxed in by them stops. A flagged Vtx can still be the Vtx a seed resolves to, which is what lets a seed sit on a barrier and grow away from it.
bUseNoGrowth.trap: A name the Vtx data does not carry silently disables the limit, the same way the growth stop does.

NoGrowthAttribute.tooltip: An attribute read on the Vtx as a boolean. If true, this point will never be grown on, but may be still used as seed.

SeedAttributesToPathTags.tooltip: Copy seed point attributes as tags on output paths.

SeedForwarding.tooltip: Which Seed attributes to forward on paths.

UPCGExPathfindingNavmeshSettings.name: Pathfinding : Navmesh
UPCGExPathfindingNavmeshSettings.purpose: Routes between seeds and goals over the level's navigation mesh instead of a cluster. It asks Unreal's navigation system for a path, then turns the corridor it gets back into points. Seeds, goals and the **Goal Picker** work exactly as they do on **Pathfinding : Edges**; nothing else does. There is no cluster to wire in, and therefore no heuristics, no search algorithm and no node picking: what shapes a route here is the navigation data itself, the agent it is queried for, and whether the level has a navmesh built at all.
UPCGExPathfindingNavmeshSettings.situation: Routes have to respect level geometry and navigation volumes rather than a network you built yourself.

mechanism.text: The **Goal Picker** pairs seeds with goals first, the same way it does for the cluster nodes, and each pair becomes one navigation query. A successful query comes back as a corridor of positions; consecutive positions closer together than `Fuse Distance` are merged, the surviving ones become the path's points, and `Blending` fills in what those invented points carry. Each query that resolves is one path. A query the navigation system cannot answer produces nothing and is not reported.

off_label.claim: Raise `Fuse Distance` well past the navmesh's own spacing and the corridor collapses to its turns, which is a cheap way to get the shape of a route without its intermediate detail.
off_label.grounded_in: FNavmeshQuery::FindPath skips a corridor position whose predecessor is within FuseDistance, keeping only the last one before each larger step

inputs.note: Where routes end. One dataset. Which seed pairs with which goal is the Goal Picker's decision.

GoalPicker.semantics: The same four pickers the cluster nodes offer, deciding the same thing: how many queries the node runs and which goal each of them aims at. Pairings are settled against the two datasets alone, so a pair the navmesh cannot connect is still posed and then quietly fails.

bAddSeedToPath.tooltip: Add seed point at the beginning of the path
bAddSeedToPath.semantics: Prepends a point at the seed's own location. Both this and `Add Goal To Path` default on here, unlike their cluster counterparts, because the corridor's own first and last positions come from the navigation system and need not sit exactly on the seed and the goal.

bAddGoalToPath.tooltip: Add goal point at the end of the path
bAddGoalToPath.semantics: Appends a point at the goal's own location.
bAddGoalToPath.trap: A path is dropped outright when its total point count is two or fewer, extras included. Turning both extras off therefore discards every route the navmesh answered with a straight two-position corridor.

bRequireNavigableEndLocation.tooltip: Whether the pathfinding requires a naviguable end location.
bRequireNavigableEndLocation.semantics: Handed straight to the navigation query, so what it decides is the navigation system's behaviour rather than this node's. Left on, a goal that does not sit on navigable ground fails its query and the pair produces no path at all.

FuseDistance.semantics: Measured between consecutive corridor positions as they are read, so the merging is sequential rather than a global tolerance. The final position is kept whatever happens, moved onto the last one merged into it, so raising this shortens the middle of a path and never its ends.

Blending.tooltip: Controls how path points blend from seed to goal.
Blending.semantics: Decides what the invented corridor points carry. Positions are held fixed whatever is selected, so this only touches attributes and the other point properties.
Blending.trap: Both ends of the blend are read from the Goals data: the far end is the goal the route ran to, and the near end is the Goals point whose row number matches the seed's, rather than the seed point. Use `Seed Forwarding` where the seed's own values have to reach the path.

NavAgentProperties.tooltip: Nav agent to be used by the nav system.

hints.text: Every query needs a live navigation system with a default navigation data instance. Without one, each query returns nothing, no path is written and no error is raised: the node succeeds with an empty Paths pin. Check that the level has a Nav Mesh Bounds Volume and that navigation has been built before looking anywhere else.

None of the cluster pathfinding surface reaches this node. There is no Heuristics pin, no Search Algorithm, no Seed or Goal Picking block and no visited-count output mode. What the navigation system will and will not walk is set by `Nav Agent Properties` and by the level's navigation data, not here.

UPCGExPathfindingPlotEdgesSettings.name: Pathfinding : Plot Edges
UPCGExPathfindingPlotEdgesSettings.purpose: Routes through waypoints already in order. A plot is an ordered point dataset read as a list of waypoints: each consecutive pair is one leg, solved on its own across the cluster, and the legs are joined end to end into a single output path. One plot dataset in, one path out, so there is no Goals input and no Goal Picker here: the ordering inside the dataset is the pairing. `Output Mode` offers the same alternative **Pathfinding : Edges** does, forwarding the cluster with per-element visited counts instead of the route.
UPCGExPathfindingPlotEdgesSettings.situation: The waypoints a route has to visit are known and ordered, and what needs solving is the connections between them.

mechanism.text: A plot of N points becomes N-1 legs, each a search from one waypoint to the next, plus a closing leg back to the first when `Closed Loop` is on. Every waypoint resolves to a Vtx the same way a seed does, the legs are stitched with the shared junction counted once, and the whole run is written as one path carrying the tags of both the plot and the Edges dataset it was solved on. Several plots and several clusters are a cross product: each plot is attempted on each cluster it matches, and each success is its own path.

off_label.claim: A two-point plot is a plain seed-to-goal query with the pairing written into the data, which is a way to drive one-off routes from a dataset that is built or filtered upstream rather than from two parallel inputs and a picker.
off_label.grounded_in: BuildPlotQuery pairs points 0 and 1 into the first sub-query and only loops from index 2, so a two-point plot resolves to a single leg
