DefaultDescriptor.semantics: Its Spline Mesh Axis decides which of the mesh's axes runs along the segment, but only as a fallback: the picked entry's own descriptor answers first, this answers when the entry leaves it unset, and X answers when neither does. Every other field here reaches a component only through Force Default Descriptor.

bForceDefaultDescriptor.tooltip: If enabled, override collection settings with the default descriptor settings
bForceDefaultDescriptor.semantics: Component settings normally come from the picked entry's own descriptor, so two entries in one collection can differ in collision, shadows or LOD. This replaces all of that with the node's Default Descriptor for every segment. The forward axis is the exception and keeps reading the entry first either way, so a mesh authored along Y stays correct with this on.

TargetActor.semantics: Left empty, the components attach to the actor the generating component already targets. There is no third fallback: when neither resolves, the node errors and spawns nothing.

PostProcessFunctionNames.tooltip: Specify a list of functions to be called on the target actor after spline mesh creation. Functions need to be parameter-less and with "CallInEditor" flag enabled.

hints.text: Tangents arrive on `Attribute`, reading `ArriveTangent` and `LeaveTangent`. Plain path points carry neither, so a freshly placed node errors and builds nothing until the source is switched to `In-place` or those attributes are written upstream.

A mixed staged dataset needs no splitting before it gets here. Picks that resolved to anything other than a mesh entry are skipped, and their points leave with an empty asset path, so the same dataset can feed this node and the type-specific spawn nodes in parallel.

UPCGExPathSplineMeshSimpleSettings.name: Path : Spline Mesh (Simple)
UPCGExPathSplineMeshSimpleSettings.purpose: Bends a mesh along every segment of a path, spawning one spline mesh component per segment on an actor. Which mesh, which material override, how the segment is pushed and offset, and which way is up are all read per point, so one path can carry a different mesh on every segment. The points themselves come back out on **Paths** unchanged, so this spawns without ending the branch. **Staging : Spline Mesh** is the sibling that picks its meshes from a collection instead of an attribute.
UPCGExPathSplineMeshSimpleSettings.situation: A run of points has to become continuous geometry in the level, with the mesh bending to follow the run.

mechanism.text: One execution spawns one spline mesh component per segment on the target actor, while the input points pass through untouched on **Paths**. A segment reads everything from the point that starts it, the mesh included, and takes only its far end's location, scale and roll from the point after it. An open path of five points therefore has four segments, and the fifth point's mesh, offsets and up vector are never used; closing the path adds the seam segment and with it that point's row. A point the **Point Filters** pin rejects, or one whose mesh does not resolve, starts no segment, so the run gains a gap there.

off_label.claim: A segment's cross-section is scaled by its two end points' own scales, on the two axes the mesh does not run along. Put a varying scale on the path and one untapered mesh produces a tapering run, with no per-entry setup and no second mesh.
off_label.grounded_in: ProcessPoints fills Segment.Params.StartScale from the start point's scale and EndScale from the next point's, on the two components GetAxisForEntry leaves over after the spline mesh axis

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to build along.

inputs.label: Point Filters
inputs.note: Decides which points start a segment. With the pin empty every point does.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The input points, unchanged. The meshes are components in the level, not data on a pin.

AssetType.semantics: The attribute route ships selected, and it registers the attribute it reads as consumable, so a `Cleanup Consumable Attributes` pass downstream drops it from the forwarded points. The constant route loads its mesh once before any path is touched and stops the node outright when it cannot; the attribute route gathers every path across every input first, and stops the node only when none of them resolve.

AssetPathAttributeName.tooltip: The name of the attribute to write asset path to.
AssetPathAttributeName.semantics: Read at the point that starts the segment, which is what puts the last point of an open path out of reach: its mesh never spawns, because no segment starts there.
AssetPathAttributeName.trap: A row that resolves to nothing skips that segment with nothing in the log, so a misspelled asset path in the middle of a run reads as a hole in the geometry rather than as an error.

MaterialAttributeName.tooltip: The name of the attribute to write material path to.
MaterialAttributeName.semantics: Read at the same point as the mesh, so a segment's material comes from its start point. A row that resolves to nothing leaves the mesh's own material in place rather than clearing the slot, so a partial material attribute degrades to the defaults instead of to blank geometry.

MaterialSlotConstant.tooltip: The index of the slot to set the material to, if found.

TargetActor.semantics: Falls back to the actor the PCG component sits on. Where neither resolves, that path spawns nothing and logs an invalid target actor error, and its points still come out on **Paths**, so the branch keeps flowing with no geometry behind it.

Tangents.tooltip: Per-point tangent settings. Can't be set if the spline is linear.
Tangents.semantics: Decides the curve each segment bends along. Set to No Tangents the node falls back to the two points' rotations, taking each end's tangent from that point's forward axis, which makes **Path : Orient** upstream the thing that shapes the run.
Tangents.trap: `Arrive Scale` and `Leave Scale` are crossed over on this node. A segment's start tangent is its start point's leave vector and its end tangent is the next point's arrive vector, but the start is multiplied by the arrive scale and the end by the leave scale. Leave the two scales equal and nothing shows; set them apart and each end bends by the other's amount.

EndOffsetValue.semantics: Both offsets are read at the point that starts the segment, not one at each end. A per-point attribute driving them therefore describes a whole segment from its start point, and the point where two segments meet supplies its predecessor's end offset from one row and its own start offset from another.
EndOffsetValue.trap: Feeding one attribute to both rows will not make the run continuous: at a shared point the segment before it reads its end offset from the point before that. Two rows have to be authored to line up, or the join steps.

fields.name: bRelativeStart

MutationDetails.semantics: Pushes a segment's ends outward past the points they sit on, the start backwards along its start tangent and the end forwards along its end tangent, and lengthens the tangents to match. Segments then overlap their neighbours, which is what covers the wedge of empty space a corner otherwise leaves between two straight meshes. `Relative` reads the amount as a fraction of that segment's own length, so one value holds across segments of different sizes.

SplineMeshUpMode.tooltip: How the spline mesh up vector is determined.
SplineMeshUpMode.semantics: Read once per segment, at the point that starts it, so the whole segment shares one up vector and neighbouring segments can disagree. Constant hands every segment the same vector, which is stable and rolls with nothing. Attribute reads the row below per point. From Tangents derives the vector from the segment's own tangents, which follows a run through a vertical stretch where a constant vector would collapse.

SplineMeshUpVectorAttribute.tooltip: Attribute to read the spline mesh up vector from.
SplineMeshUpVectorAttribute.semantics: A fresh node ships with this pointed at `$Rotation.Up`, filled in by the node's own constructor rather than by the declaration, so the attribute route reads each point's own up axis until you change it. That pairs it with **Path : Orient** without any attribute existing on the data.

StaticMeshDescriptor.semantics: Beyond the component settings it carries `Spline Mesh Axis`, which names the axis of the mesh that runs along the segment and ships on Default, resolving to X here. It decides the other two things on this page that talk about cross-section axes: which two components of a point's scale become the segment's end scales, and which plane the start and end offsets move in.

PropertyOverrideDescriptions.semantics: Applied per segment against the input point data, so an override reads its value at the point that starts the segment, in step with the mesh and the offsets. A description that fails to apply logs a warning naming the segment index and the run carries on.

PostProcessFunctionNames.tooltip: Specify a list of functions to be called on the target actor after spline mesh creation. Functions need to be parameter-less and with "CallInEditor" flag enabled.

UPCGExPathStitchSettings.name: Path : Stitch
UPCGExPathStitchSettings.purpose: Joins separate paths into longer ones by their ends. Two paths whose ends fall within `Tolerance` of each other are chained, the chain is walked from one free end to the other, and what comes out is a single dataset carrying all of it in order; a chain that closes back on itself is written out as a closed path. `Method` decides whether the two points at each join both survive or collapse into one. Nothing else about the paths is consulted unless you ask: alignment, matching rules and sorting rules each narrow which joins are allowed or which win.
UPCGExPathStitchSettings.situation: A set of path fragments that describe one continuous run and have to be handed downstream as one.

mechanism.text: One execution takes many paths and returns fewer. Every path is reduced to its two end points, ends within `Tolerance` of each other become candidate joins, and the candidates are taken in order of quality until no end has more than one partner. Each resulting chain is emitted as one dataset with its members laid end to end, reversed wherever the chain enters a path through its own end rather than its start, and a path that joined nothing is forwarded exactly as it came. Under `Connect` every point of every member survives; under `Fuse` each join gives up one point, so a chain of five paths loses four. Closed paths never take part and are forwarded untouched, and paths of fewer than two points are dropped.

off_label.claim: With Tolerance large and Only Match Start And Ends off, the node stops being about continuity and becomes a nearest-ends chainer: every fragment in a region gets linked to whichever fragment end is closest, which turns a field of unordered segments into a small number of long runs whose shape nobody chose.
off_label.grounded_in: Candidates are collected by octree query on the endpoint bounds alone, and are only rejected on distance, partition and, optionally, alignment

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to join. Closed paths are forwarded untouched rather than considered.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match Rule sub-nodes splitting the input into groups that may only stitch within themselves. Sits under the advanced pins while `Matching Details`' mode is Disabled, and becomes required as soon as it is not.
inputs.condition: required when Matching Details' Mode is anything but Disabled

inputs.label: SortRules
inputs.note: Sorting Rule sub-nodes ordering the paths before candidates are weighed, which is what settles a tie between two joins of equal quality. Left empty, the order the paths arrived in settles it.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: One dataset per chain, plus every path that joined nothing, forwarded as it arrived. A chain that closed on itself carries the closed-path marker.

Method.semantics: `Connect` keeps both points at every join, so two coincident points sit at each seam and the output count is the sum of the inputs. `Fuse` gives up one point per join instead.

FuseMethod.semantics: Which of the two points meeting at a join is meant to survive, the start point of the path being entered or the end point of the one being left.
FuseMethod.trap: The end that gets trimmed is fixed rather than derived from the direction each path is walked in, and a chain walks some of its members backwards. Where the choice disagrees with a member's direction, that join keeps both of its points and the chain loses a point from its own outer end instead. The total count still drops by one per join either way.

MergeOperation.semantics: Declared with three choices, none of which is read anywhere in the node. A fused join always keeps one of the two original points exactly as it was, which is what the shipped `None` describes.

bOnlyMatchStartAndEnds.tooltip: If enabled, stitching will only happen between a path's end point and another path start point. Otherwise, it's based on spatial proximity alone.
bOnlyMatchStartAndEnds.semantics: Restricts joins to an end meeting a start. Off, an end can meet another end and a start another start, which is what lets a chain reverse a member and is why a run of fragments authored in inconsistent directions still chains.

DotComparisonDetails.tooltip: If enabled, foreign segments must be aligned within a given angular threshold.
DotComparisonDetails.semantics: The constant-only variant of the shared dot comparison block: the same domain, operator and threshold, without the attribute row. What it is fed depends on `Mode`.

AlignmentMode.tooltip: How alignment between paths is evaluated.
AlignmentMode.semantics: What alignment is measured between. `Segments` compares the two terminal segments to each other, so it answers whether the paths are heading the same way. `Bridge` compares each terminal segment to the gap being closed, so it answers whether the join continues the run rather than doubling back. `Combined`, which ships selected, requires both.

BridgeScoring.tooltip: How the bridge alignment score is computed from both path directions.
BridgeScoring.semantics: How the two bridge readings, one per path, collapse into the one number the comparison tests. `Minimum` takes the worse of the two so both paths have to agree; `Average` lets a strongly aligned path carry a weakly aligned one.

bStrictAlignment.tooltip: When enabled, candidates that fail the alignment threshold are hard-rejected. When disabled, alignment is only used as a sorting preference (better-aligned candidates win).
bStrictAlignment.semantics: Whether alignment rejects or merely ranks. Off, which is what ships, a candidate failing the threshold is still eligible and is only weighed below the ones that passed, so a badly aligned join still happens when nothing better is available. On, it is discarded.
bStrictAlignment.trap: Turning `Requires Alignment` on without this changes which joins win, never which joins are possible, so a pair that should never have met still meets when it is the only candidate.

Tolerance.tooltip: Maximum distance between endpoints for stitching to occur.
Tolerance.semantics: The maximum distance between the two end points, and also the size of the box each end is registered in for the search, so it is both the test and the reach. Ends further apart than this are never even considered.

SortDirection.tooltip: Controls the order in which data will be sorted
SortDirection.semantics: What it orders is the paths, not the joins, so it changes which of two equally good candidates is taken first and nothing about which candidates exist. With the **SortRules** pin empty it has nothing to reverse.

MatchingDetails.tooltip: Matching rules that constrain which paths can stitch together.
MatchingDetails.semantics: Splits the input into groups before any candidate is collected, and a join is only ever considered between two paths in the same group. Paths that match no group are put in a group of their own, so they stitch to nothing rather than to everything.

CarryOverDetails.semantics: Decides which attributes and tags survive a merge, which is a question that only arises here because the members were separate datasets carrying separate metadata. An attribute missing from one member arrives at its default on that member's points.

TagsToAttributes.tooltip: Tags to convert to attributes: simple tags become boolean (presence), tag:value pairs become their typed value.

fields.name: FilterMode
fields.tooltip: How the names are processed.

fields.name: Matches
fields.tooltip: List of matches that will be checked. Any success is a pass.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNames
fields.tooltip: A list of names separated by a comma, for easy overrides. The limitation is that they all use the same shared filter mode.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNameFilter
fields.tooltip: Unique filter mode applied to comma separated names

fields.name: bPreservePCGExData
fields.tooltip: If enabled, PCGEx attributes & tags won't be affected.  Cluster-related nodes rely on these to work!

TagsToAttributes.semantics: Turns each member's tags into per-point attributes before the merge, which is the only way a tag that belonged to one fragment stays attached to that fragment's stretch of the joined path. A plain tag becomes a boolean, a tag carrying a value becomes that value's type.

bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.tooltip: If enabled, collections that have less than 2 points won't be processed and be omitted from the output.
bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.semantics: Reaches inputs of fewer than two points only, and they are dropped whatever it says: nothing forwards them here. Closed paths come back either way, since a forwarded loop keeps its points.

UPCGExPathToClustersSettings.name: Path : To Clusters
UPCGExPathToClustersSettings.purpose: Turns ordered points into connected ones. A path point is permanently binary, one segment behind it and one ahead, and this is the node where that ceiling comes off. `Fuse Paths` is what makes the crossing worth doing: with it on, points from separate paths that land in the same place weld into one Vtx, and the degree-three junction that weld creates is the thing no path could hold. With it off the conversion is mechanical, one cluster per input path, and the two halves never meet.
UPCGExPathToClustersSettings.situation: Several paths were routed across the same site and now have to be read as one network, with the places they touch treated as junctions.

mechanism.text: Every input path becomes a run of edges between its consecutive points, and a path carrying the closed-loop tag also gets the edge from its last point back to its first. `Fuse Paths` decides the rest. Off, each path becomes a cluster of its own. On, every input collapses into one cluster: points closer together than the fuse distance become a single Vtx whose attributes blend, two paths that produced the same connection collapse to one edge, and an edge whose two ends welded into the same Vtx is dropped instead of becoming a connection from a Vtx to itself. Inputs of fewer than two points are skipped with a warning. Nothing on the output records which path a Vtx came from, or which of its points came first.
steps: Points within the fuse distance collapse into one Vtx, and every edge that named them follows.
Point/Edge intersections split an edge wherever a Vtx sits on it, which is what turns a path merely touching another into a junction.
Edge/Edge intersections add a Vtx wherever two edges cross and split both, including edges the previous stage created.

off_label.claim: With `Fuse Paths` on and the fuse distance set wide, a single path folded back on itself comes out as a cluster with junctions where the folds meet, which is one way to detect self-contact on a path that ordinary path nodes cannot see.
off_label.grounded_in: The fusing processor keys every point of every input through the same union table, so two points of one path weld on the same terms as points from two paths.

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to convert. Datasets of fewer than two points are skipped, and the node warns once when any were.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: One dataset per input path with `Fuse Paths` off. One dataset for everything with it on.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One dataset per connected component, so a fused result whose paths never touched still comes out as several Edges datasets against one Vtx dataset.

bFusePaths.tooltip: Whether to fuse paths into a single graph or not.
bFusePaths.semantics: The switch between two shapes of output. On, everything arrives in one cluster and the whole fusing surface below is live. Off, each path is converted on its own and no point from one path can ever meet a point from another, whatever their positions.
bFusePaths.trap: The fusing, intersection and blending blocks carry no edit condition, so they stay on screen and fully editable with `Fuse Paths` off, where none of them does anything.

PointPointIntersectionDetails.semantics: The fuse distance inside this block is what decides whether two points become one Vtx, and it is measured in world units against the point locations, never against their bounds. Too small and paths that visually meet stay separate; too large and points along a single path start welding to their own neighbours, which shortens the path and can collapse an edge away entirely.

PointEdgeIntersectionDetails.semantics: This is the stage that handles a path ending against the middle of another rather than at one of its points. Without it, that endpoint welds to nothing and stays a leaf sitting on top of an edge it is not connected to.

EdgeEdgeIntersectionDetails.semantics: Crossings become new Vtx, so two paths that pass through each other come out joined at a degree-four Vtx. The angle limits inside the block narrow which crossings count, which is how a near-parallel overlap can be left alone while a genuine crossing is split.

DefaultPointsBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged together for fused points.
DefaultPointsBlendingDetails.semantics: Governs what a welded Vtx inherits from the several points that became it. It also covers the Vtx that the two intersection stages invent, which belong to no input point at all.

DefaultEdgesBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged together for fused edges.

CustomPointEdgeBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged together for Point/Edge intersections.

CustomEdgeEdgeBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged together for Edge/Edge intersections (Crossings).
CustomEdgeEdgeBlendingDetails.semantics: One toggle, two defaults displaced. The Vtx a crossing creates are blended by this block in place of `Default Points Blending`, and every edge point of the fused cluster is blended by it in place of `Default Edges Blending`. Turning it on to shape crossings therefore also rewrites how the ordinary edge points are built.

fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

GraphBuilderDetails.semantics: Applies in both modes, and it is the last thing that can drop a result: the small and big cluster limits are measured per connected component, so an unfused conversion of many short paths can lose most of them here rather than in the conversion.

hints.text: Closed loops are read from the tag a path carries, not from its geometry. A path whose last point sits on top of its first without the tag comes out as an open chain with two coincident Vtx, and with `Fuse Paths` on those two weld, which closes the loop by a different route and blends their attributes together.

UPCGExPCGDataAssetCollection.name: Collection | PCGDataAsset
UPCGExPCGDataAssetCollection.purpose: A weighted list of PCG data assets, where a row can also be a level. Rebuilding staging exports a level-sourced row into a generated PCG data asset: mesh actors become staged points, plain actors become an embedded Actor Collection carrying their property deltas, nested level instances become staged level picks, and the generated asset carries its own Collection Map so all three resolve. One pick then places the whole arrangement, spawned back through Staging : Load PCGData. External Storage decides whether everything generated lives inside the collection asset or as separate assets in a content folder you name.
UPCGExPCGDataAssetCollection.situation: A level was dressed by hand, and it needs to become one row that a single pick can place.

mechanism.text: A row is either a reference or a recording. Rows filled by hand or dropped in from the Content Browser arrive set to the source matching what was dropped, and every row's staged bounds are the combined bounds of all spatial data in the asset it resolves to. Rebuilding staging re-resolves every row, and level-sourced rows are re-exported from scratch each time, then merged: mesh and nested-level storage is pooled into two collection-level lists shared by every row, actor storage stays on the row, and each row's generated asset gets its own Collection Map covering all three. What a row stages is the Source question; where the generated assets live is the External Storage question.

off_label.claim: In external mode the shared mesh collection is an ordinary Mesh Collection asset you can open. Tags and categories authored on its rows survive re-exports, so a captured level's meshes can be labelled once and matched by tag downstream. Property overrides on the same rows are re-derived from the source actors on every export and do not survive.
off_label.grounded_in: CompactShared's preserved pass copies Tags, Category and EntryId onto the merged entry and deliberately skips PropertyOverrides; ExternalizeSharedAndActorCollectionsFor renames the shared collection out as a standalone asset.

off_label.claim: Point one row at a level and turn External Storage on, and the shared mesh collection that falls out is a deduplicated inventory of every mesh that level used, authored without typing a mesh list.
off_label.grounded_in: CompactSharedMeshFor merges the entry's captured mesh contributions into a UPCGExMeshCollection, which ExternalizeSharedAndActorCollectionsFor writes to the export folder.

LevelExporter.tooltip: Exporter used to convert level-sourced entries into embedded PCGDataAssets during staging. If unset, a default exporter is used. Instanced so custom exporters can expose their own settings. Editor-only: level harvesting is an authoring operation; cooked data carries the baked result.
LevelExporter.semantics: One instance serves every level-sourced row in the collection. Left unset, the export uses the default exporter class from the plugin's collection settings, and the built-in Default Level Data Exporter when that is unset too. Editor-only: cooked data carries the baked export and no level is read at runtime.
LevelExporter.trap: A Blueprint exporter overrides the simple export entry point, which captures no collection data. An asset produced that way carries raw mesh and actor attributes with no pick hashes and no Collection Map, so the staging routes have nothing to resolve against. Capturing contributions is a C++ override.

MachineryState.tooltip: Owned machinery state (per-type processor seam, Phase C1): external-storage settings (bUseExternalAssets / ExportFolder) plus the shared/external collection storage the PCGDataAsset machinery operates on. Always present (default subobject); the same state class an Omni host instantiates per present PCGData entry type. Shared subobjects it references stay outered to THIS collection (host package), exactly like on an Omni host.
MachineryState.semantics: Off, everything the export generates lives inside the collection asset: the two shared collections, and per row a generated data asset and an actor collection. On, with an export folder set, those same objects are renamed out into standalone assets in that folder and the collection keeps soft references to them. Names are built from the collection's own identifier, so they survive rebuilds and a re-export overwrites the same files instead of minting new ones. Saving the collection in the editor saves those packages alongside it. Turning it back off pulls every one of them back inside the collection and clears the references; the files they lived in are left on disk.
MachineryState.trap: Per-row asset names carry the row's position in the list, so reordering rows re-points them at each other's files. The two shared collections are named from the collection alone and are unaffected.

fields.name: AssetGrammar
fields.tooltip: Per-entry grammar configuration. Shared between leaf and subcollection entries; for subcollections this slot is populated only when SubGrammarMode == Override (it then replaces the subcollection's own SubCollectionGrammar wholesale). Customization gates EPCGExGrammarAxisSize values based on bIsSubCollection.

fields.name: ScaleToFitSource

fields.name: JustificationSource
fields.tooltip: Where this entry's Justification comes from when a staging node considers entry overrides.

fields.name: SubCollection
fields.tooltip: Subcollection to draw picks from when bIsSubCollection is enabled. Accepts any collection type; consuming nodes type-check resolved entries, so mixed-type nesting must be routed through type filters downstream. Kept populated when bIsSubCollection is toggled off so the ref survives iteration. Do not rename: legacy per-type entry members were also named "SubCollection", so their on-disk tags deserialize straight into this property.

fields.name: Source
fields.tooltip: Source mode toggle (default = DataAsset for backward compatibility)

fields.name: Level
fields.tooltip: Level reference (used when Source == Level)

Entries.semantics: Source decides what a row stages, and the two modes have little in common. Data Asset points at a finished PCG data asset and generates nothing: the row stages that asset's path and the combined bounds of its spatial data. Level points at a world, and every staging rebuild loads it, hands it to the exporter, and replaces the row's generated asset with a fresh one, so the row stages the generated asset instead. Level mode also scans the world's persistent level for socket-provider actors and bakes what it finds as managed sockets on the row. Switching a row from Level back to Data Asset discards its generated asset and everything captured from the level. A row flagged as a sub-collection ignores Source and accepts a collection of any type, not only another PCGDataAsset Collection.
Entries.trap: The Source tooltip says the default is Data Asset. The code default is Level, so a row added by hand starts pointing at a world.

hints.text: Level-sourced rows only stage in a host that runs the export machinery. This collection does, and so does an **Omni Collection**. Anywhere else the row is skipped with a warning and stages nothing, and a generated asset that arrived with a copied row is discarded rather than carried over.

Exporting is authoring work: it runs in the editor at staging-rebuild time, and what ships is the baked result. Duplicating the collection re-runs the merge so the copy's hashes are stamped against its own identifiers.

UPCGExPCGDataAssetLoaderSettings.name: Staging : Load PCGData
UPCGExPCGDataAssetLoaderSettings.purpose: The spawn route for picks that resolved to a PCG data entry. Each picked asset is loaded once and its contents are instantiated at every point that picked it, so one pick places a whole authored arrangement rather than one asset. What comes out is the asset's own data, sorted onto output pins declared by name, and it can be staged points again: the Collection Maps embedded in the loaded assets come back merged on the Map pin, so a captured scene re-enters the ordinary spawn routes.
UPCGExPCGDataAssetLoaderSettings.situation: A staged dataset whose picks name PCG data entries, and the arrangements those entries hold have to come back into the graph at each point.

mechanism.text: One execution consumes staged points and produces the contents of the assets they picked; the input points are not forwarded, so nothing that arrived leaves. Each unique picked asset is loaded once, and every piece of spatial data inside it is copied per point and composed with that point's transform, scale included, while non-spatial data is emitted once per unique asset however many points picked it. A point whose pick is missing, unresolvable, or resolved to an entry of another collection type produces nothing. Each piece keeps the pin name it carried inside the asset: an exact match against a declared custom pin routes it there, and anything else lands on Out carrying that name as a tag. Cluster tags are rewritten per point, so one instance's Vtx and Edges stay paired to each other and not to another instance's.

off_label.claim: Turn Merge Embedded Collection Maps off and declare a custom output pin labelled CollectionMap, and each loaded asset's own embedded map comes out unmerged, one per unique asset, which is how you read what a captured level shipped with instead of the union of everything.
off_label.grounded_in: the strip branch at the top of FProcessor::CompleteWork skips embedded CollectionMap data only while merging is on; with merging off it falls through to RegisterNonSpatialData, which routes by pin name through Context->RegisterOutput and deduplicates by asset

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The staged points. A point contributes the contents of the asset its pick names; the point itself is not part of the output.

inputs.label: Map
inputs.note: The Collection Map the picks resolve against. A map that rebuilds no valid mapping is an execution error, and points missing the staging layer's pick attribute error out per dataset.

inputs.label: Point Filters
inputs.note: Restricts which points instantiate anything. A rejected point is skipped whole, contents and all.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: Loaded content that matched no declared pin, each piece carrying its original pin name as a tag. Spatial content arrives once per staged point, everything else once per unique asset.

outputs.label: One pin per Custom Output Pins row
outputs.note: Content whose pin name inside the asset matches the row's label exactly, arriving without the name tag. The row is added to the node verbatim, so its declared type and multiple-data setting are what the editor shows.
outputs.condition: one pin per Custom Output Pins row that carries a label

outputs.label: Map
outputs.note: The Collection Maps embedded in the loaded assets, unioned into one. It is what keeps the staged points coming out of this node resolvable.
outputs.condition: when Merge Embedded Collection Maps is on

StagingLayer.tooltip: Staging layer this node reads staged picks from. None = default layer (PCGEx/CollectionEntry); otherwise the layer name is appended (PCGEx/CollectionEntry/<layer>).

CustomOutputPins.tooltip: Custom output pins for routing data by pin name. Data from the PCGDataAsset will be routed to matching pins by exact name. Data that doesn't match any custom pin goes to the default "Out" pin.
CustomOutputPins.semantics: Matching is against the pin name each piece of data carried inside the asset, and a row left without a label is ignored. Content routed to a declared pin arrives clean, while everything else lands on Out with its original pin name as a tag, which is how the names worth declaring get discovered in the first place.

bRefreshSeeds.tooltip: If enabled, will refresh seeds on output points.
bRefreshSeeds.semantics: Seeds are recomputed from each spawned point's location after the instance transform lands, so two copies of one asset in different places stop sharing seeds. It reaches point data inside the asset and nothing else.

bOmitEmptyData.tooltip: If enabled, will not output empty data, even if they have possibly meaningful @Data attributes
bOmitEmptyData.semantics: Empty means a point dataset with no points, or a spline or polyline with no segments.
bOmitEmptyData.trap: The data still leaves the node. What gets skipped is the transform pass, so the empty data is emitted at the asset's own frame and reported as a failed transform unless the unsupported-type warnings are quieted.

bFilterByTags.tooltip: If enabled, only spawn data from the PCGDataAsset that matches these tags. Empty means all data.

IncludeTags.tooltip: Tags to include. If empty, all data is included.

ExcludeTags.semantics: Exclusion is evaluated first and wins, so data carrying both an included and an excluded tag is dropped. The tags tested are the ones each piece carries inside the asset, never the input points' tags.

TargetsForwarding.tooltip: Which target attributes to forward on spawned point data.

TargetsForwarding.semantics: A forwarded attribute lands on the spawned data as a whole rather than per element, so every point of one instance carries the same value, read from the staged point that spawned it. An attribute of that name already inside the asset is replaced.

bForwardInputTags.tooltip: If enabled, forward input data tags to spawned data.
bForwardInputTags.semantics: The tags come from the staged points' own data, and only the per-point copies receive them; content emitted once per asset keeps the asset's tags alone.

bMergeEmbeddedCollectionMaps.tooltip: When enabled, scans loaded data assets for embedded CollectionMap entries, merges them into a single output, and strips them from duplicated data.
bMergeEmbeddedCollectionMaps.semantics: Assets exported from a level carry their own Collection Map beside their staged points. On, those maps never reach the outputs as data: they are unioned and re-emitted as the single Map output, which is what makes the staged points coming out of this node resolvable. Off, each one comes out as ordinary data on Out, once per unique asset, tagged with its original pin name.
bMergeEmbeddedCollectionMaps.trap: The merged Map covers only the collections the loaded assets carried. The Map this node consumed is not folded into it, so a downstream node reading both these points and points staged upstream needs the two Maps combined first.

bQuietUnsupportedTypeWarnings.tooltip: Quiet warnings about unsupported spatial data types that cannot be transformed
bQuietUnsupportedTypeWarnings.semantics: Surface, primitive and landscape data cannot be transformed: they are copied per point and emitted at the asset's own frame, and the warning is the only sign of it. Point data, splines and volumes are transformed. Polyline data that is not a spline is emitted untransformed and reports nothing at all.

bQuietInvalidEntryWarnings.tooltip: Quiet warnings about missing or invalid entries
bQuietInvalidEntryWarnings.semantics: Skipped points are silent already. A pick that is missing, unresolvable, or resolved to an entry of another collection type produces nothing and says nothing, so this has no message to suppress.

hints.text: The staged points do not come out of this node. Every output pin carries loaded content, so a downstream node that needs the points themselves takes them from upstream.
The point transform carries whatever fitting the staging pass applied, so a fitted point scales the entire arrangement it loads, not one asset inside it.

UPCGExPickClosestClustersSettings.name: Cluster : Pick Closest
UPCGExPickClosestClustersSettings.purpose: Narrows a batch of clusters down to the ones nearest a set of points you place, and keeps, drops or marks each cluster on that verdict. It decides at the level of whole clusters: nothing inside one is touched, and a cluster is either in the output or it is not. It can also bring the deciding point's attributes across, as values written onto both halves or as tags.
UPCGExPickClosestClustersSettings.situation: A generator produced clusters across a whole site and only the ones near a handful of placed markers should go downstream.

mechanism.text: Each point on **Pickers** measures its distance to every cluster, then claims the nearest one. A cluster claimed by at least one point is picked; the rest are not. `Action` turns that verdict into output. Clusters come through whole and unchanged, or as copies when target forwarding is on. The Vtx dataset is shared by every cluster paired with it, so it comes out as soon as any one of them does.

off_label.claim: Distance is measured from the target point to the cluster, and the cluster is never touched, so a single target with `Action` on Keep reduces a batch of clusters to the one nearest a chosen spot. That is the shortest way to say pick the cluster nearest here.
off_label.grounded_in: Each processor holds one distance per target and the picking loop assigns each target exactly one cluster, independent of how many targets there are.

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The Vtx dataset the clusters share.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The Edges datasets, one per cluster. This is what gets picked or not picked.

inputs.label: Pickers
inputs.note: The points that do the choosing, as one dataset. Ordinary point data, despite the label: this pin does not take **Picker :** sub-nodes.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: The shared Vtx dataset, emitted once if any of its clusters survived.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: The Edges datasets that survived, unchanged.

SearchMode.tooltip: What type of proximity to look for
SearchMode.semantics: Closest vtx measures to Vtx positions. Closest edge measures to the closest point along an edge, which is a point on the line between two vertices and not the edge point's own position, so a long edge passing near a target scores well even when both its ends are far away.

PickMode.tooltip: Whether to allow the same pick for multiple targets or not.
PickMode.semantics: Only Best lets several targets claim the same cluster, which is what you want when there are more targets than clusters. Next Best skips clusters another target already claimed and takes the nearest one still free, so a set of targets spreads across a set of clusters one for one and no more clusters are picked than there are targets. Targets are served in the order they arrive on **Pickers**, so where two of them want the same cluster the earlier one gets it, and a target left with nothing unclaimed in reach claims nothing.

Action.semantics: Keep emits the picked clusters, Omit emits the rest, and Tag emits every cluster with `Keep Tag` or `Omit Tag` added according to its verdict. The two tag names are read only under Tag.
Action.trap: Under Omit and Tag the clusters that reach the output are the ones no target claimed, and there is no target to read values from, so those clusters carry nothing from `Target Forwarding` or `Target Attributes To Tags`. Both blocks stay on screen and act only on whatever picked clusters the action lets through.

TargetBoundsExpansion.tooltip: Expand target bounds by this amount when searching for nearby clusters.
TargetBoundsExpansion.semantics: The first search is a box test around each target, built from that target's own scaled extents with this value added to every axis. It is an extent, so it reaches this far in each direction rather than being a box of this size, and a target point with no extents still searches a box built from this value alone.

bExpandSearchOutsideTargetBounds.tooltip: If enabled, search beyond target bounds if no cluster is found within.
bExpandSearchOutsideTargetBounds.semantics: On, every target eventually claims something, so `Action` on Keep can never come back empty while there is a cluster to pick. Off, a target whose expanded box touches no cluster claims nothing, and clusters no target reached are left unpicked.

KeepTag.tooltip: Tag to apply to kept clusters.

OmitTag.tooltip: Tag to apply to omitted clusters.

TargetAttributesToTags.tooltip: Copy target point attributes as tags on output clusters.
TargetAttributesToTags.semantics: Tags land on both halves and accumulate rather than replace, so a Vtx dataset whose clusters were claimed by several different targets ends up carrying a tag from each of them.

TargetForwarding.tooltip: Which Seed attributes to forward on paths.

TargetForwarding.semantics: Enabling it switches the output from a pass-through to a copy, which is what makes the picked clusters writable in the first place. The values written are those of the one target that claimed the cluster.
TargetForwarding.trap: Both halves are written, and the Vtx dataset is shared. When several clusters on one Vtx dataset are picked by different targets, each of them writes its own target's values onto that same Vtx dataset, so the Vtx half ends up carrying one target's values rather than each cluster's. The Edges half is per cluster and is correct.

hints.text: Picking is per cluster, and a cluster is one Edges dataset. A Vtx dataset paired with a single Edges dataset is all or nothing, so if a generator handed you one big cluster rather than several, this node has nothing to choose between.

UPCGExPickerAttributeSetRangesSettings.name: Picker : Ranges from Set
UPCGExPickerAttributeSetRangesSettings.purpose: Reads its spans from data rather than holding them. Each value it reads is a pair, the start and the end of one range, so where Picker : Indices from Set contributes one index per value this contributes a whole block. It is Picker : Range with the two ends supplied by the graph instead of by the panel, and as many ranges as the data holds.
UPCGExPickerAttributeSetRangesSettings.situation: Blocks of consecutive entries worked out upstream and written as pairs, that now have to drive a node taking pickers.

mechanism.text: Pairs are read once, when this node runs, from every attribute named in the list, across every dataset on the Ranges pin, and gathered into one set of distinct pairs. With the list left empty, the first attribute of each input is read instead. Each pair becomes a range in its own right: swapped when it is backwards, then resolved end by end and expanded into every index between them, both ends included. Ranges are resolved separately and their indices land in one set, so overlapping pairs collapse where they meet.

inputs.label: Ranges
inputs.note: Any data carrying the attributes to read the pairs from. Several inputs are read and their pairs pooled.

outputs.label: Picker
outputs.note: Wire it to the Pickers pin of a node that takes pickers.

fields.name: TruncateMode
fields.tooltip: How to truncate relative picks

fields.name: Safety
fields.tooltip: How to sanitize index pick when they're out-of-bounds

fields.name: Attributes
fields.tooltip: List of attributes to read ranges of indices from FVector2. Use negative values to select from the end.

UPCGExPickerAttributeSetSettings.name: Picker : Indices from Set
UPCGExPickerAttributeSetSettings.purpose: Reads its indices from data rather than holding them. Where Picker : Constant carries one value authored in the panel, this carries as many as the wired data supplies, which is what makes a selection computable upstream. Its twin, Picker : Ranges from Set, reads spans instead of single numbers.
UPCGExPickerAttributeSetSettings.situation: A selection worked out earlier in the graph and written to an attribute, that now has to drive a node taking pickers.

mechanism.text: Values are read once, when this node runs, from every attribute named in the list, across every dataset on the Indices pin, and gathered into one set of distinct values. With the list left empty, the first attribute of each input is read instead. Each gathered value is then resolved exactly as an authored one would be: scaled in normalized mode, counted back from the end when negative, then put in range by Safety. Reading happens once and resolving happens per collection, so one picker serves consumers of different sizes.

inputs.label: Indices
inputs.note: Any data carrying the attributes to read the index values from. Several inputs are read and their values pooled.

outputs.label: Picker
outputs.note: Wire it to the Pickers pin of a node that takes pickers.

UPCGExPickerConstantRangeSettings.name: Picker : Range
UPCGExPickerConstantRangeSettings.purpose: Names a contiguous span of indices, authored on the node. Where Picker : Constant holds one value, this holds two and every index between them, both ends included. In normalized mode the two ends are fractions of the collection, which is how the first quarter or the middle half is expressed without knowing how many entries there are.
UPCGExPickerConstantRangeSettings.situation: A block of consecutive entries, described by where the block starts and ends rather than by listing it.

mechanism.text: Two values are resolved into two indices and every index from one to the other is picked, both ends included. A range authored backwards is swapped when the node runs, so start and end can be given in either order. Each end is resolved on its own: scaled in normalized mode, counted back from the end when negative, then brought into range by Safety. The two ends are only turned into a span once both have survived that.

UPCGExPickerConstantSettings.name: Picker : Constant
UPCGExPickerConstantSettings.purpose: Names one index, authored on the node. It is the picker for the first, the last, or the one at the halfway mark, and it holds a single value rather than a span, which is what separates it from Picker : Range. Nothing is read from a pin, so the selection is fixed in the graph and resolves against whatever collection the consumer hands it.
UPCGExPickerConstantSettings.situation: One entry out of a set whose size is not known when the graph is authored, named by its position rather than by anything it carries.

mechanism.text: One value is resolved into one index. In discrete mode it is used as an index directly; in normalized mode it is scaled by the last index first. Negatives count back from the end, and Safety decides what a value still outside the collection becomes. The node subtitle shows the authored pick, so the panel says what will be selected before anything runs.

UPCGExPickerFactoryProviderSettings.name: Picker Definition
UPCGExPickerFactoryProviderSettings.purpose: The base every Picker : node inherits. It never appears in the palette, and this page carries what they all share: the Picker pin they all emit on, the settings that decide what an authored value means, and how several pickers on one pin combine. Their consumers are Cherry Pick Points, Promote Attributes, Filter : Picker, and the Uber Filters, which take pickers to narrow what they test.
UPCGExPickerFactoryProviderSettings.situation: Reading any Picker : page and needing to know what Treat As Normalized changes, or what happens to a pick that lands outside the collection.

mechanism.text: A picker answers one question, which indices, and it is asked at execution by the node consuming it. That node supplies the count, so the same picker resolves against four entries or four hundred without being touched. Several pickers on one pin are gathered into one set of indices, which makes the combination a union: order does not matter, and picks two of them share collapse to one. Nothing in a picker names a dataset, which is what lets one be reused across nodes and across collections of different sizes.
steps: In normalized mode the authored value is scaled by the last index, then landed on a whole number by Truncate Mode.
A negative result is counted back from the end, so -1 becomes the last index.
Anything still outside the collection is put back in range by Safety.
A pick Safety left out of range is dropped, and contributes nothing to the set.

outputs.label: Picker
outputs.note: What every Picker : node emits. Consumers read it on a pin named Pickers.

hints.text: What the indices index is decided by the consumer. Cherry Pick Points and the Uber Filters resolve them against the points of each input dataset, one dataset at a time. Filter : Picker resolves them against the points when it is testing points and against the datasets of the collection when it is testing a whole collection, so the same picker means two different things depending on where the filter is used.

Safety defaults to Ignore, which drops an out-of-range pick without a word. An empty pick set is not a no-op downstream: on Cherry Pick Points it means every point is discarded, so a picker aimed past the end of a short dataset empties it rather than leaving it alone.

Negative values are resolved before Safety, so -1 is the last entry rather than an out-of-range index for Safety to rescue. Only a value that is still outside the collection after that wrap reaches Safety at all.

A sub-node from another family dropped onto a Pickers pin connects, logs an invalid-input warning and is discarded, after which the node runs with whatever survived. When it was the only thing on the pin, the next thing reported is a missing-required-input error naming Pickers, which names the emptied pin rather than the wire that emptied it.

UPCGExPickerFilterProviderSettings.name: Filter : Picker
UPCGExPickerFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Turns an index selection into an ordinary filter verdict. Pickers name indices and only a handful of nodes take them directly; wiring them here instead produces a filter, which every node with a filter pin accepts, so index selection reaches the rest of the plugin without those nodes knowing pickers exist. Several pickers on the pin pool into one selection, so an element passes when any of them named its index. It also serves the consumers that judge whole datasets, where the indices address positions among the datasets on the pin rather than elements inside one.
UPCGExPickerFilterProviderSettings.situation: The elements to act on are known by where they sit in the data rather than by anything they carry.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this filter once per element. Every wired picker resolves its indices against the element count of the dataset being tested, the results are pooled into one set, and an element passes when that set holds its index; Invert flips that. Resolution runs per dataset, so one copy of this node reaches the same position inside each dataset that arrives rather than counting through them all in sequence. What an index means stays the picker's own business: absolute by default, counted back from the end when negative, read as a position across the set when that picker is switched to normalized, and either dropped or folded back into range by that picker's own `Safety` setting.

off_label.claim: Because the pickers resolve against each dataset separately, one Filter : Picker wired into a consumer marks the first, last or nth element of every dataset it meets: a picker naming index -1 reaches the final element of each one, whatever their lengths.
off_label.grounded_in: FPickerFilter::Init calling AddPicks with InPointDataFacade->GetNum(), once per facade, and the negative-index wrap in UPCGExPickerConstantFactory::AddPicks

inputs.label: Pickers
inputs.note: The picker sub-nodes naming the indices. Several are pooled into one selection rather than having to agree.

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter type, so every filter pin accepts it, and it is also accepted by the consumers that evaluate whole datasets.

hints.text: An empty Pickers pin is an error rather than a policy here. The node logs a missing input and emits no filter at all, so the consumer runs with one fewer condition instead of with a condition that rejects everything.

Pickers whose indices all fall outside a dataset leave an empty selection for it, which is what the default `Safety` of Ignore does with an out-of-range index. An empty selection fails every element in that dataset, and passes every one of them when Invert is on.

UPCGExPointsProcessorSettings.name: Points Processor Settings
UPCGExPointsProcessorSettings.purpose: The base almost every point-processing node inherits, sitting between the root settings and the node itself. It is what makes a node one that takes points in and gives points out, and the settings it contributes are about that contract: which inputs are accepted, and what happens to the ones that cannot be processed.
UPCGExPointsProcessorSettings.situation: Reading a node page and needing to know which of its settings are its own and which reach it from the point-processing base.

mechanism.text: A point processor takes a main input, works over its elements, and emits a main output. What it inherits from here is the machinery around that: input validation, the failure policies, and the shared execution settings from the root block beneath. The node's own settings decide what happens to each element; nothing here does.

hints.text: This base never appears in the palette. Its page exists so the settings it contributes are explained once rather than on every node that inherits them.

UPCGExPointsToBoundsSettings.name: Points to Bounds
UPCGExPointsToBoundsSettings.purpose: Reduces a whole dataset to the box that contains it. Everything that was scattered becomes one point whose bounds enclose the lot, carrying whatever its contents blended to, which turns a cloud into something a single test or a single spawn can act on. It can also leave the points alone and record the measurement instead.
UPCGExPointsToBoundsSettings.situation: A group of points that needs to be treated as one object downstream, or measured without being changed.

mechanism.text: The extent of every point in a dataset is measured and reduced to one box. `Output Mode` decides what happens to the dataset: collapse it to a single point sitting at that box, or leave every point where it is and write the measurement to the data domain. When collapsing, the surviving point's attributes come from blending its contents, so the result describes the group rather than any one member. The box can be axis-aligned or fitted to the cloud's own orientation.

off_label.claim: In Write Data mode with nothing else enabled it is a pure measurement: every point survives untouched and the dataset gains its own extent as data-domain values, ready for a filter or a normalisation that needs to know how big the input was.
off_label.grounded_in: The Write Data output mode leaves points unaffected and writes the results to the data domain instead of collapsing.

bOutputOrientedBoundingBox.tooltip: Output Object Oriented Bounds. This only accounts for positions and ignores point bounds.
bOutputOrientedBoundingBox.semantics: Fits the box to how the cloud is actually oriented rather than to the world axes, which is what stops a diagonal arrangement producing a box far larger than its contents.
bOutputOrientedBoundingBox.trap: It measures positions alone and ignores the points' own bounds, so a set of large points reports a box that their volumes stick out of. The axis-aligned path is the one that accounts for point extents.

bUseMinBoxFit.tooltip: If enabled, use precise min box fit.

BoundsSource.tooltip: Which point bounds should be used

OutputMode.semantics: The switch between changing the data and describing it. `Collapse` replaces a dataset with one point, so the count of points leaving the node has nothing to do with the count arriving. `Write Data` keeps every point and records the measurement on the dataset instead, which is what to reach for when the bounds are wanted as information rather than as geometry.

BlendingSettings.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged into the final point.
BlendingSettings.semantics: Decides whether the collapsed point inherits from its contents or arrives with defaults. Left on, the surviving point's attributes describe the group, which is usually the point of collapsing at all.

fields.name: TransformAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Attribute name for the transform output.

fields.name: DensityAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Attribute name for the density output.

fields.name: BoundsMinAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Attribute name for the bounds minimum output.

fields.name: BoundsMaxAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Attribute name for the bounds maximum output.

fields.name: ColorAttributeName
