UPCGExSampleNearestPointSettings.name: Sample : Nearest Point
UPCGExSampleNearestPointSettings.purpose: Reads a second point set from each of your points and writes back what it found there. The question it answers is which targets a point should listen to and how much each one counts, and everything else follows from that: distances and angles as attributes, target attributes blended onto the point, the point moved onto what it sampled. It is the sampler for point targets, and the one whose weighting settings the other samplers reuse.
UPCGExSampleNearestPointSettings.situation: Points that need a value carried over from a scattered reference set, whether that is the single nearest one or a falloff across everything in range.

mechanism.text: Every point resolves its own `Min Range` and `Max Range`, gathers the targets that fall between them, and turns that gather into one weighted set. `Sample Method` decides whether the set keeps one target or all of them, and `Weight Mode` decides what a target's closeness is worth. Everything the node writes comes from that set: the outputs read it, the blending block averages target attributes across it, and `Apply Sampling` can move the point onto the transform it produced. A point that gathers nothing counts as a failure and is still written to, with fallbacks rather than blanks.
steps: Targets outside the range band are discarded before anything is weighted.
Weights are computed across whatever survived, then attributes and outputs are written from it.
Apply Sampling moves the point last, after everything has been read.

off_label.claim: Setting `Max Range` to 0 turns the node into a whole-set operation: with no range to bound the search it visits every target, so `All (Within range)` becomes a weighted average over the entire target set and `Closest Target` becomes a global nearest.
off_label.grounded_in: FProcessor::ProcessPoints skips the range test when RangeMax is 0 and walks ForEachTargetPoint instead of the bounded FindElementsWithBoundsTest.

off_label.claim: Wiring the same data into both pins with `Ignore Self` off turns it into a self-proximity measure, since each point then finds itself at distance zero and every other point beyond it.
off_label.grounded_in: bIgnoreSelf adds PointDataFacade->GetIn() to the ignore list; with it cleared nothing excludes the source data from the target search.

bProcessFilteredOutAsFails.semantics: Decides what happens to a point the Use Value If filters rejected. Left on, it takes the failure fallbacks like any point that found nothing, which overwrites whatever those attributes held. Turned off, the point is skipped and its existing values survive, which is what makes a second sampler able to fill in what the first one left alone.

bPruneFailedSamples.tooltip: If enabled, points that failed to sample anything will be pruned.
bPruneFailedSamples.semantics: Removes points that sampled nothing from the output rather than writing fallbacks onto them. The count of points leaving the node stops matching the count arriving, so anything downstream pairing by index against the original data no longer lines up.

bIgnoreSelf.tooltip: If enabled, source points won't sample themselves as targets.
bIgnoreSelf.semantics: Only does anything when the same data reaches both pins. It excludes the sampling dataset from the target search, which is what stops every point finding itself at distance zero and sampling nothing else.

hints.text: A point that samples nothing is still written to. Success goes false, the transform and look-at outputs receive the point's own transform, distance receives `Max Range`, the sample count receives 0 and the sampled index receives -1. Nothing is left at its previous value unless the point was skipped by a filter with `Process Filtered Out As Fails` off.

UPCGExSampleNearestSplineSettings.name: Sample : Nearest Spline
UPCGExSampleNearestSplineSettings.purpose: Reads real splines rather than paths made of points. The targets arrive as polyline data, so what a point samples is a continuous curve with its own tangents and its own scale, and the result can be a position anywhere along it rather than at one of its control points. It is the sampler to reach for when the reference geometry was authored as a spline in the level.
UPCGExSampleNearestSplineSettings.situation: Points that need to align to, or measure against, a spline component rather than a path the graph built.

mechanism.text: Each point finds its closest position on each spline, keeps whichever splines fall inside its range band, and `Sample Method` decides whether one of them wins or all of them are weighted together. Because the target is a curve rather than a list of points, the sampled position is continuous and carries the spline's own transform, which is what the transform and look-at outputs are built from. `Sample Inputs` narrows which splines are eligible by whether they close, before anything is measured.

off_label.claim: Turning on the specific-alpha mode makes every point read the same place on a spline, which turns the node into a broadcast: one spline's transform at a chosen position copied onto an entire point set, with no proximity involved.
off_label.grounded_in: The alpha path replaces the closest-position search with a fixed evaluation along the spline, resolved per point through the Sample Alpha selector.

inputs.label: Targets
inputs.note: Polyline data, which is spline components rather than PCGEx paths. Paths built from points belong on **Sample : Nearest Path** instead.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The same points, carrying whatever was enabled in Outputs and Apply Sampling.

SampleInputs.semantics: Filters the splines by whether they close, before any distance is measured. A spline the mode excludes is not a distant candidate, it is absent, so a point with nothing eligible in range fails rather than falling back to the other kind.

bSplineScalesRanges.tooltip: If enabled, spline scale affect range.
bSplineScalesRanges.semantics: Lets each spline widen or narrow the range band by its own scale, so a tapering spline reaches further where it is thicker. The range is then no longer one figure the reader can check against a distance: two points at the same distance from the same spline can disagree about whether they are in range.

The range band still decides which splines are eligible, so a point can be admitted by distance and then read a position on the far end of the curve.

SampleAlphaMode.tooltip: How to interpret the sample alpha value.
SampleAlphaMode.semantics: Decides how the alpha figure is read: a fraction of the whole spline, a segment-indexed time, or a distance in world units along it. The same number means three different places, and only the fraction is bounded to the spline's extent by its own definition.

UPCGExSampleNearestSurfaceSettings.name: Sample : Nearest Surface
UPCGExSampleNearestSurfaceSettings.purpose: Finds the closest point on real collision geometry, for each of your points. The other samplers read points you supplied; this one reads the level, so what it finds is whatever the physics world has within reach. It answers where the surface is, which way it faces, and whether the point was inside it.
UPCGExSampleNearestSurfaceSettings.situation: Scattered points that need to sit on, or measure against, geometry that exists in the level rather than in the graph.

mechanism.text: Each point sweeps a sphere of its own `Distance` radius and keeps the nearest surface it touched. Every overlapped component is asked for its closest point, and the winner supplies the location, the normal and the distance. `Surface Source` narrows what may be touched, and switching it changes the node's pins rather than filtering afterwards. Nothing found inside the radius is a failure, and the radius is the only reach there is: a surface beyond it is not a distant result, it is no result.

off_label.claim: Writing `Is Inside` on its own turns the node into a containment test against level collision, which no filter offers directly. The distance and location outputs can be left off, and a point reports whether the world encloses it.
off_label.grounded_in: bIsInside is set from MinDist == 0 on the overlap result, and refined against the impact normal when Trace Complex is on.

The other two each add a required pin and restrict the search to what arrives on it, so narrowing the search is a wiring change rather than a filter applied to results.

On fresh attributes that is the type's default; on attributes an earlier node wrote, it is that earlier value. Read the distance against the search radius if you need to know a sample failed.

UPCGExSampleNeighborsSettings.name: Cluster : Sample Neighbors
UPCGExSampleNeighborsSettings.purpose: Runs the neighbour samplers over a cluster. Each Vtx looks outward through its own connections and reads what it finds there, which is how a value spreads along the structure rather than through space. The samplers on its pin decide what is read and written; this node decides nothing on its own and declares no settings.
UPCGExSampleNeighborsSettings.situation: A cluster whose Vtx should each learn something from what they are connected to, rather than from what is near them.

mechanism.text: Every sampler on the pin runs its own pass over the whole cluster. For each Vtx the walk reaches outward to the depth that sampler asked for, gathers its neighbours, and the sampler writes whatever it computes from them. Passes are independent, so several samplers reading the same neighbourhoods is normal, and their order only matters where two of them write the same attribute.

inputs.label: Samplers
inputs.note: The neighbour samplers to run. Without at least one the node has nothing to do.

hints.text: Reach is measured in connections, not in distance. Two Vtx sitting beside each other with no edge between them are not neighbours here, whatever a spatial sampler would say about them.

UPCGExSampleOverlapStatsSettings.name: Sample : Overlap Stats
UPCGExSampleOverlapStatsSettings.purpose: Measures how much each point is crowded by points from other datasets, and writes the answer without removing anything. Overlap here is between datasets rather than within one, so a point is never counted against its own neighbours. **Discard By Overlap** makes the same measurement and acts on it; this one only reports, which is what makes it the node for seeing the numbers before choosing a threshold.
UPCGExSampleOverlapStatsSettings.situation: Several scattered layers that are expected to conflict, and a need to see where and how badly before deciding what to cull.

mechanism.text: Every point's bounds are tested against the points of every other dataset, and two counts come out of it: how many other datasets touched this point, and how many individual points did. `Test Mode` decides what shape the test uses and how exact it is, and `Min Threshold` decides how much overlap has to exist before it counts at all. The relative outputs are the same counts normalised, so they answer how crowded this point is compared with the rest rather than by how many.

off_label.claim: Tagging on has-any-overlap and has-no-overlap turns it into a dataset-level triage: the tags travel with the data and a downstream filter can route whole layers by whether they collided at all, without reading any per-point attribute.
off_label.grounded_in: The tagging settings are evaluated per dataset from whether any of its points recorded an overlap, independently of the per-point attribute writes.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: Every dataset to be compared. They are all tested against each other, so a single dataset on its own records no overlaps at all.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The same datasets, carrying whatever counts were enabled, plus any tags.

TestMode.semantics: Trades exactness for cost, and the source is candid about which way each errs. `Fast` compares only the datasets' overall bounds, so it answers whether two layers occupy the same region rather than whether any two points do. `Box` tests transformed boxes and can miss overlaps. `Sphere` tests spheres and reports some that are not real. There is no exact option here.
TestMode.trap: `Fast` gives every point in a dataset the same answer, because nothing per-point is tested. A per-point attribute written under it varies between datasets and is flat within them.

BoundsSource.tooltip: Point bounds to be used to compute overlaps

Expansion.tooltip: Expand bounds by that amount to account for a margin of error due to multiple layers of transformation and lack of OBB
Expansion.semantics: Pads every point's bounds before testing, to absorb the error that accumulates through layers of transformation. It makes overlaps easier to find rather than more accurate, so a large value reports crowding that the geometry does not have.

MinThreshold.tooltip: The minimum amount two sub-points must overlap to be added to the comparison.  The higher, the more "overlap" there must be.
MinThreshold.semantics: How much two points must overlap before it counts. `Threshold Measure` decides whether the figure is a world-space distance or a fraction of the points' average size, and the shipped configuration is the fraction, so the same number behaves differently on data of a different scale.

ThresholdMeasure.tooltip: How to interpret the min overlap value.  Discrete means distance in world space  Relative means uses percentage (0-1) of the averaged radius.

OverlapCountAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write unique overlap count to. Unique overlap count is the number of time a different point data set overlapped this point.

OverlapSubCountAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write total overlap sub-count to. Total overlap count is the number of time another point overlapped this point. This count can get really high, really fast.
OverlapSubCountAttributeName.semantics: Counts individual overlapping points, where the plain overlap count counts distinct datasets. One point sitting under a dense cluster from one other layer scores 1 on the first and many on the second, which is the distinction to reach for when density matters more than variety.

RelativeOverlapCountAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write relative unique overlap count to. Relative Unique overlap count is this collection' OverlapSubCount divided by the max of all collections combined

RelativeOverlapSubCountAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write relative total overlap sub-count to. Relative Total overlap count is is this collection' OverlapCount divided by the max of all collections combined

hints.text: Overlap is only ever measured between datasets. Points crowding each other inside one dataset record nothing here, which is what **Self Pruning** is for.

UPCGExSampleSocketsSettings.name: Sample : Sockets
UPCGExSampleSocketsSettings.purpose: Reads the sockets authored on a static mesh and outputs them as points. Every input point names a mesh, through an asset path attribute or through the constant on the node, and the node emits one point per socket that mesh carries, placed in the point's own frame. This is the collection-free route to sockets: no Collection Map, no staged pick, the sockets read straight off the mesh asset. Staging : Load Sockets is the counterpart for points that came out of a collection.
UPCGExSampleSocketsSettings.situation: Points already carry the asset path of the mesh they stand for, and something has to land on that mesh's authored sockets.

mechanism.text: One execution emits one point per socket of the mesh each input point resolves to, and the input points themselves are not part of the output. Each socket point sits at the socket's own transform composed into its host point's frame, takes a seed computed from that world location, and carries the host point's attributes; beyond transform and seed, point properties stay at their defaults. Sockets are read from the mesh asset itself, so a mesh carrying none contributes nothing, and points the Point Filters pin rejects contribute nothing either. Socket points come out grouped by host, in host order, each host's sockets in the mesh's own order, and the Sockets pin carries one dataset per input dataset that produced at least one.

off_label.claim: One input point plus Asset Type set to Constant turns the node into a readout of a single mesh: the output is that mesh's socket set, with names and tags available as attributes, without anything being staged or spawned.
off_label.grounded_in: the Constant branch in Boot, which loads the named mesh and hands the same one to every point, and the per-socket writers in FSocketHelper::CompileRange

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points naming the meshes to read. Accepts multiple datasets, each processed on its own.

inputs.label: Point Filters
inputs.note: Narrows which points get read. Rejected points emit no sockets, and since the node forwards nothing, they leave no trace in the output.

outputs.label: Sockets
outputs.note: The socket points, and the node's only output. One dataset per input dataset that produced at least one socket point.

AssetType.semantics: In Attribute mode the named attribute is read as an asset path, so string, name and soft object path attributes all work, and a value in the @Data domain governs its whole dataset. Only paths resolving to a static mesh survive the load; anything else is dropped and the points holding it emit nothing.
AssetType.trap: The node cancels its own execution when no valid asset path is found across every input, or when the constant mesh fails to load, so a misspelt attribute name costs the whole node rather than a few points.

AssetPathAttributeName.tooltip: The name of the attribute to read asset path from.

hints.text: An asset path that resolves to anything other than a static mesh is dropped during loading, and the points holding it emit no sockets and no message. Fewer socket points than expected is the only symptom.
Each socket point's seed is computed from its own world location, so two sockets landing in the same place get the same seed, and moving a host re-rolls everything downstream that reads it.

UPCGExSampleSurfaceGuidedSettings.name: Sample : Line Trace
UPCGExSampleSurfaceGuidedSettings.purpose: Fires a ray from each point and reports what it hit. **Sample : Nearest Surface** asks what is closest in every direction; this one asks what is in one particular direction, which is what makes it the node for projecting points onto ground, finding the ceiling above them, or testing line of sight. Beyond the hit location and normal it can read the surface's material, its UVs and the texture values underneath.
UPCGExSampleSurfaceGuidedSettings.situation: Points that need to land on whatever is beneath them, or to answer whether anything stands between them and somewhere else.

mechanism.text: A ray leaves `Origin`, travels along `Direction` for `Distance`, and the first thing it meets supplies the result. Both the origin and the direction are read per point, so the rays need not be parallel or start where the points are. `Surface Source` decides what may be hit and changes the node's pins to match. The hit's impact normal builds an orientation through `Rotation Construction`, which is what `Apply Sampling` can then put on the point. A ray that reaches its full length without hitting anything is a failure.

off_label.claim: Two of these back to back, one down and one up, measure the thickness of whatever a point sits in without any volume authoring: the first finds the floor, the second the ceiling, and the distance outputs subtract.
off_label.grounded_in: Origin and Direction are per-point selectors, so a second trace can start from the first one's written location and travel the opposite way.

off_label.claim: `Is Inside` reports that the ray hit a back face, so tracing in any direction with a long enough distance answers whether the point started inside closed geometry.
off_label.grounded_in: IsInside is written as FVector::DotProduct(Direction, HitResult.Normal) > 0, which is true when the surface faces away from the incoming ray.

inputs.label: Actor References
inputs.note: Points carrying actor reference paths, which become the only surfaces the ray can hit.
inputs.condition: only when Surface Source is Actor Reference

inputs.label: Primitives
inputs.note: Primitive component data, which becomes the only geometry the ray can hit.
inputs.condition: only when Surface Source is Primitives

inputs.label: Texture Params
inputs.note: Texture Param factories naming which material parameters to read off the surface that was hit.
inputs.condition: only when the render material output and its texture parameter extraction are both enabled

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The same points, carrying whatever was enabled in Outputs and Apply Sampling.

pins.dynamic: The input pin set follows Surface Source and the render-material outputs. Any surface with texture extraction off declares no extra pins at all.

SurfaceSource.semantics: Decides what the ray may hit, and rewires the node to match. `Any surface` traces the physics world under the collision settings. The other two each add a required pin and the ray can hit nothing else, so narrowing what is traceable is a wiring change rather than a filter on results.

ActorReference.tooltip: Name of the attribute that contains a path to an actor in the level, usually from a GetActorData PCG Node in point mode.

Origin.semantics: Read per point, so a trace can start somewhere other than the point it belongs to. Nothing constrains it to be near the point, which is what lets one pass trace from a height down onto the points' own positions.

Direction.tooltip: The direction to use for the trace
Direction.semantics: Read per point and used as given, so its length does not extend the trace: how far the ray travels is `Distance` alone. Rays are independent, so a per-point direction attribute gives each point its own aim.
Direction.trap: A direction attribute that is zero-length leaves the ray with no direction to travel in, and the point can only fail. `Invert` flips whatever was read, which is the setting to reach for rather than negating the attribute upstream.

Distance.semantics: The length of the ray, resolved per point. It is also what a failed point receives in the distance attribute, so a point that hit nothing reports the full length of the ray it fired.

ApplySampling.tooltip: Whether and how to apply sampled result directly (not mutually exclusive with output)

RotationConstruction.tooltip: How hit transform rotation should be constructed. First value used is the impact normal.
RotationConstruction.semantics: Decides which axis of the built orientation the impact normal becomes. `Cross Axis` supplies the second direction, and the rest follows from the two, so a point aligned to a surface still needs a second axis to settle its twist about that normal.
RotationConstruction.trap: A cross axis pointing along the impact normal leaves the twist undefined, which shows up as points that flip about their own normal between neighbouring hits on a curved surface.

CrossAxis.tooltip: Second value used for constructing rotation

fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

fields.name: Constant
fields.tooltip: Direction vector when using constant input.

fields.name: bFlip
fields.tooltip: Negate the direction vector after reading.

SuccessAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'boolean' attribute to write sampling success to.

LocationAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'vector' attribute to write sampled Location to.

LookAtAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'vector' attribute to write sampled LookAt to.

NormalAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'vector' attribute to write sampled Normal to.

DistanceAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'double' attribute to write sampled distance to.

bOutputNormalizedDistance.tooltip: Whether to output normalized distance or not

bOutputOneMinusDistance.tooltip: Whether to do a OneMinus on the normalized distance value

DistanceScale.tooltip: Scale factor applied to the distance output; allows inverting it with -1

IsInsideAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'bool' attribute to write sampled point inside or outside the collision.
IsInsideAttributeName.semantics: True when the ray hit a back face, which means it started inside the geometry it hit. This is a different question from the one **Sample : Nearest Surface** answers under the same name, where being inside means the nearest surface point is the point's own position.

UVCoordsAttributeName.tooltip: Create an attribute for UV Coordinates of the surface hit. Note: Will only work in complex traces and must have 'Project Settings->Physics->Support UV From Hit Results' set to true.

UVChannel.tooltip: This UV Channel will be selected when retrieving UV Coordinates from a raycast query.

FaceIndexAttributeName.tooltip: Create an attribute for index of the hit face. Note: Will only work in complex traces.

bWriteVertexColor.tooltip: Whether to attempt to compute the vertex color and write it to the point $Color

ActorReferenceAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'string' attribute to write actor reference to.

HitComponentReferenceAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'string' attribute to write actor reference to.

PhysMatAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'string' attribute to write actor reference to.

RenderMatAttributeName.tooltip: Create an attribute for the render material.

RenderMaterialIndex.tooltip: The index of the render material when it is queried from the hit.

AttributesForwarding.tooltip: Which actor reference points attributes to forward on points.

fields.name: FilterMode
fields.tooltip: How the names are processed.

fields.name: Matches
fields.tooltip: List of matches that will be checked. Any success is a pass.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNames
fields.tooltip: A list of names separated by a comma, for easy overrides. The limitation is that they all use the same shared filter mode.

fields.name: CommaSeparatedNameFilter
fields.tooltip: Unique filter mode applied to comma separated names

fields.name: bPreservePCGExData
fields.tooltip: If enabled, PCGEx attributes & tags won't be affected.  Cluster-related nodes rely on these to work!

fields.name: bEnabled
fields.tooltip: Is forwarding enabled.

fields.name: bPreserveAttributesDefaultValue
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will preserve the initial attribute default value.

bProcessFilteredOutAsFails.tooltip: If enabled, mark filtered out points as "failed". Otherwise, just skip the processing altogether. Only uncheck this if you want to ensure existing attribute values are preserved.

bPruneFailedSamples.tooltip: If enabled, points that failed to sample anything will be pruned.

bQuietUVSettingsWarning.tooltip: Suppress warnings about UV query settings not being enabled in project settings.

hints.text: A ray that hits nothing does not receive `false` here. The failure path writes location, normal, look-at and distance, and leaves success, is-inside, the actor reference, the physical material, the UVs and the face index at whatever they already held. Read the distance against the trace length if you need to know a sample failed.

UPCGExSampleTextureSettings.name: Sample : Texture
UPCGExSampleTextureSettings.purpose: Reads texture values at coordinates the points already carry. The point supplies a UV, the texture data supplies the pixels, and a **Texture Param** says which parameter to read and what to call the result. It is the last step of the texture route rather than the whole of it: something upstream has to have produced both the UVs and the texture data.
UPCGExSampleTextureSettings.situation: Points carrying UV coordinates that need a mask, a heightmap or a colour read out of the texture those coordinates belong to.

mechanism.text: Each point reads its UV from `UV Source` and looks that coordinate up in the texture data on the pin. Which texture and which channels are read comes entirely from the Texture Param factories, so the node itself holds almost no configuration: the parameters decide what is sampled and where it is written, and several of them on the pin write several attributes in one pass. A point whose UV resolves to no texture is a failure and can be pruned.

inputs.label: Texture Data
inputs.note: The texture objects the points reference. **Get Texture Data** is what usually produces these.

inputs.label: Texture Params
inputs.note: Texture Param factories naming which parameter to read and what to write. Without one the node has nothing to sample.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The same points, carrying an attribute per texture parameter that resolved.

UVSource.semantics: The coordinate to look up, read per point. Nothing here generates UVs, so this names an attribute something upstream already wrote: **Sample : Line Trace** can produce them from a surface hit, and a graph can author them directly.

bProcessFilteredOutAsFails.tooltip: If enabled, mark filtered out points as "failed". Otherwise, just skip the processing altogether. Only uncheck this if you want to ensure existing attribute values are preserved.

bPruneFailedSamples.tooltip: If enabled, points that failed to sample anything will be pruned.
bPruneFailedSamples.semantics: Removes points whose UV resolved to no texture. The count leaving the node stops matching the count arriving, so anything pairing by index against the original data no longer lines up.

bQuietDuplicateSampleNamesWarning.tooltip: Suppress warnings about duplicate sample attribute names across texture params.
bQuietDuplicateSampleNamesWarning.semantics: Two Texture Params writing the same sample attribute name is a collision the node warns about, because the second write lands on top of the first and one parameter's result disappears. Silencing it is right only when the duplication is deliberate.

hints.text: Both input pins are required, so this node cannot run alone. The usual shape is **Get Texture Data** feeding the texture pin and a **Texture Param** feeding the other, with the same parameter definition wired to both.

UPCGExSampleVtxByIDSettings.name: Sample : Vtx by ID
UPCGExSampleVtxByIDSettings.purpose: Reconnects points to the cluster vertices they came from. Anything that left a cluster carrying a copy of a Vtx's endpoint id can be matched back to that Vtx here and take values off it. The match is by id and not by position, so it survives both sides moving, and it is exact rather than nearest: a point either names a Vtx that exists or it counts as a failure.
UPCGExSampleVtxByIDSettings.situation: Points carry an id copied off a cluster earlier in the graph and now need transforms or attributes from the vertices those ids name.

mechanism.text: Each point reads an id from the attribute named in `Vtx Id Source` and looks it up across the Vtx datasets on the **Vtx** pin. A point whose id matches nothing counts as a failure and is left alone. What lands on a match is what you asked for and nothing else: the **Blend Ops** you wired decide which attribute values come across, and `Apply Sampling` decides whether the matched Vtx transform and the look-at are written onto the point. Every input point is duplicated into the output, so the count is unchanged unless `Prune Failed Samples` is on.

off_label.claim: The id source accepts an int64 and reduces it the same way the cluster attribute is packed, so `PCGEx/VData` copied straight off a Vtx works as the id without any unpacking step of your own.
off_label.grounded_in: The element reads Vtx Id Source as int32 first and falls back to int64, taking the first half of the packed value, which is the same half the lookup is keyed on.

inputs.label: Sources
inputs.note: The points to sample onto. Every one of them is duplicated into the output.

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The Vtx datasets to look ids up in. Several are accepted and are indexed together.

inputs.label: Point Filters
inputs.note: Decides which points are sampled at all. A point that fails counts as a failure unless `Process Filtered Out As Fails` is cleared, in which case it is skipped and left exactly as it arrived.

inputs.label: Blend Ops
inputs.note: What a matched Vtx contributes to its point. With nothing wired the node still matches and still applies sampling, but no attribute value crosses over.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The input points, duplicated, with whatever the blend ops and `Apply Sampling` wrote. The points that matched nothing are still here unless they were pruned.

VtxIdSource.tooltip: Name of the attribute that stores the vtx id (first 32 bits of the PCGEx/VData)
VtxIdSource.semantics: The attribute is read as an int32 first and as an int64 second, and an int64 is reduced to its first half before matching, which is the same half the cluster attribute packs the id into. A name that resolves to neither type stops the node with an error rather than failing every sample.

ApplySampling.tooltip: Whether and how to apply sampled result directly (not mutually exclusive with blending)

LookAtAxisAlign.tooltip: The axis to align transform the look at vector to.
LookAtAxisAlign.semantics: The direction being aligned runs from the matched Vtx out to the point, so the chosen axis ends up pointing away from what was sampled. Pick Backward when you want the point facing the Vtx instead.

LookAtUp.tooltip: The value to use as Up vector for the look at transform.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

HasSuccessesTag.tooltip: If enabled, add the specified tag to the output data if at least a single point has been sampled.

HasNoSuccessesTag.tooltip: If enabled, add the specified tag to the output data if no points were sampled.

bProcessFilteredOutAsFails.tooltip: If enabled, mark filtered out points as "failed". Otherwise, just skip the processing altogether. Only uncheck this if you want to ensure existing attribute values are preserved.

bPruneFailedSamples.tooltip: If enabled, points that failed to sample anything will be pruned.
bPruneFailedSamples.semantics: The one setting here that changes the point count. What counts as a failure is an id that matched nothing, plus, while `Process Filtered Out As Fails` is on, every point the filters rejected. Turning both on makes this node delete the points the filters excluded, which is rarely what the filters were for.

hints.text: The **Vtx** pin is unforgiving in two ways. A dataset with no cluster Vtx attribute on it is skipped in silence, so a plain point dataset wired here produces nothing but failed samples and no warning. And ids are only unique inside one Vtx dataset, so wiring several unrelated ones means an id that appears in more than one of them resolves to whichever was read last.

UPCGExSanitizeClustersSettings.name: Cluster : Repair
UPCGExSanitizeClustersSettings.purpose: Rebuilds a cluster from the endpoint ids its two halves carry, and emits whatever still holds together. It is the way back in from a round trip through vanilla nodes: it trusts nothing it is handed, resolves every edge again, and discards what no longer resolves. That is also why it is expensive, so it earns its place once, at the point of re-entry, rather than as a precaution between cluster nodes.
UPCGExSanitizeClustersSettings.situation: Cluster data came back from vanilla nodes and the cluster nodes downstream either refuse it or read the wrong vertices.

mechanism.text: Every edge is resolved again through the ids on both halves, then the whole structure is recompiled. An edge naming an id that is no longer present is dropped, so is one whose two ids land on the same Vtx, a second edge between the same pair collapses into the first, the survivors are re-split by connected component into one Edges dataset each, and any Vtx left holding nothing is pruned. Both halves come out renumbered under a fresh pair id, so what arrives downstream is a new cluster rather than the one you sent in. Edge points are rewritten by `Cluster Output Settings`, which by default moves each one to the midpoint between its endpoints.

off_label.claim: Because the recompile splits by connected component, one Edges dataset holding several disconnected islands comes back as one Edges dataset per island. That makes this a way to separate components that arrived fused, without going near a generator.
off_label.grounded_in: FBatch::OnInitialPostProcess calls GraphBuilder->Compile, whose FGraph::BuildSubGraphs isolates connected components and emits a subgraph per component.

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The cluster's Vtx dataset. Read for its endpoint ids, and duplicated into the output.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The cluster's Edges datasets. Read for the pair of ids each edge names; the points themselves are rebuilt rather than forwarded.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: The surviving vertices, renumbered, under a fresh pair id.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: The surviving edges, one dataset per connected component, so one cluster in can come out as several.

GraphBuilderDetails.semantics: The only setting the node has of its own, and the last thing that can drop a result. Remove Small Clusters and Remove Big Clusters are measured per connected component after the re-split, so a repair that broke one damaged cluster into fragments can then have those fragments discarded here rather than by the damage.

hints.text: When nothing compiles, neither pin carries anything. The input is not passed through as a fallback, so a repair that finds no resolvable edge at all leaves the branch downstream empty rather than unchanged.

UPCGExSearchAStar.name: A*
UPCGExSearchAStar.purpose: The one algorithm here that asks the heuristics where the goal is. Every algorithm here asks them what an edge costs; this one also asks, at each Vtx it reaches, what the remaining distance to the goal is worth, and ranks its frontier on the sum of the two. A stack that answers that second question well lets the search ignore most of the cluster. It is picked in the `Search Algorithm` slot on **Pathfinding : Edges** and **Pathfinding : Plot Edges**.
UPCGExSearchAStar.situation: A point-to-point route across a cluster where the heuristics have some sense of direction, and examining the whole cluster to find it would be wasted work.

mechanism.text: The search grows a frontier out of the seed, always taking the Vtx whose total looks cheapest. That total has two parts: the cost accumulated crossing edges to reach the Vtx, and the goal-distance answer for the Vtx itself, both supplied by the heuristics stack. A Vtx is reached again only when a cheaper way in is found, and once it has been taken off the frontier its route is settled. The route handed back is the chain of settled steps from the goal back to the seed, and it is a shortest route under the cost model when the goal-distance answer never exceeds the real remaining cost.

bEarlyExit.tooltip: Exit the search early once a valid path is found. Disabling explores all possible paths.
bEarlyExit.semantics: A performance switch, and only that. The goal's route is frozen the moment the goal comes off the frontier, and the loop either stops there or marks it settled and carries on exploring, which can no longer reach back and change it. The route is the same either way, so turning this off buys nothing except a longer search.
bEarlyExit.trap: Turning it off does not make a search find a better route under an unusual cost model. Nothing after the goal is settled can improve the answer.

hints.text: The goal-distance half of the answer comes from the same stack as the edge costs, so a stack with no opinion about where the goal is gives this algorithm a flat estimate and it explores as broadly as Dijkstra. **Heuristics : Attribute** on its own is the usual way to end up there; pairing it with a distance or azimuth heuristic is what restores the focus.

A route is a shortest route only while the goal-distance answer stays at or below the real remaining cost. Heuristic scores are normalised against the cluster and then scaled by `Weight Factor`, so a heavily weighted goal-distance heuristic overshoots, and the search settles for the first route it reaches rather than the cheapest. Lowering that heuristic's weight relative to the edge-cost ones is the fix.

UPCGExSearchBellmanFord.name: Bellman-Ford
UPCGExSearchBellmanFord.purpose: The algorithm for a cost model that can go below zero. The other three settle each Vtx once and trust that settling was final, which a negative cost breaks; this one keeps improving every Vtx until nothing improves any more, so a cheap detour discovered late still wins. Negative costs come from a `Weight Factor` set below zero, since a heuristic's own score is floored at zero. It is picked in the `Search Algorithm` slot on **Pathfinding : Edges** and **Pathfinding : Plot Edges**, and it is much the most expensive of the four.
UPCGExSearchBellmanFord.situation: A stack where one heuristic is weighted negatively to reward a feature rather than penalise it, and the routes the other algorithms return skip past the rewarded edges.

mechanism.text: There is no frontier. Every edge in the cluster is priced by the heuristics stack and offered as a cheaper way into the Vtx it leads to, and that runs over the whole cluster again and again, at most one time fewer than the cluster has Vtx, stopping as soon as a complete round improves nothing. The goal-distance question is never asked, so nothing about where the goal sits shapes the work or shortens it. What comes back is the cheapest route under the stack, or nothing at all when the goal was never reached or when the cycle check fired.

off_label.claim: Leave `Detect Negative Cycles` on and the node doubles as a check on the stack itself: a query that fails on a cluster where the same seed and goal succeed under Dijkstra says a negative weight has made some loop free to walk forever, which is a scoring mistake rather than a routing one.
off_label.grounded_in: The detection sweep in FPCGExSearchOperationBellmanFord::ResolveQuery returns false for the whole query, independently of whether the goal was reached.

bDetectNegativeCycles.tooltip: If enabled, the search will fail if a negative weight cycle is detected
bDetectNegativeCycles.semantics: The check is a full extra sweep of the cluster after the relaxation rounds finish, and it covers every Vtx the seed can reach rather than the route alone. A loop that is cheaper each time round therefore fails the query even when it sits nowhere near the seed and the goal, and the failure is silent: no path is emitted for that query and nothing is logged.
bDetectNegativeCycles.trap: A cluster's edges run both ways, so a single edge whose cost is negative in both directions is already a loop that pays to walk. One negative `Weight Factor` on a heuristic that scores an edge the same way round either way is enough to fail every query in that cluster.

bEarlyExit.tooltip: Exit the search early once a valid path is found. Disabling explores all possible paths.
bEarlyExit.semantics: Read by nothing on this algorithm. The relaxation rounds always run until a complete round improves nothing, whatever this is set to, and the goal being reached early does not stop them.

hints.text: Turning `Detect Negative Cycles` off does not make a negative loop safe, it only stops the query failing. The relaxation rounds still end after their fixed count, so what comes back is whatever the route looked like when they ran out, which is an arbitrary number of trips round the loop rather than a route anyone chose.

The work is the whole cluster's edges swept once per Vtx in the worst case, so cost scales with the size of the cluster rather than with the distance between seed and goal. A short route across a large cluster costs the same here as a long one.

UPCGExSearchBidirectional.name: Bidirectional
UPCGExSearchBidirectional.purpose: Two searches instead of one, started at either end and grown until they touch. Neither half asks the heuristics how far the goal still is; both just accumulate edge costs, so this is **Dijkstra** run from both ends at once, and the saving is that each half only has to reach halfway. It is picked in the `Search Algorithm` slot on **Pathfinding : Edges** and **Pathfinding : Plot Edges**.
UPCGExSearchBidirectional.situation: Long routes across a large cluster, where a single frontier grown from the seed would sweep most of the cluster before it arrived.

mechanism.text: One frontier grows out of the seed and another out of the goal, taking one Vtx each in turn, both ranked on accumulated edge cost alone. The backward half asks the heuristics with the seed and the goal exchanged, so a heuristic that has an opinion about direction leans it toward the seed just as the forward half leans toward the goal. A Vtx settled by both halves is a candidate meeting point, and the cheapest total across all of them decides the route, which is then assembled from the two chains that met there. With costs at or above zero the result is a cheapest route under the stack, the same one **Dijkstra** would return.

bEarlyExit.tooltip: Exit the search early once a valid path is found. Disabling explores all possible paths.
bEarlyExit.semantics: Read by nothing on this algorithm. Both frontiers are drained whatever this is set to; what stops the work early is the cheapest meeting found so far, which lets the two halves skip expanding anything that could no longer beat it.

hints.text: The two halves have to agree on what an edge costs for the assembled route to be the cheapest one. A heuristic that prices an edge by which way it is crossed, or by where the seed and the goal are, gives two different answers for the same edge, so **Heuristics : Azimuth** and **Heuristics : Inertia** in particular make the two halves disagree and the meeting point lands somewhere neither would have chosen alone. Pick **Dijkstra** or **A\*** when the stack has a sense of direction.

Both halves carry their own copy of everything a search needs, so a query here costs about twice the working memory of the other three on the same cluster. That is the trade the halved depth is bought with.

UPCGExSearchDijkstra.name: Dijkstra
UPCGExSearchDijkstra.purpose: Spends more of the cluster to remove the one thing that can bend A* off course. It asks the heuristics what every edge costs, exactly as the other three do, and it never asks them how far the goal still is, so nothing pulls the frontier toward the destination and the route it returns is the cheapest one under the stack as written. Reach for it when a carefully weighted stack is producing routes that look like they are cutting corners. It is picked in the `Search Algorithm` slot on **Pathfinding : Edges** and **Pathfinding : Plot Edges**.
UPCGExSearchDijkstra.situation: A cost model whose weights are the point of the setup, where a route that merely arrives is worth less than the route those weights actually describe.

mechanism.text: The frontier grows out of the seed in order of accumulated cost, always taking the cheapest Vtx reached so far. Each edge leaving it is priced by the heuristics stack and added to the running total, and a Vtx keeps the cheapest way in that has been found for it. Once a Vtx comes off the frontier its route is settled and no later step revisits it. Because the frontier is ordered by real cost rather than by cost plus a guess, the first settle of any Vtx is its cheapest route, and the goal's route is a shortest route under the stack.

off_label.claim: Turn `Early Exit` off and the search settles every Vtx that the seed can reach at all, which makes an unreachable goal cost as much as the most distant reachable one. On a cluster with several components, keeping it on is what stops a failing query from sweeping its whole island first.
off_label.grounded_in: The bEarlyExit test in FPCGExSearchOperationDijkstra::ResolveQuery is the only break out of the dequeue loop; with it off the loop runs until the scored queue drains.

bEarlyExit.tooltip: Exit the search early once a valid path is found. Disabling explores all possible paths.
bEarlyExit.semantics: A performance switch, and only that. The goal's route is frozen the moment the goal comes off the frontier, and the loop either stops there or marks it settled and keeps exploring, which can no longer reach back and change it. The route is the same either way.
bEarlyExit.trap: Turning it off does not buy a better route. Nothing after the goal is settled can improve the answer.

hints.text: Settling a Vtx once is what makes this the cheapest route, and it holds only while edge costs stay at or above zero. A heuristic's own score is floored at zero, so the way to break that is a negative `Weight Factor`, which puts negative costs into the stack and lets a longer detour come out cheaper than the settled route. **Bellman-Ford** is the algorithm that handles those.

UPCGExSegmentCrossFilterProviderSettings.name: Filter : Segment Cross
UPCGExSegmentCrossFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Judges each element by the segment it starts, and asks whether that segment crosses any of the shapes on the Targets pin. Point paths, splines and polygons are all accepted there and all reduced to runs of segments before the test, so the comparison is always segment against segment. The verdict lands on the point the segment starts from, which is what makes this the filter to reach for when a crossing has to become a cut, a flag or a split at the right point.
UPCGExSegmentCrossFilterProviderSettings.situation: A run of points has to be marked wherever the line between two of them passes through a boundary.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this once per element. The element and one neighbour give a segment, and that segment is compared against the segments of every shape on the Targets pin until one comes within Tolerance of it in space; the first match settles the verdict, and nothing counts how many. Direction picks the neighbour: To Next takes the point ahead, To Prev the one behind. Closure is read from the tested data, so a closed path wraps and every point starts a segment, while an open one leaves the point at the far end starting none, and that point answers as a segment that crossed nothing would.

off_label.claim: Feed one path into both the consumer and the Targets pin, turn Ignore Self off, and the filter becomes a self-crossing test: each segment is compared against the rest of its own path, with the vertex two neighbouring segments share discounted by the default strictness.
off_label.grounded_in: the bIgnoreSelf guard in FHandler::FindClosestIntersection, which skips only the target whose data matches the tested data, together with the Strict default rejecting a contact that lands on either segment endpoint in FSegment::FindIntersection

inputs.label: Targets
inputs.note: The shapes to test against. Point paths, splines and polygons are all accepted, and every dataset on the pin is pooled into one search. A point dataset holding fewer than two points is dropped with a warning.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match rules deciding which target shapes each tested dataset is allowed to see. The pin is always present, sitting among the advanced pins until Data Matching is switched on.
inputs.condition: when Data Matching Mode is All or Any

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node produces. It carries the point-filter type, so every filter pin accepts it, Vtx and Edge pins included.

hints.text: The comparison is three-dimensional. Two segments that appear to meet when the graph is viewed from above are a crossing here only if they come within Tolerance of each other in space, so a boundary drawn at ground level and a path running above it register nothing.

Building the segment takes a real neighbour, so pins that evaluate a point in isolation drop this filter with a warning rather than running it. The Stop Conditions pin on Tensors : Extrude and Tensors Transform is where that turns up.

UPCGExSegmentLengthFilterProviderSetting.name: Filter : Segment Length
UPCGExSegmentLengthFilterProviderSetting.purpose: Measures the straight-line distance from each element to another element of the same dataset, picked by index, and compares it against a threshold. Out of the box that other element is the next one along, so the measurement is the segment leaving each element and the filter reads as a segment-length test on a path. The index is open, though: an offset of -1 measures the segment arriving instead, and Pick mode measures everything to one named element. Only locations enter the measurement, so element bounds and orientation change nothing.
UPCGExSegmentLengthFilterProviderSetting.situation: An ordered point set where spacing decides what survives, or where a gap has to be found.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this filter once per element: a second index is resolved, the distance between the two locations is measured, and one comparison against the threshold is the verdict. Index Mode decides how the index value is read, as an offset from the element's own position or as a position named outright, and Index Safety then folds anything landing outside the dataset back inside. The second index never leaves the dataset the element belongs to, so a consumer holding several datasets runs a separate copy over each, each with its own ends. The verdict lands on the element the measurement starts from, never on the segment, which is what decides who survives when a segment is judged too short.

off_label.claim: Set Index Safety to Ignore, Invalid Point Fallback to Pass, and the comparison to `<` against a threshold of 0. Every element that resolves a partner then fails, and the only survivors are those whose index landed outside the dataset, which on an open path is the end the offset points away from. Closed data has the tile override applied instead and produces no survivors at all, so the same filter reports whether the data is closed.
off_label.grounded_in: FSegmentLengthFilter::Test returning the Invalid Point Fallback only when SanitizeIndex yields -1, which only Index Safety of Ignore ever produces, and Init forcing Tile safety on data carrying `@Data.IsClosed` while Tile on closed loops is set

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter passport, so every filter pin accepts it, Vtx Filters and Edge Filters included.

hints.text: **Uber Branch** and **Break** need a filter that can judge a whole dataset, and this one never can, whatever its operands are set to. They log a warning, skip it and carry on, so a stack holding only this filter ends up empty, and an empty stack passes every dataset. A **Filter Group** holding it inherits the refusal. **Uber Filter (Data)** refuses nothing: it falls back to testing elements and counting passes.

The node subtitle reads back the whole test, `Dist to 1 > 100.0` on a fresh node. It shows the index value alone, so the same subtitle means the next element along under Offset and element number one under Pick.

UPCGExSelectorAntiRepeatFactoryProviderS.name: Selector Modifier : Anti-Repeat
UPCGExSelectorAntiRepeatFactoryProviderS.purpose: Breaks visible repetition in a sequence of picks without changing what the collection offers. It wraps another selector and asks it again, with a different seed, whenever the answer matches one of the last few picks made nearby, so the entries and their weights stay exactly as authored and only the order of the answers moves. With nothing wired into its Selector pin it re-rolls a plain weighted pick, which makes it a usable node on its own. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh, or by another modifier's Selector pin.
UPCGExSelectorAntiRepeatFactoryProviderS.situation: Points picked in order along a path or a row, where two neighbours landing on the same entry is what reads as wrong.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per point and keeps the entry it returns. The answer comes from the selector wired into the Selector pin, or from a plain weighted roll when nothing is wired; when that answer is already in the recent-pick window, the same selector is asked again with a different seed, until it returns something the window does not hold or the attempts run out. Whatever comes back last is recorded, repeat or not, so a repeat the node was forced to accept ages out of the window like any other pick. The window covers one run of points at a time, a run being a contiguous stretch of the incoming points the consumer processes as a unit, and it is kept separately per collection and per category. It is emptied at every run boundary, so the guarantee holds along a run and never across two.

off_label.claim: Wrapped around Selector : Best Fit, a re-roll stays inside the scored pool, because a different seed only moves the roll among the entries that already qualified. That makes it a spread control over a fit: the substitute a point gets is still a size match, and Top K decides how much room there is to move. At Top K 1 the pool is one entry and the re-rolls change nothing.
off_label.grounded_in: The retry loop calling ChildOp->Pick with PCGExRandomHelpers::GetSeed(Seed, Attempt), against FPCGExEntryBestFitTopKPickerOp::Pick, whose pool is built from scores alone and whose seed drives only the final weighted roll

inputs.label: Selector
inputs.note: The selector to re-roll. Leaving it empty is a supported configuration: the node then re-rolls a plain weighted pick. Connecting several is not; the lowest Priority wins, the rest are ignored, and the node warns and points at Selector Modifier : Cascade.

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory this node produces, carrying the wrapped selector inside it. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into the Selector pin of another modifier; the consumer runs it once per point to decide that point's entry.

fields.name: HistoryLength
fields.tooltip: Number of most-recent picks that are excluded from re-picking.

fields.name: MaxAttempts
fields.tooltip: Max re-rolls (with salted seeds) before accepting a repeat anyway. Guards categories smaller than the history.

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories).
BaseConfig.semantics: Category scoping decides which pool the wrapped selector draws from, and with it how much room the window has: a window of two over a category of three is close to a rotation, the same window over thirty entries is a light touch. Each category also carries its own window inside a run, so a per-point category attribute splits one run into as many independent windows as it resolves names.

hints.text: Where the runs fall is not something the graph decides. A dataset under the project's Small Points Size (1024 points by default) is processed as a single run, so the window spans it end to end. Above that, the consumer splits the dataset into roughly four runs per CPU core, and the window empties at every boundary: a repeat can surface there, and the same graph on a machine with a different core count splits in different places and produces different picks.

Three selectors ignore the seed by construction: Selector : Interleaved reads point order, Selector : Noise Field reads world position, Selector : Closest Match is a pure nearest-value match. Asking one of them again with a different seed returns the same entry, so wrapping one spends the whole attempt budget and changes nothing.

The window holds the top-level entry. A pick landing on a sub-collection entry then descends by a plain weighted roll on the child's own weights, and that roll is outside the history, so two neighbours can take different sub-collection entries and still spawn the same asset.
The node's title in the graph carries the window size in brackets, reading Modify : Anti-Repeat (2) for a History Length of 2.

UPCGExSelectorBestFitFactoryProviderSett.name: Selector : Best Fit
UPCGExSelectorBestFitFactoryProviderSett.purpose: Answers the per-point pick by size. Every entry in the scoped category is scored against the point's own bounds, and the pick is rolled among the closest-scoring ones. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh. Three metrics decide what closeness means, absolute volume, per-axis extents, or proportions with size discounted, and a pool strategy decides how much variety survives the scoring.
UPCGExSelectorBestFitFactoryProviderSett.situation: Points whose bounds were sized upstream, and a collection whose entries span a range of sizes that should line up with them.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per point and records the entry it returns, so the point count stays the consumer's business and the factory only decides which entry. Scoring state, each entry's staged extent with its volume and its weight, is built once per collection and category and reused for every point, so the per-point cost is one pass over the candidates plus a roll. When Selector Modifier : Quota wraps it, entries the quota has exhausted are dropped before scoring, so the best score is measured over what is still available rather than over the whole category.

off_label.claim: Top K spans the whole range from strict to free. At 1 the pool collapses to the best score and the roll has nothing left to choose; at or above the number of candidates K clamps to that count, the pool becomes the entire category, and scoring stops affecting the outcome at all.
off_label.grounded_in: FMath::Clamp(FMath::RoundToInt(PoolSizeGetter->Read(PointIndex)), 1, N) and the cutoff-based pool build in FPCGExEntryBestFitTopKPickerOp::Pick

off_label.claim: Scoring reads the entry's altered staging bounds, the box an entry bounds modifier derives, while the asset itself keeps its original bounds. Padding or scaling an entry's bounds retargets which points that entry wins without changing anything that reaches the scene.
off_label.grounded_in: Entry->Staging.AlteredBounds in UPCGExSelectorBestFitFactoryData::BuildSharedData, and FPCGExStagingBoundsModifier::ComputeAlteredBounds, whose contract leaves the bounds applied to the mesh untouched

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory this node produces. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into the Selector pin of a selector modifier; the consumer runs it once per point to decide that point's entry.

fields.name: Metric
fields.tooltip: How entry extents score against the point's extent.

fields.name: AxisMask
fields.tooltip: Which axes contribute to the score. Ignored by ClosestVolume.

fields.name: AxisAggregation
fields.tooltip: How per-axis scores combine when more than one axis is selected.

fields.name: VolumeInfluence
fields.tooltip: For ClosestAspectRatio: blends volume distance into the aspect score. 0 = pure aspect.

fields.name: bApplyPointScale
fields.tooltip: If true, multiply the point's local extents by its transform scale before comparing.

fields.name: PoolStrategy
fields.tooltip: Pool selection strategy. TopK uses a fixed-size pool; Tolerance pools all entries within a ratio of the best score.

fields.name: TopK
fields.tooltip: Size of the top-K pool (rounded, clamped to [1, N]). Attribute-driven for per-point pool sizing.

fields.name: Tolerance
fields.tooltip: Tolerance ratio. Pool = entries with score ≤ best * (1 + Tolerance). 0 = exact-tie only.

Config.semantics: Scoring compares the point's own bounds against the entry's staged bounds, before any fitting the spawn stage applies, so the entry that wins is the one whose authored size is closest, not the one that will read best after Scale to Fit. Every metric is lower-is-better and the pool is then a weighted roll, so entry weights still decide inside the pool and a heavy entry can take the pick from a closer-scoring light one. An Axis Mask with nothing enabled scores every entry identically, which turns the pick into a plain weighted roll.
Config.trap: Tolerance is a ratio of the best score, not an absolute distance. When some entry fits a point almost exactly the best score approaches zero and the window closes with it, so the pool holds only entries tied at that score whatever the tolerance is set to.

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories).
BaseConfig.semantics: Category scoping decides the candidate list before any scoring runs, so best always means best within the category, never within the collection. Scoring state is cached per collection and category, so a per-point category attribute builds one candidate list for each distinct name it resolves to.

hints.text: A flat entry never gets picked. Candidacy is decided by the volume of the entry's staged extent box, so a plane, a decal, or any asset with one near-zero axis leaves the candidate list silently while the rest of the category carries on. A category holding nothing but those picks nothing at all, and the consumer reports it as a missing input naming the entries' staging bounds.
The node's title in the graph carries the metric as an extra line, reading Select : Fit Volume, Select : Fit Per-Axis, or Select : Fit Aspect.
A selector shapes only the first pick. A pick landing on a sub-collection entry size-matches the subtree's aggregate bounds, and the leaf inside it is then a plain weighted roll.

UPCGExSelectorCascadeFactoryProviderSett.name: Selector Modifier : Cascade
UPCGExSelectorCascadeFactoryProviderSett.purpose: Chains selectors so a point one of them cannot answer falls through to the next. Children are tried in Priority order, lowest first, and the first child returning a pick ends the walk for that point. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh, or by another modifier, and the whole chain runs under this node's Base Config rather than the children's. A chain ends at a selector that never declines, which in practice is Selector : Classic in weighted-random mode.
UPCGExSelectorCascadeFactoryProviderSett.situation: A picking rule that answers for most of a dataset and leaves a remainder it has no entry for, where that remainder still needs one.

mechanism.text: The consumer asks the chain once per point, and the chain asks its children in Priority order, stopping at the first one that returns a pick. Priority is read from each child node and sorted ascending, so the order is authored on the children rather than here, and children sharing a Priority are ordered by nothing the node exposes. Each child's random rolls are salted by its position in that order, so two children that would roll the same entry standalone disagree on the same point, while the first position keeps the unsalted roll, which makes a one-child cascade pick-identical to that child wired straight into the consumer. A point no child answers leaves the chain without a pick and reaches the consumer as any unpicked point does.

off_label.claim: A child that cannot bind is dropped instead of failing the chain, so a cascade doubles as a compatibility guard: pair a selector that needs a collection property with a plain weighted-random child, and collections that lack the property still stage, on the fallback.
off_label.grounded_in: the PrepareForData failure branch in FPCGExEntryCascadePickerOp, which logs the skipped child and continues, erroring only once no child binds

off_label.claim: The chain reads only this node's Base Config, so wrapping a single child is how one selector node gets two different category scopes or seeds without being duplicated: two cascades, one child each, both wired to the same selector.
off_label.grounded_in: FSelectorHelper::Init reading BaseConfig off the outermost factory only, plus the unsalted seed at child position 0 in FPCGExEntryCascadePickerOp::Pick

inputs.label: Selectors
inputs.note: The children to try, in Priority order, lowest first. Anything that outputs on a Selector pin qualifies, modifiers included, so chains nest.

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The chain this node produces. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into another modifier; the consumer walks the whole chain once per point.

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories). Children's BaseConfigs are ignored.
BaseConfig.semantics: The consumer reads the Base Config of the factory wired into its own Selector pin and no other, which is why the children's are inert rather than merged or overridden. The same rule applies upward: a cascade nested inside another modifier hands the decision to that one, so in a stack only the outermost node's seed, categories and sub-distribution are ever read. Category scoping resolves before any child runs, so every child in the chain sees the same slice of the collection and none of them can widen or narrow it.
BaseConfig.trap: A child authored and tested on its own changes behaviour the moment it is wired here, because its Seed, Categories and Sub Distribution stop being read. Nothing warns; the picks differ.

Priority.tooltip: Selector priority. Drives ordering when multiple selectors are consumed by a single pin (e.g. Selector Modifier : Cascade tries the lowest priority first). Forwarded to the factory data; GetInputFactories sorts ascending.
Priority.semantics: This is the cascade's own Priority, which decides where it sits when the cascade is itself wired as a child of another modifier. It takes no part in ordering this node's children, whose order comes from the Priority set on each of their own nodes.

hints.text: Children sharing a Priority value are ordered by nothing the node exposes, and every selector starts at Priority 0, so a chain whose children were left at the default carries no authored order at all. Give each child a distinct Priority whenever which one gets first refusal matters. The setting sits under each child node's advanced properties.

Selector : Best Fit and Selector : Closest Match do not decline point by point. Either one answers for every point as soon as its category holds anything it can use, so a chain reading Best Fit then Classic never reaches the Classic child. Their fall-through happens once, at initialization, when the category holds nothing scorable and the child leaves the chain entirely. Per-point fall-through comes from the selectors that gate on the point's own values: Range-Based when no range contains them, Curve-Remapped Weight when every curve is at or below zero at that point's driver, Density-Weighted set to skip out-of-range points, Quota set to skip on exhaustion, and Classic in Indexed mode with Index Safety on Ignore and an index out of bounds.

A Selector Modifier : Quota wired as a child of a cascade keeps its counts exact, but which points receive the capped entries stops being decided by point order and starts depending on thread scheduling, so the same graph can hand back different results run to run. Wrap the cascade in the quota instead of the other way around, and the deterministic assignment holds.

A child that cannot bind to the data, a missing attribute or a category with nothing it can use, is dropped from the chain rather than failing it. The warning names the child by its position in Priority order rather than by node, and it surfaces on the consuming node instead of here, next to whatever the child itself logged. When no child binds, that same node errors and picks nothing.

UPCGExSelectorClassicFactoryProviderSett.name: Selector : Classic
UPCGExSelectorClassicFactoryProviderSett.purpose: Answers the per-point pick with the plain strategies: a roll that follows the entries' authored weights, a roll that ignores them, or a number read per point and used as a position in the entry list. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh. It is also the selector the deprecated Legacy mode builds for itself out of its inline settings, so an old graph migrates by wiring this node configured the same way and switching the mode to External.
UPCGExSelectorClassicFactoryProviderSett.situation: A collection whose authored weights already say how often each entry should appear, or a graph carrying a per-point number that names the entry outright.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per point and records the entry it returns, so the point count stays the consumer's business. Mode is the only thing that decides how the answer is reached, and all three modes answer from the same candidate list: the entries of the scoped category, valid ones only, in the collection's own order. Weighted Random and Random consume the point's seed, Index consumes an attribute and no seed at all, and every mode returns exactly one entry or nothing.

off_label.claim: Random is a way to audition a collection with its weights flattened. The roll ignores the weight table entirely, so an entry authored at 1 shows up as often as one authored at 100, and the collection asset is never touched.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExEntryRandomPickerOp::Pick calling FCategory::GetPickRandom, a uniform RandRange over the candidate count, against FPCGExEntryWeightedRandomPickerOp::Pick calling GetPickRandomWeighted

off_label.claim: The weight-ordered Pick Modes turn Index into a rank picker. Feeding a normalized attribute with Remap Index To Collection Size on selects by where an entry sits in the weight ordering, so a point can ask for the heaviest or the lightest entry without knowing what the collection holds.
off_label.grounded_in: FCategory::GetPickWeightAscending and GetPickWeightDescending addressing the weight-sorted Order array, reached through Target->GetPick(Sanitized, IndexConfig.PickMode)

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory this node produces. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into the Selector pin of a selector modifier; the consumer runs it once per point to decide that point's entry.

fields.name: Mode
fields.tooltip: Distribution strategy.

fields.name: IndexConfig
fields.tooltip: Index picking configuration. Only used when Mode is Index.

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories).

hints.text: The node's title in the graph carries the mode as an extra line, reading Select : Weighted Random, Select : Random, or Select : Indexed on followed by the attribute the index is read from.

UPCGExSelectorClosestMatchFactoryProvide.name: Selector : Closest Match
UPCGExSelectorClosestMatchFactoryProvide.purpose: Answers the per-point pick by matching values. Each axis pairs a property declared on the collection with an attribute on the point, and the entry whose values sit closest to the point's own wins outright: no pool, no roll, no seed. Axes stack and carry their own weights, so one pick can answer to a cost, a footprint and a biome name at once. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh.
UPCGExSelectorClosestMatchFactoryProvide.situation: Points already carrying the values that should decide their asset, and a collection whose entries declare properties of the same name.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per point and records the entry it returns, so the point count stays the consumer's business and the factory only decides which entry. Every entry in the scoped category is scored: each axis contributes the distance between the point's attribute value and the entry's property value, multiplied by that axis's weight, and the per-axis distances sum into one number per entry. The lowest total wins, and the seed takes no part, so the same values always return the same entry. Candidacy is settled before any scoring, and an entry that cannot produce a value for every configured axis is never scored. When Selector Modifier : Quota wraps it, the nearest entry that still has capacity wins instead.

off_label.claim: An axis at Weight 0 stops contributing to the score and keeps contributing to candidacy, which makes it a presence gate: the pick is restricted to entries that declare the named property, decided entirely by the remaining axes. The point attribute still has to be readable, since an axis that cannot read it drops out and takes the gate with it for that dataset.
off_label.grounded_in: Weight multiplies the accumulated distance in TPCGExClosestMatchAxisEvaluator::Accumulate, while the ValidEntryIndices build in UPCGExSelectorClosestMatchFactoryData::BuildSharedData ignores Weight entirely

off_label.claim: A name, string or asset-path axis scores zero on a match and its full weight on a mismatch, so weighting it above the largest total any numeric axis can reach turns it into a hard partition: the name decides which entries stay eligible, and the numeric axes choose among them.
off_label.grounded_in: FTypeOps MatchScore returns 0.0 or 1.0 for FName, FString, FSoftObjectPath and FSoftClassPath, routed through PCGExClosestMatch::Distance and scaled by the axis weight

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory this node produces. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into the Selector pin of a selector modifier; the consumer runs it once per point to decide that point's entry.

fields.name: Axes
fields.tooltip: One or more axes summed (with weights) into the per-entry distance score.

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories).
BaseConfig.semantics: Category scoping decides the candidate list before anything is compared, so closest always means closest within the category, never within the collection. Entry-side values, and the range Normalize measures them against, are captured per collection and category, so a per-point category attribute gives each category its own scale.

hints.text: Ties go to the entry authored earliest in the category, every time, because nothing rolls to break them. Distances over floats rarely tie, but equality axes tie constantly and coarse integer values tie often, so a configuration whose axes cannot separate two entries collapses onto one of them across the whole dataset.

Normalize is type-gated. It remaps float, double, vector and rotator axes; integer, boolean, quaternion, name, string and asset-path axes use raw distance whatever the toggle reads. Left enabled on one of those, it looks like it is balancing units while nothing is being remapped. It also steps aside when either side's observed values collapse onto a single value, falling back to raw distance for that axis; on vectors and rotators the collapse is per component, so a flat component contributes nothing while the others still remap.
