Normalize maps each side by the range it actually observes, and the point side's range comes from the dataset being staged. Splitting one point set in two and staging the halves separately renormalizes each half against its own spread, so identical points can come out holding different entries.

The two failure surfaces read differently. A property name the collection does not declare, or one typed as a transform, disables that axis quietly at the collection side. An attribute the dataset cannot supply warns and names the axis by its position in the list. When nothing survives at all, the consumer reports a missing input pointing at the axis property names and types.

UPCGExSelectorCurveRemappedFactoryProvid.name: Selector : Curve-Remapped Weight
UPCGExSelectorCurveRemappedFactoryProvid.purpose: Answers the per-point pick with a gradient. Each entry carries its own float curve as a collection property, the curve is evaluated at a value read from the point, and the height it returns is that entry's likelihood there. A curve at or below zero drops the entry, so the same curves that shape the odds also declare the band each entry is eligible in. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh.
UPCGExSelectorCurveRemappedFactoryProvid.situation: Points carrying one measured value, and a collection whose entries should take over from one another across that value's range.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per point and records the entry it returns. Candidates are the entries of the scoped category that resolve the named Float Curve property, and an entry resolving none never enters the pool whatever its weight. For a point, one driver value is read, every candidate's own curve is evaluated at it, and those heights are the weights of a single weighted roll, so the collection redistributes itself continuously as the driver moves. A height at or below zero removes its entry from the roll instead of making it unlikely, which is what lets one authored curve carry both the weighting and the eligibility band. When no candidate has a positive height at that value, the point gets no pick.

off_label.claim: Set Time Source to a constant and the curve family becomes a global mix control: every point reads the same driver, so one value re-weights the whole dataset at once and stepping it walks the collection through the transitions the curves describe.
off_label.grounded_in: TimeGetter->IsConstant() branch in FPCGExEntryCurveRemappedPickerOp::OnInitForData, where the effective-weight table is point-invariant and the same roll table serves every point

off_label.claim: With Multiply By Entry Weight off and curves authored as flat plateaus, the response carries no magnitude, and the pick becomes a uniform roll among whichever entries are eligible at that driver value: a per-entry eligibility mask with no weighting in it.
off_label.grounded_in: EffectiveWeight returning max(0, Curve(t)) unmultiplied, fed to RollWeightedStreaming, which is a uniform roll when every surviving weight is equal

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory this node produces. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into the Selector pin of a selector modifier; the consumer runs it once per point to decide that point's entry.

fields.name: CurvePropertyName
fields.tooltip: Name of the collection property (Float Curve type) supplying each entry's response curve.

fields.name: TimeSource
fields.tooltip: Per-point time value the curves are sampled at. Out-of-range values follow the curve's own extrapolation (clamped for LUT mode).

fields.name: bMultiplyByEntryWeight
fields.tooltip: If enabled, the curve response is multiplied by the entry's authored Weight; otherwise the curve alone drives probability.

fields.name: CurveLookup
fields.tooltip: Curve evaluation strategy (direct rich-curve eval vs baked lookup table).

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories).
BaseConfig.semantics: Category scoping settles the candidate list before any curve is read, so an entry outside the scoped category never contributes even when it carries the curve. The curve state is built per collection and category, and so is the missing-curve failure: a category where nobody authored one fails while the rest of the collection keeps working.

hints.text: An entry that resolves no curve under this name leaves the pool silently while the rest of the category carries on. When nothing in the category resolves one, which is what both a mistyped name and an empty name look like, the pool is empty and the consumer reports it as a missing input naming the property.

A driver value where every curve sits at or below zero produces no pick at all. Staging : Distribute prunes points with no pick by default, so a gap between the authored bands shows up as missing points downstream and not as an error.
A selector shapes only the first pick. A pick landing on a sub-collection entry uses that entry's own curve, and the leaf inside it is then a plain weighted roll.
The node's title in the graph carries the property name as an extra line, reading Select : Curve followed by the name, or Select : Curve-Remapped while the name is empty.

UPCGExSelectorDensityWeightedFactoryProv.name: Selector : Density-Weighted
UPCGExSelectorDensityWeightedFactoryProv.purpose: Answers the per-point pick with a scalar the point already carries. One value per point bends the weighted roll between two poles, a flat table where every entry is equally likely and the collection's own authored weights, and Weight Modulation can push past the authored weights into a wider spread. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh. The driver is the point's Density property out of the box and can be pointed at any attribute or property that reads as a double, or set to a constant.
UPCGExSelectorDensityWeightedFactoryProv.situation: A collection whose weighting should be felt strongly in some places and barely at all in others, with a per-point scalar already saying where.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per point and records the entry it returns, so the factory only decides which entry. Per point it reads one density value and builds the odds over the entries of the scoped category, then rolls once. Both modes are anchored on the same two tables, the collection's authored weights and a flat one where every entry is equally likely; density and Density Influence decide where the point's table sits against those two. The roll is a fixed fraction of that table for a given point and seed, so a density change moves a point only when a band boundary crosses its fraction, and re-driving density re-rolls a share of the points rather than all of them. When Selector Modifier : Quota wraps it, exhausted entries leave the table before the roll and the odds are spread over what is still available.

off_label.claim: Set Density Source to a constant and the node stops being per-point: it becomes a global reshaper of the collection's own weight spread, leaving the collection asset untouched. In Weight Modulation at full influence the constant sweeps from a flat roll at 0, through the authored weights at 0.5, to a widened spread at 1; in Randomness Modulation it sweeps the flat-to-authored half of that range.
off_label.grounded_in: the DensityGetter->IsConstant() branch in OnInitForData, which builds one cumulative table for the whole data, over the same Exponent and EffectiveDensity math as the per-point path

off_label.claim: With Out Of Range Policy on Skip Point, a driver that deliberately leaves the 0 to 1 range doubles as a point mask: the out-of-range points come back with no pick, and Staging : Distribute prunes them by default.
off_label.grounded_in: the early return of -1 under EPCGExDensityOutOfRangePolicy::SkipPoint in Pick and PickFiltered, which the consumer reads as an unresolved point

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory this node produces. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into the Selector pin of a selector modifier; the consumer runs it once per point to decide that point's entry.

fields.name: Mode
fields.tooltip: Algorithm for how density influences the pick.

fields.name: DensitySource
fields.tooltip: Per-point density source (attribute or constant). Defaults to the point's $Density property.

fields.name: DensityInfluence
fields.tooltip: Blend factor (0..1) between plain weighted random (0) and full density-driven pick (1).

fields.name: OutOfRangePolicy
fields.tooltip: Behavior when density falls outside the expected [0, 1] range.

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories).

hints.text: The node's title in the graph carries the mode as an extra line, reading Select : Weight Mod or Select : Randomness Mod.

Density shapes only the entry pick. The material-variant sub-pick inside a mesh entry keeps rolling on Sub Distribution from the shared config, and a pick that lands on a sub-collection entry resolves its leaf by plain weighted random on the child's own weights.

UPCGExSelectorFactoryProviderSettings.name: Selector Definition
UPCGExSelectorFactoryProviderSettings.purpose: The abstract base every Selector and Selector Modifier inherits. It never appears in the palette, and this page carries what all of them share: the Base Config block holding Sub Distribution, category scoping and the seed, plus the Priority value that orders selectors when several reach one pin. Each selector page describes what its own controls do with those inputs; what the shared settings mean is stated here and holds across the family.
UPCGExSelectorFactoryProviderSettings.situation: Reading any selector page and needing to know what its Sub Distribution, Category, Seed or Priority settings do, since those are the same on every one of them.

mechanism.text: A selector node produces one factory on its Selector pin, and the consumer runs that factory once per point to decide which entry the point gets. The consumer reads the Base Config of the factory wired into its own pin and no other, so in a stack of modifiers only the outermost node's settings are ever read. Categories resolve first: with Use Categories on, the candidate list is the scoped category's entries and the pick happens inside it, never across the collection. The pick then rolls from a per-point seed that starts as the point's own Seed and grows only by what Seed Components enables. Sub Distribution is a second pick made after the entry is settled, choosing a material variant inside mesh entries and doing nothing on the other collection types.

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory the node produces. Every selector and modifier outputs on this pin, and every consumer reads it: Staging : Distribute, Staging : Spline Mesh, and the Selector pins on the modifiers themselves, which is how selector stacks nest.

Priority.tooltip: Selector priority. Drives ordering when multiple selectors are consumed by a single pin (e.g. Selector Modifier : Cascade tries the lowest priority first). Forwarded to the factory data; GetInputFactories sorts ascending.
Priority.semantics: Priority is read only when more than one selector reaches a single pin, and factories arriving on a pin are sorted by it ascending, lowest first. Selector Modifier : Cascade orders its children that way; Selector Modifier : Anti-Repeat and Selector Modifier : Quota keep the lowest and warn that the rest are dropped; Staging : Distribute errors outright when it receives more than one. Every selector ships at 0, so a stack whose parts were left alone carries no authored order at all. The setting sits under the node's advanced properties.

hints.text: Seed Components treats Settings and Component as one switch. Enabling either one folds both the node's own Seed and the PCG component's seed into the roll, so a graph that meant to vary picks per component also re-rolls them whenever the node's Seed changes. Local is the only component that acts alone, and it is what makes Local Seed reach the roll.

Some selectors do not read the per-point seed for their entry pick at all: Selector : Interleaved reads point order, Selector : Noise Field reads world position, and Selector : Closest Match is a pure nearest-value match. On those the seed still drives what follows the pick, descent into a sub-collection and the material-variant sub-pick. Selector : Interleaved and Selector Modifier : Quota also read Local Seed unconditionally as a phase offset on their sequences, which their own pages cover.

A blank category key is a real value. It routes to the uncategorized entries and never widens to the whole collection, so points left without a category attribute value do not quietly receive categorized entries. Missing Category Behavior takes over only when the key names a category the collection does not have, or when the key is blank and the collection has no uncategorized entries.

UPCGExSelectorInterleavedFactoryProvider.name: Selector : Interleaved
UPCGExSelectorInterleavedFactoryProvider.purpose: Answers the per-point pick from a position in a sequence, with no roll involved. Each point supplies an ordinal, the point index by default, which maps to a position in the unit range and lands inside one entry's weight band. Consecutive ordinals land far apart, so the authored weight proportions hold while identical picks stay spread along point order. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh, and redirecting the ordinal to any scalar attribute moves the pattern onto whatever that attribute orders.
UPCGExSelectorInterleavedFactoryProvider.situation: An ordered run of points where the entry proportions have to hold and repeats must not bunch together.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per point and records the entry it returns, so the point count stays the consumer's business and the factory only decides which entry. The pick is a pure function of the point's ordinal: the same ordinal gives the same entry on every point, every dataset and every execution, with no per-point randomness in it. Entries occupy contiguous bands across the unit range, laid out in the order the category holds them, and consecutive ordinals land at maximally separated positions in that range. Over any stretch of consecutive ordinals the entry mix converges on the band widths, which is where the weight proportions come from. A heavy entry still lands on adjacent points in proportion to its share; what the sequence removes is the long run of one entry that independent rolls produce.

off_label.claim: Two points sharing an ordinal always get the same entry, and nothing else feeds the pick. An ordinal carrying group identity, a partition index or a cluster id, hands every member of that group the same entry with no lookup table anywhere.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExEntryInterleavedPickerOp::Pick reads only OrdinalGetter->Read(PointIndex) into Frac((Ordinal + 0.5) * GoldenRatioConjugate + EffectivePhase); the Seed parameter is never read

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory this node produces. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into the Selector pin of a selector modifier; the consumer runs it once per point to decide that point's entry.

fields.name: OrdinalSource
fields.tooltip: Per-point ordinal driving the low-discrepancy sequence. Defaults to the point index, which yields the classic golden-ratio interleave along point order. Any scalar attribute works -- distinct ordinals map to well-spread sequence positions.

fields.name: Phase
fields.tooltip: Constant phase offset added to the sequence, in [0, 1]. Rotates which entries the sequence starts on.

fields.name: bUseWeights
fields.tooltip: When enabled, entries occupy sequence bands proportional to their Weight; otherwise all entries get equal bands.

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories).

hints.text: The node's title in the graph follows this toggle, reading Select : Interleaved Weighted or Select : Interleaved Uniform.

A selector shapes only the first pick. A pick landing on a sub-collection entry descends by plain weighted roll on the child's own weights, and that roll does read the per-point seed, so which leaf inside a sub-collection a point ends on is decided by its seed and not by its ordinal.

Under Selector Modifier : Quota, a band whose entry is exhausted falls to the nearest still-available entry by position in the collection's entry list, so the order entries are authored in decides what a capped entry falls back to.

UPCGExSelectorNoiseFieldFactoryProviderS.name: Selector : Noise Field
UPCGExSelectorNoiseFieldFactoryProviderS.purpose: Answers the per-point pick from where the point is. A noise stack wired into its own Noise pin is sampled at the point's world position, and the value lands in one of the entries' bands, so neighbouring points read near-identical values and receive the same entry: variety arrives as patches and gradients rather than as per-point scatter. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh. The per-point seed takes no part in the answer, so everything that varies the result lives on the wired noise definitions.
UPCGExSelectorNoiseFieldFactoryProviderS.situation: A scatter that should read as regions, where one stretch of ground favours one set of assets and the next stretch favours another.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per point and records the entry it returns, so point count stays the consumer's business and the factory only decides which entry. The scoped category's entries are laid end to end across the sampled range in the order the collection lists them, each holding one band, and the value read at the point's position selects the band it falls in: one entry per point, never a mix of two. Sampling happens in world space, so the pattern is anchored to the level, and the same points placed elsewhere read a different part of the field. When Selector Modifier : Quota wraps it, a point whose band is exhausted falls to the nearest band still available, so a spent entry's patches convert to their neighbours in the list instead of dispersing.

off_label.claim: The order entries sit in inside the collection is the order their bands sit in across the field, so reordering the list changes which assets end up bordering each other without changing how much ground any of them covers.
off_label.grounded_in: BuildCumulativeWeights fills Cumulative parallel to FCategory::Entries, which FCategory::RegisterEntry appends in the collection's authored order, and PickFromNormalized indexes that same array

off_label.claim: A remap curve on a wired noise definition redistributes the sampled values, and so redistributes the ground each band receives. It is how one entry is made to cover most of the area while the collection's weights stay as authored for every other consumer.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExNoise3DOperation::ApplyRemap evaluates RemapLUT before the value reaches FPCGExEntryNoiseFieldPickerOp::Pick

inputs.label: Noise
inputs.note: One or more Noise3D definitions. Several inputs combine into a single field per their own blend modes and weights, and that combined field is what every point samples.

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory this node produces. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into the Selector pin of a selector modifier; the consumer runs it once per point to decide that point's entry.

fields.name: bUseWeights
fields.tooltip: When enabled, entries occupy noise-value bands proportional to their Weight; otherwise all entries get equal bands.

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories).
BaseConfig.semantics: The seed settings do not reach the entry pick, which reads position and nothing else. They still drive the entry's own sub-pick, so material variants keep varying point to point inside a patch that is otherwise one repeated asset. Category scoping applies before the bands are laid out, so a per-point category attribute gives each category its own band layout over the same field.

hints.text: Picks are pinned to world position, not to the points carrying them. Anything that moves the points before staging, an offset, a transform node, or moving the actor that generates them, walks them into a different part of the field and changes which entries they receive.

The sampled value is clamped into the zero-to-one range before the band lookup, so a noise definition whose Scale pushes its output past one does not widen the field, it flattens everything above one into the last band. What shows up in the level is the final entry in the list taking over.

UPCGExSelectorQuotaFactoryProviderSettin.name: Selector Modifier : Quota
UPCGExSelectorQuotaFactoryProviderSettin.purpose: Puts a budget on each entry and enforces it around another selector. Two numeric collection properties supply the figures: a maximum an entry may be picked, and a minimum it must be picked. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh, and it wraps whatever selector is wired into its own Selector input, or a plain weighted roll when that input is empty. Maximums come out exact; minimums land within one of the authored figure.
UPCGExSelectorQuotaFactoryProviderSettin.situation: A collection holding a few entries that must appear a fixed number of times across a scatter, with the rest free to fill in around them.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per point, and the factory only decides which entry; how many points there are stays the consumer's business. Every entry in the scoped category carries a remaining count, and an entry with none left is dropped from the candidate list the inner selector rolls over, so the inner selector chooses among what is still available instead of picking and being refused. Ahead of that, a share of the points is reserved for entries carrying a minimum: membership in that share is a pure function of the point's index, spread evenly through point order, and a reserved point never reaches the inner selector. Caps and minimums are read per entry through the collection's property tiers, so a figure declared once on the collection gives every entry its own counter of that size rather than a budget they share.

off_label.claim: A maximum of zero is a hard gate rather than a budget, so the cap property doubles as an entry allowlist. The value resolves through the collection's property tiers, so one category override row can blank out or admit a whole category without touching any weight or the entry list.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExPickAvailability::IsAvailable treating 0 as unavailable, over counters initialised from Entry->TryGetPropertyValue<double> and its entry, category, collection resolution

off_label.claim: With a minimum and no maximum, the reservation is the whole behaviour: a low-discrepancy sequence over point index hands one entry an evenly spread share of the points with no clumping, and the wrapped selector fills everything else. That is a spacing tool as much as a guarantee.
off_label.grounded_in: ReservationU, the golden-ratio conjugate sequence over PointIndex, and the ReservationFraction branch at the head of FPCGExEntryQuotaPickerOp::ResolvePick

inputs.label: Selector
inputs.note: The selector the quota wraps. Left empty, the quota constrains a plain weighted roll, which makes the node worth using on its own. Connecting several is not a merge: the lowest Priority wins, the rest are dropped, and the node warns and points at Selector Modifier : Cascade.

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory this node produces. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into another modifier's Selector pin; the consumer runs it once per point and receives the budgeted answer.

fields.name: MaxPropertyName
fields.tooltip: Numeric collection property supplying each entry's MAX pick count (cap). Entries without the property (or with negative values) are uncapped; zero = never pickable.

fields.name: MinPropertyName
fields.tooltip: Optional numeric collection property supplying each entry's MIN pick count. Minimums are satisfied by deterministic low-discrepancy reservation (accurate to ±1, spread evenly across point order) and always resolve PER INPUT DATA. Entries without the property have no minimum.

fields.name: Mode
fields.tooltip: How property values translate into counts.

fields.name: Scope
fields.tooltip: Which point population the MAX caps apply to.

fields.name: ExhaustedBehavior
fields.tooltip: Behavior once every available entry is exhausted.

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories).

hints.text: Capped entries are claimed in ascending point-index order, and both consumers drive that ordering, so the counts and the assignment are each reproducible run to run. Point order being the claim priority also means anything upstream that reorders or inserts points reassigns which points get the scarce entries.

A cap sits on the entry the category holds, so capping a sub-collection entry limits how often the subtree is entered, never how often a given leaf inside it comes out. Descent below the first hop is a plain weighted roll on the child's own weights, and no counter follows it down.

UPCGExSelectorRangeBasedFactoryProviderS.name: Selector : Range-Based
UPCGExSelectorRangeBasedFactoryProviderS.purpose: Answers the per-point pick by containment: each entry declares the band of values it covers, and a point picks among the entries whose bands contain its value. The bands are read from the collection's properties, so which entry serves which value is authored on the collection and this node only says where to look. It produces a factory on the Selector pin, consumed by Staging : Distribute and Staging : Spline Mesh. Axes stack, each with its own per-point value and its own pair of range properties, and an entry qualifies only when every axis contains its value; three overlap policies then decide between the entries that qualify.
UPCGExSelectorRangeBasedFactoryProviderS.situation: A collection whose entries were authored with the band of values each one covers, and points carrying the value that has to land in one of them.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per point. Each axis reads one value from the point and tests it against every entry's authored range on that axis; an entry becomes a candidate only when all of its axes contain their value, so adding an axis narrows the candidate list and never widens it. The overlap policy then picks one candidate, and the point count stays the consumer's business. Entries whose range fails to resolve on any axis are candidates for nothing, and a point that no candidate contains gets no pick at all.

off_label.claim: An entry whose Min and Max are equal has a band of width zero, which under Narrowest Wins scores below every real band and takes the pick outright. Paired with the [|] boundary, so the degenerate band still matches its one value, that turns a single entry into an exact-value override sitting on top of the broad bands.
off_label.grounded_in: the hypervolume product and its strictly-lower comparison in FPCGExEntryRangeNarrowestPickerOp::Pick, plus the ClosedClosed branch of ContainsOnAxis

off_label.claim: An axis whose band resolves the same on every entry discriminates nothing and gates everything: while the point value sits outside that shared band no entry matches at all, so a second axis doubles as an on/off switch for the whole selector without touching the bands that do the sorting.
off_label.grounded_in: the AND early-exit in MatchesAllAxes and the collection-default tier of FPCGExAssetCollectionEntry property resolution, which hands every unoverridden entry the same value

outputs.label: Selector
outputs.note: The factory this node produces. Wire it into the Selector pin on Staging : Distribute or Staging : Spline Mesh, or into the Selector pin of a selector modifier; the consumer runs it once per point to decide that point's entry.

fields.name: Axes
fields.tooltip: One or more axes. With multiple axes, an entry must contain the point value on every axis (AND policy).

fields.name: OverlapMode
fields.tooltip: What to do when the point value falls in multiple entries' ranges. For multi-axis, NarrowestWins scores by hypervolume (product of per-axis widths).

BaseConfig.tooltip: Shared distribution configuration (seed, entry distribution, categories).
BaseConfig.semantics: Category scoping decides the candidate list before any band is tested, so an entry outside the scoped category never matches however well its band fits the value. The seed settings reach only both rolls this selector can make, the `Weighted Random` pick and the `Narrowest Wins` tie-break, and a First Match configuration ignores them outright.

hints.text: The default `Boundary Mode` is `>|<`, which excludes both endpoints. Bands authored to meet at a shared value, 0 to 0.5 and 0.5 to 1, leave a point sitting exactly on 0.5 matching nothing, and the outer ends of the covered span behave the same way. Bucket behaviour, where every value across the covered span belongs to exactly one band, is `[|<`.
Axis rows in the panel are titled by their `Min Property Name`, which `XY` mode never uses, so a multi-axis setup in `XY` shows a stack of rows all reading None.

Bands that do not cover the full spread of the incoming values are not an error. Points landing in a gap get no pick, and Staging : Distribute prunes unpicked points by default, so an over-tight set of bands reads as missing points downstream rather than as a complaint on this node.
The node's title in the graph carries the policy as an extra line, reading Select : Range Weighted, Select : Range First, or Select : Range Narrowest.

UPCGExSelfPruningSettings.name: Self Pruning
UPCGExSelfPruningSettings.purpose: Thins a dataset by removing points that overlap each other. Where **Discard By Overlap** works between datasets and removes whole layers, this works inside one and removes individual points, which is what makes it the node for turning a dense scatter into one where nothing collides. It can also report the overlap count instead of acting on it.
UPCGExSelfPruningSettings.situation: A scatter dense enough that instances would intersect, needing thinning without a fixed grid or a re-scatter.

mechanism.text: Every point is tested against its neighbours in the same dataset, and where two overlap one of them goes. Which one is decided by sorting: the rules on the pin order the points, and the point that sorts worse is the one removed. `Mode` switches the whole node between doing that and merely writing how many overlaps each point had. The bounds tested are the points' own, expanded independently for the point being judged and for the neighbours it is judged against.

off_label.claim: Write Result mode turns it into a density measure with no removal at all: each point learns how crowded it is, and a filter downstream can act on that with a threshold the node itself does not offer.
off_label.grounded_in: Mode selects between pruning and writing the overlap count, and the count is written in both discrete and normalised forms.

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to thin. Each dataset is treated on its own, so points in different datasets never prune each other.

inputs.label: Sorting Rules
inputs.note: Decides which of two overlapping points survives. Without rules the order comes from the randomisation setting instead.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The surviving points, or in Write Result mode every point carrying its overlap count.

outputs.label: Discarded
outputs.note: The points that were pruned away. The setting describes it as authoring-time only, so it is a graph-building aid rather than part of a shipping route.
outputs.condition: only when the discard output is enabled

Mode.tooltip: Whether to prune points or write the number of overlaps
Mode.semantics: Switches between removing points and measuring them, and nothing else in the panel changes meaning with it. In `Write Result` no point leaves, so the sorting rules and the discard output have nothing to do; in `Prune` the count settings have nothing to write.

SortDirection.tooltip: Whether to sort hash components or not.

bRandomize.tooltip: Sort over a random per-point value
bRandomize.semantics: Ships on, and adds a small per-point jitter to the sort so that points which would otherwise tie are broken apart rather than resolved by index. Without it a uniformly scattered set prunes in a pattern that follows point order, which reads as directional thinning.
bRandomize.trap: It changes which points survive between runs unless the seed is fixed, so a graph that needs a repeatable result has to either clear this or control the seed upstream.

RandomRange.tooltip: Sort over a random per-point value

NumOverlapAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the attribute to write the number of overlap to.

Units.tooltip: Discrete mode write the number as-is, relative will normalize against the highest number of overlaps found.

bOutputOneMinusOverlap.tooltip: Whether to do a OneMinus on the normalized overlap count value

bOutputDiscard.tooltip: If enabled, output the pruned-away points to a separate 'Discarded' pin. Authoring-time only.
bOutputDiscard.semantics: Adds the Discarded pin. The setting calls itself authoring-time only, so it is there to inspect what a configuration removes while tuning it rather than to feed a shipping branch.

bPreciseTest.tooltip: If enabled, does very precise and EXPENSIVE spatial tests. Only supported for pruning.
bPreciseTest.semantics: A much more expensive spatial test, and it works in `Prune` only. The count written in `Write Result` is always the cheaper approximation, so a graph cannot preview the precise result before pruning with it.

PrimaryMode.tooltip: If and how to expand the primary bounds (bounds used for the main point being evaluated)
PrimaryMode.semantics: Expands the bounds of the point being judged. Together with the secondary expansion it decides how much clearance is demanded: the two are separate so that a point can be tested as though it were larger than the neighbours it is tested against, which thins more aggressively than growing both.

PrimaryExpansionValue.tooltip: Primary Expansion value. Uniform, discrete offset applied to bounds.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

SecondaryMode.tooltip: If and how to expand the primary bounds (bounds used for neighbors points against the main point being evaluated)
SecondaryMode.semantics: Expands the bounds of the neighbours a point is tested against, rather than the point itself. Setting only this and leaving the primary alone asks whether anything nearby has grown into this point, which is a different question from whether this point has grown into anything.

SecondaryExpansionValue.tooltip: Secondary Expansion value. Uniform, discrete offset applied to bounds.

fields.name: Input
fields.tooltip: Whether to use the constant value or read from an attribute.

fields.name: bCleanupAttribute
fields.tooltip: Allow this attribute to be registered as consumable, i.e. deleted from the consuming node's outputs when its 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' toggle is enabled. Disable to always preserve the attribute.

fields.name: Attribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute or property selector to read from when Input is set to Attribute.

hints.text: Pruning happens inside each dataset separately. Two datasets whose points sit on top of each other are both left intact, which is what **Discard By Overlap** handles instead.

UPCGExSettings.name: Settings
UPCGExSettings.purpose: The settings every PCGEx node carries, whatever it does. They are about how a node executes rather than what it computes: how its data is prepared, how it threads, what it protects, and how loudly it complains. A node's own page describes what it does; this page describes what it shares with every other one.
UPCGExSettings.situation: A node behaving oddly around threading, caching or warnings, where the cause is in the shared block rather than in the node.

mechanism.text: These settings sit beneath every node's own, in an Inherited group, and are read before the node's work begins. Most are performance choices whose only visible effect is time. Two are not: the protected attributes list changes what a node may overwrite, and the consumable cleanup setting changes what survives the node at all. Those two alter results, and the rest alter cost.

BulkInitData.tooltip: If enabled, will pre-allocate all data on a single thread to avoid contention. Not all nodes support this.

CacheData.tooltip: Cache the results of this node. Cached data persists until inputs change, avoiding re-computation.

CacheLoadedResources.tooltip: Cache the resources loaded by this node. Only accounted for if the node actually relies on external resources.

ScopedAttributeGet.tooltip: Whether scoped attribute read is enabled or not. Disabling this on small dataset may greatly improve performance. It's enabled by default for legacy reasons.
ScopedAttributeGet.semantics: Reads attributes in bounded scopes rather than all at once, which lowers peak memory on large datasets at some cost in time. It changes nothing about the result, so it is a setting to reach for when a graph runs out of room rather than when it runs slowly.

StealData.tooltip: This node will not make any copy of the data and instead modify the inputs directly. When enabling this you must make absolutely sure the data plugged into this node is not plugged in any other node. Only supported by nodes set-up in a way that makes in-place mutations possible. 'Cleanup Consumable Attributes' and 'Flatten Output' then also apply to the stolen inputs (including forwarded pass-through pins), and because upstream caches keep referencing the mutated data, re-running only this node against cached inputs is not idempotent.

bFlattenOutput.tooltip: Flatten the output of this node. Merges hierarchical data into a single flat collection.
bFlattenOutput.semantics: Collapses the output's metadata into a plain form, which costs time and makes what follows cheaper. On a long chain it is usually worth doing once near the end rather than at every step.

bCleanupConsumableAttributes.tooltip: If the node registers consumable attributes, these will be deleted from the output data.
bCleanupConsumableAttributes.semantics: Removes attributes a node declared it had consumed, so a value read and folded into something else does not travel onward. It changes what leaves the node rather than how it runs, which makes it the one performance-shaped setting in this block that is really about data.

CommaSeparatedProtectedAttributesName.tooltip: If the node registers consumable attributes, this a list of comma separated names that won't be deleted if they were registered.

ProtectedAttributes.tooltip: Attribute names to exclude from cleanup. Works alongside the comma-separated string list above.
ProtectedAttributes.semantics: Names attributes a node must not overwrite, which is the counterpart to the cleanup above. It is how a graph keeps an identifier or a reference intact through a node whose settings would otherwise claim that name.

bPropagateAbortedExecution.tooltip: Whether the execution of the graph should be cancelled if this node execution is cancelled internally

bQuietInvalidInputWarning.tooltip: Suppress warnings about invalid input data (e.g., missing attributes, wrong data types).
bQuietInvalidInputWarning.semantics: Silences the complaint about input the node could not use. Worth reaching for where a mixed stream legitimately contains data this node ignores, and worth leaving alone otherwise, since it is often the only sign that a wire is going somewhere unintended.

bQuietMissingInputError.tooltip: Suppress errors about missing required input connections.

bQuietCancellationError.tooltip: Suppress error messages when node execution is cancelled.

hints.text: These appear as an Inherited settings group on every node page rather than being repeated in full. A node whose own panel seems to be missing a familiar toggle usually has it here.

UPCGExShapeBuilderFactoryProviderSetting.name: ShapeBuilder Definition
UPCGExShapeBuilderFactoryProviderSetting.purpose: The base every Shape sub-node inherits, and the page for the settings they all share. A shape node describes a form to build; it does not build anything itself. **Create Shapes** is what runs them, and every seed point it processes becomes a shape of whatever form the builders on its pin describe. What resolution, fitting and orientation mean is the same on every one of them and is stated here.
UPCGExShapeBuilderFactoryProviderSetting.situation: Reading one of the Shape nodes and needing to know which of its settings are its own and which reach it from here.

mechanism.text: A shape builder emits a factory on the Shape Builder pin. When its consumer runs, each seed point is handed to the builder, which produces the points of one shape around it. Every builder carries the same shared block beneath its own settings, and it settles four things: how dense the shape is, how it is sized against the seed, which way the form is turned, and which way its points face. `Resolution Mode` is the one to read first, because it decides whether the figure beside it is a density, so larger shapes get more points, or a fixed count every shape gets regardless of size.

outputs.label: Shape Builder
outputs.note: The form definition, read by **Create Shapes**. Several builders on one pin produce several shapes per seed rather than a choice between them.

hints.text: Builders on the pin do not compete. Each one produces its own shape for every seed, so wiring several is how one seed set becomes several overlapping forms.

The shared block guards the low end and not the high one: shapes resolving to fewer points than `Min Point Count` are dropped, while the matching upper guard ships off. A resolution set as a density on large seeds can therefore produce shapes with many thousands of points before anything objects.

`Source Axis` and `Target Axis` are read as a pair: they name the shape's own reference direction and the seed direction it should be brought onto. Orienting the points themselves is a separate setting, so a ring can lie flat while its points each face the centre.

UPCGExShiftPathSettings.name: Path : Shift
UPCGExShiftPathSettings.purpose: Rotates a path's data around a chosen point, so that point's values end up at the front and everything before it wraps to the back. The point count and the point positions are untouched: what moves is what each slot along the path is carrying. `Shift Type` decides how much of that moves, from the metadata alone to every native property alongside it, and the pivot itself is chosen by a fraction of the path, a raw index, or the first point that passes a filter.
UPCGExShiftPathSettings.situation: A closed path whose seam falls in the wrong place, where the run is right and only the point it is written down from is wrong.

mechanism.text: One execution takes paths and returns them with the same number of points, in the same order, in the same places. The pivot resolves to one index, and the values living at index `pivot` onward are moved to the front while the values before it wrap around behind them. Nothing is interpolated and nothing is dropped: every value that was on the path is still on it, one slot elsewhere. A pivot that lands on the first or the last point leaves the path untouched, since a rotation by zero and a rotation by the whole length are the same rotation.

off_label.claim: Shifting Properties while leaving Metadata alone breaks the pairing between a point's position and its attributes on purpose, which is a way to slide a whole authored attribute pattern along a run without moving any geometry.
off_label.grounded_in: The Properties value passes every allocated native property except MetadataEntry to InheritProperties, so attributes stay where they were

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to rotate.

inputs.label: Shift Conditions
inputs.note: The pivot becomes the first point that passes, scanning from the start, or from the end while `Reverse Shift` is on. A path where nothing passes keeps whatever pivot was left over, which is not a defined position.
inputs.condition: present and required while Input Mode is Filter

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The same points, carrying rotated values.

ShiftType.tooltip: What data is shifted (index, metadata, properties, etc.).

InputMode.tooltip: How the shift amount is determined.
InputMode.semantics: `Relative` takes a fraction of the path's last index, so one setting cuts every path at its own midpoint whatever its length, while `Discrete` names the same absolute position on every path.

RelativeConstant.tooltip: Relative shift amount as a fraction of path length (0-1).
RelativeConstant.semantics: Multiplied by the path's last index, not by its point count, so 1.0 lands on the final point and rotates by nothing. It is not clamped, and a value outside 0 to 1 is put back in range by `Index Safety`.

Truncate.tooltip: How to truncate the computed index.

DiscreteConstant.tooltip: Number of positions to shift by.
DiscreteConstant.semantics: An index rather than an amount, so 2 makes the third point the new first. It ships at 0, which is a rotation by nothing, so a node in `Discrete` mode does nothing until this is set.

IndexSafety.tooltip: How to handle out-of-range indices after shift.
IndexSafety.semantics: `Tile`, the shipped value, wraps a pivot that falls outside the path, so a discrete pivot larger than the path keeps working on shorter paths rather than failing on them. It is not consulted in `Filter` mode, where the pivot came from a real point.

bReverseShift.semantics: Turns the rotation around, so the pivot's values move toward the back rather than the front, and it also measures the pivot from the other end for `Relative` and `Discrete`. In `Filter` mode it changes nothing about the rotation and only reverses the scan, so the pivot becomes the last point that passes rather than the first.

CherryPickedProperties.semantics: A bitmask over the native properties. Selecting the metadata entry here is equivalent to `Metadata`, which is why it can collide with the list below.

CherryPickedAttributes.semantics: Attribute names, one per row, and only names that resolve to a real attribute are used; a property path typed here is skipped.
CherryPickedAttributes.trap: Attributes of container or extended types are silently left where they were. Everything else in the list rotates, so a partial result is the shape a mixed list produces.

bQuietDoubleShiftWarning.tooltip: Suppress warning when path data has already been shifted.
bQuietDoubleShiftWarning.semantics: The warning it silences is real: naming attributes here while also selecting the metadata entry in the property bitmask rotates the same values twice, once through the entry and once through the buffer, so they end up two rotations away.

bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.tooltip: If enabled, collections that have less than 2 points won't be processed and be omitted from the output.
bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.semantics: The only gate this node has. Nothing checks the input size on the way in, so a path of fewer than two points is processed as a no-op and then dropped here while this is on.

UPCGExShrinkPathSettings.name: Path : Shrink
UPCGExShrinkPathSettings.purpose: Eats a path in from its ends. Either end can give up a number of points or a length of run, and where the cut lands between two points, `Cut Type` decides whether a new point is placed exactly there or an existing one is taken as the new end. A negative distance does the opposite and pushes the end outward along the direction it was already going, so the same node lengthens a path as well as shortens it. The **Stop Conditions** pin puts a floor under the whole thing by naming points the shrink is not allowed to pass.
UPCGExShrinkPathSettings.situation: Runs that have to stop short of whatever they lead to, a road ending before a building or a cable stopping clear of its anchor.

mechanism.text: One execution takes paths and returns them with points removed from one or both ends and their two surviving end points moved. Both ends are worked at once and each consumes its own amount, so the output count is the input count less whatever the two ends between them took. Closed paths are refused outright with a warning and forwarded untouched, because a loop has no ends to eat. A path that shrinks down below two points is dropped rather than emitted short, and so is one whose two ends ate past each other. Where nothing was removed at either end the input is forwarded exactly as it arrived.
steps: Each end resolves its amount, a count or a distance, from its own settings block.
An end whose own point already passes a stop condition gives up its amount entirely and shrinks by nothing.
The two ends then walk inward together, each stopping at its amount or at the first point that passes a stop condition, whichever it reaches first.

off_label.claim: A negative distance runs the whole node backwards: instead of eating in, the end point is pushed out along the line of its terminal segment by that much and no point is removed anywhere. It is the shortest way to extend a path by an exact length without inventing geometry, and the node's own keywords list extend alongside reduce.
off_label.grounded_in: ShrinkByDistance handles StartAmount and EndAmount below zero by offsetting NewStart and NewEnd along the terminal segment direction, then zeroes the amount so no masking runs

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to shrink. Closed paths are passed through with a warning rather than processed.

inputs.label: Stop Conditions
inputs.note: Points that pass halt the shrink coming toward them, and that point becomes the new end. Left empty nothing stops the shrink and both ends consume their full amount.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The shortened paths. A path reduced below two points, or whose ends crossed, is not emitted at all.

ShrinkEndpoint.tooltip: Which endpoints to shrink (start, end, or both).
ShrinkEndpoint.semantics: Which ends are eaten. `Start` and `End` zero the other end's amount outright, which also means the second settings block stops being read at all.

SettingsMode.tooltip: Whether both endpoints use shared settings or separate settings.
SettingsMode.semantics: Whether one block drives both ends or each has its own. `Shared` reads the primary block for both; `Separate` hands the end its own secondary block. It only appears while both ends are being shrunk.

ShrinkMode.tooltip: Shrink by distance traveled or by point count.
ShrinkMode.semantics: `Count` removes a number of points and never places a new one, so what is left is a subset of the original points. `Distance` measures the run and can cut between two points, which is where `Cut Type` starts to matter and where a new endpoint can appear.

PrimaryDistanceDetails.tooltip: Distance-based shrink settings for the first endpoint (or both if shared).

fields.name: AmountInput
fields.tooltip: Whether the distance is a constant or read from an attribute.

fields.name: DistanceAttribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute to read the shrink distance from.

fields.name: Distance
fields.tooltip: Distance to shrink the path endpoint by.

fields.name: CutType
fields.tooltip: How to handle the cut point when shrinking by distance.

PrimaryDistanceDetails.semantics: The distance is measured along the path, following the run rather than the straight line to the end. Its `Cut Type` decides what happens where the distance runs out between two points: `New Point` moves the surviving point to the exact spot, `Previous (Ceil)` keeps the point before it so the path stays a little longer than asked, `Next (Floor)` takes the point after so it comes out shorter, and `Closest (Round)` picks whichever of the two is nearer.
PrimaryDistanceDetails.trap: An attribute source is read from one point only: the primary block reads the path's first point for the start amount and its last point for the end amount. A value that varies along the path is never sampled anywhere else.

SecondaryDistanceDetails.tooltip: Distance-based shrink settings for the second endpoint.
SecondaryDistanceDetails.edit_condition: ShrinkMode == EPCGExPathShrinkMode::Distance && ShrinkEndpoint == EPCGExShrinkEndpoint::Both && SettingsMode == EPCGExShrinkConstantMode::Separate

fields.name: AmountInput
fields.tooltip: Whether the distance is a constant or read from an attribute.

fields.name: DistanceAttribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute to read the shrink distance from.

fields.name: Distance
fields.tooltip: Distance to shrink the path endpoint by.

fields.name: CutType
fields.tooltip: How to handle the cut point when shrinking by distance.

SecondaryDistanceDetails.semantics: The end's own block, read from the path's last point when its source is an attribute. It exists only while both ends are shrunk under `Separate`.

PrimaryCountDetails.tooltip: Count-based shrink settings for the first endpoint (or both if shared).

fields.name: ValueSource
fields.tooltip: Whether the count is a constant or read from an attribute.

fields.name: CountAttribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute to read the point count from.

fields.name: Count
fields.tooltip: Number of points to remove from the path endpoint.

PrimaryCountDetails.semantics: A count of points to remove, clamped at zero so it cannot run backwards the way a distance can. An attribute source is read from the first point for the start and the last point for the end.

SecondaryCountDetails.tooltip: Count-based shrink settings for the second endpoint.
SecondaryCountDetails.edit_condition: ShrinkMode == EPCGExPathShrinkMode::Count && ShrinkEndpoint == EPCGExShrinkEndpoint::Both && SettingsMode == EPCGExShrinkConstantMode::Separate

fields.name: ValueSource
fields.tooltip: Whether the count is a constant or read from an attribute.

fields.name: CountAttribute
fields.tooltip: Attribute to read the point count from.

fields.name: Count
fields.tooltip: Number of points to remove from the path endpoint.

SecondaryCountDetails.semantics: The end's own count block under `Separate`, and an attribute source here is read from the path's last point alone, the way the primary block's is read from its first.

bEndpointsIgnoreStopConditions.tooltip: If enabled, endpoint points themselves won't trigger stop conditions.
bEndpointsIgnoreStopConditions.semantics: Clears the stop verdict on the path's first and last points before anything runs. Without it, a stop condition that happens to pass on an end point stops that end before it removed anything, so the shrink silently does nothing on that side.

bPreserveFirstMetadata.tooltip: If enabled, the point cut from the start will inherit from the original first point
bPreserveFirstMetadata.semantics: The point that ends up first carries the attributes of whichever original point it came from, which after a distance cut is the point the cut passed through. Turning this on hands it the original first point's attributes instead, so anything keyed to the path's start survives being trimmed.

bPreserveLastMetadata.tooltip: If enabled, the point cut from the end will inherit from the original last point

bQuietClosedLoopWarning.tooltip: Suppress warning when attempting to shrink a closed loop path.
bQuietClosedLoopWarning.semantics: Only silences the message. A closed path is forwarded untouched either way, and splitting it into an open run is what makes it shrinkable.

bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.tooltip: If enabled, collections that have less than 2 points won't be processed and be omitted from the output.
bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.semantics: Reaches inputs of fewer than two points, which are dropped rather than forwarded whatever this says. What it does control is closed paths: they are forwarded whole, and while this is on they survive the output gate because a forwarded loop still has its points.

hints.text: A path that shrinks below two points, or whose two ends eat past each other, is discarded rather than emitted short. Fewer paths out than in is the symptom, and nothing is logged.

UPCGExSimplifyClustersSettings.name: Cluster : Simplify
UPCGExSimplifyClustersSettings.purpose: Takes Vtx out of a cluster without changing what it connects. Everything that carries structural meaning stays: leaves, Vtx holding more than two edges, and any Vtx a filter protects. What goes is the filler between them, the binary Vtx that only pass a connection along. `Prune Leaves` is the one setting that goes further and removes rather than collapses, taking whole dead-end runs out of the cluster.
UPCGExSimplifyClustersSettings.situation: A cluster came out of a generator or a mesh import carrying far more Vtx along its runs than the connectivity needs.

mechanism.text: The unit of work is a chain: a run of Vtx that each hold exactly two edges, bounded at either end by a Vtx that does not. Every bounding Vtx survives, and so does any Vtx a filter marked as a breakpoint, which splits the chain there and makes it two. Each chain is then replaced by a path joining the same two ends, so nothing that was connected becomes disconnected. What is removed is interior Vtx: with `Merge Above Angular Threshold` off the whole chain collapses to one edge, and with it on an interior Vtx survives where the turn at it is sharper than the threshold. Every emitted edge records how many originals it absorbed. `Prune Leaves` is the exception to all of this, dropping chains that end in a leaf outright, and a component made only of such a chain goes with them.

off_label.claim: Wire **Keep Conditions** with a filter that passes a scattering of Vtx and leave the angular threshold off, and the node becomes a resampler for a cluster's runs: everything between two kept Vtx collapses to one edge, so the surviving Vtx are the ones the filter chose and nothing else.
off_label.grounded_in: A breakpoint becomes a chain endpoint when the cached chains are split, and a chain with no angular rule is emitted as a single edge between its two endpoints.

inputs.label: Vtx
inputs.note: The cluster's Vtx dataset.

inputs.label: Edges
inputs.note: The cluster's Edges datasets, one per cluster. Each is simplified independently.

inputs.label: Keep Conditions
inputs.note: Vtx that pass are protected, which makes them chain endpoints and splits any chain running through them. Unconnected, nothing is protected and the chains fall where the topology puts them. It takes point filters rather than Vtx filters.

inputs.label: EdgeFilters
inputs.note: Reaches the Vtx through the edges: `Edge Filter Role` decides whether the endpoints of a passing edge are protected or made collapsible.

outputs.label: Vtx
outputs.note: The surviving Vtx, rebuilt through the graph builder. Vtx no emitted edge names are gone from it.

outputs.label: Edges
outputs.note: One dataset per connected component. Each edge point stands for the run of original edges it absorbed.

bOperateOnLeavesOnly.tooltip: If enabled, only check for dead ends.
bOperateOnLeavesOnly.semantics: Narrows the work to the chains that end in a leaf. Every other chain is emitted with all of its original edges intact, so the interior of the cluster comes through untouched however the angular settings are configured.
bOperateOnLeavesOnly.trap: `Prune Leaves` is decided first. With both on, the leaf chains are removed and the rest is passed through whole, so the node deletes dead ends and simplifies nothing.

EdgeFilterRole.tooltip: Define the behavior of connected edge filters, if any
EdgeFilterRole.semantics: Sets which side of the edge verdict protects. **Preserve** starts every Vtx collapsible and protects the endpoints of edges that pass. **Collapse** starts every Vtx protected and makes the endpoints of passing edges collapsible, so the cluster is left alone apart from where the filters point.
EdgeFilterRole.trap: The edge verdict is applied after the **Keep Conditions** verdict and overwrites it on the endpoints it touches. With both pins wired and the role set to Collapse, a Vtx that Keep Conditions protected is still collapsed when a passing edge meets it.

AngularThreshold.tooltip: If enabled, uses an angular threshold below which nodes are merged.
AngularThreshold.semantics: The turn measured at each interior Vtx, between the direction coming in and the direction going out. A Vtx whose turn is under the threshold is filler and goes; one whose turn is over it is a corner and stays. Zero therefore keeps every Vtx that bends at all, and 180 collapses the chain whole.
AngularThreshold.trap: The switch above this also decides what happens to closed loops. With the angular threshold off, a closed loop is emitted with every one of its original edges, so the setting that collapses every open chain to a single edge leaves loops entirely alone.

bInvertAngularThreshold.tooltip: Removes hard angles instead of collinear ones.
bInvertAngularThreshold.semantics: Keeps the straight runs and removes the corners, which is the shape you want for reading where a cluster runs flat rather than for reducing its Vtx count.

bFuseCollocated.tooltip: If enabled, will consider collocated binary nodes for collocation and remove them as part of the simplification.
bFuseCollocated.semantics: A second reason to drop a Vtx, applied after the angular test and measured against the last Vtx that was kept rather than against the immediate neighbour. A long run of tight corners therefore thins out to roughly one Vtx per tolerance, instead of keeping every corner.

FuseDistance.tooltip: Distance used to consider point to be overlapping.
FuseDistance.semantics: World units, and it never takes a closed loop below three Vtx, because a cycle cannot be expressed with fewer.

bPruneLeaves.semantics: The only setting here that removes rather than collapses, and it takes the whole chain, not the leaf Vtx alone: everything from the leaf back to the first Vtx that is not binary leaves the cluster.
bPruneLeaves.trap: A connected component that is nothing but a run with a leaf at either end is one leaf chain, so this deletes it entirely. Repeated runs of the node keep peeling: a branch exposed as a new dead end by the previous run is pruned by the next.

fields.name: IsUnionAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to mark point as union or not

fields.name: UnionSizeAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to mark the number of fused point held

fields.name: IsSubEdgeAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to mark edge as sub edge or not

EdgeUnionData.semantics: What the collapse can be made to record. The union size on an emitted edge is the count of original edges it stands for, which is the only place the length of the vanished run survives, and it is worth writing when anything downstream has to weight edges by how much cluster they replaced.

EdgeBlendingDetails.tooltip: Defines how fused point properties and attributes are merged together for Edges (When an edge is the result of a simplification).
EdgeBlendingDetails.semantics: Decides what an emitted edge point inherits from the edges it absorbed. An edge standing for a run of forty has forty sources, so an average and a sum give very different answers here than they would on a one-to-one edit.

EdgeCarryOverDetails.tooltip: Meta filter settings for edge data.

fields.name: bPreserveAttributesDefaultValue
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will preserve the initial attribute default value.

fields.name: Attributes
fields.tooltip: Attributes to carry over.

fields.name: bDataDomainToElements
fields.tooltip: If enabled, data domain attributes are promoted to the elements domain (the single @Data value is broadcast to every point). Off by default; Merge Points is the node that enables it. Not used by all nodes.

fields.name: Scope
fields.tooltip: Scope

fields.name: Tags
fields.tooltip: Tags to carry over.

fields.name: bTestTagsWithValues
fields.tooltip: If enabled, will test full tag with its value ('Tag:Value'), otherwise only test the left part ignoring the right `:Value` ('Tag').

GraphBuilderDetails.semantics: The last thing that can drop a result. With `Prune Leaves` on, a simplification that stripped a component down to nothing leaves the component gone, and the small-cluster limit here can take out what the pruning merely shrank.

hints.text: Connectivity comes through intact. Each chain is replaced by a path between the same two Vtx, so anything that could be reached before can still be reached, and the component count is unchanged. `Prune Leaves` is the single setting that breaks that promise, and it only ever removes dead ends.

UPCGExSkinnedMeshCollection.name: Collection | Skinned Mesh
UPCGExSkinnedMeshCollection.purpose: A weighted library of skinned meshes, row for row the Mesh Collection with a skinned asset in place of the static one. Picking, staging and the pick hash are identical; spawning goes through the vanilla Skinned Mesh Spawner, driven by the Staging Data (Skinned) selector. What the type changes is the row: one skinned asset, one component descriptor where a mesh row carries an instanced one and a plain one, and sockets baked only when the asset is a skeletal mesh.
UPCGExSkinnedMeshCollection.situation: The library holds skeletal meshes, and the picks have to reach a spawner that renders skinned geometry.

mechanism.text: Authoring is the Mesh Collection's: weighted rows, categories, tags, sub-collections, fitting and property overrides all behave as they do there. A staging rebuild loads each row's skinned asset to bake its path and bounds, and lifts sockets from it when the asset is a skeletal mesh, each socket carrying its source bone name as the socket tag. Consumption is the vanilla Skinned Mesh Spawner: the Staging Data (Skinned) selector reads the pick hash and the Collection Map, follows through on the rows that resolved to skinned entries, skips every other type, and hands the spawner one instance list per row. Hosted inside an Omni Collection, this type's collection-level settings appear as its Type Globals block, and skinned rows there resolve against that block instead.

off_label.claim: A skinned row bakes each socket with its source bone name in the socket tag, so Staging : Load Sockets can narrow socket points by bone through its tag filters, or write the bone name onto them as an attribute.
off_label.grounded_in: FPCGExSkinnedMeshCollectionEntry::UpdateStaging passes USkeletalMeshSocket::BoneName into the staged FPCGExSocket's Tag field, which FPCGExSocketOutputDetails filters on and writes

GlobalDescriptor.semantics: One descriptor covers this type where a Mesh Collection carries two, since skinned meshes spawn through a single component type. Rows read it when their Descriptor Source is Global, and every row reads it when Global Descriptor Mode is Overrule, whatever each row asked for.
GlobalDescriptor.trap: Neither this block nor a row's own Skinned Mesh Settings reaches the spawned component while the staged selector keeps Use Template Descriptor enabled, which is its default: in that state the selector pushes only the asset and the row's tags onto its own template descriptor.

Entries.semantics: A skinned row holds one asset reference, the same weighted material variants a mesh row offers, and a single Skinned Mesh Settings block whose source Descriptor Source names: Local reads the row's own block, Global reads the collection's. Every other field on the row is the shared entry anatomy and behaves as it does on any collection type.
Entries.trap: Material variants are rolled and packed into the pick hash, and nothing applies them: the descriptor skinned meshes spawn through carries no material overrides in this engine version, so a variant roll changes the recorded pick and never the rendered materials.

hints.text: The Skinned Mesh Spawner has no Collection Map input of its own. The selector reads the Map from the node's override pin, the same wiring the static mesh route needs, and resolves nothing without it.

Descriptor Source offers None on a skinned row, and picking it hides the Skinned Mesh Settings block without clearing it. Descriptor resolution treats None exactly like Local, so the row still resolves to whatever the hidden block holds.

UPCGExSkinnedMeshSelectorStaged.name: Staging Data (Skinned)
UPCGExSkinnedMeshSelectorStaged.purpose: Skinned-mesh spawning is what the vanilla Skinned Mesh Spawner already does, and this is what teaches it to read staged picks. It is not a node: it is the mesh selector the spawner runs, and from there it resolves every point's pick against the Collection Map and hands the spawner its instance lists, carrying the entry's skinned asset, its tags and its component descriptor. Picks that resolved to something other than a skinned mesh entry contribute nothing, so a mixed staged dataset can be wired straight in, and mesh entries have their own selector for the vanilla Static Mesh Spawner.
UPCGExSkinnedMeshSelectorStaged.situation: A staged dataset reaches a Skinned Mesh Spawner, and the skeletal meshes have to come out with the descriptors and tags their collections authored.

mechanism.text: One execution takes the points on the spawner's input and the Collection Map on the spawner's override pin: every attribute set wired there is examined, the ones carrying a Map are read, and anything else on that pin stays the spawner's business. Points are grouped by their pick, and the spawner receives one instance list per distinct pick, however many points share it. Picks that resolve to an entry which is not a skinned mesh contribute no instances, and their points are otherwise untouched.
steps: The entry's component descriptor is resolved: the selector's own Template Descriptor while Use Template Descriptor is on, the entry's own descriptor (or its collection's globals) when it is off.
The entry's tags are appended to the component tags either way.
Force Disable Collisions clears collision on the resolved descriptor, so it wins over whichever descriptor supplied it.

StagingLayer.tooltip: Staging layer this selector reads staged picks from (and strips from output points). None = default layer (PCGEx/CollectionEntry); otherwise the layer name is appended (PCGEx/CollectionEntry/<layer>). Other layers' attributes pass through untouched.

bApplyMaterialOverrides.semantics: Skinned mesh entries author weighted material variants and the pick records which one was rolled, and the descriptor skinned meshes spawn through carries no material overrides in this engine version, so this setting changes nothing in either state. The By Attribute Material Overrides fields inherited from the vanilla selector are not read here either.

bForceDisableCollisions.semantics: Applied after the descriptor is resolved, so it clears collision whichever descriptor supplied it, the selector's Template Descriptor or the entry's own.

bUseTemplateDescriptor.tooltip: If enabled, will ignore the collection descriptor details and only push asset, materials & tags from the collection. Uses the inherited TemplateDescriptor from UPCGSkinnedMeshSelector.
bUseTemplateDescriptor.semantics: On, every instance is built from the Template Descriptor this selector inherits from the vanilla one, and the entry contributes only its skinned asset and its tags. Off, each entry brings its own component descriptor, or its collection's globals when the entry defers to them or the collection overrules, and its tags are appended to that.
bUseTemplateDescriptor.trap: Collections that author per-entry component details have every one of them ignored while this is on, and it is on by default. Template Descriptor stays editable in both states, since it belongs to the vanilla selector rather than to this one, and nothing in the panel greys out to signal that none of what it holds survives.

bUseTimeSlicing.semantics: Spreads the grouping of points across several executions instead of doing it in one pass, so a large staged dataset does not hold the editor for the duration. The result is identical either way.

bOutputPoints.semantics: On, the spawner's point output is a copy of its input with this layer's pick attribute removed. Picks on other layers survive, so points staged on several layers stay staged for the consumers of those layers.
bOutputPoints.trap: Off leaves the output empty rather than passing the points through. The Skinned Mesh Spawner allocates an output holding no points and this selector is what fills it, so switching this off means the pin carries a dataset with zero points.

bQuietMissingStagingDataWarning.tooltip: When enabled, silently skips input data that is missing the staging hash attribute instead of logging an error.
bQuietMissingStagingDataWarning.semantics: Skipped data produces no instances and comes out with zero points, silently.

hints.text: A mesh selector is a vanilla concept: the swappable brain inside a mesh spawner. It is unrelated to the Selector sub-nodes that decide picks upstream, which are a PCGEx system of their own. The two meet in this one place.

## The Skinned Mesh Spawner exposes no selector picker

The Static Mesh Spawner carries a Mesh Selector Type property, which is how the static counterpart gets installed. The Skinned Mesh Spawner has no equivalent in this engine version: its mesh selector is shown read-only in the details panel and stays the vanilla one. This page describes what this selector does once the spawner runs it.

## The Map goes into the spawner's override pin

The Skinned Mesh Spawner has no Map input of its own, so wire the Collection Map into the node's override pin. Without it the selector resolves nothing, reports that it found no Map in the overrides, and spawns nothing, while its point output still carries the points as if the node had run.

The vanilla selector this one extends contributes Mesh Attribute and By Attribute Material Overrides to the details panel, and neither is read here: the staged pick decides the asset. Template Descriptor is the one inherited field this selector uses.

UPCGExSmoothingInstancedFactory.name: Smoothing
UPCGExSmoothingInstancedFactory.purpose: The half the two smoothing rules share. A rule never moves anything: it is handed the points and a blender, and its whole job is to name, one point at a time, which other points contribute and how much each contributes. **Path : Smooth** owns what those contributions are applied to, which is why the same two rules smooth positions, colours and custom attributes without knowing which is which, and it owns how strong the result is and which points are processed at all.
UPCGExSmoothingInstancedFactory.situation: Reading **Moving Average** or **Radius** and needing to know which half of the result the rule decides and which half the node above it decides.

mechanism.text: A rule is handed the dataset, whether the path is closed, and a blender, and is asked once per point for the set of contributors to that point. Every value it names is read from the points as they arrived and never from the result being built, so a point that has already been smoothed is never a source for the next one: the outcome does not depend on the order points are visited in or on how the work is split across threads, and one execution is one pass over the path. A rule produces contributors and weights and nothing else. Whether those weights are honoured, and what they are applied to, is settled by the blending surface on **Path : Smooth**.

UPCGExSmoothSettings.name: Path : Smooth
UPCGExSmoothSettings.purpose: Pulls each point toward the points around it. The rule picked from the `Smoothing Method` dropdown decides what counts as around it and how heavily each neighbour counts; what actually moves is decided separately, by the blending surface, so one node smooths positions, colours or any attribute depending only on how that surface is set up. The **Point Filters** pin chooses which points are touched at all, and the two ends of an open path can be held still on their own.
UPCGExSmoothSettings.situation: A path whose run between points wobbles, where the overall shape is right and the point-to-point noise is not.

mechanism.text: One execution takes paths and returns the same points in the same order. Nothing is added or removed, and a path of fewer than two points is refused with a warning. Every contribution is read from the points as they arrived, so nothing a point picks up feeds into its neighbours and one execution is one pass: more smoothing means a larger `Smoothing` or a second node, not an iteration count. `Smoothing` is the rule's reach and its unit is the rule's business; `Influence` scales the weights the rule hands back.

off_label.claim: Set the inline block to blend `Position` alone and the node stops being a smoother of geometry only: point a Blend Op at a scalar attribute instead and the same neighbour weights turn into a blur over that attribute, with positions untouched.
off_label.grounded_in: The rule hands the blender an index and a weight and never names a channel; every channel comes from FPCGExBlendingDetails or the Blend Ops factories

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to smooth.

inputs.label: Point Filters
inputs.note: Points that fail are left as they arrived. They still count as sources for the points that are smoothed, so a filter here holds part of a path still while the rest relaxes around it.

inputs.label: Blend Ops
inputs.note: Blend Op sub-nodes naming what the contributions are applied to and how. Read only while `Blending Interface` is `Individual`; in `Monolithic` the pin drops under the node's advanced pins and is ignored.

inputs.label: Overrides : Smoothing
inputs.note: Attribute set whose entries overwrite the selected rule's own properties by name. Sits under the node's advanced pins.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The same points in the same order, with whatever the blending surface admitted moved.

bPreserveStart.semantics: Runs the rule for the first point with an influence of zero, which both rules take as an instruction to leave the point alone.
bPreserveStart.trap: It is indexed, not geometric. On a closed path the array's first point is an ordinary point on the loop, so pinning it while its neighbours move puts a kink at an arbitrary place on the ring.

bPreserveEnd.semantics: The same instruction at the other end of the array, with the same caveat on a closed path.

SmoothingMethod.semantics: Holds the two rules, and a fresh node ships with **Moving Average** selected.
