OutputStagingLayer.semantics: Reading and writing the same layer overwrites the picks in place and the pre-swap decision is gone downstream. Writing to another layer keeps both readable, and every staging consumer picks the layer it reads by name, so one dataset can carry several themes at once.
OutputStagingLayer.trap: The target layer is written for every point, including points the Point Filters rejected and points no variant covered, so it is a complete copy of the source layer rather than a sparse overlay of the swaps.

EntryDistributionSettings.tooltip: Re-picks the micro cache selection (secondary index, e.g. mesh material variants) of swapped points from the VARIANT entry's micro cache -- when disabled, swapped points get their secondary pick reset instead. Unswapped points are never touched. Same semantics as Distribute's Distribution (Micro-cache).

fields.name: Distribution
fields.tooltip: Distribution type

fields.name: IndexSettings
fields.tooltip: Index settings

EntryDistributionSettings.semantics: A swapped pick always loses its secondary index, because that index pointed into the source entry's own material pool. Enabled, the swapped point gets a fresh secondary pick from the variant entry's pool instead of an empty one. Unswapped points are never touched either way.
EntryDistributionSettings.trap: Only mesh entries carry a re-pickable pool, so a swap landing on any other entry type leaves the secondary pick cleared, and the node warns once when nothing it swapped to has one.

hints.text: Swapping does not re-fit. The transforms were fitted against the source entry's bounds, so a variant asset with a different footprint keeps the old fit. Chase a footprint-changing swap with Staging : Fitting.

UPCGExStateFactoryProviderSettings.name: State : Point
UPCGExStateFactoryProviderSettings.purpose: One named condition, wrapped so that **Write States** can fold it into a flag mask. The state owns a filter stack and nothing else: when that stack passes on a point it applies one bitmask operation to the point's shared mask, and when it fails it applies a second, independent one. It can also echo the two masks it was configured with onto its own output pins, which is how a downstream **Filter : Bitmask** gets the same value without it being typed twice.
UPCGExStateFactoryProviderSettings.situation: A condition that several later nodes need to test, cheap enough to answer once and carry as a bit rather than re-evaluating per consumer.

mechanism.text: This node produces no data of its own. When **Write States** reaches a point it asks each state whether its filters all pass there, then hands the verdict back, and the state applies its pass operation or its fail operation to that point's shared int64. A state never names an attribute and never creates one, so several states stack onto one number and the consumer alone decides where that number is written. `Priority` orders the stack, lowest first.

inputs.label: Filters
inputs.note: The condition this state tests. Point, Filter Group and Data filters all work; the pin also declares Vtx filters, which the point-level consumer cannot run. Required: with nothing wired here the factory is never built.

outputs.label: State
outputs.note: The state this node defines, for the **States** pin on **Write States**.

outputs.label: BitmaskPass
outputs.note: An attribute set holding a single int64 named OnPassBitmask: the mask this state would apply on a pass, or 0 when the pass half is switched off.
outputs.condition: when Output Bitmasks is on

outputs.label: BitmaskFail
outputs.note: The same for the fail half, named OnFailBitmask.
outputs.condition: when Output Bitmasks is on

Name.tooltip: Unique name for this state definition.
Name.semantics: Labels the node in the graph and reaches no data. Nothing downstream can select a state by it.

Priority.semantics: Orders this state against the others on the consumer's **States** pin, lowest first. Collisions between states land on bits rather than on names, so a state with a higher number gets the last word on a bit an earlier one set. Equal priorities are not resolved by the order the wires were drawn.

bOutputBitmasks.semantics: Governs the two advanced bitmask pins only. The masks they carry are the ones typed on this node, resolved once when the graph runs, so they say what the state is configured to do and never what it did to any point.

hints.text:
## The two halves of a state

`On Test Pass` guards `Pass State Flags`, the bitmask and operation applied when every filter passes. `On Test Fail` guards `Fail State Flags`, applied when any of them fails. Both ship enabled, exactly one of the two fires per point, and switching a half off leaves the shared mask alone in that case rather than clearing it.

Each half is a bitmask block carrying its own operation, and the rows inside the block reach the point's mask on their own terms as well as through that operation. A `Mutations` row set to OR still sets its bit when the half's operation is AND, and a **Bitmask Collection** row in `Compositions` set to SET still overwrites the mask when the half's operation is OR. Use the half's operation to describe the block as a whole, and the row operations to describe individual bits, rather than mixing the two.

A filter that cannot bind what it needs is dropped from this state's stack with a warning, and a state left holding no filters tests true on every point, so its pass mask lands everywhere. A misspelled attribute name inside the filter therefore reads as the state matching everything rather than as an error on this node.

The **Filters** pin declares the wider cluster-filter type, so a **Vtx Filter :** connects. The point-level **Write States** runs the stack through a point filter manager, which refuses a cluster filter with `Using a Cluster filter without cluster data` and drops it. Cluster-aware conditions belong on **Cluster : Write States** instead.

UPCGExStringCompareFilterProviderSetting.name: Filter : Compare (String)
UPCGExStringCompareFilterProviderSetting.purpose: Compares one text value read on the element against a second, either a constant you type or another attribute on that same element. Both operands come from the element being tested, which is what separates it from the rest of the string family: Filter : Self Compare (String) reads one attribute at two indices of the same dataset, Filter : Compare Nearest (String) reads one operand off a separate dataset, and Filter : Regex replaces the operator list with a pattern language. The operators reach past exact match into length comparison, ordering, substring tests and wildcard matching, so a great deal of the work that looks like it needs a regex lands here. Point both fields at `@Data.` attributes and the filter answers once per dataset instead of once per point, which is what lets Uber Filter (Data) route whole collections on it.
UPCGExStringCompareFilterProviderSetting.situation: Text already written onto the points, and the next node should act only where it matches, contains or outranks a second string.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per element and decides what the answer means; the filter itself reads no data of its own and writes nothing. Operand A is read on the element being tested, Operand B is either the constant or a second attribute read on that same element, and both arrive as text whatever type they are stored as. The verdict is the chosen operator applied to the pair in that order, so Operand A is always the left-hand side and Swap Operands is what reverses it.

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter passport, so it is accepted on every filter pin, Vtx Filters and Edge Filters included.

fields.name: OperandA
fields.tooltip: Operand A for testing -- Read as text (string comparison).

fields.name: Comparison
fields.tooltip: Comparison

fields.name: CompareAgainst
fields.tooltip: Type of OperandB

fields.tooltip: Operand B for testing -- Read as text (string comparison).

UPCGExStringCompareNearestFilterProvider.name: Filter : Compare Nearest (String)
UPCGExStringCompareNearestFilterProvider.purpose: Judges each element by a text value carried on the closest point of another dataset. That other dataset arrives on the Targets pin, and reaching outside the data being filtered is what this node has that the rest of the string family does not: Filter : Compare (String) reads both operands on the element, Filter : Self Compare (String) reads one attribute at two indices of the same dataset, and Filter : Regex tests a single value against a pattern. Because it holds target data of its own, it also carries the whole spatial apparatus: a search radius, a choice of how distance is measured against bounds, and rules pairing target datasets with the inputs they apply to.
UPCGExStringCompareNearestFilterProvider.situation: Two datasets in play, where the label deciding each element of the first one is stored on the second.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per element, and the comparison spans two datasets: Operand A is read on the closest point found on the Targets pin, Operand B on the element being tested, both as text. Every dataset wired to Targets joins one pool and the closest point can come from any of them, minus the tested element's own data while Ignore Self is on. Max Distance, read on the tested element and multiplied by the scale under it, bounds the search, and at its default of 0 the search is unbounded. An element with no qualifying target inside that radius fails, without the comparison running at all. The verdict is always one per element: Uber Branch and Break skip this filter with a warning that it cannot be used with collections, and Uber Filter (Data) falls back to counting element passes.

inputs.label: Targets
inputs.note: Several datasets can be wired here; they join one pool, and the closest point may come from any of them.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match rule sub-nodes deciding which target datasets may pair with each tested dataset. While Data Matching is Disabled the pin stays collapsed under the node's advanced pins.
inputs.condition: when Data Matching is set to All or Any

fields.name: DistanceScale
fields.tooltip: Constant scale applied to the Max Distance value. A non-positive result (e.g. a negative scale) means an unbounded search.

fields.name: bIgnoreSelf
fields.tooltip: Exclude the point's own data from the nearest search.

fields.name: DataMatching

fields.name: Comparison

fields.name: bSwapOperands
fields.tooltip: Swap operands. Useful to invert "contains" checks. Has no effect on equality comparisons.

hints.text: Missing Data Policy answers two failures here: a Targets pin that arrives empty, and a target dataset that does not carry Operand A. Both are settled before any element is tested, and the default of Fail replaces this node's output with an always-false filter rather than stopping the graph. Neither says anything under Pass or Fail; only Error logs, naming the selector in the Operand A case.

UPCGExStringRegexFilterProviderSettings.name: Filter : Regex
UPCGExStringRegexFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Tests one text value on the element against a regular expression. A pattern language is what this node has that the rest of the string family does not: Filter : Compare (String) offers a fixed operator list plus `*` and `?` wildcards, Filter : Self Compare (String) applies that list between two indices of one dataset, and Filter : Compare Nearest (String) applies it across two datasets. Reach for this one where the acceptable shape needs character classes, alternation, quantifiers or anchors. Point Operand A at a `@Data.` attribute and the filter answers once per dataset instead of once per point, which is what lets Uber Filter (Data) route whole collections on it.
UPCGExStringRegexFilterProviderSettings.situation: Text on the points whose acceptable shapes cannot be written as one equality, prefix or substring test.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per element and decides what the answer means; the filter itself reads no data of its own and writes nothing. Operand A is read on the element being tested and arrives as text whatever type it is stored as, then the pattern is searched for inside it. A hit anywhere in the value is a pass, so a pattern needs `^` and `$` to mean the whole value, and the shipped default of `.*` passes everything including an empty one. Invert flips that verdict afterwards. Matching is case-sensitive here, where every operator on Filter : Compare (String) ignores case; an inline `(?i)` at the front of the pattern folds case back in.

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter passport, so it is accepted on every filter pin, Vtx Filters and Edge Filters included.

fields.name: OperandA
fields.tooltip: Attribute whose value will be tested against the regex pattern.

fields.name: RegexPattern
fields.tooltip: Regex pattern to match against. Uses ICU regular expression syntax.

fields.name: bInvert
fields.tooltip: Invert the filter result (pass becomes fail and vice versa).

UPCGExStringSelfCompareFilterProviderSet.name: Filter : Self Compare (String)
UPCGExStringSelfCompareFilterProviderSet.purpose: Compares one text attribute against itself at a second index of the same dataset. There is one selector and no Operand B: the two sides are the same attribute read at two positions, which is what this node has instead of the second operand Filter : Compare (String) gives you, and instead of the separate dataset Filter : Compare Nearest (String) reaches into. Index Mode decides whether that second position is an offset from the element's own index or a position named outright. The full string operator list applies to the pair, so the question against the neighbour can be equality, length, ordering, substring or wildcard.
UPCGExStringSelfCompareFilterProviderSet.situation: An ordered dataset where the question is how a label changes from one element to the next, or how each element reads against one reference element.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this factory once per element; the filter reads nothing else and writes nothing. One selector supplies both sides: Operand A is read on the element being tested and read again at a second index of the same dataset, arriving as text whatever type it is stored as, so this node can only ever compare an attribute with itself. Index Mode decides which index that is, adding the Index value to the element's own position under Offset or naming a position outright under Pick; Index Safety decides what a position outside the dataset resolves to, and Invalid Index Fallback is the verdict for an element left without one. The second index never leaves the dataset the element belongs to, so a consumer holding several datasets runs a separate copy of the filter over each one, each with its own ends.

off_label.claim: An attribute-driven index under Pick turns this into a general pairwise text test inside one dataset. Write a partner index upstream, the index a sampler resolved for instance, and each element is compared against the element that index names rather than against a neighbour.
off_label.grounded_in: FStringSelfCompareFilter::Test using the per-point Index value directly as the target index when Index Mode is Pick, read through GetValueSettingIndex over Config.IndexAttribute

outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter passport, so it is accepted on every filter pin, Vtx Filters and Edge Filters included.

UPCGExSubdivideSettings.name: Path : Subdivide
UPCGExSubdivideSettings.purpose: Adds points inside the segments of a path and leaves the points already there exactly where they were. How many each segment gets comes from a spacing, a fixed count, or a Manhattan staircase, and what the new points are worth is decided by the `Blending` dropdown rather than by this node. The **Point Filters** pin picks which segments are subdivided, and the two additional outputs mark which points are new and how far along their segment each one landed.
UPCGExSubdivideSettings.situation: A path whose points sit too far apart for whatever reads it next, deformation, sampling or spawning, where the run itself is already right.

mechanism.text: One execution takes paths and returns the same points in the same order with new ones inserted between them. Nothing moves and nothing is removed, so the output count is the input count plus whatever every segment was granted, and a run that granted nothing anywhere comes back as a copy of its input. A segment starts at each point and reaches the next, so on an open path the last point starts none and can never be subdivided; close the path and the seam segment from the last point back to the first subdivides like any other. New points land on the straight line between the two points bracketing them, `Manhattan` excepted, and each one is given a fresh seed derived from where it landed after blending has run.

off_label.claim: Driving the amount from an attribute turns the node into its own per-segment gate: a segment whose value truncates to zero keeps its start point and gains nothing, so a single attribute decides both where subdivision happens and how dense it is, with the Point Filters pin left empty.
off_label.grounded_in: AmountGetter->Read(Index) feeds PCGExMath::TruncateDbl, and ProcessRange skips any segment whose NumSubdivisions is 0

inputs.label: Paths
inputs.note: The paths to subdivide.

inputs.label: Point Filters
inputs.note: Tested per point and read as a verdict on the segment that point starts. A segment whose start point fails keeps its own start point and gains nothing. Left empty, every segment is subdivided.

inputs.label: Overrides : Blending
inputs.note: Attribute set whose entries overwrite the picked blend rule's own properties by name. Sits under the node's advanced pins.

outputs.label: Paths
outputs.note: The original points in their original order, with the new ones between them.

SubdivideMethod.tooltip: Reference for computing the blending interpolation point point
SubdivideMethod.semantics: Decides what the amount is counted in. `Distance` reads it as a spacing and grants a segment as many points as fit, so long segments get more and the count varies along the path. `Count` reads it as the number of points to add and grants every admitted segment the same number whatever its length, cutting it into that many spans plus one. `Manhattan` ignores the amount entirely and steps between the two points one axis at a time, so the run between them stops being straight.

Distance.semantics: A spacing in world units, and the first new point sits exactly that far from the segment's start. The count is the segment length over this value, rounded by `Truncate Method`, so at the shipped `Floor` the node lays down whole steps from the start and what is left at the far end is the remainder: always shorter than one step, never longer. `Redistribute Evenly` is what removes it.
Distance.trap: A segment whose length divides evenly by the spacing has no remainder, so its last invented point lands on the segment's own end point and the output carries two points in one place.

Count.semantics: The number of points added to each segment, not the number of spans it ends up with: a count of 3 cuts one segment into four equal spans. Spacing is derived from the segment, so segments of different lengths end up with different spacing.

TruncateMethod.tooltip: How the subdivision count is rounded. Applies to Count as well, whose amount is read as a double.
TruncateMethod.semantics: Under `Distance` the count it rounds is the segment length over the spacing, so it is also what decides the remainder at the far end.
TruncateMethod.trap: With `Redistribute Evenly` off, `Ceil` and `Round` can grant a segment one point more than it holds: the spacing is still stepped off from the start, so that last point lands past the segment's own end, off the path entirely. The shipped `Floor` cannot do it, and neither can `None`, which lands on the same count.

bRedistributeEvenly.semantics: Keeps the count that the spacing worked out and then spreads that many points evenly across the whole segment, so the spacing you typed becomes an approximate target and every gap in the segment ends up equal. What it does not do is change how many points a segment gets.

ManhattanDetails.semantics: The zero to two points `Simple` promises follow from how many axes the segment actually crosses: an axis-aligned segment gets none and comes through unsubdivided, a segment moving in two axes gets the one corner between them, and one moving in all three gets two. The grid methods keep stepping at the grid size until they arrive, so their count follows that size against the segment's extent. `Order` decides which axis is walked first, which is what shapes the staircase.

Blending.semantics: The dropdown deciding what every point this node invents is worth. It hands the picked rule the two points bracketing a gap and the run between them; the rule and its settings own the rest.

SubPointFlagName.semantics: True on the points this node invented, false on the ones that came in. It is the cheapest way to hand the new points alone to a downstream filter, since nothing else about them differs.

AlphaAttributeName.semantics: Written on every output point, not only the new ones. A new point carries how far along its segment it sits, 0 at the start and 1 at the end, measured along the run the points actually make: under `Manhattan` that run is the staircase. An original point carries `Default Value` instead.

DefaultAlpha.semantics: The value every original point receives. It ships at 1, which is also the far end of the range the new points use, so leaving it alone makes an original point indistinguishable from a point that landed at the very end of a segment. Any value outside 0 to 1 separates the two.

bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.tooltip: If enabled, collections that have less than 2 points won't be processed and be omitted from the output.
bOmitInvalidPathsOutputs.semantics: Honoured here in the off position: a path of fewer than two points is refused before any work, forwarded untouched, and then dropped again at output time while this is on. Turning it off is what lets it through.

UPCGExSubPointsBlendInheritEnd.name: Inherit Last
UPCGExSubPointsBlendInheritEnd.purpose: Every invented point in a gap comes out holding a copy of the point the gap ends at. It hands the blend a weight of 1 and arrives with `Default Blending` already set to `Copy (Target)`, and both of those name the same value, the gap's last point. **Inherit First** is the same sub-node aimed at the other bracket.
UPCGExSubPointsBlendInheritEnd.situation: Points invented along a segment should carry the values of the point ahead of them, with nothing mixed in from behind.

mechanism.text: Every new point in a gap gets the same weight, 1, and `Default Blending` decides what that weight is worth. This sub-node arrives with it on `Copy (Target)`, which reads the gap's last point and never looks at the weight, so each invented point comes out holding a copy of that point for every attribute and property in scope. `Lerp` reaches the same values by the other road, since a weight of 1 lands on the same bracket. Nothing varies across the gap, so path direction is the whole result: reverse the path and the same sub-node inherits from the other end.

hints.text: On a closed path the final gap wraps, so the point it ends at is the path's own first point and the invented points in that gap inherit from the start of the path.

UPCGExSubPointsBlendInheritStart.name: Inherit First
UPCGExSubPointsBlendInheritStart.purpose: Every invented point in a gap comes out holding a copy of the point the gap starts at. It hands the blend a weight of 0 and arrives with `Default Blending` already set to `Copy (Source)`, and both of those name the same value, the gap's first point. **Inherit Last** is the same sub-node aimed at the other bracket.
UPCGExSubPointsBlendInheritStart.situation: Points invented along a segment should carry the values of the point behind them, with nothing mixed in from ahead.

mechanism.text: Every new point in a gap gets the same weight, 0, and `Default Blending` decides what that weight is worth. This sub-node arrives with it on `Copy (Source)`, which reads the gap's first point and never looks at the weight, so each invented point comes out holding a copy of that point for every attribute and property in scope. `Lerp` reaches the same values by the other road, since a weight of 0 lands on the same bracket. Nothing varies across the gap, so path direction is the whole result: reverse the path and the same sub-node inherits from the other end.

hints.text: This sub-node and **Inherit Last** arrive on different values of `Default Blending`, and that is the only place they differ. Set both to the same weight-ignoring mode and they become the same node: `Average` gives both the mean of the two bracketing points, `Copy (Source)` gives both the gap's first point, `Copy (Target)` gives both its last. Only a mode that reads the weight, `Lerp` among them, keeps them apart on a shared setting.

UPCGExSubPointsBlendInstancedFactory.name: Sub-Point Blending Operation
UPCGExSubPointsBlendInstancedFactory.purpose: Every path node that invents points has to decide what those points are worth, and this family is where that decision lives. It is a `Blending` dropdown in the details panel of seven nodes, **Path : Subdivide**, **Path : Insert**, **Path : Hatch**, **Path × Path Crossings**, **Path × Bounds Intersection**, **Pathfinding : Navmesh** and **Pathfinding : Plot Navmesh**, with four choices under it: **Interpolate**, **Inherit First**, **Inherit Last** and **No Blending**. All four carry the settings block on this page, which is what decides the mode, the attributes in scope, and the per-property and per-attribute exceptions. Those same seven nodes each carry an advanced **Overrides : Blending** pin: an attribute set whose names are matched one to one against the picked sub-node's own settings, so the choice can be driven from data.
UPCGExSubPointsBlendInstancedFactory.situation: Points a path node invented came back carrying values nobody chose, and the setting that chose them is that node's `Blending` dropdown.

mechanism.text: Work happens one gap at a time. The consumer hands over the two points bracketing a gap, the run of new points lying between them, and the length of that gap measured through those new points; each new point then receives a single weight, and the sub-node picked is the only thing deciding what that weight is. `Default Blending` decides what a weight means, and applies it between the two bracketing points across every attribute and all nine point properties; each sub-node arrives with its own value already in that setting. Three things sit outside it: the attributes the consumer writes itself, which it protects by name; data-domain attributes, which are skipped; and `Position`, which the family ships pinned to `None` so the placement the consumer computed survives.

off_label.claim: A new point never has a neighbour on one side only. Where a consumer adds points beyond a path's end, as **Path : Insert** does with its extensions, the outermost invented point is promoted to being a bracket and keeps whatever the consumer gave it, and the rest blend between that point and the path's real endpoint.
off_label.grounded_in: the pre-path and post-path extension blocks in PCGExPathInsert, which pass the outermost inserted point as the From or To bracket and scope the blend to the remainder

hints.text: `Seed` is one of the nine properties and blends by default. Under **Inherit First** or **Inherit Last** every invented point in a gap ends up carrying the same seed as the point it inherited from, so anything downstream that randomises per point repeats across the whole gap. **Path : Subdivide** writes a fresh spatial seed after blending and escapes this on its own; the nodes that write theirs before the blend do not. Set `Seed`'s override to `None` wherever it matters.

UPCGExSubPointsBlendInterpolate.name: Interpolate
UPCGExSubPointsBlendInterpolate.purpose: The one sub-node in the family that gives each invented point a weight of its own. **Inherit First** and **Inherit Last** hand every point in a gap the same weight; this one varies it across the gap, so whatever `Default Blending` makes of weight 0 at one end and weight 1 at the other is spread across the points in between. It arrives with that setting on `Lerp`, the mode that reads the weight. `Blend Over` decides what the variation is measured against.
UPCGExSubPointsBlendInterpolate.situation: The points a node invented along a segment should carry a value that ramps from the point the gap starts at to the point it ends at.

mechanism.text: Each new point in a gap receives its own weight, and `Default Blending` turns that weight into a value drawn from the two points bracketing the gap. `Blend Over` is the only thing deciding the weight, and neither of its two varying modes reaches 1: the weight is measured across the new points and divided by a span that runs all the way to the bracketing point at the far end, so the last new point always stops short of the far bracket's own values.

BlendOver.semantics: `Distance` is the only mode that reads where a point actually sits, measuring along the gap through the new points, so unevenly spaced points receive unevenly spaced weights and none of them lands on 0. `Count` ignores position and divides each point's rank within its own gap by the number of new points there, so four new points get 0, a quarter, a half and three quarters however they are spaced, and the first of them is a copy of the gap's first bracket. `Fixed` reads neither and hands the same `Lerp` value to every point in every gap. A gap that measures zero length falls back from `Distance` to `Count`.

Lerp.semantics: Fills the slot the varying weight would have filled, so every point in every gap comes out identical. At 0 it reproduces **Inherit First** and at 1 **Inherit Last**; the values between are the only way to ask for a fixed mix of the two bracketing points.

UPCGExSubPointsBlendNone.name: No Blending
UPCGExSubPointsBlendNone.purpose: Skips the blend. No blender is built, nothing reads the two bracketing points, and the invented points keep whatever the consumer left on them.
UPCGExSubPointsBlendNone.situation: The consumer already wrote the values the invented points should carry, and a blend would write over them.

mechanism.text: What a new point carries is entirely the consumer's doing, and this sub-node adds nothing to it. In **Path : Subdivide** the consumer writes a position and a seed, so every attribute on an invented point comes back at its own default value rather than at anything either neighbour holds. Where a consumer writes more than that, forwarding values onto the points it invented, those values are what remains.

hints.text: The blending block still shows in the panel, inherited from the family base, and nothing here ever reads it. A filter, a mode or an override set on this sub-node changes nothing at all.

UPCGExTagCheckFilterProviderSettings.name: Data Filter : Tag Check
UPCGExTagCheckFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Asks whether a dataset carries a tag, and answers for the dataset as a whole. Tags come in two shapes: a bare marker such as `Enemy`, and a pair written `Key:Value` such as `Spawner:Cave`, split at the first colon when both halves have text in them. `Strict` is what decides whether a pair is matched by its key alone or by its whole text, and what the value of a pair actually says is the subject of **Data Filter : Tag Value** instead.
UPCGExTagCheckFilterProviderSettings.situation: Datasets marked upstream by whichever branch produced them, where only one of those markings should carry on.

mechanism.text: Each of the dataset's tags is compared against `Tag Name` under `Match`, and the first that matches passes the whole test. The tag is the left side of the comparison and what you typed is the right. `Strict` chooses what a `Key:Value` pair contributes to that comparison: its key on its own, or the whole pair as one string. A bare marker is compared whole either way, and a dataset carrying no tags fails.

outputs.label: Data Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. The Data Filter family qualifies for dataset-level evaluation by construction, with no condition on how the node is configured, so every filter pin in the plugin takes it, **Uber Branch** and **Break** included.

UPCGExTagValueFilterProviderSettings.name: Data Filter : Tag Value
UPCGExTagValueFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Compares what a `Key:Value` tag carries, and answers for the dataset as a whole. `Tag Name` and `Match` select the tags that take part by their key, and `Value Type` states whether their values are read as numbers or as text. Bare markers hold no value and are out of reach here; asking whether a tag is present at all is **Data Filter : Tag Check**.
UPCGExTagValueFilterProviderSettings.situation: Datasets stamped upstream with a graded value, where only the ones past a threshold should reach the next stage.

mechanism.text: Every `Key:Value` tag whose key matches `Tag Name` under `Match` is gathered, and a dataset where none matched fails outright. Each gathered value already has a type, fixed when the tag was read: a whole number, a decimal, a vector, a boolean, or text. `Value Type` states which of those the comparison expects, and a value it cannot reach fails the comparison instead of being converted. `Multi Match` combines the verdicts when more than one tag was gathered.

off_label.claim: In `String` mode the operator list includes length comparisons, so the node can gate on how long a tag's text value is without regard for what it says.
off_label.grounded_in: The length variants of EPCGExStringComparison, reached through PCGExCompare::Compare on the gathered tag value

outputs.label: Data Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. The Data Filter family qualifies for dataset-level evaluation by construction, with no condition on how the node is configured, so every filter pin in the plugin takes it, **Uber Branch** and **Break** included.

UPCGExTangentsInstancedFactory.name: Tangents (Base)
UPCGExTangentsInstancedFactory.purpose: Tangent rules decide, per point, how a curve arrives at that point and how it leaves it. Five ship, and they all answer with the same pair of vectors: **Path : Write Tangents** stores that pair as two vector attributes, while **Create Spline**, both Spline Mesh nodes and **Copy to Path** carry a `Source` picker that reads two named attributes, runs a rule in place, or asks for no tangents at all. Its default is the attribute route, reading `ArriveTangent` and `LeaveTangent`, which are the names **Path : Write Tangents** writes by default. Direction decides which way the curve leans through the point and length decides how far it holds that lean, so a long tangent carries the curve past the straight line between neighbours and a zero-length one flattens it onto that line.
UPCGExTangentsInstancedFactory.situation: A path is about to become a spline or a run of spline meshes, and the curve running between its points has to be decided.

mechanism.text: A rule is called once per point and handed the point positions plus three indices: the point, its predecessor and its successor. It fills in both vectors, and the two scales the consumer read at that point arrive as arguments, so the rule does the multiplying rather than the consumer. On a closed path every point is an interior point, because the neighbour indices wrap. An open path's first and last are not, and the base answers for them rather than the rule: the first gets the whole vector running from it to the second point, the last the whole vector from the second-to-last to it, and arrive and leave both get that same vector. `Start Override` and `End Override` put a rule of your choosing in place of that answer, and on a closed path neither is ever consulted.

hints.text: Only two of the five rules answer differently at an open path's ends. **From Transform** and **Zero** define their own first-point and last-point behaviour; **Auto**, **Catmull-Rom** and **From Neighbors** fall through to the base's. Choosing one of those three as `Start Override` or `End Override` changes nothing at the two endpoints.

`Arrive Scale` and `Leave Scale` belong to the consumer. **Path : Write Tangents** carries them on the node as full vectors, the other four inside their own Tangents block, where the constant is one number spread across all three axes. Both multiply component by component in world axes, so an uneven scale swings the tangent off the direction the rule computed as well as changing its length.

UPCGExTensorDotFilterProviderSettings.name: Filter : Tensor Dot
UPCGExTensorDotFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Turns alignment with a tensor field into a pass or fail. The tensors wired into the Tensors pin composite into one field, the filter samples it at each element's own transform, and the sampled direction is set against a vector read from the element. The comparison is a dot product, so what decides the verdict is how closely the two point the same way, at whatever cutoff Dot Comparison Details names. It answers per element only, so the consumers that judge whole datasets never take it.
UPCGExTensorDotFilterProviderSettings.situation: A field is already shaping the scene, and the next node should touch only the elements facing along it, or only the ones facing across it.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this filter once per element. The field is sampled at the element's transform and both the sampled direction and Operand A are normalised, so nothing either side does to its own length reaches the verdict; what meets the threshold is the dot product of the two bearings. An element the field cannot answer for, one sitting where no tensor reaches, fails outright and never reaches the comparison at all.

off_label.claim: Set the cutoff so nothing the field reaches can fail it, a Scalar threshold of -1 with the greater-or-equal operator against a unit-length Operand A, and the filter reports coverage instead of alignment: every element the field reaches passes, and every element it does not reach fails.
off_label.grounded_in: FTensorDotFilter::Test returning false on a failed sample before the dot comparison is reached

inputs.label: Tensors
inputs.note: The tensors that make up the field. Several are accepted and composite into one, so the dot is taken against the composite and never against one tensor at a time.

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter passport, so it is accepted on every filter pin, Vtx Filters and Edge Filters included.

hints.text: An empty or unusable Tensors pin is what Missing Data Policy governs on this node, which is why the setting is live here. At its shipped value of Fail the node still emits a filter, a constant one failing every element; at Pass, a constant one passing every element; at Error the node cancels instead of producing anything.

UPCGExTensorFactoryProviderSettings.name: Tensor Definition
UPCGExTensorFactoryProviderSettings.purpose: The base every **Tensor :** node inherits. It never appears in the palette, and this page carries what the fourteen of them share: the **Tensor** pin they all emit on, the per-source **Potency** and **Weight** with their falloff curves, and the **Tensor Weight** deciding a tensor's share once several of them stack. Anything with a **Tensors** pin reads them: **Tensors : Extrude**, **Tensors Transform**, **Probe : Tensor**, **Heuristics : Tensor** and **Filter : Tensor Dot**.
UPCGExTensorFactoryProviderSettings.situation: Reading any tensor page and needing to know what its Potency, Weight and falloff curves are doing, or how far one effector reaches.

mechanism.text: A tensor answers one question: what does the field say at this transform. It hands back a direction carrying a length, a rotation, and a count of the sources that reached that spot; a count of zero means it has nothing to say there and it drops out of the field. What separates the fourteen is where the answer comes from, with six reading effector points, four reading a path or a spline, and four needing no source at all. What they share is how one answer is built. Every source in reach contributes a direction, a **Potency** setting that direction's length and a **Weight** setting its share, both scaled by their own falloff curve read at the distance to the source. Those contributions are averaged by weight into the one direction the tensor reports. **Tensor Weight** sits outside that sum: it is the share the whole answer claims once several tensors composite.

inputs.label: Effectors
inputs.note: The points a tensor draws its field from, read as ordinary point data: each one is a source with a position, an orientation and a reach. Only the effector-driven tensors carry this pin. The path and spline tensors take a **Paths** or **Splines** pin in its place, and **Tensor : Constant**, **Tensor : Inertia (Constant)** and **Tensor : Noise** take no source pin at all.
inputs.condition: on Tensor : Pole, Flow, Spin, Inertia, Null and Noise (Bounded)

inputs.label: Parent Tensor
inputs.note: An advanced pin, and a copying shortcut: only the first tensor on it is read, and the settings on this node are then overwritten from it. A parent of the same tensor type replaces the whole panel here, which is how one authored configuration drives many nodes. A parent of a different type shares nothing the panel shows, so nothing visible transfers.

outputs.label: Tensor
outputs.note: What every **Tensor :** node emits. Any pin labelled **Tensors** takes it, and several of them on one pin is what makes a field.

Priority.tooltip: Tensor Priority, only accounted for by if sampler is in any Ordered- mode.

hints.text: Tensors are read in the order they arrive on the pin, and nothing reorders them. That order leaves the composited direction alone, which is a weighted sum, and it does reach the composited rotation, which is folded in one tensor at a time starting from whichever arrived first.

An effector reaches as far as its own scaled bounds, measured as a sphere whose radius is the length of the bounds extent, so scaling an effector point scales its reach and a point with no bounds reaches nowhere. The lookup that finds candidate effectors reads the point's `Steepness` too, searching a box of twice the extents at a Steepness of 0 and one times the extents at 1, so a high-Steepness effector stops short of its own sphere.

**Sampling Mutations** appears on the tensors that support it and reshapes that tensor's own answer before the field is composited: **Invert** mirrors it, **Scale** multiplies it per axis, and **Bidirectional** turns it around where it disagrees with an axis of the transform being sampled. The consumers carry a second, separate block of the same kind that acts on the finished field.

UPCGExTensorSampler.name: Tensor Sampler (Default)
UPCGExTensorSampler.purpose: The sampler every consumer starts on, and the base the other three extend. A sampler settles two things the tensors do not: how many places the field is read to answer one question, and how those readings fold into a single direction. This one reads once, at the position it was asked about. It also owns the step the other three build on, where the tensors on a pin become one field, so what is written here holds for all four.
UPCGExTensorSampler.situation: Reading a field that changes little between one step and the next, or working out what the other samplers are spending their extra reads on.

mechanism.text: One reading is one pass over every tensor on the pin. Each is asked at the same transform, the ones that answer are kept, and their directions are averaged by the share each claims through its **Tensor Weight**; their rotations are folded in one at a time, in the order the tensors arrive. A tensor reaching nothing there is left out of the average instead of counted as zero, so a field with gaps still answers wherever anything covers it, and with only one tensor answering its reading is handed back untouched, weights and all. When nothing answers the read fails, and the consumer decides what that means: an extrusion ends, a point stops moving, a filter fails. This sampler takes one reading. The other three take more, which is the whole of the difference between them.

Radius.semantics: The step length in world units that the stepping samplers work in: **Six Points** offsets its six reads by it, **RK4** scales its four stages into it, and **Adaptive RK** takes it as the full step it then subdivides. This sampler reads at the position it was given and never consults it. It is a sampling distance and not a reach: how far a tensor carries is set on the tensor.

MinStepFraction.tooltip: Minimum step size as fraction of base radius
MinStepFraction.semantics: Read by **Adaptive RK** alone, which clamps the step it chose between this fraction of `Radius` and `Max Step Fraction`. Raising it puts a floor under how finely a tight bend can be followed.

MaxStepFraction.tooltip: Maximum step size as fraction of base radius
MaxStepFraction.semantics: Read by **Adaptive RK** alone, and the ceiling of the same clamp. Above 1 it lets a straight stretch of field be crossed in a step longer than `Radius`.

ErrorTolerance.tooltip: Error tolerance for step size adaptation
ErrorTolerance.semantics: Read by **Adaptive RK** alone, and the numerator of the step it picks: the chosen step is this value divided by the turn rate measured at the probe, before the two fractions clamp it. Lowering it shortens the step everywhere and buys accuracy with reads.

MaxSubSteps.semantics: Read by **Adaptive RK** alone, and the cost ceiling: it caps how many sub-steps one answer may cost, each of them four reads. A bend tight enough to hit the cap is walked in steps longer than the tolerance asked for, so this is where accuracy is traded back for time.

hints.text: A sampler is chosen from a class dropdown, inside **Tensor Sampling Settings** on the consumer, and never wired in as a sub-node. The five values below live in that same block, on the consumer, and are copied onto the sampler when the run starts, so the consumer is the only place they can be authored.

Setting a tensor's **Tensor Weight** to zero to mute it is safe while another tensor still answers at that position. Where every tensor answering sits at zero, the shares cannot be worked out and the reading comes back as not-a-number, which reaches the consumer as a position or a rotation made of them.

Only this sampler and **Adaptive RK** report a rotation that describes the field. **Six Points** and **RK4** build theirs by multiplying their stage rotations together, and **Six Points** then shrinks the result to a sixth of unit length, so neither is an orientation for the position asked about. Every consumer reading the sampled direction is unaffected; the one reading the rotation is **Tensors Transform** in its `Absolute` and `Relative` modes.

UPCGExTensorSamplerAdaptive.name: Tensor Sampler (Adaptive RK)
UPCGExTensorSamplerAdaptive.purpose: Measures how sharply the field is turning before it commits to a step, then walks that step in as many four-reading passes as the turn rate calls for. A straight stretch is crossed in one pass and a tight bend in several, so the same accuracy holds through both without paying bend prices everywhere. Its cost varies from point to point, which none of the other three do, and it is the only one reading all five values in the block.
UPCGExTensorSamplerAdaptive.situation: A field that runs smooth over most of its extent and turns hard in a few places, where a step short enough for the bends would be wasted on everything else.

mechanism.text: Two readings measure the turn: one at the probe, one a quarter of a **Radius** further along it. The angle between them sets the step this sampler wants, **Error Tolerance** divided by that turn rate, clamped between **Min Step Fraction** and **Max Step Fraction** of **Radius**. A full step of one **Radius** is then split into that many equal sub-steps, capped at **Max Sub Steps**, and each sub-step is a four-reading pass in the manner of **RK4** that advances the probe before the next one runs. One last reading supplies the rotation, so the orientation reported describes the field where the step landed. An answer costs three readings plus four for every sub-step. A sub-step that runs off the field ends the walk there, and the shortened step still counts as a success.

hints.text: This is the one sampler whose reported rotation is an orientation the field gives, and it is taken at the end of the step rather than at the probe, which is up to one **Radius** away. **Tensors Transform** and **Tensors : Extrude** read it in their `Absolute` and `Relative` modes; both ship on `Align`, which reads the direction.

**Tensors Transform**'s optional **Effectors Pings** attribute counts the sources reached by the first reading of every sub-step, so under this sampler it scales with how many sub-steps that point happened to take. Two points sitting in the same coverage can report figures a factor of **Max Sub Steps** apart.

All five values in **Tensor Sampling Settings** reach this sampler, and it is the only one of the four for which that is true. **Radius** sets how far the step goes, scaled by the length of the readings that build it in the same way **RK4** works, and the other four decide how finely it is walked.

UPCGExTensorSamplerRK4.name: Tensor Sampler (RK4)
UPCGExTensorSamplerRK4.purpose: Reads the field four times in a chain and answers with where a step lands, rather than with the direction sitting under the probe. Each read starts from where the one before it pointed, and what that buys is a curve staying on the field instead of drifting off the outside of every bend, which is what one reading per step does once the step is long enough to see. The cost is fixed at four readings per answer, whatever the field is doing there.
UPCGExTensorSamplerRK4.situation: An extrusion through a curving field is cutting the corners and ending up outside the streamline it started on.

mechanism.text: Four readings, each a full pass over the tensors on the pin, chained by what the last one said. The first is taken at the probe, the second half a step along the first reading, the third half a step along the second, the fourth a full step along the third. Every offset is measured from the probe, so the four sit around it instead of walking away from it. They are then folded together in the classical one, two, two, one proportion, and what comes back is where a step of one **Radius** lands. That step is **Radius** scaled by the length of the reading that set it, and a reading is as long as the effectors' **Potency** makes it. A probe standing on nothing fails all four stages together, so this sampler answers wherever **Default** does.

hints.text: Two of the values handed back are accumulated across the four stages rather than measured once. The rotation is the four stages' rotations multiplied together, which describes no orientation, and it reaches **Tensors Transform** and **Tensors : Extrude** only in their `Absolute` and `Relative` modes; both ship on `Align`, which reads the direction. The source count behind **Tensors Transform**'s optional **Effectors Pings** attribute is the total across all four readings, so it runs at roughly four times the figure one reading would report.

The last three stages read at a probe whose rotation has been turned by the reading before them, so anything that answers from the probe's own orientation gives a different answer there: **Tensor : Inertia**, **Tensor : Inertia (Constant)**, **Tensor : Surface**'s reference axis, and any tensor with **Bidirectional** switched on. A stage's own weight scales how far the probe moves and not how far it turns, so all three take the full turn whatever the length of their offset.

**Radius** is the only one of the five values in **Tensor Sampling Settings** this sampler reads; the other four reach **Adaptive RK** alone. It sets how far out the three later stages read and how long the returned displacement is, and that length is then replaced by **Size** in the same block whenever **Normalize** is on, which is how it ships.

UPCGExTensorSamplerSixPoints.name: Tensor Sampler (Six Points)
UPCGExTensorSamplerSixPoints.purpose: Reads the field in six places around the probe and averages them, so detail finer than the distance between them stops reaching the answer. The six sit one **Radius** out along each world axis, which makes **Radius** the setting deciding how much smoothing there is. Six readings go into one answer where **Default** takes one, and that is the whole of the cost.
UPCGExTensorSamplerSixPoints.situation: A noise tensor in the stack is making an extrusion wander from step to step, and what is wanted is the trend under the grain.

mechanism.text: Six readings, each a full pass over the tensors on the pin, taken at the probe pushed one **Radius** along each world axis in both directions. Their directions are summed and divided by six, which is the whole of the smoothing. The probe position is not one of the six, and that is what decides whether the read succeeds: a probe standing on a tensor still fails when all six offsets land on nothing, and a probe standing on nothing still answers when one of them lands on something. The offsets are measured in world space, so the point's own rotation does not turn the pattern with it.

hints.text: Two of the values handed back are accumulated across the six readings rather than measured once. The rotation is the six rotations multiplied together and then shrunk to a sixth of unit length, so it describes no orientation, and it reaches **Tensors Transform** and **Tensors : Extrude** only in their `Absolute` and `Relative` modes; both ship on `Align`, which reads the direction. The source count behind **Tensors Transform**'s optional **Effectors Pings** attribute is the total across all six readings, so it runs at roughly six times the figure one reading would report.
**Radius** is the only one of the five values in **Tensor Sampling Settings** this sampler reads. The other four reach **Adaptive RK** alone.

UPCGExTensorsTransformSettings.name: Tensors Transform
UPCGExTensorsTransformSettings.purpose: Walks points through a field without turning them into paths. Each point reads the tensors wired in at its own position, moves by what it finds, and repeats for as many iterations as it is given, so a scatter comes out drifted along the field and, if asked, turned to face it. The dataset survives whole: same count, same order, same attributes, new transforms. Five optional attributes record what happened to each point, including whether it stopped before the iterations ran out.
UPCGExTensorsTransformSettings.situation: A scatter already exists and should be pushed, combed or swirled by a field instead of being regenerated from it.

mechanism.text: Points come out one for one, in input order, carrying everything they arrived with; only their transforms change. On each iteration a point reads the field at its current position and moves by the direction and length that reading gives, so a run of iterations is a walk the node takes and does not record. A point that reads nothing, or that a stop filter catches, is finished: it keeps its last position and sits out every remaining iteration, which is why raising the iteration count costs less than it looks. The **Filters** pin decides which points take part at all, and the ones it rejects pass straight through untouched.

off_label.claim: One iteration with **Transform Position** off and `Rotation` on `Align` turns the node into a field-alignment pass: nothing moves, and every point ends up facing whichever way the field points where it already stands.
off_label.grounded_in: the rotation branch reads the sampled direction and is applied independently of bTransformPosition, and with the position unchanged a second iteration would read the same answer

off_label.claim: **Max Iterations Reached** doubles as a coverage report: with the stop pin empty it is written only for the points the field reached on every pass, so the points it leaves false are the ones sitting in the field's gaps.
off_label.grounded_in: a failed read deactivates the point for the rest of the run, so its update count stops short of the iteration count and the flag is written from that comparison

inputs.label: In
inputs.note: The points to move. Several datasets can be wired, and each is walked on its own.

inputs.label: Filters
inputs.note: Narrows which points the walk applies to. Rejected points are copied to the output untouched, so this thins the effect rather than the dataset.

inputs.label: Tensors
inputs.note: The tensor sub-nodes composited into the field. With none, the node errors out.

inputs.label: Stop Conditions
inputs.note: Point filters marking where a point is not allowed to be. A point that satisfies one stops there and takes no further iteration. Unwired, only the iteration count and the field's own gaps end a walk.

outputs.label: Out
outputs.note: The same points with new transforms, one dataset out per dataset in, and the optional report attributes on them.

bTransformPosition.tooltip: Whether to update point positions using tensor sampling.
bTransformPosition.semantics: Off, the points hold their positions and every iteration reads the field at the same place, so the answer never changes and the iteration count stops mattering for the movement. Under `Relative` the same rotation is still applied on each pass and compounds, which is the one thing that keeps growing with iterations while nothing moves.

bTransformRotation.tooltip: Whether to update point rotations using tensor sampling.

Rotation.semantics: `Align` is the only value that reads the sampled direction: it turns the point so `Align Axis` runs along the step. `Absolute` replaces the point's rotation with the one the field reports, and `Relative` composes that rotation onto the one the point already carries, so under `Relative` the turn accumulates across iterations. The field's rotation is built with its own forward along the composited direction, so `Absolute` and `Align` at `Forward` put the point's forward in the same place and differ in what fills the other two axes: `Align` keeps the point's current up as a hint, `Absolute` has no hint to keep.
Rotation.trap: The field reports a rotation worth using only under the Default and Adaptive RK samplers. Six Points and RK4 build theirs by multiplying their stage rotations together, so `Absolute` and `Relative` under either of those give an orientation unrelated to the field. `Align` reads the direction instead and is unaffected, which is also the shipped value.

AlignAxis.tooltip: The axis to align with movement direction.
AlignAxis.semantics: Names the local axis that ends up running along the step, so `Up` lays the point's +Z along the field and `Backward` points its -X that way. The point's current up vector goes in as the secondary hint, which is what stops a run of iterations from rolling arbitrarily about the step.

Iterations.tooltip: Number of iterations to apply tensor transforms.
Iterations.semantics: Each iteration is a fresh read at the point's new position, so raising it bends the walk with the field where a single long step would run straight. Step length is set in the sampling block, not here.
Iterations.trap: One pass always runs. A value of 0 or below still applies a single step, and both report flags then come out false for every point that moved.

StopConditionHandling.tooltip: How to deal with points that are stopped
StopConditionHandling.semantics: `Exclude` drops the step the filter caught, leaving the point where it stood when the condition became true. `Include` applies that step first and stops afterwards, so the point ends one step inside the region the filter describes. Neither removes anything from the output: the enum is shared with the extrusion, where the choice is about a path's last point.

EffectorsPingsAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write the total number of effectors that affected the transform, all iterations combined. This is hardly a measure of anything, but it's an interesting value nonetheless

UpdateCountAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'int32' attribute to write the number of iterations that affected the point before it stopped.

TraveledDistanceAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'double' attribute to write the approximative distance travelled by this point.
TraveledDistanceAttributeName.semantics: Summed over the positions the point was read at, in world units, and along the walk rather than end to end, so a point that curled back on itself still reports the whole journey.
TraveledDistanceAttributeName.trap: The last step applied is never counted, because the distance is accumulated at the start of each iteration and nothing closes the sum afterwards. At one iteration the value is always 0, and at more it is short by the length of the final step.

GracefullyStoppedAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'bool' attribute to tag the point with if transform stopped before the maximum number of iterations.
GracefullyStoppedAttributeName.semantics: Written from the count of iterations that moved the point, so it means the walk ended early for any reason: a stop filter, or the field having nothing to say where the point stood.
GracefullyStoppedAttributeName.trap: A point the **Filters** pin rejected never moved at all, counts zero iterations, and is written as gracefully stopped alongside the points that genuinely stopped short.

MaxIterationsReachedAttributeName.tooltip: Name of the 'bool' attribute to tag the point with if it has reached the max number of iterations set. Faster alternative to comparing multiple attributes.
MaxIterationsReachedAttributeName.semantics: The complement of **Gracefully Stopped** at any iteration count of 1 or more, offered separately so a downstream filter can test one attribute instead of comparing two.

TensorHandlerDetails.tooltip: Tensor sampling settings. These are applied on the flattened sample, e.g after & on top of individual tensors' mutations.
TensorHandlerDetails.semantics: Where the step length comes from. With **Normalize** on, which is how it ships, the composited direction is scaled to unit length and multiplied by **Size**, so nothing the tensors say about magnitude reaches the movement and **Size** alone sets how far a point travels per iteration; it reads per point, so an attribute on the input drives it. **Uniform Scale** multiplies afterwards, **Invert** turns the step around, and **Sampler Settings** picks which sampler reads the field and carries its parameters. This block acts on the finished field, after each tensor's own **Sampling Mutations** have acted on its answer.
TensorHandlerDetails.trap: **Invert** turns the reported rotation around as well as the direction, and the turn it applies is not the mirror of the sample, so `Absolute` and `Relative` under **Invert** give an orientation that does not correspond to the inverted step. `Align` reads the direction and is unaffected.

hints.text: Stop filters are evaluated directly, without the attribute buffers a normal filter pass sets up, so filters that need one are dropped before the run starts. The dropped ones are named in a warning and the node carries on with whatever survived; when none survive, the warning says so and nothing stops the walks at all. **Filter : Distance** is the common casualty, since it opts out as soon as its threshold is read from an attribute.

A point standing where no tensor reaches stops there on the first pass and never moves. **Tensor : Constant** at a low weight covers the whole field and is the usual fix for a run where most of the points barely shifted.

UPCGExTexParamProviderSettings.name: Texture Param
UPCGExTexParamProviderSettings.purpose: Names one texture parameter on a material and says what a consumer should write when it finds it. A material exposes its textures by name, so the node reading them needs to be told which name to look for and what to call the results. It emits a factory on the Texture Param pin, read by **Get Texture Data**, **Sample : Texture** and **Sample : Line Trace**, and several of these on one pin describe several parameters at once.
UPCGExTexParamProviderSettings.situation: Materials that expose a mask or a heightmap under a known parameter name, and a graph that wants that texture's values on its points.

mechanism.text: The factory carries a name to look for and a set of names to write to, and the consumer does the work. `Material Parameter Name` is the key looked up on whatever material the consumer resolved; a material without that parameter contributes nothing for this factory and the consumer carries on with the others. `Texture ID Attribute Name` receives what was found, and `Sample Attribute Name` receives the value read out of it. `Sampled Channels` decides which of R, G, B and A are read, always in that order whatever order you tick them in, and `Output Type` decides the shape they are packed into. `Scale` multiplies the result on the way out.

outputs.label: Texture Param
outputs.note: The parameter definition, read by every node that resolves textures off a material. **Get Texture Data** and **Sample : Texture** declare the pin required outright, so neither runs without one. **Sample : Line Trace** declares it only while its render-material output and that output's texture extraction are both on, and does not show the pin at all otherwise.

Config.tooltip: Texture parameter configuration for sampling and output.

fields.name: MaterialParameterName
fields.tooltip: Name of the texture parameter to look for, when used in node that are set up to require this info.

fields.name: TextureIDAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to output the path to

fields.name: SampleAttributeName
fields.tooltip: Name of the attribute to output the sampled value to

fields.name: OutputType
fields.tooltip: Type of the attribute to output the sampled value to

fields.name: SampledChannels
fields.tooltip: What components will be sampled. Output is truncated or sparse depending on the selected output type.

fields.name: Scale
fields.tooltip: Apply a scale factor to the output value

fields.name: TextureIndex
fields.tooltip: Index into the texture array to sample (-1 for non-array textures).

hints.text: The node's subtitle is built from the two output attribute names, so a graph with several of these on one pin reads as a list of what each one writes without opening any panel.

UPCGExTimeFilterProviderSettings.name: Filter : Time
UPCGExTimeFilterProviderSettings.purpose: Reads a point's location as a position along a path. The paths, splines and polygons wired to the Targets pin are the ruler: each element is projected onto the closest one, which gives a figure running from 0 at the start of that path to 1 at its end, and the comparison judges that figure. Time here is parametric position and nothing temporal, so no lifetime, age or simulation step is involved. Compared against a constant it keeps a band of the path, and compared against an attribute it lets every element carry its own cutoff.
UPCGExTimeFilterProviderSettings.situation: Which elements survive depends on how far along a path they sit rather than on how close to it they are.

mechanism.text: The consumer runs this filter once per element. The element's location is projected onto the wired paths, the closest projection yields a figure between 0 and 1, and Comparison judges that figure against Operand B. The figure counts segments rather than distance: it is the projection's place in the path's own point order divided by the number of segments, so on a path whose points are unevenly spaced 0.5 lands on the middle segment and not at the halfway point. Pick decides which paths get a say, and Time Consolidation decides how several answers collapse into one.

inputs.label: Targets
inputs.note: The paths the position is measured along. Point paths, splines and 2D polygons are all accepted, and several of them can be wired at once.

inputs.label: Match Rules
inputs.note: Match rules deciding which target paths each tested dataset is allowed to see. The pin is always present, sitting among the advanced pins until Data Matching is switched on.
inputs.condition: when Data Matching Mode is All or Any

outputs.label: Filter
outputs.note: The filter this node defines. It carries the point-filter type, so every filter pin accepts it, Vtx and Edge pins included.

hints.text: An empty Targets pin routes through Missing Data Policy rather than Initialization Failure Policy, and so does a pin whose every target was dropped: a path of fewer than two points, or a spline with no segment. Each drop logs its own warning, but the empty result that follows logs nothing at all unless that policy is set to Error.

UPCGExTopologyClusterSurfaceSettings.name: Topology : Cluster Surface
UPCGExTopologyClusterSurfaceSettings.purpose: Fills in the faces of a cluster. The edges already say which Vtx are joined, so the enclosed loops are already decided, and this turns each of them into geometry rather than inventing connectivity. That is what separates it from **Topology : Point Surface**, which triangulates a scatter and has to work out neighbours for itself.
UPCGExTopologyClusterSurfaceSettings.situation: A cluster whose cells were built deliberately, and now need to exist as a mesh rather than as a diagram.

mechanism.text: The cluster's edges enclose loops, each loop becomes a face, and the faces are appended to one dynamic mesh. Nothing here decides which points connect: that was settled when the cluster was built, so changing the surface means changing the cluster. The constraints on which loops qualify are the cell settings the node inherits, and everything past the triangulation belongs to the topology block.

outputs.label: Mesh
outputs.note: The dynamic mesh built from the cluster's enclosed loops.

hints.text: The surface follows the cluster exactly, so a hole in the mesh is a hole in the connectivity. Fixing it means adding edges upstream rather than adjusting anything here.

UPCGExTopologyPathSurfaceSettings.name: Topology : Path Surface
UPCGExTopologyPathSurfaceSettings.purpose: Fills a path in. The path is an outline, so the shape is already decided and this turns its interior into geometry. It is the simplest of the topology nodes to reason about: one closed path, one filled surface, with nothing to settle about connectivity because the outline says everything.
UPCGExTopologyPathSurfaceSettings.situation: An authored or generated outline that should become a solid piece of ground, water or floor.

mechanism.text: Each path is treated as a boundary and its interior is triangulated into a dynamic mesh. The outline's own order is what defines the region, so a path that crosses itself describes a region no filling can resolve cleanly. Everything past the triangulation, the material, the UVs and the normals, comes from the topology block.

outputs.label: Mesh
outputs.note: The dynamic mesh, filled from the path outline.

Topology.tooltip: Topology settings. Some settings will be ignored based on selected output mode.

hints.text: A path that crosses itself has no unambiguous interior, and the filling that results is whatever the triangulation makes of it rather than an error. **Clipper2 : Triangulate** is the node that offers a fill rule for deciding those cases deliberately.

UPCGExTopologyPointSurfaceSettings.name: Topology : Point Surface
UPCGExTopologyPointSurfaceSettings.purpose: Turns a loose scatter into a surface, by triangulating the points themselves. Nothing has to be connected first: the points are projected, a Delaunay triangulation over them decides which triples become faces, and the result is a dynamic mesh. It is the topology node for data that has no structure yet, where **Topology : Cluster Surface** wants a cluster and **Topology : Path Surface** wants an outline.
UPCGExTopologyPointSurfaceSettings.situation: Scattered points that should read as ground, water or any continuous sheet, without a cluster having been built first.

mechanism.text: The points are projected onto a plane, triangulated there, and the resulting faces are lifted back onto the original positions. Because the connectivity is decided in the projection, the plane is what determines which points end up neighbours, while the heights are whatever the points already had. One mesh comes out per input dataset. Everything past the triangulation, the material, the UVs and the normals, is the topology block's business.

outputs.label: Mesh
outputs.note: The dynamic mesh, one per input dataset.

ProjectionDetails.semantics: Decides the plane the triangulation runs on, which decides which points become neighbours. On terrain-like data a projection along the world up gives the expected sheet; any other plane connects points that are near each other as seen from that direction, which on the same data produces a different surface entirely.
ProjectionDetails.trap: The projection has to be one the data is genuinely spread across. Points arranged in a vertical wall projected downward collapse onto a line, and the triangulation over that is degenerate.

RepairDegenerate.semantics: How far the repair pass may go when fixing triangles with no real area, while repair is enabled above. Degenerate faces are the usual reason a mesh looks correct and shades wrong, so this is about shading as much as geometry.

Topology.tooltip: Topology settings. Some settings will be ignored based on selected output mode.

bQuietBadVerticesWarning.tooltip: Suppress warning when the mesh contains degenerate or bad vertices.

UPCGExTransformPointsSettings.name: Transform Points
UPCGExTransformPointsSettings.purpose: Offsets, rotates and scales points by a random amount within a range you set. It is the variation the asset collections apply, available as a node, so the same jitter can be put on points that are not being staged. Each of the three has its own range, its own snapping and its own choice of whether the change is applied in world space or the point's own.
UPCGExTransformPointsSettings.situation: Placed points that read as too regular, needing controlled variation without a scatter being redone.

mechanism.text: For each of offset, rotation and scale, a value is drawn between the minimum and the maximum and applied to the point. Snapping then rounds the result to a step, which is what keeps variation from breaking an alignment the points were placed on. The absolute setting on each decides whether the change is applied in world space or relative to the point's own orientation, which is the difference between nudging everything the same way and nudging each point along its own axes.

UPCGExTupleSettings.name: Tuple
UPCGExTupleSettings.purpose: Authors a small table on the node and emits it as an attribute set. Composition names the columns, each column being one attribute with a type and a default value, taken from the schemas authored here or from imported Property Schema assets; Values holds the rows, each row carrying one value per column. A column can also hold a Collection Entry, a pick into an asset collection, which lands as a staged pick with the Collection Map it resolves against emitted on a second pin. Tuple : Distribute picks a row per point and writes it onto points; this node hands the whole table downstream as data.
UPCGExTupleSettings.situation: A graph needs a handful of named, typed values that belong together as rows, authored in one place instead of assembled from separate constant nodes.

mechanism.text: One attribute set out, holding one attribute per column of the Composition and one entry per row of Values. Each column becomes one attribute, named after the column and typed by the property it holds, with the value authored on the column as that attribute's default. A row writes only the columns it has enabled, so a disabled cell leaves its entry sitting on the column default and a row that enables nothing is a full row of defaults. Nothing is read from the graph: the node takes no input, and the same configuration always emits the same set.

off_label.claim: Build the Composition entirely from imported Property Schema assets, add one row, and enable nothing on it. The emitted set is then that schema's declared defaults, read into the graph without a collection or an actor in the picture.
off_label.grounded_in: Composition.Resolve walks locals then the imported assets depth-first, and each attribute is created with the resolved property's own value as its default; a row whose override is disabled never reaches WriteMetadataValue.

outputs.label: Tuple
outputs.note: The attribute set: one attribute per column of the Composition, one entry per row of Values.

outputs.label: Map
outputs.note: The Collection Map for the picks this node wrote: one row per collection, carrying its index and its asset path, with every sub-collection reachable from it listed too.
outputs.condition: when Output Map is on and an enabled cell holds a collection pick; the pin sits collapsed as an advanced pin otherwise

Composition.tooltip: Tuple composition defines the columns (property types and names).

fields.name: Schemas
fields.tooltip: Schema array (locals -- always take precedence over imported entries with matching names)

fields.name: ImportedSchemas
fields.tooltip: Imported schema assets, resolved in array order after locals. Hard refs -- assets stay loaded as long as the owning collection exists. Recursion through imported assets' own ImportedSchemas is supported with cycle detection.

fields.name: ImportOverrides
fields.tooltip: Per-entry value overrides for imported entries. EditAnywhere is required so the detail panel's GetChildHandle can reach this property's children -- the registered FPCGExPropertySchemaCollectionCustomization takes over rendering entirely (CustomizeChildren controls every visible row), so this never appears as a top-level array editor in the inspector. The array is kept parallel with the imports-only schema via ReconcileImportOverrides (which delegates to FPCGExPropertyOverrides::SyncToSchema). UE per-instance UPROPERTY delta serialization handles three-layer composition: asset default -> template (collection on CDO) -> instance (collection on actor instance). Each layer overrides the previous via bEnabled toggles on individual entries. Locals do not appear here -- they are edited in-place on Schemas.

Composition.semantics: Each column contributes one attribute named after the column and typed by the property it holds, and the value authored here is that attribute's default, which is what an entry carries when its row leaves the column disabled. Columns come from the schemas authored here and from any imported Property Schema assets, locals first, so a local column and an imported one sharing a name is the ordinary locals-win override rather than a collision. A Float Curve column has no attribute form and is skipped, contributing nothing for any row.
Composition.trap: Two local columns sharing a name stop the node before it runs, with an error naming the duplicate and no output at all.
